lines.translation_en: Hidden dragon; do not act.
Dragon appears in the field; beneficial to see a great person.

lines.text_zh: 君子終日乾乾，夕惕若；厲，无咎
lines.translation_en: The noble person is active and creative all day, and in the evening remains wary and alert; danger, but no blame.
At times leaping in the abyss; no blame.
Flying dragon in the heavens; beneficial to see a great person.
Dragon at the zenith; there is regret.

special.translation_en: A group of dragons appears without heads; auspicious.

taoist.title: Creative Strength, Timely Practice
taoist.essence: Qian is not fixed power but a living rhythm of origination, penetration, benefit, and firmness, inviting the restoration of original true yang through disciplined, timely practice.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Pure yang heaven meeting heaven, six firm lines, images the unceasing creative power of the dragon. Liu Yiming reads this as the alchemical phase of advancing yang fire to restore one’s original true yang and innate knowing. The hexagram maps the four seasons of one strength—origination, penetration, benefit, firmness—and calls for a discipline that moves from hidden nurture to full expression, never mistaking force for vitality.
taoist.historical_core: In Liu Yiming’s commentary, Qian is the hexagram of ‘advancing the yang fire’ and ‘establishing destiny.’ He equates the strength of Qian with the precelestial true yang innate in every person, obscured after contact with acquired habits but not destroyed. Yuan heng li zhen become four seasonal movements of one strength and also four stages of inner work: the hidden stirring of life, its pervasion, its completion, and its consolidation. Each line is then read as an alchemical step, from nourishing the first faint vitality to completing the sacred embryo and releasing it at the right moment.
taoist.modern_meaning: Present-day readers may see Qian as an invitation to cultivate inner coherence through ordinary effort and rhythm. The hidden dragon asks for quiet preparation before visibility; the appearing dragon suggests honoring the undimmed heart in relationships; the daily-nightly vigilance of line three points to integrating effort with honest self-review; the leap from the abyss invites timing rather than impulse; the flying dragon points to mature service; the overbearing dragon warns against burnout, control, and rigidity. Rather than passive non-doing, this hexagram describes active, disciplined cultivation: the gradual reclaiming of vitality, clarity, and purpose through small consistent practices. It does not promise outcomes, but frames possibility: when one follows the season of a situation, strength can become flexible, life-giving, and less likely to turn into strain. The ‘headless dragons’ of the closing line suggest letting go of a fixed self-image so that strength can take the form each moment requires.
taoist.advice: When the impulse to push arises, pause and ask whether this is the season for hidden nurture, steady work, a considered leap, or generous influence. Tend the faint signs of true strength before exposing them. Match effort to timing; let self-review be as regular as effort. If strength becomes strain or pride, soften without abandoning practice.
taoist.shadow: Rigidity, over-exertion, premature visibility, spiritual pride, and denial of rest. The overbearing dragon exhausts itself and others; hidden vitality is mistaken for weakness and forced into display before its time.
taoist.reflection_question: Where is disciplined strength trying to emerge, and what season is it actually in?
taoist.evidence_zh: 乾者，健也。剛強不屈之義。

lines.interpretation: The first line marks the earliest stirring of true strength. Liu Yiming compares it to a hidden dragon: the seed of authentic vitality is present, but still tender. This is not a time to force visibility or assert one’s power. It invites quiet nourishment, protecting the emerging inner resource from exposure, impatience, and self-display. The work is real, but hidden. One can build foundations without announcing them, trusting that the life-force grows best when not yet used.
lines.reflection: What emerging strength in me needs shelter more than expression right now?
lines.evidence_zh: 初九，在健之初，健德方振，如潛藏之龍，正當培養正氣之時，未可自恃其健，故曰“勿用”。

lines.interpretation: Strength now acquires balance. The dragon appears in the field: authentic nature begins to show itself without losing its rootedness. Liu Yiming calls this ‘attaining centrality,’ where firmness and yielding stay in proportion. The great person is one who has not lost the heart of a newborn child. This line may point to learning from such an exemplar, or to becoming one. It asks that we let inner clarity become visible in daily life, not for performance but as natural radiance.
lines.reflection: Who or what reminds me of the undimmed heart I want to live from?
lines.evidence_zh: 九二，健而得中，不偏不倚，剛柔相當，如見龍在田，生氣常存，天良不昧，聖胎有象。所謂大人者，不失其赤子之心者也，故曰“利見”。

lines.interpretation: Here practice becomes daily. The noble person is active and creative from morning onward, yet in the evening remains wary and alert. Liu Yiming sees vast qi and correctness: by day one strives, by night one reviews. This is not anxiety but rigorous self-examination. Danger is present because sustained effort can become mechanical or smug. The line suggests that vigilance and effort together prevent blame. Rest is not abandonment; it is part of the discipline. Even when exhausted, one can reflect honestly.
lines.reflection: How can I bring as much honesty to my evening review as to my daytime effort?
lines.evidence_zh: 九三，浩氣充塞，剛而得正，日則勉於行，夕則察其過，日乾夕惕，健行不息，雖有危厲，故能無咎。

lines.interpretation: The inner work has matured, yet timing still matters. The dragon sometimes leaps, sometimes remains in the abyss. Liu Yiming says the sacred embryo is complete but not yet released; one must examine conditions and guard against danger. This is not hesitation but discernment. A threshold has been reached: to leap may bring transformation, to remain may allow ripening. Either choice can be correct if it follows the actual season rather than fear or ambition. No blame arises from respecting the moment.
lines.reflection: What threshold in my life is ripe for a leap, and what still asks to stay in the depths?
lines.evidence_zh: 九四，健德已成，聖胎完全，待時脫化，如龍或躍而起，或在於淵，審查氣候，防危慮險，故可無咎。

lines.interpretation: Strength reaches a centered, correct expression. The flying dragon moves through heaven, hidden and visible without fixed form. Liu Yiming describes a state where form and spirit become wondrous, and one can complete oneself and aid others. This is not dominance but mature influence: the ability to act for the whole without losing inner alignment. It invites us to let our cultivated vitality become generous, responsive, and unforced. Greatness here is not celebrity but integrity that nourishes others.
lines.reflection: How might my inner work become a quiet benefit to others, without becoming a role I perform?
lines.evidence_zh: 九五，剛健中正，陰陽混化，身外有身，形神俱妙，與道合真，不但成己，而且成物，如飛龍在天，隱顯不測，隨時濟物。

lines.interpretation: The top line warns of excess. The dragon flies too high, becoming parched and unable to generate life. Liu Yiming calls this strength advancing too far: only firm, never yielding; knowing advance but not retreat. What once was power now becomes strain, pride, or ruin. The timely cultivation of the earlier lines is lost. The line invites honest recognition of one’s limits and the courage to step back. Regret here can become a teacher if it leads to softening rather than self-punishment.
lines.reflection: Where has my strength become strain or pride, and what would need to soften for life to move again?
lines.evidence_zh: 上九，進健太過，獨剛不柔，知進而不知退，如亢旱之龍，龍至於亢，不能生物。健至太過，必敗其事。

special.interpretation: ‘Using nine’ is the art of using strength without a fixed head. The dragons appear in a group, yet no single one leads. Liu Yiming reads this as following the time: be hidden when hiding fits, appear when appearing fits, leap at the leap, fly at the fly. Strength becomes flexible, never too much, never too rigid. This is not formless passivity but practiced responsiveness. One uses strength without being used by it. The fixed identity of the one who must always lead dissolves into moment-by-moment appropriateness.
special.reflection: Can I let my strength change shape with the moment, or am I still leading with a fixed identity?
special.evidence_zh: 用九者，即用健也。龍之為靈昭昭也，變化不測，能上能下，能大能小，能隱能顯，迎之不見其首，隨之不見其後。

confucian.title: Creative Strength, Timely Action
confucian.essence: Cheng Yi reads Qian as Heaven's nature: creative strength without rest. The four virtues—origination, flourishing, advantage, uprightness—trace the sage's timely advance from concealment to mature rulership, with vigilance against overreach.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: Qian is the creative principle, Heaven as nature and disposition. It begins all things, sustains growth, fulfills rightness, and completes through uprightness. The six dragon lines map the rhythm of internal power seeking right timing: hidden, emerging, laboring, testing, reigning, and overreaching. Its pure yang force is not aimless dominance but disciplined strength that must know when not to lead and when to refrain.
confucian.historical_core: In Cheng Yi's commentary, Qian is the hexagram of Heaven, doubled to exhaust change under Heaven. The four virtues are read as cosmological and moral: beginning, growth, fulfillment, completion. The dragon lines narrate the sage's career: Shun's fishing and farming, the ascent of hidden virtue, trial offices, and finally obtaining Heaven's position. The commentary also values the ruler seeing worthy ministers and warns the top line against fullness. 'Using the nine' rejects pure firmness as excessive; firmness must be tempered by yielding to be central. This reflects the Northern Song Neo-Confucian emphasis on principle, timeliness, and hierarchical sage-ruler ethics.
confucian.modern_meaning: For modern readers, Qian's creative strength is less a royal career than the inner pattern of bringing any disciplined initiative to maturity. Hidden dragon, do not act asks us to hold back when capacity is unformed, avoiding premature exposure rather than forcing visibility. The appearing dragon values trust in ordinary speech and careful conduct, blocking what distorts while preserving sincerity. The all-day vigilance line reminds us that even capable people in responsible but uncertain positions need steady self-review and honest work, not bravado. The leaping line honors experimentation that follows timing, not restless jumping; we test when the moment is fitting and return to rest when not. The flying dragon speaks to using visible influence to seek collaborators of genuine virtue, not sycophants. The arrogant dragon warns that fullness cannot last; successes that ignore limits turn into regret. 'A group of dragons without heads' suggests shared, non-egotistic leadership, where one does not claim primacy. These are not predictions; they are reflective images for timing, self-cultivation, and the responsibilities of creative power.
confucian.advice: When creative energy rises, pair it with earned readiness. Do not hide forever, but do not leap before substance is visible. In public roles, attach to genuine partners, keep ordinary words trustworthy, and maintain evening self-check. At high visibility, avoid the illusion that strength alone sustains leadership. Prefer shared, headless influence over self-promotion.
confucian.shadow: Overconfident force that imagines itself immune to timing; brilliance demanding constant visibility; rigidity that refuses cooperation; the fall from fullness into regret. Pure yang without yielding becomes tyranny, and unled dragons may devolve into scattered ego rather than shared authority.
confucian.reflection_question: Where is my creative strength currently being forced ahead of its proper timing, and what would patient readiness look like?
confucian.evidence_zh: 乾健也健而无息之謂乾

lines.interpretation: Initial position is the beginning point, yang qi just sprouting. Cheng Yi reads the hidden dragon as the sage in lowly obscurity, not yet fit to act. The task is not permanent withdrawal but concealment and nourishment while waiting for the right time. In modern terms this is the phase of unripe skill or unborn project; exposure too early dissipates it. We do not despise hiddenness; we use it to deepen.
lines.reflection: What in me needs concealment and nourishment before it can be rightly used?
lines.evidence_zh: 初九在一卦之下為始物之端陽氣方萌聖人側微若龍之潛隱未可自用當晦飬以俟時

lines.interpretation: The dragon appears above ground; virtue begins to be seen. Cheng Yi likens this to Shun's time of farming and fishing—publicly visible but not yet holding office. The line is not about self-display but mutual recognition between those of great virtue. In modern terms, emerging capacity benefits from finding worthy collaborators: peers, mentors, communities. The field is ordinary life where trustworthy speech and careful conduct make one's quality legible. We show up where we are.
lines.reflection: Who are the people of genuine virtue I should seek out in my current field?
lines.evidence_zh: 田地上也出見於地上其德已著以聖人言之舜之田漁時也利見大德之君以行其道君亦利見大德之臣以共成其功天下利見大德之人以被其澤

lines.interpretation: The third line is a minister's seat above the lower body: honored but not yet in highest authority, with virtue becoming known. Cheng Yi calls it the time when Shun's dark virtue ascended and was heard. Because visibility brings danger, unremitting daytime activity and night watchfulness are needed. Modern interpretation: when competence increases and others begin to rely on us, we sustain steady effort and an honest evening review, not publicized self-importance. Danger is met by conscientiousness.
lines.reflection: What danger accompanies my growing responsibility, and how do I practice daily vigilance without anxiety?
lines.evidence_zh: 三雖臣位已在下體之上未離於下而尊顯者也舜之𤣥德升聞時也日夕不懈而兢惕則雖處危地而无咎

lines.interpretation: The abyss is the dragon's place of rest. 'Perhaps' is a word of uncertainty; leaping or not depends solely on meeting the right time to reach safety. Cheng Yi points to Shun's period of being tested through offices. The line teaches experimental movement without compulsion. In modern life, career leaps, public launches, or role changes should be tested when season and preparation align, not forced by restlessness. We may return to rest without shame.
lines.reflection: Is my impulse to leap coming from readiness and timing, or from discomfort with resting?
lines.evidence_zh: 淵龍之所安也或疑辭謂非必也躍不躍惟及時以就安耳聖人之動無不時也舜之歴試時也

lines.interpretation: This is full arrival: the flying dragon in heaven, the sage having obtained the position of Heaven. Cheng Yi does not make this a solitary triumph; the ruler benefits from seeing persons of great virtue below to accomplish the affairs of the world. Modern application: whenever we gain influence, we should seek worthy teammates and not imagine ourselves self-sufficient. Great visibility is for attracting shared purpose, not for dominating. Leadership is completed through reciprocal recognition.
lines.reflection: When I gain influence, whose deep virtue do I intentionally seek out, and do I make room for them?
lines.evidence_zh: 進位乎天位也聖人既得天位則利見在下大徳之人與共成天下之事天下固利見夫大徳之君也

lines.interpretation: The central correct fifth position is the extreme of obtaining the time; passing beyond it is overbearing. The top line reaches the limit of overbearing and has regret. Fullness cannot last. Cheng Yi adds that only the sage knows advance and retreat, survival and ruin, without error. For modern readers, this warns against believing that peak success removes limits. After a high point, pushing further out of habit breeds remorse. We are invited to recognize endings before they become excess.
lines.reflection: Where am I past the peak but still pushing, and what would a timely retreat look like?
lines.evidence_zh: 九五者位之極中正者得時之極過此則亢矣上九至於亢極故有悔也有過則有悔

special.interpretation: Using nine is the way of dwelling in Qian's firmness. Pure yang is excessive; firmness and yielding tempering each other is central. Seeing a group of dragons without a head means observing the meaning of all yang lines and refusing to make oneself the head. In modern terms, strong initiatives thrive when no one's ego claims primacy. The ability to lead without being the sole face of leadership is not weakness; it is the proper management of creative power. Claiming first place through force invites conflict.
special.reflection: In my collaborations, where do I insist on being first, and what might emerge if I let shared authority operate without my head?
special.evidence_zh: 用九者處乾剛之道以陽居乾體純乎剛者也剛柔相濟為中而乃以純剛是過乎剛也見羣龍謂觀諸陽之義无為首則吉也以剛為天下先凶之道也

classical.name: Kun (Earth)
classical.judgment_zh: 坤：元亨。利牝馬之貞。君子有攸往，先迷後得主。利西南得朋，東北喪朋。安貞，吉。
classical.judgment_en: Kun: Supreme success. It is favorable to be steadfast as a mare. When the noble one has somewhere to go, at first he loses his way and later gains a lord. It is favorable to gain companions in the southwest and to lose companions in the northeast. Security and perseverance bring good fortune.
classical.image_zh: 地勢坤，君子以厚德載物。
classical.image_en: The disposition of the earth is Kun; the noble person carries all things with generous virtue.
classical.historical_note:
Translated from the received Zhouyi base text for hexagram 2 (Kun): judgment, Great Image, six line statements, and yong liu. The Tuan, small-image, and Wenyan passages in the source are traditional commentary and are not included here.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Treading on hoarfrost; hard ice is about to come.
Straight, square, and great; without practice, nothing is unfavorable.

lines.text_zh: 含章，可貞。或從王事，无成有終。
lines.translation_en: Containing hidden brightness, one may be steadfast. If one follows the king’s affairs, there is no attainment, but there is completion.
Tie up the sack; no blame and no praise.
Yellow lower garment; supreme good fortune.
Dragons fight in the open; their blood is dark and yellow.

special.translation_en: It is beneficial to be perpetually steadfast.

taoist.title: Receptive Yin Discipline
taoist.essence: Kun, pure yin, teaches disciplined receptivity: follow true yang, refine false compliance, and rest in correct stillness so the Dao-mind arises and nature is cultivated through earth's yielding pattern.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: The archetype is the yielding earth and the moon that faithfully follows the sun—not submission to whim, but a receptive power that contains, ripens, and manifests hidden brightness. It represents the capacity to receive, hold, and complete a process: the vessel that carries blessing without self-display, the inner ground that must be stilled and corrected before true yang can root itself.
taoist.historical_core: In the received Zhouyi, hexagram 2 Kun is pure yin: 'Kun: originating and penetrating; beneficial for the correctness of a mare.' Liu Yiming, however, treats it as an inner-alchemical instruction—'the hexagram of circulating the yin talisman, the study of cultivating the nature.' For him the yielding way is not ethical passivity but disciplined compliance with the true yang. He interprets the moon's waxing and waning as the growth of hun-soul within po-soul and of po-soul within hun-soul as gain and loss of light, and reads each line as a stage of refining the human mind so the Dao-mind may govern. His closing 'using six' calls for perpetual correctness in compliance, returning to the pre-acquired 'original face.'
taoist.modern_meaning: In contemporary terms, this hexagram addresses the receptive side of growth: learning to listen, follow timing, and contain energy without forcing. Liu Yiming's commentary warns that what feels like compliance may actually be compliance with desire or habit. The practice is to distinguish true yielding from false yielding. This means cultivating a still inner space, allowing a deeper direction to arise, and then following it consistently. It may apply to caregiving, creative incubation, collaborative work, or any situation where influence comes through steady presence rather than control. The text does not promise outcomes; it describes a discipline of refining motivation and remaining correct over time. The moon's phases suggest that knowing when to advance and when to retreat is itself a skill, not passivity.
taoist.advice: When circumstances call for receptivity, do not confuse it with self-abandonment. Watch the first signs—small habits or concessions harden into larger patterns. Cultivate inner spaciousness, let the mind settle, and act only from that settled correctness. Follow a trustworthy principle, not every external demand. Persist gently but firmly, and let your influence emerge through quiet consistency rather than force.
taoist.shadow: Falsely yielding to desire or habit; self-negation disguised as humility; refusal to act when firmness is needed; resentment hidden beneath compliance; or cold withdrawal that avoids both blame and responsibility.
taoist.reflection_question: Where am I mistaking compliance with habit or pressure for genuine yielding to what is true?
taoist.evidence_zh: 此運陰符之卦，修性之學

lines.interpretation: At the first step of yielding, the path is not yet fixed: it may turn true or false. Liu Yiming warns that the slightest incorrectness lets guest qi enter, and one yin draws a crowd of yin—frost already implies hard ice. This line is a call to early discernment. Receptivity begins with small acts, attitudes, and permissions; if they are not aligned, they accumulate into a frozen pattern. The work is to notice the first cooling, the first compromise, and correct it before it becomes a fixed condition.
lines.reflection: What first small sign, if left uncorrected, is already cooling into a fixed pattern in my life?
lines.evidence_zh: 稍有不正，客氣潛入，必至一陰生而群陰畢集

lines.interpretation: The second line describes yielding that is centered and correct. Because the mind is centered, it is straight and careful; because action is correct, it is square and measured. This is not imitation or rote learning—Liu Yiming says 'without practice nothing is unfavorable' because the foundation is already aligned. In modern terms, when inner honesty and outer boundaries match, you do not need to rehearse every response; right action flows naturally. This is the mature form of receptivity: accommodating without losing shape.
lines.reflection: Where can I allow my natural straightness and clear boundaries to act without over-rehearsing?
lines.evidence_zh: 中則其心直而能謹慎。正則其行方而有裁制，內直外方，循規蹈矩，自能大其德業

lines.interpretation: Line three holds inner brilliance without display. The nature is yielding but the will is firm; one may outwardly comply with duties—'follow the king's affairs'—yet not lose oneself. Liu Yiming reads the absence of 'accomplishment' not as failure but as preserving inner truth while completing what is required. This speaks to working within institutions or relationships that demand accommodation. You may not get credit, and your hidden gift may remain unseen, but the process can still reach a true completion.
lines.reflection: What hidden strength am I being asked to carry faithfully, without needing recognition?
lines.evidence_zh: 性柔志剛，含藏章美，順守其正，不以外假而傷內真

lines.interpretation: This line counsels closing the bag: inner thoughts do not leak out, outer thoughts do not enter. It is a time of protected stillness, not of display. Liu Yiming calls it complying with time and destiny—neither inviting misfortune nor seeking praise. This can be a season of retreat, confidentiality, or quarantine of the heart. The danger is mistaking this necessary closure for permanent withdrawal. When used rightly, it protects a process that is not yet ready for exposure.
lines.reflection: What in me needs to be sealed and protected for now, without seeking either blame or approval?
lines.evidence_zh: 內念不出，外念不入，順時順命，不致禍而不求福，如括結囊口

lines.interpretation: Line five is the ripest form of yielding: the yellow lower garment, hidden beneath outer garments yet coloring the whole presence. The center is empty, the virtue full enough to move others without words. Liu Yiming says it is trusted without speaking and transforms without teaching. This is not charismatic performance but the radiance of integrated inner work. It reminds us that authority can arise from humility, and that lasting influence often emerges from what is worn closest to the body, not displayed.
lines.reflection: What quiet quality in me, if fully embodied, might influence others without needing to be announced?
lines.evidence_zh: 柔順虛中，德足服人，不言而信，不教而化，如黃裳著體

lines.interpretation: The top line shows corruption of yielding: self-importance turns receptivity into rigidity. Refusing to yield and demanding that others yield produces open conflict—dragons fighting in the wild, blood dark and yellow. Liu Yiming says one is injured before gaining anything from others. This warns against the false strength that compensates for inner uncertainty. When we over-assert, we lose the very harmony that would have allowed us to receive. The blood is both yin and yang, a sign of mutual wounding.
lines.reflection: Where am I turning receptivity into self-assertion, and what is the cost?
lines.evidence_zh: 自尊自大，以柔為剛，不能順人，欲人順己，如龍戰於野

special.interpretation: The 'using six' instruction closes the hexagram by calling for perpetual correctness in compliance. Liu Yiming insists that true yielding is not occasional or convenient; it must be constant to the point of death, without concealment or deceit. When yin is stabilized in the correct, it reveals the firmness hidden within it, and the acquired temperament gives way to the original, uncontrived nature. This is the culmination: receptivity not as weakness but as the enduring ground that permits return to the source.
special.reflection: What would it mean for me to practice yielding as a lifelong, consistent commitment rather than an occasional tactic?
special.evidence_zh: 能永順其正，柔中即有剛，不隱不瞞，至死不變

confucian.title: The Generous Constancy of Earth
confucian.essence: Kun is yielding compliance that nonetheless moves firmly, receiving Heaven's work and bringing it to completion. Its strength is constancy: supportive, unassuming, and capable of carrying what is entrusted.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: In Cheng Yi's reading, Kun is the counterpart of Qian: not weakness but receptive strength. The mare's yielding yet firm movement images how one can follow without losing direction. Earth's thick virtue supports all things and joins with Heaven's limitlessness. This archetype calls for containing one's brightness, holding to one's place, and completing tasks without claiming the outcome. Its power is moral depth, steady service, and the discernment to act at the right time.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Kun within a hierarchical cosmos and court where yin follows yang, minister follows ruler, and wife follows husband. He calls the wife's occupation of the honored position an 'extraordinary change' and uses examples from ancient history; these statements reflect Song Confucian social order and should not be taken as endorsements for today. His core teaching is moral: keep to one's allotted part, contain hidden merit, complete tasks for the larger order, and watch the gradual growth of yin before it hardens.
confucian.modern_meaning: Today, this hexagram can be read as a reflection on supportive leadership, quiet competence, and ethical boundaries. Its historical language of subordinates should not be applied literally to modern relationships; instead, the underlying principle is that completing shared work requires knowing when to step back, when to speak, and when to be silent. One might recognize the power of consistent, unglamorous effort—building trust, maintaining integrity, and allowing others' contributions to be seen. The warning about frost becoming ice invites attention to small habits and social dynamics before they harden. The image of carrying things with generous virtue suggests caring for one's community or environment without needing public recognition. In contemporary settings, this can mean collaborative service, principled restraint, and the courage to hold one's ground without fighting.
confucian.advice: Cultivate steady receptiveness rather than force. Attend to small signals before they intensify; keep inner rightness and outer clarity; hide your brightness when sharing credit serves the larger work; in closed or risky times, practice careful silence. Hold to your center without overstepping, and let constancy, not contention, bring completion.
confucian.shadow: Receptivity can slide into self-erasure, silence into complicity, or patience into passivity. When one clings to a subordinate stance beyond what the moment requires, unresolved small issues may accumulate until conflict becomes inevitable.
confucian.reflection_question: Where am I being asked to support completion without claiming the outcome?
confucian.evidence_zh: 君子觀坤厚之象以深厚之徳容載庶物

lines.interpretation: At the first step, hoarfrost underfoot signals that harder ice is forming. Cheng Yi treats this as a moral warning: yin begins subtly, and small tendencies grow by habituation. In reflective practice, this line points to the value of noticing early signs—a habit, a relationship dynamic, a drift in one's values—before they become fixed. Attention at this stage may be quiet and preventive; it does not promise control, only the chance to respond while the pattern is still soft.
lines.reflection: What small pattern in my life is still in its frost stage, and how might I respond to it now?
lines.evidence_zh: 陰始凝而為霜漸盛則至於堅永小人雖微長則漸至於盛故戒於初

lines.interpretation: Straight, square, great: three qualities that, in Cheng Yi's commentary, complete the way of earth. Straightness is inner correctness; squareness is outer rightness; greatness emerges from both without deliberate practice. This line suggests that when one acts from settled integrity, one need not rehearse or force outcomes. There is a natural effectiveness available to those whose inward and outward selves align. In practice, this may look like clarity, fairness, and a calm confidence that does not require external validation.
lines.reflection: What might become effortless if I aligned my inner values with my outward actions?
lines.evidence_zh: 以直方大三者形容其徳用盡地之道矣由直方大故不習而无所不利不習謂其自然

lines.interpretation: Cheng Yi reads this line through the minister who contains hidden splendor and follows a larger task without claiming completion. Goodness is real but held back, not suppressed forever; it is expressed when the time is right. One may be steadfast, serve, and allow the work to reach its end without needing to be named as the author. The modern reflection is on collaboration: offering skill and insight while letting shared purpose, rather than personal recognition, carry the conclusion.
lines.reflection: Can I contribute to a shared outcome without needing my name attached to it?
lines.evidence_zh: 為臣之道當含晦其章美有善則歸之於君乃可常而得正

lines.interpretation: A tied sack: no blame, no praise. Cheng Yi places this in a time when above and below are closed off, when speaking exposes one to harm. The counsel is not permanent silence but careful concealment of one's knowledge in a dangerous interval. In reflective terms, this line may describe seasons when discretion protects what is not yet ready to be shared. It asks for restraint without bitterness, knowing that not every moment is for visibility.
lines.reflection: Where might careful silence be the most honest and protective choice right now?
lines.evidence_zh: 若晦藏其知如括結囊口而不露則可得无咎不然則有害也

lines.interpretation: Yellow lower garment: supreme good fortune. For Cheng Yi, yellow is the color of the center and the lower garment signifies dwelling below. One who keeps to the center and accepts an allotted place enjoys great good—not through ambition but through proper measure. The line warns against yin occupying the honored position; in present-day terms, this might caution against claiming authority that does not fit the role. Fulfillment can come from embodying one's station with beauty and restraint.
lines.reflection: Where might staying centered in my present role be the stronger form of leadership?
lines.evidence_zh: 守中而居下則元吉謂守其分也

lines.interpretation: Dragons fight in the open; their blood is dark and yellow. Cheng Yi sees yin at its extreme, no longer following yang but resisting and contending. When one has advanced beyond one's proper limit, conflict and mutual wounding follow. This line does not predict doom; it reflects on the consequences of pressing a position past its natural boundary. In ordinary life, it points to burnout, power struggles, or the harm that comes when two sides refuse to yield. De-escalation may require recognizing that the fight itself is the sign of excess.
lines.reflection: Where am I pressing beyond a limit that is already telling me to stop?
lines.evidence_zh: 陰從陽者也然盛極則抗而爭六既極矣復進不已則必戰

special.interpretation: Using six: beneficial to be perpetually steadfast. Cheng Yi says the way of yin is yielding and difficult to keep constant, so the counsel is lasting firmness. This closing text invites a commitment to sustained inner discipline, not a momentary pose. Constancy itself becomes the virtue—holding to what is right through changing circumstances, ending well rather than merely beginning well.
special.reflection: What practice am I willing to sustain for the long term, even when no immediate result appears?
special.evidence_zh: 陰道柔而難常故用六之道利在常永貞固

original_chinese.title: 伊川易傳 (四庫全書本)/卷1

further_reading.title: The Yi River Commentary on the Book of Changes

hexagrams.essence: Kun, pure yin, teaches disciplined receptivity: follow true yang, refine false compliance, and rest in correct stillness so the Dao-mind arises and nature is cultivated through earth's yielding pattern.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: The archetype is the yielding earth and the moon that faithfully follows the sun—not submission to whim, but a receptive power that contains, ripens, and manifests hidden brightness. It represents the capacity to receive, hold, and complete a process: the vessel that carries blessing without self-display, the inner ground that must be stilled and corrected before true yang can root itself.
hexagrams.historical_core: In the received Zhouyi, hexagram 2 Kun is pure yin: 'Kun: originating and penetrating; beneficial for the correctness of a mare.' Liu Yiming, however, treats it as an inner-alchemical instruction—'the hexagram of circulating the yin talisman, the study of cultivating the nature.' For him the yielding way is not ethical passivity but disciplined compliance with the true yang. He interprets the moon's waxing and waning as the growth of hun-soul within po-soul and of po-soul within hun-soul as gain and loss of light, and reads each line as a stage of refining the human mind so the Dao-mind may govern. His closing 'using six' calls for perpetual correctness in compliance, returning to the pre-acquired 'original face.'
hexagrams.modern_meaning: In contemporary terms, this hexagram addresses the receptive side of growth: learning to listen, follow timing, and contain energy without forcing. Liu Yiming's commentary warns that what feels like compliance may actually be compliance with desire or habit. The practice is to distinguish true yielding from false yielding. This means cultivating a still inner space, allowing a deeper direction to arise, and then following it consistently. It may apply to caregiving, creative incubation, collaborative work, or any situation where influence comes through steady presence rather than control. The text does not promise outcomes; it describes a discipline of refining motivation and remaining correct over time. The moon's phases suggest that knowing when to advance and when to retreat is itself a skill, not passivity.
hexagrams.advice: When circumstances call for receptivity, do not confuse it with self-abandonment. Watch the first signs—small habits or concessions harden into larger patterns. Cultivate inner spaciousness, let the mind settle, and act only from that settled correctness. Follow a trustworthy principle, not every external demand. Persist gently but firmly, and let your influence emerge through quiet consistency rather than force.
hexagrams.shadow: Falsely yielding to desire or habit; self-negation disguised as humility; refusal to act when firmness is needed; resentment hidden beneath compliance; or cold withdrawal that avoids both blame and responsibility.
hexagrams.reflection_question: Where am I mistaking compliance with habit or pressure for genuine yielding to what is true?

classical.name: Zhun (Beginning Difficulties)
classical.judgment_zh: 屯：元亨，利貞。勿用有攸往，利建侯
classical.judgment_en: Zhun: primordial success; beneficial to be firm. Do not act to have somewhere to go; it benefits to establish a lord.
classical.image_zh: 雲雷，屯；君子以經綸
classical.image_en: Clouds and thunder: Zhun. Thus the noble person sets the world in order.
classical.historical_note:
Base text from Zhouyi hexagram 3. The Great Image is from the Ten Wings; only this Wing text is included here. The source notes a variant in line 1: 磐 also written 盤.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.text_zh:
磐
一作「盤」
桓，利居貞，利建侯
lines.translation_en: Lingering and hesitant; beneficial to remain steadfast; beneficial to establish a lord.

lines.text_zh: 屯如邅如，乘馬班如，匪寇婚媾，女子貞不字，十年乃字
lines.translation_en: Difficult and wavering, riding horses in rows; not robbers but a marriage alliance; the maiden remains steadfast and does not marry; after ten years she marries.

lines.text_zh: 即鹿无虞，惟入于林中，君子幾不如舍，往吝
lines.translation_en: Approaching the deer without a forester; one only enters the forest. The noble person sees the incipient signs and deems it better to give up; going brings regret.

lines.text_zh: 乘馬班如，求婚媾，往，吉无不利
lines.translation_en: Riding horses in rows, seeking a marriage alliance; going is auspicious, nothing is not advantageous.
Its fat/oil is blocked; small persistence is auspicious, great persistence is ominous.
Riding horses in rows, weeping tears of blood, flowing abundantly.

hexagrams.title: Zhun (Beginning Difficulties)
hexagrams.name: Zhun (Beginning Difficulties)

taoist.title: Living Yang at the Threshold
taoist.essence: Zhun is the first movement of true yang within difficulty; one guards the one point of living potential, corrects the mind, and waits for the living zi-hour before acting. Timing and firmness open primordial success.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: The figure of water over thunder depicts movement within danger: the hidden pre-cosmic yang stirs but is not yet strong enough to emerge safely. This is not a deadlock but a seed-time. The work is to recognize the first stirring, protect it from acquired impulses, and let it mature through patient discipline. To rush is to deepen the danger; to wait with purpose is to build the root. Thus Zhun becomes an image of initiating the yang fire.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 3 as the first hexagram of 'advancing yang' after Qian. He equates the hexagram's upper Kan and lower Zhen with 'movement within danger,' and the hidden true yang with original correct qi that appears in the 'living zi-hour.' For him, 'primordial success; beneficial to be correct' means guarding the one point of living potential, and 'do not act; establish a lord' means first correcting the mind as ruler of the body. The six lines sequence concealment and rooting; refining self and waiting; avoiding force; harmonizing the elixir; forming the sacred embryo yet still containing yin; and failing through timidity. Throughout he insists on knowing the time.
taoist.modern_meaning: Today this hexagram can be read as an inner weather report, not a forecast. It names those early moments when something authentic begins to stir—a creative calling, a boundary, a healing impulse—yet the environment feels unsafe or unready. Liu Yiming's counsel is not to declare the impulse false or to suppress it. Instead, one can name the first stirring honestly, create a private container for it, and set a rhythm of small consistent actions. The mind is the 'lord' in the sense of an ethical center, not a tyrant over others; correcting that center means clearing envy, haste, and self-dramatizing. The image of waiting for the living zi-hour teaches that mature timing is discerned, not forced. This is disciplined cultivation: one gathers energy, refines motive, and acts only when the moment is ripe. The historical language of lord and marriage becomes an inner analogy for aligning a whole life around its emerging core. Nothing here promises a particular outcome; it offers a way to keep faith with what is beginning without losing prudence.
taoist.advice: Guard the small beginning before it has strength. Keep an internal practice of witnessing without prematurely acting. When the impulse arises, ask what kind of container it needs, then build that container through repeated, disciplined attention. Let the mind be the steady ruler, not the restless judge. Move only when the timing is recognized, and then move wholeheartedly. Do not mistake waiting for passivity—it is the work of ripening.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is impatience disguised as decisiveness, or caution disguised as wisdom. One may force an immature beginning, or endlessly delay until the living moment passes; both leave the true yang buried under anxiety and the heart weeping at its own hesitation.
taoist.reflection_question: What small authentic impulse is presently asking me to guard rather than force?
taoist.evidence_zh: 屯者，前進有難之義，卦德上坎陷、下震動，動於險中，險中之動，不易出險，故謂屯。

lines.interpretation: The first line sits at the very root; the yang qi lies hidden below, like the broad foundation of a mansion. There is no visible achievement yet, only the need to dwell in correctness and make the root firm. The image of establishing a lord points to cultivating the inner ruler—an enduring center that can hold the emerging energy. This is not withdrawal from life but preparation: daily structure, clear intention, and restraint from exposing the new impulse too soon. One learns to keep the beginning intact by giving it roots.
lines.reflection: What root can I deepen now so that a still-hidden beginning may be safely held?
lines.evidence_zh: 陽氣下伏，如大廈之盤桓，利於居貞，而堅固根本

lines.interpretation: In the midst of difficulty, the second line practices refining the self and waiting for the right moment. Its horses are reined in, not out of fear, but because the conditions are not yet balanced. The image of a woman who remains faithful and refuses an early marriage describes a deep loyalty to one's own timing. The 'ten years' is not literal; it signals that some unions cannot be rushed. One stays centered, soft but not weak, and lets the inner and outer conditions ripen before committing.
lines.reflection: What alliance or commitment in me is not yet ripe enough to honor by waiting?
lines.evidence_zh: 柔順中正，煉己待時，故乘馬班如。

lines.interpretation: The third line warns against forcing progress when one lacks the inner guide. The image of chasing a deer without a forester describes acting from greed or impatience; the deeper one pushes, the more entangled one becomes. For Liu Yiming, the wise person knows the subtle signs and chooses to wait. This is not missed opportunity but protection from the inflated will. The line criticizes those who are 'in a hurry for success': their forward push brings regret, not achievement. Discernment means recognizing when not going is the more awake move.
lines.reflection: Where am I chasing something without the inner guidance that would make pursuit wise?
lines.evidence_zh: 至於明道君子，須當知幾，不如告之以待時。若不待時，急欲成功，往而前進，必有招險之吝。

lines.interpretation: Here the waiting has done its work: the true yang is in sight, and the moment to harmonize the elixir has arrived. The line changes from holding back to moving forward. Seeking the marriage alliance is no longer premature; going is auspicious because the preparation is complete. But this is not impulsiveness—it is the fruit of prior self-refinement. The invitation is to recognize the ripe opening and act without hedging, confident that the inner alignment now supports the outer step. One can say yes wholeheartedly.
lines.reflection: What prepared opportunity is now asking me to move from waiting into wholehearted action?
lines.evidence_zh: 柔而得正，煉己待時，真陽在望，正當調和丹頭之時，不可當面錯過者，是以求婚媾往吉，無不利。

lines.interpretation: The fifth line holds a formed inner reality—the sacred embryo has an image; the belly is filled. Yet the work is not finished: residual yin still surrounds it, and the danger has not fully cleared. Liu Yiming says intentional action is complete, and the phase of non-action becomes evident. 'Small persistence' means following the now-dominant non-action; 'great persistence' means forcing grand action. This is a call to trust the process and avoid grand gestures. Mature practice knows when to do less, not more.
lines.reflection: Where has my effort done enough, such that continued pushing would harm what is ripening?
lines.evidence_zh: 聖胎雖結，陰氣未退，尚在險中，如屯其膏矣。當此之時，有為事畢，無為事彰，是以小貞吉，大貞凶。

lines.interpretation: The final line sits at the threshold of emergence, yet is soft and incapable; the horses halt, and there is no plan. The true yang is near but cannot be obtained because the heart is overwhelmed. Weeping tears of blood changes nothing. Liu Yiming calls this being small and unable to become great: having arrived at the end of difficulty, one still carries a reactive self that cannot receive what is offered. The line invites an honest inventory: have I prepared the inner capacity to meet what I long for?
lines.reflection: What inner incapacity is making me weep at the door of my own becoming?
lines.evidence_zh: 上六，在屯之終，正是出屯之時，柔而無能，乘馬班如，措手無策，雖真陽在望，未許我得，泣血漣如，何益於事？

confucian.title: Beginning Difficulties
confucian.essence: Zhun names the first tangled stirring of life, when cloud and thunder have not yet become rain. Emergence depends on upright firmness, timely restraint, gathered support, and the patient ordering of what is still disorderly.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: At the birth of anything, vitality is present but knotted and not yet flowing; cloud and thunder respond without forming rain, and movement arises inside danger. Cheng Yi reads this as the archetype of incipient fullness, a time when things are not yet open but contain the way of great success. The noble person therefore weaves order into the world while waiting, not by solitary force but by establishing helpful relations and remaining upright.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi's Commentary on the Yijing locates Zhun after Qian and Kun as the first birth of the myriad things. In his cosmology, yin and yang first interact as cloud and thunder, still blocked, not yet mature rain; movement within danger defines the time. The hexagram judgment is read as a moral curriculum: Zhun has a way of 'great success,' but only through upright firmness, not through unaided effort. The noble person's response is ordering and weaving the world's affairs. Each line is interpreted by position, correspondences, and the personal virtues of firmness, centrality, restraint, and seeking worthies; these are instructions for ministers and rulers within a hierarchical social vision.
confucian.modern_meaning: In present-day terms, Beginning Difficulties describes the early phase of any undertaking—an idea, a relationship, a community, a creative work—when energy is real but blocked, and pressure can feel like danger. Cheng Yi's advice is not to wait passively or force a breakthrough. His emphasis on upright firmness points to staying connected with one's ethical center while circumstances remain unfinished. His counsel to establish lords can be reclaimed for modern contexts as building mutual support, delegating, and inviting the right partners; the historical language about lords and rulers reflects a feudal order, but the underlying pattern is that no significant beginning succeeds alone. Each line then maps common moments: the hesitant start, the pressured commitment, the tempting shortcut, the limited leader seeking help, the constrained authority needing gradual correction, and the exhausted end that cannot be sustained. Applied today, this is an invitation to examine where one rushes, where one refuses help, where one overreaches, and where one needs to let a phase end before renewal can come.
confucian.advice: When something new is still tangled, do not force it. Clarify your own integrity; stay near what is right even if progress is slow. Seek capable and trustworthy allies rather than acting alone. Read the early signs and know when to withdraw. If you hold responsibility and your power to help is blocked, correct gradually rather than by abrupt coercion. At the dead end, let the extreme pass.
confucian.shadow: Impatient haste that rushes into danger; isolated self-reliance that refuses help; greedy pursuit of immediate gain without a guide; overbearing authority that tries to correct everything at once; despair that turns difficulty into endless weeping.
confucian.reflection_question: Where is a new beginning tangled in your life, and what kind of help or upright restraint might let it unfold without force?
confucian.evidence_zh: 屯有大亨之道而處之利在貞固非貞固何以濟屯

lines.interpretation: At the outset, a capable person is still in a lower position. Cheng Yi warns against rushing forward; the difficulty would be met head-on, so one should remain steady and firm, yet not idle. This first line also depicts lowering the noble to the humble: genuine leadership in an uncertain time earns trust by placing itself below others and seeking allies. The appropriate move is not a grand leap but a grounded, deliberate beginning that gathers support before acting.
lines.reflection: When you feel ready but the way is blocked, what would steady waiting—and seeking help—look like for you?
lines.evidence_zh: 方屯之初不磐桓而遽進則犯難矣故宜居正而固其志

lines.interpretation: A pressured commitment must hold its own center. The second line is pressed by an advancing force and cannot yet unite with its true partner. Cheng Yi reads this as integrity under coercion: the maiden does not yield to an improper match, even when it delays union for a long time. The ten years symbolize the full cycle of endurance, not a literal deadline. Persistence in one's deeper values can keep the way open for eventual restoration; but the present moment is about saying no to the wrong pressure.
lines.reflection: Where in your life are you being pressed to compromise, and what integrity is worth that long wait?
lines.evidence_zh: 六二居屯之時而又乘剛為剛陽所逼是其患難也

lines.interpretation: This line describes acting on a tempting opportunity without proper guidance. Approaching a deer without a forester means chasing desire into the forest; the further one goes, the more lost one becomes. Cheng Yi praises seeing the incipient signs and choosing to stop. In a tangled time, not every apparent opening should be pursued. The noble person recognizes when the cost of pressing forward exceeds the value of the goal and releases the chase without shame.
lines.reflection: What currently looks like an opportunity but may actually be a desire leading you off the path?
lines.evidence_zh: 君子見事之幾微不若舍而勿逐往則徒取窮吝而已

lines.interpretation: A limited but well-placed person can still bring relief by seeking capable help. The fourth line is soft and near the ruler; on its own it cannot rescue the situation, so it hesitates. Cheng Yi says that recognizing this insufficiency and going to seek worthy support is itself clarity. This is not weakness but wise humility in a position of responsibility. When one's own gifts are insufficient, the fruitful act is to form an alliance with someone whose strength complements the need.
lines.reflection: What responsibility are you carrying that would benefit from seeking a partner whose strengths differ from yours?
lines.evidence_zh: 知己不足求賢自輔而後往可謂明矣

lines.interpretation: Those in authority may have a title but find their help and influence blocked. Cheng Yi interprets the blocked fat as beneficence that cannot flow downward. He warns that abruptly seizing back power or forcing large-scale correction leads to disaster. Instead, small, gradual correction—cultivating virtue, employing worthies, restoring good practice step by step—allows the blockage to loosen. This is not passive quietism; it is disciplined, sustained reform that avoids violent rupture.
lines.reflection: Where do you hold formal responsibility but little actual influence, and what small faithful correction might be possible now?
lines.evidence_zh: 故小貞則吉也小貞則漸正之也

lines.interpretation: The extreme of beginning difficulty is exhaustion. The top line rides but cannot advance; it weeps tears of blood. Cheng Yi calls this the end of a cycle: when one is at the extreme of danger with no support, neither dwelling nor moving brings peace. Such a state, in his structural reading, cannot be sustained long. The commentary implies that if there were firmness and help, even this extreme could be crossed. Without that, the only wisdom is to recognize the dead end.
lines.reflection: What situation has reached an extreme of distress, and what would it mean to acknowledge that it cannot continue as it is?
lines.evidence_zh: 屯難窮極莫知所為故至泣血顛沛如此其能長久乎

The mind is the 'lord' in the sense of an ethical center, not a tyrant over others; correcting that center means clearing envy, haste, and self-dramatizing. The image of waiting for the living zi-hour teaches that mature timing is discerned, not forced. This is disciplined cultivation: one gathers energy, refines motive, and acts only when the moment is ripe. The historical language of lord and marriage becomes an inner analogy for aligning a whole life around its emerging core. Nothing here promises a particular outcome; it offers a way to keep faith with what is beginning without losing prudence.
hexagrams.advice: Guard the small beginning before it has strength. Keep an internal practice of witnessing without prematurely acting. When the impulse arises, ask what kind of container it needs, then build that container through repeated, disciplined attention. Let the mind be the steady ruler, not the restless judge. Move only when the timing is recognized, and then move wholeheartedly. Do not mistake waiting for passivity—it is the work of ripening.
hexagrams.shadow: The shadow is impatience disguised as decisiveness, or caution disguised as wisdom. One may force an immature beginning, or endlessly delay until the living moment passes; both leave the true yang buried under anxiety and the heart weeping at its own hesitation.
hexagrams.reflection_question: What small authentic impulse is presently asking me to guard rather than force?

classical.name: Youthful Folly
classical.judgment_zh: 蒙：亨。匪我求童蒙，童蒙求我。初筮告，再三瀆，瀆則不告。利貞。
classical.judgment_en: Youthful Folly: success. It is not I who seek the young and ignorant; the young and ignorant seek me. At the first divination I answer; if he asks again and again, that is disrespectful; if disrespectful, I do not answer. It is beneficial to be upright.
classical.image_zh: 山下出泉，蒙；君子以果行育德。
classical.image_en: Below the mountain a spring comes forth: the image of Youthful Folly. Thus the noble person acts decisively and nurtures virtue.
classical.historical_note:
In the source text of Six Three, the character 取 is accompanied by the variant annotation 一作「娶」. The primary reading is 取 ('take'), and the translation follows this primary reading; the variant 娶 would mean 'marry'.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Six at the beginning: Enlightening the ignorant. It is beneficial to use punishment; use release from fetters and handcuffs; going on in this way brings regret.
lines.text_zh: 發蒙，利用刑人，用說桎梏，以往吝。

lines.translation_en: Nine in the second place: To be tolerant of the ignorant brings good fortune; to take a wife brings good fortune; the son can manage the household.
Six in the third place: Do not take a woman in marriage. When she sees a man of wealth, she does not keep her own person; nothing is beneficial.
lines.text_zh: 勿用取一作「娶」女，見金夫，不有躬，无攸利。

lines.translation_en: Six in the fourth place: Confined by ignorance. Regret.
Six in the fifth place: Childlike ignorance; good fortune.
Top nine: Smiting the ignorant. It is not beneficial to act as a robber; it is beneficial to defend against robbers.

hexagrams.title: Youthful Folly
hexagrams.name: Youthful Folly

taoist.title: Nourishing the True Ignorance
taoist.essence: Ignorance begins when original spirit dims and acquired cleverness rules. Stop, still the chattering mind, and protect the hidden yang; then ignorance can revert to childlike clarity.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Meng shows danger beneath stillness: the original spirit has fallen into the post-cosmic condition, and yin is injuring yang. Yet danger can be stilled. The archetypal movement is from false ignorance—outward brightness with inward darkness—to true childlike ignorance, which does not know and does not understand yet follows the heavenly principle. This return happens through non-action when the seed is undivided and deliberate action once guest qi has entered.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming, an 18th–19th-century Daoist master, reads Hexagram 4 as the first hexagram of 'circulating the yin talisman,' following Kun. He interprets lower Kan as one yang trapped in yin and upper Gen as yin pressing on yang, an image of acquired spirit replacing original spirit. The commentary describes a fall from pre-cosmic yang into post-cosmic yin, causing the human mind to mistake false for real. His remedy includes two methods: non-action to nourish true ignorance when yin-yang is undivided, and action to transform false ignorance after guest qi enters, always with correct timing.
taoist.modern_meaning: Today this is not about remaining naïve or passively accepting confusion. The 'youthful ignorance' that seeks the teacher is the part of us willing to admit not-knowing. The 'monied man' and 'woman' in line three can be read as inner figures: desire, vanity, or the acquired self that chases external glitter and loses its own center. In a contemporary inner reading, the 'wife' and 'son' in line two can be understood as inclusive work of caring for the hidden yang within ordinary relationships and responsibilities, rather than fixed gender roles. Practice begins with restraint—not self-punishment but clear boundaries. Then comes containment: allowing yang to grow within the dark until it can manage the inner household. Without reflection one may stay trapped in familiar company; with humility one can borrow the strength of wise companions. The final 'striking' is used only against internal robbers such as resentment and craving, never as cruelty toward others. This view offers no guaranteed outcomes; it maps a disciplined return to authentic nature.
taoist.advice: When you feel confused, pause before reaching for more cleverness. Protect the small honest impulse within; create quiet boundaries around it. Seek a teacher or steady companion. If inner turbulence intensifies, use firm but non-hostile discipline—strike the inner robber, not yourself or others.
taoist.shadow: False ignorance hides behind fluent explanations, spiritual jargon, or compulsive seeking outside. It avoids silence, resists correction, and mistakes restlessness for insight, thereby preserving the very confusion it claims to hate.
taoist.reflection_question: Where am I performing cleverness to avoid the childlike not-knowing that could actually restore contact with my original nature?
taoist.evidence_zh: 此運陰符下手之卦，承上坤卦而來。坤者，行順道也。運陰符者，運其不順之陰，而歸於順也。

lines.interpretation: At the first appearance of the acquired mind, do not ignore the small inward disturbance. Liu Yiming compares this to applying punishment to the incipient human mind: clear, firm restraint before it hardens into habit. Removing the fetters too soon, or letting indulgence move forward, leads to regret. The work here is preventive—watch the first stirring of desire and set a boundary while it is still small. This is not self-punishment but the careful protection of what is true.
lines.reflection: What small inner impulse am I allowing to wander because I am unwilling to apply a clear boundary now?
lines.evidence_zh: 在蒙之初，人心方起，急須嚴加克制，如利用刑人也。

lines.interpretation: This line counsels not to root out every confusion by force. Firmness becomes true strength by yielding enough to hold yin and nourish yang, like enveloping the ignorant inside a dark yet bright container. In a modern inner sense, one can allow ordinary shortcomings and daily duties to become the field where the hidden yang grows. The image of marriage and household suggests committed care and gradual maturation, not immediate clarity. Tend the small light rather than scorning the dark.
lines.reflection: How can I turn the ordinary materials of my present life—especially the parts I call dull or dependent—into nourishment for the true yang?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛而能柔，借陰養陽，是包蒙也，蒙在包中，外暗內明

lines.interpretation: Here the danger is not ignorance itself but desire wearing the mask of pursuit. Liu Yiming uses the figure of a woman who, seeing a wealthy man, loses her own person; read inwardly, this is the acquired human mind chasing external glitter—status, praise, comfort—until it forgets its ground. The text says 'do not take her,' meaning do not grasp that current. To follow it is to be emptied, not fulfilled. Protect your center before the outward glitter.
lines.reflection: What external prize or person am I using to avoid the quieter inner work, and what am I losing in the chase?
lines.evidence_zh: 陰柔不中不正，恣情縱欲，故勿用取女。勿用者，以其人心用事，貪財好色，如淫奔之女，見金夫不有躬

lines.interpretation: This position warns of ignorance that keeps itself alive by staying in the wrong company. When one is inwardly dull, surrounding oneself only with like-minded or petty influences prevents the expansion of knowledge. Liu Yiming says it is not merely regret; one remains trapped and does not know one is trapped. The turning point is to seek out those with clearer insight. In present terms, this is the moment to stop hiding in comfortable circles and ask for help.
lines.reflection: Who am I avoiding because their clarity would expose the places where I have been hiding?
lines.evidence_zh: 性質本愚，又與小人為伍，不知親近高明之士，以擴充其識見

lines.interpretation: This is the healthy face of ignorance: a childlike mind that knows it does not know. The line describes 'stopping' where one should stop—not forcing knowing, but lending one's receptive attention to a stronger truer capacity. By borrowing firmness to aid yielding, one remains outwardly unlearned yet inwardly aligned. In modern practice, this is the discipline of humility: surrender the need to appear clever and allow the original nature to respond naturally.
lines.reflection: What would change if I stopped pretending to know and allowed a deeper, quieter knowing to respond in its own time?
lines.evidence_zh: 於止知其所止，以無能而順有能，借剛濟柔，雖蒙不蒙

lines.interpretation: At the extreme of confusion, a firm and courageous strike is needed—not against other people, but against the inner robbers of resentment and craving. Liu Yiming says it is not beneficial to become the robber; it is beneficial to guard against robbers. When guest qi has thoroughly invaded, soft measures are not enough. The aim is to rouse the Dao-mind, expel the acquired human mind, and let yang become pure and whole again. Directed inward, this fierceness restores rather than harms.
lines.reflection: Am I striking at my own confusion, or am I projecting the robber onto someone else?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛而居於蒙之極，是能懲忿窒欲，猛力以退客氣，如擊蒙也。退陰之道，不利於人心而為寇，利於道心而禦寇

confucian.title: Youthful Folly, Nurtured Correctness
confucian.essence: Unformed potential beneath a still mountain and a spring that has not yet found its way. Growth arises through sincere seeking, timely response, restraining what blocks learning, and nurturing correctness before distortion.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: Youthful Folly represents the beginner's unformed condition: not moral failure but undeveloped clarity. A spring emerges below a mountain, seeking direction; danger below and stillness above mean the person does not know where to go. The archetype is not passive waiting but disciplined receptivity: the ignorant one asks sincerely, the wise one responds only to genuine seeking. Proper order matters: first divination is answered; repeated demand is irreverent. Thus learning requires structure, relationship, and timing.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Meng as political education: Six Five, the gentle but youthful ruler, corresponds with Nine Two, the firm and central worthy who waits below. Success depends on the ruler's sincere seeking, not the worthy's self-promotion. The ancients waited for the lord to show reverence before serving. Laws and punishments come first only to remove the fetters of ignorance so teaching can enter. Nourishing correctness in the not-yet-aroused mind is the work of sagehood. This is a Confucian pedagogy of moral transformation, not egalitarian collaboration; in modern application the hierarchical roles become useful metaphors rather than endorsements.
confucian.modern_meaning: In present terms, Meng speaks to moments when we are beginners: entering a new role, learning a skill, or facing a confusion we cannot yet name. The instruction is not to force clarity but to move decisively at the right time. Like a spring under a mountain, our unformed questions need an outlet; without direction they become stagnant. The hexagram invites honest self-assessment: do we ask for help only once, sincerely, or do we return with the same question because we want reassurance rather than change? It also speaks to those in teaching or mentoring positions: wait for genuine seeking; don't chase the learner. Use structure as an aid—clear boundaries, honest feedback—not as punishment for its own sake. The historical image of a ruler employing a worthy can be translated today as leading by trusting competence, not by demanding subordination. Cultivate the untouched, still-responsive part of the mind before habits harden.
confucian.advice: Consider asking once with full sincerity, then act on what you hear. Before pursuing answers, notice what distractions keep confusion in place. If you teach or lead, allow yourself to be sought rather than imposing. Use clear limits as aids to learning, not weapons. When you are the beginner, accept structure and seek worthy companions rather than remaining isolated. Firmly correct excesses, but never become the aggressor.
confucian.shadow: The shadow is stubborn confusion that rejects guidance, or enforced teaching that becomes punishment. One may wait passively for rescue instead of seeking, become infatuated with shiny rewards, or turn correction into cruelty.
confucian.reflection_question: Where am I asking the same question repeatedly instead of acting on the first sincere answer?
confucian.evidence_zh: 蒙以養正聖功也

lines.interpretation: At the first step, clear limits are not cruelty but the removal of fetters that keep a beginner confused. Cheng Yi reads Initial Six as the common people's unformed ignorance: first make boundaries and consequences visible so that fear restrains reckless desires, creating an opening for teaching, then gradually lead to the good. Applied today, this might mean honest feedback or protective structure in a new environment. Persisting only in threat or restriction becomes coercive and cannot transform the whole person.
lines.reflection: What boundary or consequence am I avoiding that could create enough stillness for real learning?
lines.evidence_zh: 初以陰暗居下下民之蒙也爻言發之之道發下民之蒙當明刑禁以示之使之知畏然後從而教導之

lines.interpretation: Nine Two represents the capable person who does not insist on superiority. Its firm clarity corresponds with the gentle but immature ruler, and its virtue is broad inclusion: pity the dim and foolish; accept what is good even from a soft or limited source. Cheng Yi likens it to a son who can manage the family because of trusted connection, not formal authority alone. In modern terms it is the teacher, mentor, or colleague who enlarges their clarity by receiving and including others rather than acting alone. Such embrace makes good work possible.
lines.reflection: How can I broaden my understanding by including what is good in someone I find limited or difficult?
lines.evidence_zh: 必廣其含容哀矜昏愚則能發天下之蒙成治蒙之功其道廣其施博如是則吉也

lines.interpretation: Six Three is a warning against abandoning one's own integrity for glittering advantage. In Cheng Yi's historical language, a woman should follow her rightful partner through proper rites, not run toward a 'man of gold' because of wealth. The gendered image is a product of its time; the underlying principle remains useful: when confused, don't trade loyalty, propriety, or self-possession for nearby status or riches. No direction is beneficial if you lose your own person.
lines.reflection: Where am I tempted to abandon my own values for a nearby reward or influential attraction?
lines.evidence_zh: 三以陰柔處蒙闇不中不正女之妄動者也正應在上不能逺從近見九二為羣蒙所歸得時之盛故捨其正應而從之是女之見金夫也

lines.interpretation: Six Four describes the shame of isolation. Although it is yin and soft, its deeper trouble is distance from the firm and clear—the worthy persons or practices that could awaken it. Cheng Yi says it has no intimate aid and no way to develop itself. The line does not say punishment is needed; it says the condition is constricted because the one trapped does not draw near to wisdom. Reflective practice today may recognize the point at which solitude becomes stagnation rather than rest.
lines.reflection: Is my current solitude protecting my attention, or is it keeping me away from people and practices that could clarify me?
lines.evidence_zh: 四以陰柔而蒙闇无則明之親援无由自發其蒙困於昏蒙者也其可吝甚矣吝不足也謂可少也

lines.interpretation: Six Five is the auspicious figure of childlike ignorance: not childish stubbornness, but the unhardened openness that depends on another's competence. The gentle ruler occupies the honored position, yet delegates to the firm and capable worthy below; by employing the other's gifts, the achievement becomes no different from one's own. Cheng Yi prizes this as letting go of self and following what is good. In modern application it may mean a team leader who truly trusts expertise, not a call to remain dependent.
lines.reflection: What would it look like to receive another's capacity so fully that their achievement becomes our own?
lines.evidence_zh: 五以柔順居君位下應於二以柔中之徳任剛明之才足以治天下之蒙故吉也

lines.interpretation: Top Nine marks the extreme edge of ignorance, where firm action becomes necessary. Cheng Yi uses the distinction between resisting brigands and becoming one: correcting another's ignorance is defensive, but giving free rein to hardness and violence turns correction into oppression. Examples from his context—Shun's campaign and the Duke of Zhou's punishment—are historical references to justified restraint of disorder, not endorsements of force. In modern application, the challenge is to set limits against harm without becoming punitive.
lines.reflection: When I must stop harmful behavior, how do I remain a defender rather than becoming an aggressor?
lines.evidence_zh: 治人之蒙乃禦冦也肆為剛暴乃為冦也
