lines.translation_en: Returning to one's own way: what fault is there? Auspicious.
Drawn along to return; auspicious.

lines.text_zh: 車一作「輿」說輹一作「輻」，夫妻反目
lines.translation_en: The cart's axle-guard detaches; husband and wife turn against each other.
With good faith, blood departs and fear goes out; no blame.
With sincere trust, bound as one; enrich one's neighbors.

lines.text_zh: 既雨既處，尚得一作「德」載，婦貞厲，月幾望，君子征凶
lines.translation_en: Rain has come, rest has been achieved; still it can be carried. The wife's persistence is dangerous; the moon is nearly full; the noble one's march brings misfortune.

hexagrams.title: Small Restraint
hexagrams.name: Small Restraint

taoist.title: Small Restraint: Nourishing the Great
taoist.essence: Smallness, rightly held, restrains the strong so that true yang is nourished. Humility must not collapse into weak quietism; disciplined timing protects and stores the great within the small.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: This hexagram embodies the phase in which strong creative power is held by gentle restraint. Wind over heaven suggests influence through sustained, penetrating modesty rather than force. The small becomes a vessel: outer emptiness, inner solidity. It is not suppression but guarded nourishment, a symbolic shelter where the life impulse gathers like clouds that are not yet ready to fall.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 9 as 'making one's nourishment small' (xiǎo qí yǎng). In his view the hexagram follows Shi's work of borrowing yang to drive back yin; therefore one must first nourish yang. Proper smallness lowers the mind, hides brightness, and makes the strong not self-assertive, so virtue grows. But Liu warns that excessive smallness lets yin take charge, weakens resolve, and becomes empty quietism—'dense clouds without rain.' The decisive question is fire-time: when smallness protects the great and when it harms it.
taoist.modern_meaning: In present terms, this hexagram does not predict events; it describes a quality of attention. The 'small' is any deliberate contraction that protects something vital during a formative stage—listening before speaking, simplifying before building, restoring before performing. Liu's alchemical reading treats this as inner work: the strong, creative urge is not erased but held in a gentle container so it can mature. This is active discipline, not passive wu wei: one chooses timing, refines intention, and asks what must be made small so the whole can become stronger. It may mean learning from others, admitting limits, or rebuilding trust. The historical language of 'borrowing the other's yang' can be reframed as seeking complementary strengths rather than hierarchy. The warning remains: if smallness turns into disappearance, avoidance, or self-diminishment, it loses its nourishing function. True restraint must eventually release the stored strength at the right time.
taoist.advice: Hold your strength in a quieter form for now, but do not renounce it. Choose a small container—a consistent practice, a focused conversation, a reduced pace—that lets inner heat gather. Watch for the difference between skillful humility and self-erasure. When the time ripens, let the rain fall and allow the stored power to move forward.
taoist.shadow: Excessive smallness becomes weak quietism: talent hidden so long it forgets itself, relationships avoided, resolve thinned. The other shadow is stubborn self-assertion that refuses to be nourished by restraint—force without timing, breaking the cart.
taoist.reflection_question: Where in your life is the discipline of smallness protecting something that must later grow, and where has smallness become an excuse for withdrawal?
taoist.evidence_zh: 小畜者，小其養也。卦德上巽伏下乾健，健而巽行，巽伏其健，健不自用，故謂小畜。此以小養大之卦

lines.interpretation: Line 1 describes a return to one's own path through chosen humility. The creative strength is present but placed in a low position; it does not announce itself. Liu treats this as 'hiding brightness and nourishing obscurity,' so the inner true yang can increase without being damaged by outer display. In practical terms, this is the discipline of returning to what genuinely belongs to you—your values, your practice, your authentic nature—rather than seeking external validation. What fault is there? The line names it auspicious because the small beginning protects the greater growth.
lines.reflection: What inner truth needs your quiet protection in order to return to its own way?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛而居卑，韜明養晦，抱道而處，不以外假而傷內真，是能複於自道也

lines.interpretation: Line 2 turns restraint into shared learning. Firmness is not abandoned; it is expressed through receptivity. Liu describes a learner who asks questions without embarrassment, forms partnerships with principled companions, and lets reciprocal influence pull the self back to its original clarity. The word 'pulled back' here is not regression but repair: outer pride becomes empty while inner substance becomes solid. In application, this is about allowing trusted relationships and honest study to correct your course. Smallness succeeds because it does not isolate.
lines.reflection: Who or what can draw you back to your own depth without shaming your strength?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛以柔用，敏而好學，不恥下問，結交有道君子，彼此資益，明善複初

lines.interpretation: Line 3 is the warning of strength that refuses the small. Liu reads the broken cart and estranged couple as images of self-will: when only one's own force matters, harmony and center are lost. The axle or spokes separate; the vehicle can no longer move. In inner terms, firmness without the discipline of yielding becomes brittle. The line is not a fated failure but a natural consequence of refusing restraint. It asks you to notice where unilateral force has damaged collaboration, and to restore the missing mutual adjustment before the structure collapses.
lines.reflection: Where has your insistence on being right or strong made movement impossible for you and another?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛而自用，有己無人，乖和失中，終必敗剛

lines.interpretation: Line 4 is the pivotal turn. It acknowledges vulnerability: situated among stronger forces, there may be injury and fear. Liu does not deny the danger, but says sincere trust and correct yielding allow one to 'borrow the yang of the other's house.' In modern language, this means leaning on complementary strength without losing yourself. Through vigilant self-refinement, what was harmful can be released, and what was blameworthy can return to innocence. The line teaches that smallness is most powerful when it becomes receptive and honest about its own limits.
lines.reflection: What complementary strength could you honestly seek in order to release a fear you cannot resolve alone?
lines.evidence_zh: 柔而得正，自信一己純陰，為害最大，而能借他家之陽，警惕勉力，煉己持心

lines.interpretation: Line 5 marks the fruition of small nourishing. Here trust is not a performance; it binds the fragments into one. Liu describes the central and correct motion of yang blending with yin, the 'golden elixir' congealing as an inner symbol of wholeness. The root becomes secure, yet the work is not finished: acquired temperament must still be transformed and shared. To 'enrich one's neighbors' is to extend the gathered strength outward. This is a mature smallness that stores the great—stable enough to benefit others without display.
lines.reflection: What inner bond of trust is now stable enough to be shared without being depleted?
lines.evidence_zh: 陽剛巽進於中正，真信在中，陰陽混合，金丹凝結

lines.interpretation: Line 6 is the boundary. Rain has come, rest has been achieved, and the small phase has done its work. Liu warns against stopping there: the restrained state is a means, not a home. If smallness becomes final, yin turns back to weaken yang—like a moon nearly full, about to wane. His gendered image of the wife reflects his era; the core warning is that a yielding phase must not become permanent. True yang must now advance; otherwise solitary quietism forfeits the farther journey. This calls us to move from protective smallness to timely larger action.
lines.reflection: What small protection has completed its purpose and now needs to be released into fuller expression?
lines.evidence_zh: 假陽既息，真陽須進，小畜之終，正當大畜之時

confucian.title: Small Restraint: Refine Virtue
confucian.essence: One yin holds five yang through gentle compliance, not force. Small restraint gathers strength by refining cultural virtue, awaiting harmony before action.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: This hexagram shows gentle wind moving above heaven: the small and supple restrains the firm and strong. It is a time of gathering, where advancement is slowed not by force but by compliance and refinement. Dense clouds gather yet no rain falls, because harmony has not ripened. The noble person uses this interval to polish cultural virtue, recognizing that small accumulations prepare the way for eventual action.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Xiaochu as one yin in the fourth place holding five yang lines. Because Xun is supple, it can tie but cannot forcefully control; hence the restraint is “small.” The judgment’s dense clouds without rain arises because yin initiates from the west rather than yang leading, so the two qi are not harmonious. Yet success remains possible: inner Qian is vigorous, outer Xun is compliant, and the second and fifth lines are firm and central. Cheng Yi’s ethical focus is not prediction but how restraint and refinement accumulate virtue.
confucian.modern_meaning: In present-day terms, Small Restraint speaks to moments when progress is slowed by modest constraints—limited resources, uncertain support, or relationships that require tact. Rather than pushing harder, the hexagram suggests refining one’s capacities and cultivating trust. Dense clouds without rain remind us that preparation is not failure; sometimes the atmosphere of change must become harmonious before results can fall. A small voice can influence a larger group through sincerity and consistent presence, not through force. In workplaces, families, and communities, this means listening closely, building shared understanding, and honoring legitimate boundaries. The historical image of a wife restraining her husband is a product of its time; we translate it today as the ethical power of the less dominant party to speak truth with gentleness. The key is not manipulation but alignment: when inner purpose is firm and outer manner is gentle, even small accumulations become meaningful.
confucian.advice: Refine your cultural and interpersonal virtues before demanding visible results. Use sincerity rather than pressure. Notice whether the time is ripe: if clouds gather but no rain falls, continue preparing and aligning with others. Keep your own center firm while remaining courteous. Do not mistake a pause for defeat; small, consistent acts of trust and skill may prepare a larger breakthrough.
confucian.shadow: When small constraints become passive obstruction, they may breed resentment or subtle control. The desire to influence without force can slip into manipulation; waiting too long can become avoidance. Watch for the hidden imbalance where the weaker party clings to power through guilt or silence.
confucian.reflection_question: Where am I mistaking the need for patience for an excuse to avoid necessary speech or action?
confucian.evidence_zh: 小畜謂以小畜大所畜聚者小所畜之事小以陰故也

lines.interpretation: The first line returns by its own way. In Cheng Yi’s reading, a firm and capable beginning naturally moves upward toward those who share its aim. Because this return flows from one’s own character and path, there is no fault. The modern move is to reclaim your own direction without self-reproach: not every pause is wrongdoing, and returning to a path aligned with your values often clears away blame and opens what is already auspicious.
lines.reflection: What path have I left that is actually my own to return to?
lines.evidence_zh: 初九乃由其道而行无有過咎故云何其咎无咎之甚明也

lines.interpretation: The second line is pulled back with a companion. Cheng Yi sees the second and fifth as firm but central partners sharing the same aim; when they move together, gentle restraint cannot overpower them. This line does not suggest resisting alone, but finding an ally who shares your principles. Mutuality preserves balance: you are pulled back not into retreat but into a more coordinated return. The strength of two centered people, aligned in timing, turns a small hold into a shared advance.
lines.reflection: Who shares my aim, and how might we move together without losing our individual center?
lines.evidence_zh: 二五同志故相牽連而復二陽並進則隂不能勝得遂其復矣故吉也

lines.interpretation: A yang line too close to restraining yin loses its way. Cheng Yi explains that the third, lacking centrality, becomes overly familiar with the fourth and is controlled by it; like a cart without spokes, it cannot move. The image of husband and wife turning away reflects ancient gender hierarchy, but the underlying pattern is relational: when boundaries blur and dependence or resentment replaces respect, forward motion stops. The fault is not in the other’s influence alone, but in one’s own failure to remain centered.
lines.reflection: In a close relationship, where am I losing my balance by becoming too entangled or too reactive?
lines.evidence_zh: 故不能前進猶車輿說去輪輻言不能行也

lines.interpretation: The fourth line holds many strong forces and cannot succeed through force. Cheng Yi emphasizes sincerity as the only safe path: a single gentle position facing many firm ones would be harmed by opposition, but truthful presence can move them. Modern application is clear: when outnumbered or less powerful, do not coerce. Build trust, show honest intent, and align with the deeper interests of others. Then fear recedes, and no blame is incurred. Influence through integrity is more durable than control.
lines.reflection: Where am I trying to force an outcome that only sincerity can move?
lines.evidence_zh: 四苟欲以力畜之則一柔敵衆剛必見傷害唯盡其孚誠以應之則可以感之矣

lines.interpretation: The fifth line’s sincerity binds others to a common cause. Cheng Yi reads it as a position of influence that shares advantage with neighbors rather than hoarding it. When the upright are pressed by difficulties, those below seek support above, and those above draw strength from below. The image of the rich sharing wealth points to solidarity: success is not solitary, and trust is not a private possession. In modern life, this may mean mentoring, community building, or using resources to lift others so that all can move.
lines.reflection: What resource or strength do I hold that I am not yet sharing with those who could move with me?
lines.evidence_zh: 有孚攣如葢其鄰類皆牽攣而從之與衆同欲不獨有其富也

lines.interpretation: The top line shows small restraint reaching completion: rain has come, rest is achieved. Cheng Yi warns that this is both an accomplishment and a danger. Supple influence has accumulated to the point where it may overstep and oppose the firm. The historical image of a wife’s dangerous persistence belongs to a hierarchical past; its core insight is about any subordinate force that, having succeeded through gentleness, begins to dominate. The nearly full moon signals that further advance will bring misfortune, not because movement is wrong, but because the timing has reversed.
lines.reflection: Now that I have achieved some influence, am I overreaching beyond the gentle means that brought me here?
lines.evidence_zh: 陰柔之畜剛非一朝一夕能成由積累而至可不戒乎

classical.name: Treading
classical.judgment_zh: 履虎尾，不咥人，亨
classical.judgment_en: Treading on the tail of a tiger, it does not bite the person. Success.
classical.image_zh: 上天下澤，履；君子以辨上下，定民志
classical.image_en: Heaven above and lake below: Treading. The noble person uses this to distinguish high and low, and to settle the people's aspirations.
classical.historical_note:
Core Zhouyi text for hexagram 10, with the indicated Great Image from the Xiang commentary. The smaller line images are not included.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Plain treading: going forward is without fault.
The path of treading is smooth and broad; for the secluded person, perseverance brings good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 眇能視，跛能履，履虎尾，咥人，凶。武人為于大君
lines.translation_en: Blind in one eye but able to see; lame but able to walk; treading on a tiger's tail, it bites the person: misfortune. A warrior acts for the great lord.
Treading on the tiger's tail; fearful and cautious, in the end good fortune.
Resolute treading; perseverance is perilous.
Look to one's treading and examine the details; its return is supremely auspicious.

hexagrams.title: Treading
hexagrams.name: Treading

taoist.title: Treading in Joyful Caution
taoist.essence: Liu Yiming presents Hexagram 10 as the work of advancing inner yang through joy, not force: tread close to danger with watchful, unhurried sincerity until acquired yin transforms and pure yang returns.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: This hexagram describes any careful passage through risk where joy and firmness must cooperate. The tiger is not an external enemy but the living, potentially dangerous energy of life; treading its tail means engaging that energy without being devoured. The image asks the inner practitioner to advance step by step, with both courage and receptivity, so that what threatens can become what restores wholeness.
taoist.historical_core: In Liu Yiming’s commentary, Lü means advancing yang while guarding against danger. He reads the lower trigram Dui (joy) as the youngest daughter who can turn yin at its extreme back to yang; through her gradual, trustworthy action, the practitioner summons true yang that was lost to the post-cosmic state. The six lines map stages: firm will, hidden-perseverance, foolish self-will, firm yielding, centered decisive cultivation, and complete beginning-to-end treading. His framework is expressly inner alchemical: the 'tiger' is dangerous acquired energy, and 'no bite' arises from harmonious, attuned treading rather than passivity.
taoist.modern_meaning: In a modern contemplative context, this hexagram can be read as an invitation to bring disciplined attention to high-stakes transitions—work, relationship, creative risk, inner growth—without forcing outcomes. Liu Yiming’s language of medicine (inner material to be refined) and fire-times (timing and dosage) becomes a metaphor for inner practice: knowing when to act and when to soften, when to be firm and when to yield. Treading the tiger’s tail names the honest recognition that some necessary advances carry risk; the response is not avoidance but nuanced, persistent care. Joy is not a reward at the end but the quality of moving itself. This reading supports self-examination rather than prediction: if one treats status, ambition, or emotional intensity as raw material to refine, one can proceed with less arrogance and more attunement. The goal is not domination but restoration—returning to a more sincere, unified disposition through repeated small choices.
taoist.advice: Move forward, but do not rush. Pair firm intention with a soft, attentive step. Check the 'fire-time': if tension rises, ease the pace; if stagnation appears, summon quiet courage. Let joy inform discipline, not replace it. Review your motives at each threshold, and adjust rather than force.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is overconfidence disguised as clarity—one-eyed seeing, lame walking—that mistakes momentum for wisdom. It rushes into the tiger’s reach, ignores timing, and turns a workable risk into self-inflicted injury.
taoist.reflection_question: Where am I moving with hidden force, and am I listening for the moment to soften?
taoist.evidence_zh: 履者，前進也。卦德上乾健下兌悅，陰悅于陽，有一陰進而變為純陽之象，故謂履。此進陽防危之卦

lines.interpretation: First Nine marks the beginner’s firmness: when the will is strong and trust in the path is plain, one can begin without ornament. This is not naivety but a wholehearted commitment to the work itself. The key is to honor that initial sincerity and translate it into steady practice, knowing that a clean beginning already reduces future harm. The line cautions against hesitation disguised as humility; if the intention is sound, taking a direct first step is appropriate. It is treading by firm resolve, uncomplicated and honest.
lines.reflection: What plain, unembellished step is my strong will ready to take?
lines.evidence_zh: 初九，心強氣壯，素信於履道者，信於履而即能履，以是往而下手修為，必將進於無咎之地矣。此志念堅固之履也。

lines.interpretation: Second Nine describes a hidden, steady joy that is not dependent on external rewards. The way feels level because desire has been simplified; one is not chasing approval, pleasure, or success. This is perseverance maintained in solitude—not isolation from others, but an inner seclusion that protects one’s center. When outer conditions shift, the person remains unshaken. The work here is to cultivate satisfaction in the practice itself, so that continuity becomes natural. It is treading as quiet confidence, free from greed and mental restlessness.
lines.reflection: What external reward am I still using to make my path feel level?
lines.evidence_zh: 九二，樂在其中，自有真悅，不戀假悅，一切外物，不得而移之，是以履道坦坦也。坦坦之履，無貪無求，心安神靜，非始終如一守貞之幽人，不能為樂道忘年之履也。

lines.interpretation: Six Three warns against confident ignorance. The one-eyed person thinks they see fully; the lame person believes they stride. Without understanding the inner material and timing, one rushes forward and is bitten by the very intensity one sought to control. The martial image points to imposing willfulness rather than attuned action. This is not a condemnation of limitation, but of refusing to recognize limitation. The work is to pause, admit what is unknown, and seek precise, humble guidance before stepping farther. Otherwise, strength becomes self-injury.
lines.reflection: Where am I presenting inability as ability, and what would honest sight require me to acknowledge?
lines.evidence_zh: 六三，愚而自用，藥物不知，火候不曉，以不明為明，以不能為能，冒然行道，如眇能視、跛能履，履虎尾，咥人，自取其凶。又如武人為于大君，自招其禍。此愚而自用之履也。

lines.interpretation: Fourth Nine embodies firmness that knows how to yield. It enters with sincerity, acts with softness, and remains fearfully attentive. This is not anxiety but the protective alertness that prevents harm. Caution here enables the practitioner to stay close to danger without being consumed; the tiger’s energy is transformed through respectful distance. The line suggests that real courage includes trembling vigilance. Eventually such treading moves toward wholeness, not through domination but through refined adaptation. It is the balance of strong intention and gentle application.
lines.reflection: Where can firmness become gentler in my hands, so that vigilance opens rather than closes a situation?
lines.evidence_zh: 九四，剛而不躁，以誠而入，以柔而用，防危慮險，如履虎尾，愬愬，戒慎恐懼，不但虎不能咥，終必履于純陽之地，而得吉。此剛而能柔之履也。

lines.interpretation: Fifth Nine names mature centeredness: strong, correct, and decisive without inner conflict. At this stage the work has begun to coalesce, and the danger shifts from external risk to the risk of losing what has been gained. Therefore the line counsels constancy and a sober sense of peril even amid progress. One must not become entitled or casual. Resoluteness must be tempered by the realization that near completion requires deeper watchfulness. This is treading that moves from formed achievement toward formless integration, holding the center without grasping.
lines.reflection: What have I gained that I now need to protect by remaining undivided and sober?
lines.evidence_zh: 九五，剛健中正，從心所欲，不逾矩。履道果決而不犯難心，然履道至於中正，金丹已有象，須當貞一不二，以危厲自處，方無得而復失之患。此自有入無之履也。

lines.interpretation: Top Nine calls for careful review of the entire process. It looks back at the timing of each step and the quality of the inner material, refining what was incomplete. Completion is not a sudden leap but a circular return that honors the beginning. The goal is a blended condition—yin and yang, firm and yielding—whole and without deficiency. This is treading as mature fulfillment, where ending and beginning meet. It invites honest examination rather than self-congratulation, ensuring that what has been walked can be integrated and passed forward.
lines.reflection: As a phase ends, what needs to be reviewed so that its beginning is honestly completed?
lines.evidence_zh: 上九，剛居柔位，視其所履之火候，考其藥物之老嫩，循序而進，旋始旋終，終以全始，期以至於陰陽混合、圓成無虧而後已。此全始全終之履也。

confucian.title: Treading with Reverent Care
confucian.essence: The soft rests beneath the firm; joy responds to strength. Proper treading is propriety itself: discern roles, settle aspiration, and move with care even near danger.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: This hexagram points to the human act of walking a path of conduct, especially in proximity to overwhelming power. The lake lies below heaven, mirroring the soft support that joyfully carries the firm. To tread safely near a tiger’s tail is to align step with principle, not to disarm force but to walk so that danger has no opening. It is the archetype of propriety as a living practice.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Lü as propriety (li), what human beings walk. After things accumulate, distinctions of size, rank, and quality appear; thus propriety follows accumulation. Heaven above and Lake below show the correct order of above and below, the root of constant conduct. The noble person uses this image to distinguish high and low and settle people's minds. Cheng Yi describes ancient offices as matching virtue, while later ages chase honor and wealth, producing disorder. This hierarchy is his historical frame; it need not be reproduced as social ranking.
confucian.modern_meaning: In a present-day reading, the upper and lower trigrams are not fixed social classes but different positions, responsibilities, and sources of strength within any shared situation. Treading well means seeing the actual structure: who holds formal authority, what role each person carries, which voices are above and below in influence. Settling people’s aspirations can become clarifying a group’s purpose so that competing desires do not turn into confusion. The tiger’s tail represents moments of close contact with power, risk, or strong personalities. Caution is not passivity; it is disciplined attention to timing and proportion. The soft under the firm can be translated as humility, support, or the informed contribution of those not in charge, offered with joy rather than resentment. Resolute action has its place, but only when it consults others and remains aware of limits. The closing call to examine one’s steps invites retrospective honesty: not to predict outcomes, but to learn how each step has shaped the path.
confucian.advice: Approach influence as if near a sleeping tiger: move deliberately, know the actual order of responsibility, and offer support without losing your own plainness. When in a position of authority, do not rely only on personal decisiveness; seek counsel, especially from those with less power. Pause before forcing a step. Revisit the end of a path to see whether it has been complete.
confucian.shadow: The shadow is resolute self-will dressed as propriety, using ritual or hierarchy to silence others, or pretending plainness while quietly craving advancement. It is the one-eyed step that overestimates its vision, the lame step that claims to run.
confucian.reflection_question: Where am I walking too close to power without enough attentive care?
confucian.evidence_zh: 履禮也禮人之所履也

lines.interpretation: The first line occupies the lowest place; its plain treading is not about remaining in poverty, but about not being driven by greed and restlessness. Cheng Yi contrasts the person who advances to escape lowliness, bringing pride and blame, with the worthy who rests in plainness and then advances with purpose. Plainness is the ground of disciplined action. In a present-day context, this is the integrity of doing small, unglamorous work without pretending it is grand, so that movement forward carries real purpose rather than compensation.
lines.reflection: What would happen if I acted from my present plainness instead of from the wish to escape it?
lines.evidence_zh: 賢者則安履其素其處也樂其進也將有為也

lines.interpretation: The second line walks a smooth and broad path, but Cheng Yi warns that this is only auspicious for those who are quiet and calm within. The yang will to advance must be steadied by inner tranquility; otherwise restlessness disturbs the center. In modern terms, this is the discipline of maintaining a quiet mind amid easy outward conditions. Smooth progress can become reckless accumulation of advantage if profit and desire stir the heart. The hidden person is not passive but cultivates the still center from which clear, firm action can proceed.
lines.reflection: How can I keep inner quietness when the path ahead seems smooth and inviting?
lines.evidence_zh: 葢其中心安靜不以利欲自亂也

lines.interpretation: The third line is yin in a yang place: the will aspires to firmness, but the substance is soft. Cheng Yi compares it to the one-eyed who think they see and the lame who think they walk far. Its treading is not aligned with its actual capacity, so danger bites. The caution is against performing a role one cannot carry, especially when aggressive self-confidence masks insufficiency. In present terms, this is overclaiming competence or pushing into authority before preparation. Recognition of limits is not self-deprecation but the foundation of safe movement.
lines.reflection: Where has my aspiration outrun my actual capacity, and what step needs to be corrected?
lines.evidence_zh: 以柔居三履非其正所以致禍害被咥而凶也

lines.interpretation: The fourth line is close to the ruler and therefore close to danger. Firm in substance yet soft in will, it does not rest comfortably in its proximity. Cheng Yi reads 'trembling with fear' as the appearance of prolonged caution. This trembling is not debilitating anxiety but the vigilant care that allows one to move safely through a risky position. In modern contexts, this is the informed caution of someone near power who knows the cost of a misstep and still chooses to act, not frozen, but moving with acute attention.
lines.reflection: What fear, if honored rather than suppressed, could become careful attention in my present situation?
lines.evidence_zh: 若能畏懼則當終吉葢九雖剛而志柔四雖近而不處故能兢慎畏懼則終免於危而獲吉也

lines.interpretation: The fifth line is the resolute ruler, yang in the honored central place. Cheng Yi warns that even correct action becomes perilous when one relies solely on personal decision and does not listen. Ancient sages, he says, sought counsel even from woodcutters and grass-gatherers. Authority is not invalidated by consultation; it is made luminous. Present-day application questions the confident leader who equates decisiveness with isolation. Firmness must be tempered by genuine openness to other voices, especially those below.
lines.reflection: In a role of authority, whose counsel am I currently avoiding, and what might that avoidance reveal?
lines.evidence_zh: 若自任剛明決行不顧雖使得正亦危道也

lines.interpretation: The top line turns from forward movement to retrospective examination. Cheng Yi interprets 'return' as completeness: looking back over one's steps, checking both good and bad, and completing the circle without flaw. This is not a prediction of reward but a practice of moral account-keeping. In modern terms, it is the end-of-process review that asks whether the path was walked whole-heartedly, whether beginnings and endings cohere. What is valued is having a real end, not drifting off.
lines.reflection: At the end of this phase, what do my completed steps reveal about the path I have actually taken?
lines.evidence_zh: 旋謂周旋完備无不至也

original_chinese.title: 伊川易傳 (四庫全書本)/卷1

further_reading.title: The Yi River Commentary on the Book of Changes

hexagrams.essence: Liu Yiming presents Hexagram 10 as the work of advancing inner yang through joy, not force: tread close to danger with watchful, unhurried sincerity until acquired yin transforms and pure yang returns.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: This hexagram describes any careful passage through risk where joy and firmness must cooperate. The tiger is not an external enemy but the living, potentially dangerous energy of life; treading its tail means engaging that energy without being devoured. The image asks the inner practitioner to advance step by step, with both courage and receptivity, so that what threatens can become what restores wholeness.
hexagrams.historical_core: In Liu Yiming’s commentary, Lü means advancing yang while guarding against danger. He reads the lower trigram Dui (joy) as the youngest daughter who can turn yin at its extreme back to yang; through her gradual, trustworthy action, the practitioner summons true yang that was lost to the post-cosmic state. The six lines map stages: firm will, hidden-perseverance, foolish self-will, firm yielding, centered decisive cultivation, and complete beginning-to-end treading. His framework is expressly inner alchemical: the 'tiger' is dangerous acquired energy, and 'no bite' arises from harmonious, attuned treading rather than passivity.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: In a modern contemplative context, this hexagram can be read as an invitation to bring disciplined attention to high-stakes transitions—work, relationship, creative risk, inner growth—without forcing outcomes. Liu Yiming’s language of medicine (inner material to be refined) and fire-times (timing and dosage) becomes a metaphor for inner practice: knowing when to act and when to soften, when to be firm and when to yield. Treading the tiger’s tail names the honest recognition that some necessary advances carry risk; the response is not avoidance but nuanced, persistent care. Joy is not a reward at the end but the quality of moving itself. This reading supports self-examination rather than prediction: if one treats status, ambition, or emotional intensity as raw material to refine, one can proceed with less arrogance and more attunement. The goal is not domination but restoration—returning to a more sincere, unified disposition through repeated small choices.
hexagrams.advice: Move forward, but do not rush. Pair firm intention with a soft, attentive step. Check the 'fire-time': if tension rises, ease the pace; if stagnation appears, summon quiet courage. Let joy inform discipline, not replace it. Review your motives at each threshold, and adjust rather than force.
hexagrams.shadow: The shadow is overconfidence disguised as clarity—one-eyed seeing, lame walking—that mistakes momentum for wisdom. It rushes into the tiger’s reach, ignores timing, and turns a workable risk into self-inflicted injury.
hexagrams.reflection_question: Where am I moving with hidden force, and am I listening for the moment to soften?
hexagrams.editorial_status: integration-candidate — AI-assisted; final human review pending

classical.name: Peace
classical.judgment_zh: 小往大來，吉亨
classical.judgment_en: The small departs, the great arrives; auspicious and prosperous.
classical.image_zh: 天地交，泰；后以財成天地之道，輔相天地之宜，以左右民
classical.image_en: Heaven and earth join: this is Peace. The ruler thereby regulates and completes the way of heaven and earth, assists what is fitting for heaven and earth, and thereby guides the people.
classical.historical_note:
Hexagram 11 Tai has Qian below and Kun above. The source includes Tuan zhuan and Xiang zhuan commentaries, including line-specific small images; only the judgment, Great Image, and six line statements are translated here. In line 2, 得尚于中行 is rendered with 'honor'; Cheng Yi reads 尚 as 'partner'.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Pulling up the rush by its roots brings its kind with it; going forward is auspicious.

lines.text_zh: 包荒。用馮河，不遐遺；朋亡。得尚于中行
lines.translation_en: Embrace the wild. Use this to ford the river; do not leave the distant behind; partisanship dies away. Thus one attains honor in central conduct.

lines.text_zh: 无平不陂，无往不復，艱貞无咎。勿恤其孚，于食有福
lines.translation_en: There is no level ground without a slope; no going without a return. Be steadfast in hardship, and there will be no blame. Do not worry about trustworthiness; in nourishment there is blessing.

lines.text_zh: 翩翩，不富以其鄰；不戒以孚
lines.translation_en: Fluttering, one is not rich, yet with one's neighbor; without forewarning, there is trust.
Di Yi gives his younger sister in marriage; there is blessing, supreme good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 城復于隍，勿用師，自邑告命，貞吝
lines.translation_en: The city wall falls back into the moat. Do not use the army; issue orders from your own city. Persevering leads to regret.

hexagrams.title: Peace
hexagrams.name: Peace

taoist.title: The Alchemy of Peace
taoist.essence: Peace arises when inner firm yang and outer yielding yin are cultivated in right timing; the small departs, the great arrives. This is communication, not passive quiet, requiring disciplined alchemical work.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Tai depicts heaven below and earth above joining in intercourse. Liu Yiming reads it as the moment when true yang grows within while yielding yin complies without, restoring prior heaven and transforming later heaven. The archetype is one of balanced interchange—strength and receptivity, inner work and outer conduct—held together by timely fire-phases. Peace here is not mere absence of conflict but an achieved condition of mutual permeation that must be actively cultivated and protected.
taoist.historical_core: In Liu Yiming's commentary, Tai is '通和之義' (the meaning of communication and harmony). The lower Qian is strong within, the upper Kun yielding without; yin and yang respond to each other. He inherits the Zhouyi image of heaven and earth joining, but interprets the small departing and great arriving as alchemical: '小往則陰順，大來則陽健'—when yin yields and yang is strong, prior heaven is gradually restored and later heaven transformed. To accomplish this, he insists on advancing and retreating according to fire-phases, using firmness to bring about Tai and yielding to preserve it, moving from intentional action to non-action. The hexagram thus becomes a manual for completing nature and destiny, not a prediction.
taoist.modern_meaning: Read today, Tai speaks to the interior conditions for genuine peace in relationships, communities, and oneself. Liu Yiming's language of inner alchemy can be translated as disciplined self-cultivation: the 'yang within' is attentive initiative, clear principle, and willingness to act at the right moment; the 'yin without' is receptive listening, realistic accommodation, and patience to let timing mature. Peace is not achieved by suppressing conflict or by passive non-interference. It requires active harmonizing: recognizing when to be firm and when to yield, when to advance and when to step back. In group life, this might look like creating structures where different voices can meet—where the 'heaven' of vision joins the 'earth' of practical constraints. The text warns that every level ground has a slope; every advance has a return. Lasting peace needs ongoing maintenance, not a once-for-all fix. Liu's emphasis on 'fire-phases' invites regular review of timing and proportion, adjusting effort to the actual stage of a situation. It is a call to cultivate authentic nature while honoring obligations: not forcing outcomes, but also not abandoning initiative.
taoist.advice: Discern the season of your own situation. Where yang is needed, bring clarity and initiative; where yin is needed, practice receptivity and patience. Do not mistake passivity for peace. Use small, disciplined steps to gather strength, protect what has been built, and adjust your fire—your intensity—to the phase. Act when the time ripens, and let go into maintenance only after the foundation is firm.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is complacent harmony that avoids necessary conflict; rigidity disguised as strength; or over-yielding that lets acquired habits creep in. Peace becomes a wall that falls back into the moat because it was not maintained early.
taoist.reflection_question: Where am I mistaking passive accommodation for the living interchange that actually creates peace?
taoist.evidence_zh: 泰者，通和之義。卦德上坤順、下乾健，陽健于內，陰順於外，健順如一，陰陽相應，故謂泰。

lines.interpretation: At the first sign of inner clarity or motivation, Liu sees the whole network of allied strengths stirring, like pulling couch grass that brings the whole cluster. The teaching is to begin cultivation immediately when this yang appears—small, consistent refinement from subtle to evident. Initial impulse alone is not enough; it must be gathered while the moment is alive. In modern terms: when a genuine intention or principled impulse arises, honor it with concrete practice before distraction returns. Auspicious movement comes from acting with the time, not from waiting indefinitely.
lines.reflection: What seed of initiative is present now, and how can I support it with a first concrete step?
lines.evidence_zh: 初九，一陽潛生，諸陽皆有動機，如拔茅之茹根以及匯葉也。致泰者，乘此一陽發現，而即下手修為，漸采漸煉，由微而著

lines.interpretation: Line two describes the mature practitioner who pairs broad acceptance with decisive courage. 'Embracing the wild' is not laxity but wide measure; 'fording the river' is active will. Liu names this as civil and martial fire in balance—quiet observation with the utmost of yielding, preserving sincerity with the utmost of firmness. Applied today, this is the ability to include what is unfamiliar while still taking necessary risks. Partisanship dissolves, and one moves in the central path: neither rigid control nor accommodating drift, but responsive integrity adjusted to the present.
lines.reflection: Where am I being called to combine wide acceptance with courageous action, rather than choosing only one?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛中有柔，柔中有剛，文烹武煉，左之右之，無不宜之，得尚於中行矣。

lines.interpretation: At the third line, yang has reached fullness and the natural law of reversal appears: level ground slopes, going returns. Liu urges knowing advance and retreat, guarding steadfastness in hardship, and anticipating danger so the gain is not lost. This is not pessimism but strategic care at a peak. In ordinary life, success or stability contains the seed of its own decline only if unattended. The task is to practice maintenance before the turn, to accept that cycles are part of the work, and to hold to principle when conditions begin to shift.
lines.reflection: Where am I at a peak or plateau, and what protective adjustment is being asked of me now?
lines.evidence_zh: 當此之時，須要知進知退，艱難守貞，防危慮險，方無得而復失之咎。

lines.interpretation: This line marks the threshold where yang gives way to yin. If caution lapses, a hidden yielding influence stirs and group energy disperses, as if everyone 'flutters' and depends on others without real wealth. Liu warns that even an obtained elixir—an achieved inner peace—can be lost through inattention. The modern reading is subtle: small concessions, unexamined habits, or reliance on neighborly goodwill can erode hard-won integrity. Trust without forewarning can become spontaneous coalescence. Preserve peace by noticing the first encroachment of the merely comfortable.
lines.reflection: What small habit or accommodation is quietly dispersing focus or integrity that I have already cultivated?
lines.evidence_zh: 當陽極交陰之際，不能防危慮險，一陰潛生，群陰皆動，如翩翩不富以其鄰，無待相戒而孚合，金丹已得而復失。

lines.interpretation: At the fifth line, true peace is not maintained by force but by nourishing reciprocity. Liu reads the marriage image alchemically: yin clings to yang and yang clings to yin, same qi naturally blazing in the furnace. The ruler's gift creates blessing through relationship, not domination. Applied now, this is the quiet art of using receptivity to sustain initiative: partnership, dialogue, and mutual recognition keep the inner fire alive without overheating. It is the mature phase where one lets agreed structures and shared values do the work while still tending the flame.
lines.reflection: How can I nourish a relationship or project so that mutual commitment, rather than force, carries it forward?
lines.evidence_zh: 當正泰之時，以陰養陽，陽氣凝結，如帝乙歸妹，以祉及於臣下，陰戀陽而陽戀陰，陰陽同氣，自有天然真火，爐中赫赫長紅。

lines.interpretation: The final line is a caution. When compliance has gone to its extreme, one sees only the smoothness of peace and forgets that peace has a reverse. The city wall collapses into the moat because it was not repaired in time. Liu says that at this late moment aggressive action cannot recover the situation; one can only issue local orders and regret. In modern terms: neglect of maintenance eventually makes large interventions useless. The task is not to mobilize armies of effort after the fact but to learn from the fall and begin again at the appropriate, smaller scale.
lines.reflection: Where have I ignored early signs of erosion, and what can I learn from a current reversal without overreacting?
lines.evidence_zh: 在泰之終，順之極，只知泰之順，不知泰之逆，不防於早，必敗於終，如城傾而複於隍矣。

confucian.title: Tending Peace Through Exchange
confucian.essence: Peace is the free meeting of heaven and earth, ruler and minister, inner worth and outer care; it asks disciplined cultivation that contains what is wild, reforms boldly, and remembers that every height inclines.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: Peace is not the absence of conflict but a dynamic joining: creative strength moves upward while receptive earth opens downward, so what is small departs and what is great arrives. The image shows noble purpose taking root within and self-serving habits moving outward. This is a time to build institutions, trust capable people, and keep communication open between levels of life. Yet the very fullness of peace contains a slope toward decline, so vigilance and renewal belong to its meaning.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Tài as a political and cosmic pattern: Heaven below and Earth above exchange qi, and at court the ruler shows trust while ministers serve sincerely. In his account, yang—noble and princely—advances inward while yin—petty and common—withdraws. He calls on the ruler to 'fashion and complete the Way of Heaven and Earth,' making seasonal institutions that aid the people. His line commentary urges enough magnanimity to embrace the wild, enough boldness to cross the river, and enough impartiality to let factional ties die away. The image of Di Yi giving his daughter in marriage belongs to a patriarchal order; its ethical point is humble reliance on worthy help.
confucian.modern_meaning: In a contemporary frame, Peace invites us to notice how contrasting parts of a life or community meet: leadership with listening, planning with flexibility, tradition with renewal. It does not promise that comfort lasts; it asks us to practice what Cheng Yi calls containing uncultivated ground and crossing rivers—tolerating imperfection while acting decisively. Not leaving out the distant can mean attending to overlooked people and long-term effects, not only immediate circles. Companions disappearing can mean releasing cliquish loyalty so fairness is possible. The line about Di Yi's daughter can be read not as endorsement of hierarchy but as a call to honor competence and share authority in relationships. Because peace is cyclic, periods of ease are times for disciplined self-cultivation, fair institutions, and honest communication. The oracle voice is reflective: consider what is currently joining, what needs to be reformed, and where a slope may be forming.
confucian.advice: Cultivate spaciousness without losing nerve. Hold what is messy with patience, but do not postpone needed change. Include the overlooked and release cliquish attachments. Trust worthy partners and lower pride where needed. Watch for the first sign of reversal, and respond with small, local, honest adjustments rather than force.
confucian.shadow: Complacency turns peace into self-indulgence; fear of change preserves old abuses. When trust decays, authority may reach for force or issue commands only to the near, deepening isolation.
confucian.reflection_question: Where is ease currently asking you to combine tolerance with courageous change?
confucian.evidence_zh: 天地交而隂陽和則萬物茂遂所以泰也

lines.interpretation: The first line shows a capable person below, at a time turning toward Peace. Cheng Yi reads the linked roots as an image of mutual support: one worthy advance draws others upward. Group solidarity is not mere preference; it is how shared purpose becomes effective. In modern terms, this is an invitation to notice the communities and colleagues whose convictions align with your work. Advance is promising when it is not purely solitary but tethered to mutual responsibility. Ask who advances with you, and whose roots you are pulling.
lines.reflection: Whose roots come up with yours when you move forward?
lines.evidence_zh: 君子之進必與其朋類相牽援如茅之根然拔其一則牽連而起矣

lines.interpretation: The second line is the active center of Peace. Cheng Yi names four practices: embrace what is uncultivated, cross the river with boldness, do not leave the distant behind, and let partisan ties die. Tolerance and courage are not opposites; tolerance gives reform its timing, courage keeps tolerance from becoming slackness. Modern application may mean staying with a messy situation while making one clear change, and deliberately including people or consequences far from your immediate circle. Ask what fairness requires you to release.
lines.reflection: What distant concern are you tempted to leave out?
lines.evidence_zh: 包荒用馮河不遐遺朋亡四者處泰之道也

lines.interpretation: The third line stands at the height of Peace. The path that feels level invites a slope; every outward movement prepares a return. This is not a prediction of disaster but a call to discipline. When things are going well, do not become easy or careless. Hardship and uprightness here mean keeping a rigorous inner life, examining assumptions, and acting with steady integrity. Trust may not be fully recognized, yet nourishing work can still be blessed. The line does not say to grasp at permanence; it says to meet impermanence with faithful effort.
lines.reflection: What slope might be forming beneath your current ease?
lines.evidence_zh: 物理如循環在下者必升居上者必降泰久而必否

lines.interpretation: The fourth line moves past the height of Peace. 'Fluttering' suggests easy descent: formerly elevated habits or roles begin to lose their solid place. Not being rich while with neighbors means union is based on shared intention rather than advantage. In a personal or group setting, this can be a moment when people let go of prestige and align because they genuinely want the same direction. That alignment does not need forced promises; it emerges from inner honesty. Notice what is falling away not as shame, but as a return to fittedness, if it is met with sincerity.
lines.reflection: What shared intention is asking you to descend rather than cling?
lines.evidence_zh: 翩翩疾飛之貌四翩翩就下與其鄰同也

lines.interpretation: The fifth line uses the marriage of Di Yi's daughter as an image. In Cheng Yi's time it meant a ruler lowering privilege to trust a worthy minister. Today the historical hierarchy should be contextualized, not imitated; the ethical core is yielding status to honor competence. Softness in a high position responds to the firm wisdom of the second line. Leaders may make room for expertise; individuals may set aside pride to receive good counsel. Blessing emerges when dignity is shared rather than defended.
lines.reflection: Where is your current role asking you to honor someone else's competence?
lines.evidence_zh: 五能𠋣任其賢臣而順從之如帝乙之歸妹然降其尊而順從於陽則以之受祉且元吉也

lines.interpretation: The top line marks the end of a long Peace. The wall is not an external enemy but an accumulation returning to its own moat: resources, structures, or trust that once held now collapse inward. Cheng Yi counsels against force; when hearts no longer follow, coercion will worsen disorder. The only remaining movement is local and close, issuing honest communication from one's own sphere, yet even correct commands may feel late and small. This is not a prophecy of ruin but a sober reminder to notice decay early, while local repair is still possible.
lines.reflection: What structure in your life may be returning to its own moat?
lines.evidence_zh: 上下之情不通矣民心離散不從其上豈可用也

hexagrams.essence: Peace arises when inner firm yang and outer yielding yin are cultivated in right timing; the small departs, the great arrives. This is communication, not passive quiet, requiring disciplined alchemical work.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: Tai depicts heaven below and earth above joining in intercourse. Liu Yiming reads it as the moment when true yang grows within while yielding yin complies without, restoring prior heaven and transforming later heaven. The archetype is one of balanced interchange—strength and receptivity, inner work and outer conduct—held together by timely fire-phases. Peace here is not mere absence of conflict but an achieved condition of mutual permeation that must be actively cultivated and protected.
hexagrams.historical_core: In Liu Yiming's commentary, Tai is '通和之義' (the meaning of communication and harmony). The lower Qian is strong within, the upper Kun yielding without; yin and yang respond to each other. He inherits the Zhouyi image of heaven and earth joining, but interprets the small departing and great arriving as alchemical: '小往則陰順，大來則陽健'—when yin yields and yang is strong, prior heaven is gradually restored and later heaven transformed. To accomplish this, he insists on advancing and retreating according to fire-phases, using firmness to bring about Tai and yielding to preserve it, moving from intentional action to non-action. The hexagram thus becomes a manual for completing nature and destiny, not a prediction.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: Read today, Tai speaks to the interior conditions for genuine peace in relationships, communities, and oneself. Liu Yiming's language of inner alchemy can be translated as disciplined self-cultivation: the 'yang within' is attentive initiative, clear principle, and willingness to act at the right moment; the 'yin without' is receptive listening, realistic accommodation, and patience to let timing mature. Peace is not achieved by suppressing conflict or by passive non-interference. It requires active harmonizing: recognizing when to be firm and when to yield, when to advance and when to step back. In group life, this might look like creating structures where different voices can meet—where the 'heaven' of vision joins the 'earth' of practical constraints. The text warns that every level ground has a slope; every advance has a return. Lasting peace needs ongoing maintenance, not a once-for-all fix. Liu's emphasis on 'fire-phases' invites regular review of timing and proportion, adjusting effort to the actual stage of a situation. It is a call to cultivate authentic nature while honoring obligations: not forcing outcomes, but also not abandoning initiative.
hexagrams.advice: Discern the season of your own situation. Where yang is needed, bring clarity and initiative; where yin is needed, practice receptivity and patience. Do not mistake passivity for peace. Use small, disciplined steps to gather strength, protect what has been built, and adjust your fire—your intensity—to the phase. Act when the time ripens, and let go into maintenance only after the foundation is firm.
hexagrams.shadow: The shadow is complacent harmony that avoids necessary conflict; rigidity disguised as strength; or over-yielding that lets acquired habits creep in. Peace becomes a wall that falls back into the moat because it was not maintained early.
hexagrams.reflection_question: Where am I mistaking passive accommodation for the living interchange that actually creates peace?

classical.name: Standstill
classical.judgment_zh:
否
之匪人，不利君子貞，大往小來。
classical.judgment_en: Standstill of the wrong people: it is not favorable for the noble person to be resolute; the great departs and the small comes.
classical.image_zh: 天地不交，否；君子以儉德辟難，不可榮以祿。
classical.image_en: Heaven and earth do not intermingle—Standstill. Thus the noble person uses thrifty virtue to avoid difficulties; he must not allow himself to be honored with emolument.

lines.translation_en: Pulling up the rooted thatch, drawing along its kind. Steadfastness: good fortune. Success.
Embracing and receiving: the small person is fortunate; the great person is at a standstill. Success.
Embracing disgrace.
There is a mandate; no blame. Companions share in blessings.

lines.text_zh:
休否，大人吉。其亡其亡，繫于
包
一作「苞」
桑。
lines.translation_en: The standstill ceases; the great person is fortunate. 'It is lost, it is lost!'—fastened to a bushy mulberry.
The standstill is overturned; first standstill, then joy.

taoist.title: Standstill and the Hidden Return
taoist.essence: Pi is not a verdict but a condition of blockage: heaven and earth stop mingling, true yang scatters while false yin rules. Yet within this closed state, disciplined renewal waits for recognition and timely reversal.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: This hexagram names the state where inner yielding and outer force no longer interpenetrate. What was true becomes false; yang retreats and yin manages affairs. The noble person is obstructed, while the small—desire, habit, acquired impulse—appears ascendant. Liu Yiming treats this not as permanent loss but as a closed gate: the original yang is concealed rather than extinguished, and disciplined restraint of spirit and qi can protect the seed of return.
taoist.historical_core: In the received text, Pi says the wrong people obstruct; it is not favorable for the noble to be resolute; the great departs and the small comes. The Great Image says heaven and earth do not intermingle, so the noble uses frugal virtue to avoid difficulty and cannot be glorified by emolument. Liu Yiming, writing as an inner-alchemy commentator, identifies the 'wrong people' with evil qi and the 'noble person' with correct qi. For him the hexagram follows Lü (履) in his received sequence, differing from the standard order after Tai: when pre-cosmic unity is lost, true yin and true yang become false, evil qi enters, and correct qi retreats. The six lines then show stages of guarding yin and restoring yang.
taoist.modern_meaning: Historically, this is not a political or social judgment; it is a diagnosis of inner obstruction. When habits harden, when outward performance replaces inward contact, when desire leads and quieter knowing withdraws, Pi appears. Liu Yiming's language of true yang and evil qi may sound foreign; we can hear it as the difference between lucid, whole-hearted presence and the scattered momentum of compulsion. The modern invitation is not to flee or force change. It is to observe the closed gate honestly, to simplify, to lower expenditure of attention, and to watch for the first stirring of renewal. There is no guarantee that effort will immediately open the way, but the line commentary consistently places power in the moment of recognition: early, small acts of restraint; refusing to mistake false comfort for real nourishment; mid-blockage honesty; and late-stage readiness to act when vitality returns. This is a map of process, not a promise of outcome.
taoist.advice: When the gate is closed, do not pound on it. Retire from display, conserve your energy, and decrease what feeds the blockage. Watch for the faint movement of authenticity—whether a bodily signal, an honest reluctance, or a returning scruple—and respond without delay. Small, concrete protectiveness now is stronger than a forced reopening later.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is false comfort: mistaking acquired ease for true nourishment, collecting shame while smiling, or waiting so long that the closed gate hardens into identity. The noble posture can itself become rigid correctness that blocks.
taoist.reflection_question: Where is my outward strength currently separated from my inward receptivity?
taoist.evidence_zh: 蓋陰陽不交，真陰變為假陰，真陽變為假陽，先天失而邪氣入，邪氣入而正氣退

lines.interpretation: The first subtle yin has already taken root, like pulling up thatch roots drawing along their kind. Because this early stage still holds enough unspoiled yang, early recognition is decisive. Liu Yiming calls this guarding against yin before obstruction has fully formed. The reflective practice is not to dramatize the small warning but to meet it with simple correctness—removing one harmful association, interrupting one reactive pattern, returning to honesty before the current becomes fixed.
lines.reflection: What small habit is already pulling its kindred into my life?
lines.evidence_zh: 初六，一陰潛生，否之根已立，否之機必發，如拔茅布，以其匯矣。當斯時也，陰氣方生，陽氣未傷，若能早為致濟，猶可轉否為泰。

lines.interpretation: At the second stage, outward compliance masks an inner drift. The yielding pattern has not yet fully harmed yang, but that momentum is present. The text's 'small person' is not another human being; it is the part of us that finds ease in avoidance, flattery, or half-truth. Liu Yiming's advice is frugal virtue: reduce display, avoid entanglement with what feeds the blockage, and do not mistake apparent social smoothness for inner alignment. This is protection in the midst of early obstruction.
lines.reflection: Where am I outwardly agreeable while inwardly closing to what is true?
lines.evidence_zh: 六二，陰氣漸進，殺氣將發，外君子而內小人，是謂包承。包承之陰，雖未至於傷陽，已有傷陽之勢，在小人邪氣順行則吉，在大人正氣不通則否。修道者，儉德辟難，不為陰氣所惑，亦否中得亨之一道，此防陰于方否之時也。

lines.interpretation: The third line is the moment of false mastery. When blockage thickens, we may turn to indulgent coping and call it self-care. Liu Yiming says yin qi has congealed; one follows desire, mistakes false for true, and embraces shame without recognizing it. This is not a moralistic rebuke but a diagnostic alert: the feeling of having a workable arrangement may itself be the obstruction. The practice here is naming the shame we have been carrying as if it were comfort.
lines.reflection: What am I calling self-care that is actually reinforcing the blockage?
lines.evidence_zh: 六三，陰氣結聚，順其所欲，認假為真，以為得計，實包羞而不知其羞者，此順陰而不知有否也。

lines.interpretation: Here, at the exhaustion of the blocked pattern, a living pulse returns. Liu Yiming calls it the heavenly conscience—not a special possession of the wise but a natural endowment present in everyone, obscured by disposition and desire. Turning back does not require perfection; one honest movement of conscience can dissolve many accumulated errors. Even ordinary people, knowing and practicing this, can transform calamity into blessing. This line invites a concrete act of returning, not a grand conversion.
lines.reflection: What is the first small honest movement available to me right now?
lines.evidence_zh: 九四，在陰極交陽之際，否中藏泰，生機又現，無命者而又有命矣。人之健德，天命之良心也。此心人人具足，個個圓成，處聖不增，處凡不減，但為氣質所拘，人欲所蔽，以苦為樂，不肯回頭耳。若肯回頭，天良發現，一善可以解百惡，立登道岸，有咎者即可至於無咎。是道也，雖凡夫俗子，知而行之，災變為福，刑化為德，疇離祉乎。

lines.interpretation: The fifth line is not complacent success. When the gate begins to open, Liu Yiming warns against resting in apparent prosperity. The phrase 'It is lost, it is lost' is a deliberate practice of remembering fragility while still fastened to the sturdy mulberry—the rooted work of cultivation. To guard the Dao-mind and remove the human mind means not identifying with the returning vitality. Prosperity itself is protected by humble vigilance: before losing, guard against loss; while stable, attend to what could destabilize.
lines.reflection: What stability am I enjoying so much that I have stopped guarding its foundations?
lines.evidence_zh: 九五，剛健中正，守道心而去人心，不求否休而自休。其休者，以其能防否於正泰之時，居三陽之內，正泰之時也。其亡其亡，系于苞桑，未亡而防亡，方泰慮不泰，陰氣焉得而入之？此防陰於正泰之時也。

lines.interpretation: The final line describes the moment when blockage has run its course. Yin should retreat and yang advance; action now is not forced but takes advantage of accumulated timing. Liu Yiming speaks of heaven and the person issuing forth together—not an external miracle but the convergence of inward readiness and outer occasion. The work is to support yang, actively and without delay: first obstruction, then joy. This is the fruit of all earlier restraint, but only if one has learned the medicine and the fire-times.
lines.reflection: What long-held blockage is now ripe to be named and released?
lines.evidence_zh: 上九，在否之終，陰氣當退，陽氣當進，正當傾否之時。修道者，乘此機會，天人合發，抑陰扶陽，先否後喜，易如反掌，此進陽於否終之時也。然則不能使泰而不否者，後天循還之道。而能於否中致泰者，先天逆運之功，但須要認得藥物，知的火侯，不先不後，隨時進退耳。

confucian.title: Standstill: Preserving Integrity in Obstruction
confucian.essence: When Heaven and Earth do not intermingle, a standstill blocks communication; the noble person retires from honor, preserves frugal virtue, and waits for the moment when firm yang talent can overturn obstruction.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: This hexagram depicts a pattern of non-communication: creative strength above, receptivity below, yet they remain apart, so generative exchange fails. In Cheng Yi's moral reading, that cosmic blockage mirrors a human situation in which the way of the noble person declines and petty interests seem ascendant. The archetype is not passive despair but disciplined withdrawal: hide one's outward merit, do not seek emolument or prestige, keep relationships and principles intact, and recognize that obstruction reaches a limit and must reverse.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi explains Pi through the movement of qi and political order: when ruler and ministers do not truly communicate, the world has no functioning state. He reads the Judgment's 'not favorable for the noble person's steadfastness' as the noble person's correct way blocked, while yang departs and yin arrives. The Image says the noble person uses frugal virtue to avoid difficulty and cannot be glorified by emolument. Historically this meant withdrawing from conspicuous office under a corrupt or unresponsive regime, preserving one’s integrity rather than accepting honor. This hierarchy—ruler, minister, worthy—was a political context; it need not be endorsed as a timeless social structure.
confucian.modern_meaning: In present-day terms, Pi does not command passivity or prediction. It names moments when channels are blocked: a team stops listening, an institution rewards compliance rather than honesty, a relationship becomes formal without real exchange. Cheng Yi's caution can be translated as: do not chase recognition from a system that will compromise your ethical core; reduce external display, live with deliberate plainness, protect the space for honest speech. At the same time, his line-by-line reading says not every position is identical. A person in a junior or marginal role may need to stay united with trusted companions; a person with some authority may act only when mandate and role genuinely permit; a person at the center of responsibility must not relax at the first sign of improvement but keep watch for relapse. The historical 'ruler' and 'minister' are better understood today as relational functions—leadership, collaboration, stewardship—rather than fixed ranks. Obstruction is not a permanent fate but a phase that calls for timing, integrity, and readiness to overturn it when the moment ripens.
confucian.advice: When communication is blocked, do not force recognition. Withdraw gracefully, reduce unnecessary display, stay close to companions of integrity. If you hold legitimate authority, act only through clear, shared purpose, not personal pride; if improvement begins, remain alert. Let the period teach you what must be restored before you attempt to overturn it.
confucian.shadow: The shadow is contemptuous isolation or self-righteous withdrawal. One may call it integrity while actually hardening against all relationship, or secretly court approval while pretending to refuse honor.
confucian.reflection_question: Where am I mistaking self-protective withdrawal for principled preservation—or seeking recognition that would compromise what I know to be right?
confucian.evidence_zh: 天地不交否君子以儉徳辟難不可榮以禄

lines.interpretation: Initial Six dwells below at the beginning of obstruction. Cheng Yi says the Changes takes the reed with its clustered roots as an image of solidarity: in a blocked time, those below are noble persons, not petty. The line’s steadfastness is not a solitary spiritual stance; it is kept together with one’s kind. You may not be able to advance now, but you can preserve the root system of shared purpose. The line does not promise outward success; it describes good fortune in dwelling steadfastly, which keeps the Way alive until communication returns.
lines.reflection: Who are the companions of integrity with whom I am rooted, and am I actually remaining steadfast with them?
lines.evidence_zh: 初六能與其類貞固其節則處否之吉而其道之亨也

lines.interpretation: Six in the second is yin but central and correct. Cheng Yi contrasts two responses to obstruction. The petty person wraps and harbors a wish to bear with the superior, seeking personal advantage by flattering compliance. The great person in standstill refuses to bend the Way or violate integrity; the very blockage of personal prospects is the penetration of the Way. Cheng Yi even says that if one remains upright, then it is blocked—there is nothing to flatter. This teaches a boundary: acceptance of obstruction can be honorable only when it is chosen for principle, not when it becomes hidden collusion.
lines.reflection: Where might my smooth adaptation be a subtle form of self-serving compliance rather than genuine loyalty?
lines.evidence_zh: 大人當否則以道自處豈肯枉已屈道承順於上唯自守其否而已身之否乃其道之亨也

lines.interpretation: Six in the third is yin, neither central nor correct, and close to the powerful. In Cheng Yi’s account, this is the extreme of the petty person’s condition: unable to guard the Way or rest in its lot, it wraps up and harbors shameful schemes, and its deliberations become wicked and excessive. The line faces the uncomfortable truth that a person who clings to an inappropriate position may internalize disgrace, masking it as competence. It is a warning against becoming the very thing one claims to oppose.
lines.reflection: What shame am I quietly packaging and calling necessary in my current circumstances?
lines.evidence_zh: 其所包畜謀慮邪濫无所不至可羞耻也

lines.interpretation: Nine in the fourth has yang firmness near the ruler’s seat; Cheng Yi calls it one who has talent to rescue the standstill and has attained high position. The danger is dwelling on one’s own merit and provoking envy. The line’s no-blame condition is that every action issues from a shared or higher mandate; authority returns to its proper source, and companions share in the blessing. This is not servility; it is the art of acting in a blocked system without making oneself the heroic center.
lines.reflection: Can I act for repair without needing to be seen as the rescuer, and am I willing to align with legitimate shared purpose?
lines.evidence_zh: 若能使動必出於君命威柄一歸於上則无咎而其志行矣

lines.interpretation: Nine in the fifth has yang firmness, centrality and correctness in the honored position: enough to bring the standstill to rest and gradually arrive at Tai. But Cheng Yi insists the work is not finished. The repeated warning—'It is lost! It is lost!'—means binding oneself to a deep-rooted mulberry of long-term security while continually watching for relapse. The historical examples of Wang Yun and Li Deyu showed ruin when leaders relaxed after apparent success. In modern terms, repair at the center must include institutional memory and humble vigilance, not just a triumphant moment.
lines.reflection: What early signs of relapse am I tempted to ignore because restoration is finally beginning?
lines.evidence_zh: 大人當位能以其道休息天下之否以馴致於泰猶未離於否也故有其亡之戒

lines.interpretation: Top nine is the end of standstill. Cheng Yi says the principle of things is that at the limit it must reverse: when Tai reaches its limit, there is Pi; when Pi reaches its limit, there is Tai. But reversal is not automatic; it requires firm yang talent to overturn the obstruction. The line names a change in experience: first blockage, then joy. This is not a prediction that things will improve regardless of action; it is a structural hope conditioned on strong, principled effort at the right time.
lines.reflection: What is the next small, firm act that could begin overturning this obstruction without pretending it is already gone?
lines.evidence_zh: 否極則泰上九否既極矣故否道傾覆而變也

classical.name: Fellowship
classical.judgment_zh: 同人于野，亨。利涉大川，利君子貞。
classical.judgment_en: Fellowship in the open country; success. Favorable to cross the great river; favorable for the noble one to be steadfast.
classical.image_zh: 天與火，同人；君子以類族辨物。
classical.image_en: Heaven and fire: Fellowship. Thus the noble one sorts kindred and distinguishes things.
classical.historical_note:
The source text for the fourth line carries an inline variant note 一作「墉」; the primary reading 庸 is understood as 'wall/rampart'.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Fellowship at the gate: no blame.
Fellowship with one's clan: shame.
Concealing warriors in the brush, he ascends the high ridge; for three years he does not rise.
lines.text_zh: 伏戎于莽，升其高陵，三歲不興。

lines.translation_en: Mounting his rampart, he is unable to attack; good fortune.
lines.text_zh: 乘其庸一作「墉」，弗克攻，吉。

lines.translation_en: Fellowship: first crying and wailing, then laughter. The great army overcomes and they meet.
lines.text_zh: 同人，先號啕而後笑。大師克相遇。

lines.translation_en: Fellowship in the outskirts: no regret.
