hexagrams.name: Fellowship

taoist.title: Fellowship in the Open Country
taoist.essence: True fellowship arises after the sacred embryo is formed; it is selfless union in the open country, grounded in principle, not private preference, allowing one to cross great rivers.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: This hexagram depicts heaven above fire: inner clarity moving with outer strength. Liu Yiming reads it as the stage of mingling with the world after the alchemical embryo is formed. The archetype is the one who unites with others by shared principle, without losing inner solidity; not blending from need or partiality, but becoming like heaven and sun—covering and illuminating all without exception.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming places Tong Ren after Tai, the hexagram of balanced yin and yang where the sacred embryo is already formed. He describes the practice as mingling with the vulgar and harmonizing with the light as the next step of cultivation. For him, true fellowship demands being completely public-spirited and without selfishness, dissolving the distinction between self and other. The open country symbolizes the absence of self-other fixation; and the favorable crossing of the great river means fellowship must be sincere enough to endure danger, not just comfort. Only the noble one who unites by principle, not by a changing mind, completes self and others.
taoist.modern_meaning: Today this hexagram points to a mature form of solidarity that does not erase boundaries or dissolve into a crowd. It asks you to bring the clarity of your own inner work into groups and communities, not as a strategy of domination but as shared principle. Liu's inner alchemy suggests that only after one has formed an inner center—an embryo of disciplined selfhood—can one truly meet others without being captured by their expectations or by one's own need for approval. It is not passive nonaction; it is disciplined presence: sort kinds, distinguish things, choose the right moment, and refuse forced union. The great river is any situation of high risk where only a fellowship based on integrity can carry you. In practical terms, this could mean building alliances around values rather than identity, staying warm and clear even when relations are strained, and being willing to walk away from private cliquishness. It does not predict success, but describes the conditions under which genuine fellowship can unfold.
taoist.advice: Cultivate selfless principle before seeking allies. Withdraw your demand for personal recognition, and test whether you can remain in fellowship when conditions become difficult or dangerous. When tempted to force an ally or to cling only to those already close, return to the open country: act from shared principle, not private preference, and let timing show whether union is real.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is forced or partial fellowship: uniting with those who please you while hiding warriors behind your supposed friendliness; climbing a high mound of self-importance and wondering why no one truly meets you.
taoist.reflection_question: Where am I confusing closeness with genuine fellowship, and what would it look like to enter the open country of shared principle?
taoist.evidence_zh: 同人者，人我如一之義。卦德上乾健、下離明，明而行健，健而通明，誠中達外，成己成物，故謂同人。

lines.interpretation: At the threshold of fellowship, strength is tempered by clarity. Before stepping out the gate, discern what is right and what is possible; do not rush into union for its own sake. Liu Yiming calls this strong yet careful at the beginning. It is the discipline of testing alliances before committing, so that the first step toward others is clean and without blame. This is not aloofness but the right use of discernment before action.
lines.reflection: What do I need to discern before I leave my own gate to meet others?
lines.evidence_zh: 初九，在同人之時，剛而能明，將欲出門同人，不遽出門，先辨其是非可否，而後同。同之能以無咎者，此剛而謹始之同也。

lines.interpretation: This line shows fellowship restricted to one's own clan or inner circle. It is yielding but does not go far; one can unite only with the familiar and cannot reach the distant. Liu Yiming calls it shameful and distressing. The inner self may be comfortable, but the work of true fellowship remains incomplete. Clinging to the familiar feels safe yet breeds regret because it falls short of the open country of shared principle.
lines.reflection: Where am I limiting my fellowship to those who already resemble me?
lines.evidence_zh: 六二，居於內體，與二陽同處，是同人于宗，僅能同之於親，不能同之於疏，乃同人羞吝之道，此柔而不遠之同也。

lines.interpretation: Excessive force and self-regard produce only forced union. One hides weapons in the thicket, climbs a high mound, and tries to make fellowship a matter of others submitting. Liu speaks of three years without rising: even prolonged effort cannot bring authentic fellowship when it is unnatural and domineering. The lesson is not more aggression but recognizing that fellowship from a high position is not fellowship at all.
lines.reflection: In what relationship am I hiding warriors while claiming to seek union?
lines.evidence_zh: 九三，剛明太過，自尊自大，問或同人出於勉強，不由自然，如伏戎於莽，升其高陵也。高陵之同，順我者能同，逆我者不能同。如此之人，雖三歲之久，終不能興同人之事，此剛而勉強之同也。

lines.interpretation: Here strength meets strength, and attack fails. Yet Liu sees good fortune: when unable to unite, one does not force the attack. This is strength that can become yielding. Rather than battering the wall of another's difference, the wise pause and accept non-union for now. This restraint preserves the possibility of later fellowship. It is not passivity but a strategic and ethical limit on force.
lines.reflection: Where am I being asked to stop forcing an outcome and let principle, not pressure, decide?
lines.evidence_zh: 九四，以剛乘剛，彼強我勝，彼我不能同心，如乘其墉而弗克攻矣。然剛而能柔，不能同而不強攻，亦同人之吉道，此剛而能柔之同也。

lines.interpretation: The central line first weeps, then laughs. The path of true principle may at first lack companions; high virtue attracts slander and few understand. But after completing oneself, one seeks to complete others through public-spirited union. Liu compares this to a great army overcoming through sincerity. Persistence in correctness eventually moves beings; the weeping gives way to meeting. This is fellowship won through disciplined integrity, not popularity.
lines.reflection: Can I stay with the grief of being misunderstood long enough for true meeting to ripen?
lines.evidence_zh: 九五，剛健中正，道全德備，先無人同，而終必有同者，是同人先號咷而後笑也。夫道高者毀來，德修者謗興，知音之少，亦無足怪。然成己之後，而欲成物，大公無私，以正而同，如大師克之，久則誠能動物，方且人人尊服，而皆同之，何患知音之不遇哉！此大公無私，利涉大川之同也。

lines.interpretation: Fellowship in the outskirts is outwardly with the world but inwardly beyond it. One can be in the dust yet transcend the dust. Liu calls this harmony without drifting: great wisdom appears foolish, great skill seems clumsy, and circumstances cannot move the heart. This is not isolation but a final refinement—remaining available to others while preserving an inner distance that keeps one free from regret.
lines.reflection: How can I be in the world of relationships while remaining inwardly unshaken by its pressures?
lines.evidence_zh: 上九，剛以柔用，在塵而能出塵，處世而能出世，外雖同而內不同，如同人於郊。於郊之同，大智若愚，大巧若拙，境遇不得而移，不致悔而自無悔，此和而不流之同也。

confucian.title: Fellowship in the Open Wilds
confucian.essence: Impartial fellowship is found beyond private attachment, in open ground; correctness and clarity, not force or clan, make crossing difficulty possible.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: Heaven above and fire below share an upward reaching; the noble person uses this to sort kinds and discern differences without dissolving into faction. The single yin at the center draws many seekers, yet authentic fellowship belongs to those who can meet through centrality and correctness rather than possessive closeness. The image is not sameness but ordering: clear distinctions make impartial union possible.
confucian.historical_core: In Cheng Yi’s eleventh-century moral reading, Tong Ren follows Obstruction because a blocked age requires shared strength. He contrasts the noble person’s impartial union in the open wilds with the petty person’s private favor and faction. The second line’s bond with the fifth is central and correct, but in this hexagram private correspondence is shameful; the fifth is not read as a ruler because a ruler should unite with all under Heaven, not one favorite. The third and fourth lines show violent rivals around the one yin; their schemes fail because rightness prevails, while restraint brings good fortune.
confucian.modern_meaning: Read as an oracle today, Tong Ren does not predict whether a partnership will succeed. It asks where a person stands: in the open ground of shared principle or within a protected inner circle. Open ground can mean building alliances across difference without erasing distinction; clarity sorts kindred while respecting what is not one’s own. In workplaces, movements, families, and communities, this invites attention to the difference between genuine solidarity and unspoken favoritism. The third line’s hidden rivalry suggests that when desire for closeness becomes possessive or envious, energy may go into hidden watching, posturing, and delay rather than honest engagement. The fourth line points to the dignity of recognizing an unjust advantage and stepping back. The fifth suggests that deep loyalty can survive obstruction, but also warns against mistaking intense private attachment for broad fairness. The sixth asks whether distance and non-involvement, though safe, leave a deeper longing unfulfilled. Historical hierarchy need not be replicated; the enduring question concerns how partial loyalties coexist with just and open community.
confucian.advice: Notice whether your sense of belonging rests on shared values or on closeness to an in-group. Ask what would change if your circle widened. Where rivalry or hidden maneuvering appears, consider whether the goal itself is just. Refraining from a wrongful advantage can be a form of success. Honor sincere bonds, but do not confuse private loyalty with fairness to the whole.
confucian.shadow: Faction disguised as fellowship: clan loyalty, possessive guarding of one person, hidden rivalry, self-righteous weeping that later turns to triumph, or safe remoteness that avoids real solidarity.
confucian.reflection_question: Where does your sense of belonging become a closed door rather than an open gate?
confucian.evidence_zh: 夫同人者以天下大同之道則聖賢大公之心也

lines.interpretation: At the very beginning, no fixed attachment pulls the person inward; the union is through the gate, outside the household, so it has not yet narrowed into private favor. Cheng Yi reads this as public-mindedness without partiality. A broad, unguarded beginning keeps blame away, not because all will agree, but because no faction has formed. The question is whether early openness can be sustained once closer ties and stronger claims appear.
lines.reflection: Where am I still able to meet others without first sorting them into 'mine' and 'not mine'?
lines.evidence_zh: 九居同人之初而无繫應是无偏私同人之公者也

lines.interpretation: The second line has a legitimate bond with the fifth, but in Tong Ren that very bond becomes partial. Cheng Yi calls it 'lineage' or clan: solidarity with one's own circle. It may feel loyal, yet it narrows the wider fellowship and brings shame, because the standard is no longer shared principle but special attachment. Even a correct relationship can become a hidden limit. The line asks whether closeness is serving the whole or only protecting a favored connection.
lines.reflection: Is my loyalty to a person or group making me less available to the wider community?
lines.evidence_zh: 同於所繫應是有所偏與在同人之道為私狹矣故可吝

lines.interpretation: The third line hides soldiers in the brush and climbs a high hill to watch. It wants the object of union but knows its claim is not right. Cheng Yi sees a strong and violent character caught between desire and fear: because rightness does not support the seizure, action remains hidden and delayed for years. No open attack happens, so no recorded misfortune, but the image is one of anxious, dishonest maneuvering. This line warns that force and envy produce not victory but prolonged watching and internal burden.
lines.reflection: What desire am I stalking instead of openly testing against what is just?
lines.evidence_zh: 理不直義不勝故不敢顯發伏藏兵戎于林莽之中

lines.interpretation: The fourth is close to the fifth but wants the same second line; it climbs the dividing wall, ready to attack. Rightness does not support the assault. Cheng Yi points to the possibility of turning back: because this line is firm in a yielding place, it can recognize that the advantage is unjust and refrain. Good fortune is not conquest but restraint. The wall marks a boundary, and the wise act is to step down from it.
lines.reflection: Where is the wall I have climbed, and what would stepping down require?
lines.evidence_zh: 苟能自知義之不直而不攻則為吉也

lines.interpretation: The fifth begins in crying because it is separated from its true partner by intervening rivals. Its sense of rightness is strong, but the weeping then laughter belongs to a private bond. Cheng Yi does not read this as the ruler’s impartial path; a ruler should unite with all, not one favorite. Still, the passage honors two hearts centered in sincerity whose unity cannot be divided. Obstruction is real, but so is eventual meeting—though the triumph should not become self-congratulation at another’s defeat.
lines.reflection: When my loyalty meets resistance, is the grief grounded in shared principle or in a personal claim?
lines.evidence_zh: 五自以義直理勝故不勝憤抑至于號咷

lines.interpretation: The top line stands outside the city, in the outskirts. It has no close correspondent, so it finds no one with whom to unite. There is no regret, because nothing has been risked or wrongly grasped; but Cheng Yi says the intention to seek union is not attained and this is not a good dwelling. Safety without connection avoids blame yet remains incomplete. The line offers an honest form of solitude, without the rewards of real fellowship.
lines.reflection: Where is my distance protecting me from the vulnerability that genuine fellowship requires?
lines.evidence_zh: 郊在外而逺之地求同者必相親相與上九居外而无應終无與同者也

classical.name: Great Possession
classical.judgment_zh: 大有：元亨
classical.judgment_en: Great Possession: supreme success.
classical.image_zh: 火在天上，大有；君子以遏惡揚善，順天休命
classical.image_en: Fire is above heaven: Great Possession. The noble person thereby restrains evil and promotes good, complying with Heaven's beneficent mandate.
classical.historical_note:
Hexagram 14: 大有 with lower 乾 (☰) and upper 離 (☲). The source text includes variant notes inline: ‘大轝’ (一作「車」), ‘匪其尫’ (一作「彭」), and ‘自天佑之’ (一作「右」). Translations follow the source's primary characters. The standard received text usually has 大車以載, 匪其彭, and 自天祐之. Only the Great Image is translated; the Tuan and the small-line images are not included.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: No involvement with harm; it is not blameworthy. In hardship, there is no blame.

lines.text_zh: 大轝一作「車」以載，有攸往，无咎
lines.translation_en: A great carriage for carrying: if there is somewhere to go, there is no blame.

lines.text_zh: 公用亨于天子，小人弗克
lines.translation_en: The duke offers it to the Son of Heaven; a petty person cannot.
It is not his feebleness; there is no blame.
His sincerity meets with them; he is majestic and awe-inspiring: good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 自天佑一作「右」之，吉无不利
lines.translation_en: Assistance comes from Heaven; auspicious and nothing is unfavorable.

hexagrams.title: Great Possession
hexagrams.name: Great Possession

taoist.title: Possessing Greatness with Clarity
taoist.essence: Great Possession arises when inner strength (Qian) is governed within and outer clarity (Li) responds without. Through disciplined cultivation, what was absent is gained and what is already present grows, daily renewing virtue.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Fire above Heaven images inner light shining outward. Liu Yiming reads this as restoration of heavenly virtue after a period of obscurity: lower Qian is pure firm intent; upper Li is clear spiritual illumination. When strength governs within and brightness responds without, one walks as if beneath a sun that reveals all things. This archetype points to abundant inner possession, not accumulation of external goods, and to daily renewal through truthful practice.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming's commentary treats Hexagram 14 as a map for inner alchemy after the blockage of Pi. He defines greatness not as property but as renewal of innate heavenly virtue. For him, lower Qian is strong intent and upper Li is clear spiritual light; by using strength to govern within and brightness to respond without, one restores what was lost. The six lines trace disciplined stages: hidden cultivation, outward testing, correct firmness, firmness softened by gentleness, yielding seeking the firm, and final completion in which one's life becomes self-sovereign and Heaven's blessing follows. This is a historical Daoist contemplative framework, not a modern psychological or predictive system.
taoist.modern_meaning: In a time of noise and comparison, this hexagram invites us to distinguish true inner abundance from external display. The fire above heaven can be read as clarity founded on steady self-discipline. It suggests that we restrain harmful habits and cultivate honest strengths, not to dominate others but to become reliable in our relationships. The historical image of a duke offering to a ruler can be reframed: one offers one's best efforts to shared purposes rather than asserting rank. The line about a great cart bearing weight points to capacity tested in real circumstances; the line about a person who feigns greatness warns against self-importance without substance. This is not a prediction that all will go smoothly, but a contemplative lens for examining how we handle resources, visibility, and influence. It encourages periodic inner inventory, asking what should be quietly strengthened and what should be expressed. No outcome is guaranteed; the work is in honest, daily renewal.
taoist.advice: Consider practicing steady, unglamorous self-discipline: choose one small inner virtue to strengthen daily. When visibility comes, let it clarify rather than impress. Test capacity in ordinary responsibilities before seeking larger roles. Notice impulses to claim more than one has; soften them. Let sincerity anchor interactions. Begin with quiet inner cultivation and let outer testing follow when inner virtue is sufficient.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is self-inflation: claiming a greatness one has not cultivated, using clarity to dazzle rather than reveal, or treating inner strength as rigidity. It can also appear as hoarding insight while failing to test it in relationship.
taoist.reflection_question: Where am I presenting strength or brightness that I have not yet quietly cultivated?
taoist.evidence_zh: 此富有日新，嚴以治內之卦

lines.interpretation: At the start of inner abundance, what one has is not yet visible. The line warns against entanglement with harm, but Liu Yiming adds that even if you avoid external distractions, inner restlessness can still act as an object that disturbs the true self. The work here is quiet, hidden cultivation: face difficulty as a refining process, not as punishment. Let false impulses subside and allow the genuine to emerge. This is not a time for display or seeking validation; it is a time to guard the nascent inner resource.
lines.reflection: What inner distraction am I treating as an external problem, when it actually calls for quiet self-refinement?
lines.evidence_zh: 惟艱以處之，煉己持心，假者去而真者來，不有者能有，方能始終一無所咎矣。

lines.interpretation: When inner resources are sufficient, the image is a great cart able to bear a heavy load. Liu Yiming stresses that this capacity is not complete until tested in actual conditions. One must have somewhere to go—some responsibility, relationship, or task—and move through it without being shaken. Passing lightly does not mean avoiding difficulty; it means not being captured by outcomes. If the inner center holds under real weight, then inner and outer both become free of blame.
lines.reflection: What real situation could test my inner steadiness without becoming a source of harm?
lines.evidence_zh: 德克於內，須驗於外，唯有攸往，事上境上，輕輕過去，不動不搖，方是大有

lines.interpretation: The historical image of a duke offering tribute to the Son of Heaven is turned by Liu Yiming into an inner gesture: offering one's cultivated virtue to a higher principle. The line praises firmness that is also correct—not mere willfulness. A petty person, firm but not aligned with truth, makes something out of nothing and claims self-importance, which only opposes Heaven. In a modern frame, this asks whether our confidence serves a purpose larger than ego. Authority, if any, must be grounded in genuine virtue rather than rank.
lines.reflection: Where might my confidence be firm but not correct—more self-assertion than offering?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛而不正之小人，無而為有，予聖自雄，適以違天

lines.interpretation: This line describes a state where one has both strength and clarity but does not display them for recognition. The phrase 'does not flaunt his greatness' points to an inner abundance that appears outwardly modest. Not relying on force, not using brightness to dazzle, the person remains teachable and open. What they possess grows precisely because it is not spent on performance. Firmness that can soften is more durable than rigid strength.
lines.reflection: Where am I using my strengths to prove myself rather than to serve what is needed?
lines.evidence_zh: 有健不恃，有明不用，是匪其彭也

lines.interpretation: This line describes a state of sincere openness: one knows one's limitations and recognizes strengths in others. By seeking the firm through the yielding, dignity emerges not from self-assertion but from honest relationship. The word 'awe-inspiring' is not intimidation; it is the quiet authority that comes when trust is mutual and real. What was absent becomes present, what was small becomes great. This is a corrective to the previous line's hidden self-sufficiency: sometimes we grow by asking and receiving.
lines.reflection: Whose strength am I willing to receive without feeling diminished?
lines.evidence_zh: 以柔求剛，借剛濟柔，是以厥孚交如，威如吉也

lines.interpretation: The final line marks the ripening of the whole process: strength and clarity have become seamless, firmness and yielding are balanced, and the inner work reaches completion. Liu Yiming speaks of the golden elixir congealing and of one's life becoming self-sovereign, not through defiance but through alignment with Heaven's mandate. The blessing from Heaven is not an external reward; it is the natural accompaniment of a life that has completed its own inner mandate. This is the historical culmination of his alchemical reading, not a promise of effortless success.
lines.reflection: What would it look like for me to align my own self-direction with a principle larger than my preferences?
lines.evidence_zh: 我命由我不由天，是以自天佑之，吉無不利也

confucian.title: Great Possession Held Aright
confucian.essence: Great Possession is not mere accumulation but a patterned abundance: inner strength, outer clarity, timely response to Heaven, and trust that turns resources into shared order.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: Fire above heaven lights the multitude; all beings are seen, yet not possessed. One yielding line holds the honored center as yang lines respond, forming unity through openness rather than force. The archetype is mature stewardship: great resources, visibility, or influence gathered by integrity, made sustainable by restraint and dignity. Its abundance is moral as well as material.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Dayou as the hexagram of 'grand abundance and plenteous possession.' Its virtue is inner firmness and outer brightness, responding to Heaven and timely action. The noble person restrains evil, promotes good, and complies with Heaven's beneficent mandate. In his feudal context, lords must present their wealth to the Son of Heaven; the third line calls this a subject's constant duty. Read historically, this is hierarchical. Present-day application shifts from offering to a ruler to public accountability and common-good stewardship, while preserving the core demand: abundance must not become private hoarding or pride.
confucian.modern_meaning: Dayou speaks to contemporary forms of abundance—resources, attention, institutional authority, knowledge, social capital. Its counsel is not to renounce these but to hold them as a trust. Brightness above heaven asks that what we manage be visible, ordered, and oriented toward wider benefit. The inner firmness of Qian supplies discipline; the outer clarity of Li supplies honest self-examination. In workplaces, families, and public roles, this may look like transparency, shared decision-making, listening to those affected, and resisting the private capture of common goods. Sincerity builds reciprocal confidence, but it needs boundaries and dignity. At the height of success, the wise step back rather than overstate ownership. The hexagram encourages timely action and timely restraint, recognizing that abundance can distort as easily as it can serve.
confucian.advice: When holding plenty, ask what is not yours to keep. Act from disciplined strength and clear perception. Share credit and resources; establish honest limits. Maintain sincerity without becoming permissive. At a peak, reduce rather than display. Let abundance serve relationships, not isolate you.
confucian.shadow: Pride, possessiveness, and the fantasy that abundance proves merit. It hoards, dominates, blurs public and private, and mistakes flattery for trust, becoming the petty person who cannot offer what should be shared.
confucian.reflection_question: Where does my abundance need to become a shared trust rather than a private safeguard?
confucian.evidence_zh: 君子以遏惡揚善順天休命

lines.interpretation: At the first line, abundance is still young; the position is low and unacknowledged. Because pride and excess have not yet arisen, there is no contact with harm. Cheng Yi warns that wealth itself is not blameworthy; people bring blame through their own responses to it. The task is to enjoy what one has while remembering difficulty. Early restraint forestalls later harm. This line asks for an awareness of difficulty and cost, rather than innocence that becomes entitlement.
lines.reflection: What practice helps you notice the difficulties inside your current advantages?
lines.evidence_zh: 若能享富有而知難處則自无咎也

lines.interpretation: The second line is trusted by the central ruler because its strength is balanced by humility and the mean. Like a strong cart, it can carry heavy loads and travel far without breaking. In a time of growing abundance, the line may take responsibility and move with purpose, provided the fullness is not yet extreme. It suggests that capacity is not for display but for bearing shared weight. To act safely, match your strength to the actual burden and keep your destination clear.
lines.reflection: What burden are you currently able to carry that you have not yet assumed?
lines.evidence_zh: 如大車之材强壯能勝載重物也可以任重行逺故有攸往而无咎也

lines.interpretation: The third line occupies a position above others but below the sovereign. Historically, Cheng Yi frames this as a feudal lord's duty to present wealth to the Son of Heaven: all land and people ultimately belong to the wider order. Read for today, the point is accountability. Those who hold roles or resources on behalf of others must not treat them as private property. The petty person hoards and personalizes abundance; the mature steward returns it to the common good. This line tests whether ownership becomes service or self-dealing.
lines.reflection: Which of your resources or roles is most in danger of becoming a private possession?
lines.evidence_zh: 小人處之則専其富有以為私不知公以奉上之道故曰小人弗克也

lines.interpretation: At the fourth line, abundance has passed the middle and risks excess. Cheng Yi says the way to avoid blame is not to dwell in too much abundance—to be modest and reduce. Because the line is close to the ruler's high position, display would invite calamity. The protection is clear discrimination: seeing that fullness is about to turn, the wise person restrains themselves before reaching the brim. This is not self-diminishment for its own sake but intelligent refusal to let possessions define identity.
lines.reflection: What fullness in your life currently needs to be reduced before it becomes a source of blame?
lines.evidence_zh: 能不處其盛而得无咎者葢有明辨之智也

lines.interpretation: The fifth line is the central ruler, empty-centered and open. Cheng Yi stresses that sincerity alone is insufficient; softness without dignity invites insolence. Trust must be mutual: the ruler's sincerity calls forth the trust of others, while appropriate awe preserves respect. The balance is delicate—warmth that listens, and clarity that sets standards. In any leadership or caregiving role, this line counsels combining genuine openness with visible boundaries. Goodness arises not from permissiveness but from trustworthy presence that can also say no.
lines.reflection: Where do you need to pair sincerity with a firmer boundary?
lines.evidence_zh: 既以柔和孚信接於下衆志說從又有威嚴使之有畏善處有者也吉可知矣

lines.interpretation: The top line stands at the extreme of abundance yet does not reside in its possessions. Cheng Yi reads this as supreme brightness: knowing that fullness overflows, the noble person steps back from final ownership and honors trust and worth. Fullness without overflow is not passive withdrawal but active compliance with principle. The line's blessing is not guaranteed reward; it is the natural response of an order aligned with modesty, sincerity, and respect for others. At the end of great possession, the task is to let go gracefully.
lines.reflection: What would it look like for you to be full without overflowing?
lines.evidence_zh: 君子滿而不溢乃天祐也

hexagrams.essence: Great Possession arises when inner strength (Qian) is governed within and outer clarity (Li) responds without. Through disciplined cultivation, what was absent is gained and what is already present grows, daily renewing virtue.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: Fire above Heaven images inner light shining outward. Liu Yiming reads this as restoration of heavenly virtue after a period of obscurity: lower Qian is pure firm intent; upper Li is clear spiritual illumination. When strength governs within and brightness responds without, one walks as if beneath a sun that reveals all things. This archetype points to abundant inner possession, not accumulation of external goods, and to daily renewal through truthful practice.
hexagrams.historical_core: Liu Yiming's commentary treats Hexagram 14 as a map for inner alchemy after the blockage of Pi. He defines greatness not as property but as renewal of innate heavenly virtue. For him, lower Qian is strong intent and upper Li is clear spiritual light; by using strength to govern within and brightness to respond without, one restores what was lost. The six lines trace disciplined stages: hidden cultivation, outward testing, correct firmness, firmness softened by gentleness, yielding seeking the firm, and final completion in which one's life becomes self-sovereign and Heaven's blessing follows. This is a historical Daoist contemplative framework, not a modern psychological or predictive system.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: In a time of noise and comparison, this hexagram invites us to distinguish true inner abundance from external display. The fire above heaven can be read as clarity founded on steady self-discipline. It suggests that we restrain harmful habits and cultivate honest strengths, not to dominate others but to become reliable in our relationships. The historical image of a duke offering to a ruler can be reframed: one offers one's best efforts to shared purposes rather than asserting rank. The line about a great cart bearing weight points to capacity tested in real circumstances; the line about a person who feigns greatness warns against self-importance without substance. This is not a prediction that all will go smoothly, but a contemplative lens for examining how we handle resources, visibility, and influence. It encourages periodic inner inventory, asking what should be quietly strengthened and what should be expressed. No outcome is guaranteed; the work is in honest, daily renewal.
hexagrams.advice: Consider practicing steady, unglamorous self-discipline: choose one small inner virtue to strengthen daily. When visibility comes, let it clarify rather than impress. Test capacity in ordinary responsibilities before seeking larger roles. Notice impulses to claim more than one has; soften them. Let sincerity anchor interactions. Begin with quiet inner cultivation and let outer testing follow when inner virtue is sufficient.
hexagrams.shadow: The shadow is self-inflation: claiming a greatness one has not cultivated, using clarity to dazzle rather than reveal, or treating inner strength as rigidity. It can also appear as hoarding insight while failing to test it in relationship.
hexagrams.reflection_question: Where am I presenting strength or brightness that I have not yet quietly cultivated?

classical.name: Humility
classical.judgment_zh: 謙：亨，君子有終
classical.judgment_en: Humility: pervading; the noble one has completion.
classical.image_zh: 地中有山，謙；君子以裒多益寡，稱物平施
classical.image_en: Within the earth there is a mountain: Humility. The noble one thereby reduces what is excessive and increases what is scarce, weighing things and equalizing distribution.

lines.translation_en: Humble, humble noble one: using this to cross the great river; auspicious.
Sounding humility: steadfastness is auspicious.
Toiling humble noble one: has completion; auspicious.
Nothing is not advantageous; spread humility.

lines.text_zh: 不富，以其鄰，利用侵伐，无不利
lines.translation_en: Not rich; with its neighbours, it is advantageous to use invasion and attack; nothing is not advantageous.
Sounding humility; it is advantageous to use marching armies; subdue one's own cities and states.

taoist.title: Modesty as Inner Alchemy
taoist.essence: Modesty is not self-deprecation but the alchemical discipline of stopping false yang within and responding with yielding compliance without, so prior-heaven qi may gather.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: The mountain rests beneath the earth: outward receptivity holds an inner, unwavering stillness. This image points to strength that does not need to display itself, and to a lowering that creates space for true vitality. In Liu Yiming's reading, the yielding outer nature protects the firm inner core, allowing false activity to cease and true yang to be nourished.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming, an 18th-century Daoist master, reads Qian as the practice of 'using yin to protect yang.' The lower Gen trigram is inner stopping; upper Kun is outer compliance. Gen is the place where the false self 'dies'; Kun is where life is nurtured through true compliance. Stopping false yang preserves true yang; circulating true yin withdraws false yin. Modesty becomes disciplined cultivation: lower the mind, empty oneself, and the prior-heaven qi congeals into the elixir. This is not passive quietism but a rigorous inner work requiring beginning-to-end commitment.
taoist.modern_meaning: In contemporary terms, Qian invites a discipline of inner stillness and outer consideration. The mountain within the earth suggests that true confidence does not need to advertise itself; one can hold a clear boundary while remaining open and receptive. Rather than suppressing ambition, this practice reframes it: stopping the demand for recognition, comparing, or inflating self-image creates room for quiet competence and genuine connection. In relationships, it means listening from a place of fullness, not self-abandonment; in work, it means contributing without needing to be seen as the source. Liu Yiming's language of true and false yang can be translated as distinguishing between authentic aliveness and acquired posturing. The work is not to become small but to stop feeding self-importance and to circulate a more honest, receptive presence. This asks for ongoing cultivation, not a single decision, and it matures through repeated, ordinary choices. It also includes timing: knowing when to yield and when to hold firm, so that humility does not become passivity and firmness does not become domination.
taoist.advice: When the impulse to prove yourself arises, pause and ask what is actually needed. Practice lowering the mind without collapsing your inner boundary: listen, wait, and let your competence speak through steady action. Cultivate a daily discipline that stops self-display and nourishes quiet clarity. Enter difficult crossings with a lowered center and a firm inner stop.
taoist.shadow: False modesty that self-aggrandizes, or a show of humility that masks pride. It also includes self-belittlement that avoids responsibility, using 'not enough' as an excuse to hide.
taoist.reflection_question: Where am I using outer modesty to avoid inner work, or inner firmness to avoid outer engagement?
taoist.evidence_zh: 剛止於內，柔順於外，內剛而外柔

lines.interpretation: This line begins from a low, flexible position. It does not announce its virtue but refrains from putting itself first. In Liu Yiming's reading, this is modesty doubled: a yielding disposition that remains modest whether conditions are smooth or contrary. Such a person can face a 'great river'—a major transition or risk—without forcing outcomes, because the inner ground is already lowered and receptive. The practice is to start small, with ordinary deference, before attempting larger inner crossings. True strength here is not in spectacle but in the willingness to be taught.
lines.reflection: What does it look like for me to practice modesty when no one is watching, especially in small beginnings?
lines.evidence_zh: 順固能謙，逆亦能謙

lines.interpretation: This line points to a centered yielding that openly acknowledges what it does not have. The 'sounding' of modesty is not self-promotion but a clear showing of one's emptiness and a genuine regard for another's capacity. Liu Yiming says that when the mind is emptied, the belly can be filled—meaning that the receptivity of the lower center allows real nourishment. This is the modesty of yielding complying with firmness: not weakness, but an intelligent alignment with stronger forces. In practice, it may mean naming a limitation clearly, then creating space for skill or guidance to enter.
lines.reflection: Where might I need to voice my lack honestly so that another's strength can support the work?
lines.evidence_zh: 虛心即能實腹

lines.interpretation: The single firm line amid yielding lines carries the work of transformation. Here modesty is labor: not passivity but sustained effort that gradually enlightens the surrounding field. Liu Yiming says the virtue grows daily greater while the mind grows daily smaller. The practice is to hold one's inner firmness without lording it over others, so that others naturally become more modest themselves. This is 'toiling modesty'—the discipline of a true-hearted person who serves without needing reward. Completion comes not from a single act but from enduring, steady application that refines both self and environment.
lines.reflection: How can I sustain the labor of quiet influence without becoming proud of my own effort?
lines.evidence_zh: 其德日大，其心日小

lines.interpretation: This line describes modesty that spreads in all directions: toward those with virtue and those without, toward those above and those below. It is a flexible correctness that does not reserve humility for favored relationships but lets it become a consistent posture. Liu Yiming calls this 'spreading modesty,' saying it moves left and right, present wherever one finds oneself. The practice is to extend the same quiet openness to everyone, refusing to use humility selectively as a social strategy. This yields a state of 'nothing not beneficial,' because the self is no longer blocking the flow of circumstance.
lines.reflection: Toward whom do I find it hardest to be genuinely modest, and what would it take to include them?
lines.evidence_zh: 左之右之，隨在皆然

lines.interpretation: This line addresses leadership with a centered, humble heart. It is not enough to be modest oneself; genuine modesty can transform those nearby, but must also reach what is far and resistant. Liu Yiming says if one can only influence the near and compliant, it is not true modesty; one must also meet the distant and contrary with clear boundaries. The mention of 'invasion and attack' is not about aggression but about the necessary firmness when humility alone is misread as weakness. The practice is to remain empty-minded while setting conditions, so that influence can extend without domination.
lines.reflection: Where must I combine humility with firm boundaries so that my influence can reach difficult situations?
lines.evidence_zh: 謙至逆順不拘，遠近皆通

lines.interpretation: The top line marks a failure: modesty proclaimed from a high place becomes self-aggrandizement. Liu Yiming reads this as having self and no others—a show of humility that cannot actually humble itself, much less transform others. The military language points to the destructive consequence of false modesty: even those close and compliant may need to be brought back by force, and distant opposition becomes harder. The lesson is not to use force but to recognize the danger of using humility as a performance. When one cannot lower oneself from a position of status, the inner work has stopped.
lines.reflection: In what area have I turned modesty into a public performance that protects my status rather than doing inner work?
lines.evidence_zh: 自尊自大，有己無人

confucian.title: Mountain Within Earth
confucian.essence: True humility stores high capacity within lowly bearing; it reduces excess, replenishes scarcity, and lasts to completion through principled yielding rather than self-abasement.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: Humility is not self-effacement but the choice to hold real strength inside a modest position, like a mountain under earth. It succeeds by not claiming success, so the noble person is honored while yielding and grows brighter while hiding. The source commentary treats this as the highest human virtue, warning that fullness invites decrease and humility attracts increase.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Qian as the corrective after Dayou: once something is great it must not become full. The hexagram image—mountain beneath earth—shows loftiness stored in lowliness. He says the noble person's intention is preserved in humility; understanding principle, he delights in Heaven and does not contend, inwardly full, yielding without self-display. The Tuan commentary traces this pattern through Heaven, Earth, ghosts and spirits, and human feeling: the full are diminished, the humble increased. The Image directs reducing excess and increasing scarcity to equalize distribution.
confucian.modern_meaning: Cheng Yi wrote within a hierarchical world where ruler, minister, and commoner had fixed duties; that framework need not be reproduced today. His underlying point remains useful: when skill, power, or resource is concentrated, the wise move is not to hoard or perform humility but to redistribute excess toward what is lacking. Humility here means accurate self-assessment, principled restraint, and a consistent practice of making room for others. It is not passive silence: Fifth and Sixth lines require firmness, boundary-setting, and even correction. The commentary praises completion—the capacity to maintain humility over time without resentment or silent superiority. In contemporary terms this might look like sharing credit, reducing one's own dominance in conversation or decision-making, and attending to unequal distributions of labor, recognition, or material security. The goal is balance, not self-punishment; humility becomes sustainable when it flows from principle rather than fear.
confucian.advice: Examine where your current strength or advantage is accumulating. Rather than displaying or denying it, ask what should be reduced and what should be replenished. In relationships and work, yield the floor, credit, or resource without abandoning your responsibilities. Where humility has become excessive, restore firm boundaries and name problems directly.
confucian.shadow: False humility that seeks praise, or self-diminishment that avoids standing up for oneself or others. It can rigidify into a refusal to correct injustice or to use necessary authority.
confucian.reflection_question: Where is my present strength being used to fill rather than to balance?
confucian.evidence_zh: 謙有亨之道也有其徳而不居謂之謙人以謙㢲自處何徃而不亨乎君子有終君子志存乎謙巽達理故樂天而不競内充故退讓而不矜安履乎讓終身不易自卑而人益尊之自晦而徳益光顯此所謂君子有終也

lines.interpretation: The first line occupies the lowest place and is yielding; Cheng Yi calls it humility doubled, not a fault but the normal condition of a soft line at the bottom. It shows a self-governing practice that begins from the lowest position and does not seek recognition. That lowliness, when joined by others, can carry one through danger. In modern terms, it suggests staying close to the ground of a task, willing to learn and serve without performing importance; this creates trust and safe passage through difficult beginnings.
lines.reflection: What would it mean for me to begin from the lowest, least impressive place without pretending to be weak?
lines.evidence_zh: 初六以柔順處謙又居一卦之下為自處卑下之至謙而又謙也故曰謙謙

lines.interpretation: Second line has humility accumulated in the center, so it issues outward in voice and countenance. Cheng Yi stresses that this sounding humility is not forced; it is owned by the heart. Because it is centered and correct, constancy is auspicious. Modern reading: when inner alignment is real, your speech and expression naturally carry humility rather than arrogance or apology. It invites you to check whether your words match inner conviction; authenticity cannot be performed for long.
lines.reflection: Is my outward humility an expression of inner clarity, or a performance I think others expect?
lines.evidence_zh: 二以柔順居中是為謙徳積於中謙徳充積於中故發於外見於聲音顔色故曰鳴謙居中得正有中正之徳也故云貞吉

lines.interpretation: Third line is the strongest yang line in a lowly position, honored by others and entrusted by the ruler. It has real merit yet remains humble; Cheng Yi names the Duke of Zhou as its historical type. The danger is self-flattery: even if one tries humility, remembered achievements can corrode endurance. Lasting humility requires peaceful practice, not a strategy to preserve position. Today, this speaks to capable leaders who do the heavy work but let others receive credit; they can sustain it only if ego does not accumulate.
lines.reflection: What achievement am I still carrying in a way that quietly demands recognition?
lines.evidence_zh: 三以陽剛之徳而居下體為衆隂所宗履得其位為下之上是上為君所任下為衆所從有功勞而持謙徳者也故曰勞謙古之人有當之者周公是也

lines.interpretation: Fourth line sits close to the ruler and above a meritorious minister. Cheng Yi frames it in hierarchical terms: its place is full of fear, so it must spread humility in every movement. That historical station need not be copied, but the underlying relational wisdom is useful: when you hold power near authority and above capable peers, your actions should distribute humility rather than assert rank. Nothing is lost by making room; you keep the rule by not overstepping your role while remaining active.
lines.reflection: Where am I positioned between strong people, and how can I make that position safer through shared credit?
lines.evidence_zh: 四居上體切近君位六五之君又以謙柔自處九三又有大功徳為上所任衆所宗而已居其上當恭畏以奉謙徳之君卑巽以讓勞謙之臣動作施為无所不利於撝謙也

lines.interpretation: Fifth line is a ruler not rich yet having neighbors because humility attracts trust. But Cheng Yi warns the ruler's way cannot be only gentle; martial firmness is needed to subdue what patterned virtue cannot. The text's invasion language reflects ancient statecraft, and should not be taken as a modern call to force. Its present-day meaning: legitimate authority, family leadership, or organizational responsibility sometimes requires clear consequences and firm correction, not endless accommodation. Humility without timely strength ceases to be rulerly; it becomes neglect.
lines.reflection: Where has my humility become an excuse for not exercising needed authority?
lines.evidence_zh: 五以君位之尊而執謙順以接於下衆所歸也故不富而能有其鄰也鄰近也不富而得人之親也為人君而持謙順天下所歸心也然君道不可專尚謙柔必須威武相濟然後能懐服天下故利用行侵伐也

lines.interpretation: Top line is humility at its extreme but in a high place. Its intention to be humble is not fulfilled, so it sounds out; Cheng Yi says this is excess and needs firm self-governance. 'Marching armies against one's own city' is a historical image for using strict force to correct one's private self, not for external aggression. Modern reflection: when you have suppressed yourself too long or become theatrically modest, restore firm boundaries and direct correction inward before addressing the outer field.
lines.reflection: Where has humility turned into self-effacement, and what firmness would restore balance?
lines.evidence_zh: 六以柔處柔順之極又處謙之極極乎謙者也以極謙而反居高未得遂其謙之志故至發於聲音又柔處謙之極亦必見於聲色故曰鳴謙雖居无位之地非任天下之事然人之行己必須剛柔相濟上謙之極也至於太甚則反為過矣故利在以剛武自治邑國己之私有行師謂用剛武征邑國謂自治其私

classical.name: Ease
classical.judgment_zh: 豫：利建侯行師。
classical.judgment_en: Ease: It is beneficial to establish lords and deploy armies.
classical.image_zh: 雷出地奮，豫。先王以作樂崇德，殷薦之上帝，以配祖考。
classical.image_en: Thunder comes forth from the earth with vigor: Ease. The former kings made music to honor virtue and presented it richly to the Lord on High, accompanying their ancestors.
classical.historical_note:
Hexagram 16 in the received Zhouyi text; lower trigram Kun (Earth), upper trigram Zhen (Thunder). The Great Image belongs to the Ten Wings and is kept separate from the base hexagram and line statements. The line 4 phrase includes the textual variant note '一作「簪」' in the source, indicating some editions read 朋盍簪.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Crying out in ease: misfortune.
Firm as a rock, not waiting for the day to end: perseverance brings good fortune.
Gazing upward for ease: regret. Delay brings further regret.

lines.text_zh: 由豫，大有得。勿疑。朋盍戠一作「簪」。
lines.translation_en: From ease: great gain. Do not doubt. Companions gather [戠]; one version reads 簪, 'hairpin'.
A lasting illness, yet never perishing.
Darkened ease; what has been completed is changed: no blame.
