hexagrams.name: Ease

taoist.title: Joy Through Timely Movement
taoist.essence: Joy is not indulgence but the fruit of timely movement: lower earth receives upper thunder, inner compliance allows true yang to rise. When fire times are exact and the heart rules the body, whole-hearted action becomes effortless.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: The archetype is the heart as a lord or general: one yang among yin, not overpowered, but transforming confusion into gathered order. Joy appears when desire no longer performs; authentic nature moves and ordinary patience follows. The image is thunder breaking from earth—music honoring virtue, inner vitality breaking through stagnation. Yet this is not passive waiting; it requires establishing disciplined inward rule and moving only when the moment is ripe.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 16 as inner-alchemy instruction. He defines Yu as joy (樂) and identifies its virtue as 'upper Zhen movement, lower Kun compliance.' Following Dayou, he frames this as using yin to attract yang: the heart is master of the body 'like the lord, like the general.' Joy depends on moving in accord with fire times—'haste and slowness have their method, advancing and withdrawing accord with their joints.' The six lines then diagnose false joys: display, envy, stubborn emptiness, darkened indulgence—while the second and fourth lines show true constancy and unifying strength. His final image is thunder emerging beyond earth, yang qi rising, and the world blooming.
taoist.modern_meaning: In present-day practice, Ease can be misread as relaxation or emotional comfort. Liu's reading points elsewhere: joy is the signal that one's inward timing is correct. It asks for self-inquiry rather than mood management. The heart-as-lord is not a literal ruler but a metaphor for a centered, ethical core that can coordinate impulses, desires, and relationships. Moving in accord with the time may mean declining an opportunity that flatters desire but violates the moment; it may mean acting firmly when gentleness would only postpone. The discipline is not harshness but precision—recognizing when effort is needed and when effort interferes. Building inner order, as one builds trust in any community, allows joy to arrive without chasing it. Today, joy need not be loud or performative; it can be the quiet steadiness of a rock, the gathered force of scattered attention, the willingness to change a completed pattern. This is practiced only by attending to one's actual nature and timing, not by passive waiting.
taoist.advice: Do not advertise an unfelt joy or borrow someone else's. Practice becoming firm as rock toward inner truth: examine what is yours to do now, and what is merely restless desire. When the moment is ripe, move decisively; otherwise, wait without hollow stillness. Gather scattered attention around a single clear intention. Let joy be a sign of right timing, not a goal forced by display or avoidance.
taoist.shadow: Ease curdles into performance, envy, and stubborn emptiness. The heart chases borrowed joy or locks itself away, mistaking numbness for peace. Dark indulgence completes then collapses into sorrow; no outer blame absolves the inner flight from timing.
taoist.reflection_question: Where am I forcing or displaying joy instead of allowing disciplined inner movement to reveal the season?
taoist.evidence_zh: 豫者，樂也。卦德上震動、下坤順，順時而動，動而通順，故謂豫。

lines.interpretation: At the beginning of Ease, Liu names 'crying-out joy': a self-display that mistakes stimulation for gladness. When the heart keeps company with habitual pettiness and gives up on itself, it takes suffering for pleasure. The line warns that advertising one's enjoyment, especially before it is real, hardens a person into shallow identifications. Authentic joy cannot be performed. The discipline here is to notice the impulse to broadcast a mood and ask whether it covers an inner lack. Refuse to decorate misery with noise; begin by standing honestly in the unglamorous place before joy can ripen.
lines.reflection: Am I performing satisfaction to avoid facing a deeper unease?
lines.evidence_zh: 初六，居豫之初，又在三陰之下，性質本愚，且與小人為伍，自暴自棄，以苦為樂，是謂鳴豫。

lines.interpretation: Second Six shows firmness without strain. Liu describes one who is 'like one wedged in rock,' delighting in Heaven and knowing destiny, not letting external falsity injure inner truth. This is not cold detachment; it is the capacity to refuse joy beyond one's proper share immediately, before the day ends. Inner truth becomes a boundary that does not need anger. In present terms, it is the quiet confidence to say no to invitations, images, and ambitions that dilute the core. Perseverance brings good fortune because the center is not negotiated away.
lines.reflection: What joy or opportunity must I release immediately to keep my inner truth intact?
lines.evidence_zh: 六二，無貪無求，樂天知命，如介於石，確然有守，不以外假而傷內真，至於非分之樂，不俟終日，則即去之。

lines.interpretation: Third Six is the joy of looking upward: one abandons one's own vitality and envies another's apparent happiness. Liu says before gaining from another, one has already lost oneself. The lesson is not to suppress aspiration but to recognize when comparison dislodges the center. Quick regret turns the energy back to oneself; delayed regret deepens entanglement. If you find yourself tracking what others have, pause before envy becomes a direction. The real loss is not missing their advantage; it is deserting the seed of your own joy before it can show itself.
lines.reflection: Whose life am I watching more closely than my own, and why?
lines.evidence_zh: 六三，舍己之樂，仰望他人之樂，是謂盱豫。豫至於盱，未得於人，先失其己，致悔之道。

lines.interpretation: Nine in the fourth place is the one yang among yin, the source of joy and great attainment. Liu compares it to tangled hair gathered into a single hairpin: unity governs confusion, stability halts disorder. This is not domination but magnetic ordering. When the heart stops being pulled by every impulse, scattered energies align. The line says not to doubt this process; doubt scatters what is ready to gather. In practice, choose one principle and let it bind many impulses without rigidity. Joy comes from integrative strength, not from controlling every detail.
lines.reflection: What one clear intention can gather my scattered energies now?
lines.evidence_zh: 九四，以一陽而居於群陰之中，不為群陰所惑，且能點化群陰，皆來順之，是謂由豫大有得也。

lines.interpretation: Fifth Six warns against a false spiritual quiet. Yielding but not firm, empty but not solid, it is like an illness that never dies. Liu calls this attachment to stubborn emptiness: one guards a small constancy and rests content in a lesser vehicle, while true yang remains just beyond reach. This is the shadow of contemplative practice—peace that is avoidance, openness that lacks vitality. Joy is absent because life is neither fully entered nor fully renewed. The task is not to force motion but to remain available to real yang when it stirs, rather than building a safe hollow.
lines.reflection: Am I mistaking withdrawal or numbness for spiritual stillness?
lines.evidence_zh: 六五，柔而不剛，孤寂守靜，空而不實，如有疾而不能樂矣。

lines.interpretation: Top Six is darkened ease: only moving along with enjoyment, not reversing and operating joy. Liu says one who follows desires into fixed enjoyment will discover that what has been completed must change; extreme joy gives birth to sorrow. The line contains a hidden mercy: the completed pattern can change, and no blame is placed on others. The fault is only one's own unwillingness to reverse. When pleasure has hardened into compulsion, the first movement is to name it. Then the end can release into a different beginning, not by shame but by turning attention back toward discipline.
lines.reflection: What familiar pleasure has become a closed room, and what small reversal can open it?
lines.evidence_zh: 上六，在豫之終，只知順行其樂，不知逆運其樂，是謂冥豫。

confucian.title: Compliant Movement's Ease
confucian.essence: Ease arises when motion follows principle and gathers willing response; joy becomes durable through discipline, sincerity, and timely correction rather than indulgence.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: Thunder emerging from cultivated earth: an inner charge that moves with receptive order. This is not passive rest but harmonized action—celebration, music, and shared purpose arise when firm leadership meets consent. The archetype invites us to notice where ease is earned by alignment and where it curdles into self-congratulation, shallow display, or dependency on powerful figures.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Yu through principle and role ethics: Zhen above moves while Kun below complies; because action follows li, all respond. The judgment 'beneficial to establish lords and move armies' reflects his feudal world, where ruling many states and assembling multitudes requires harmonious joy. The Great Image links this to ritual music exalting virtue and honoring Heaven and ancestors. In his line reading, the fourth yang is a minister bearing the world's burden under a weak ruler; the fifth is a ruler endangered by indulgence; the second shows the noble one's timely self-restraint. Historical hierarchy is positioned, not prescribed.
confucian.modern_meaning: Read today, Yu asks how joy, shared momentum, and celebration can be sustained without self-deception. The thunder-above-earth image suggests that meaningful movement grows from receptive ground: a team, family, or inner life where energy aligns with shared principle rather than coercion. Cheng Yi's concern with 'compliant movement' translates into attention to timing—acting when conditions can welcome the action. His warning against shallow display (line 1) becomes a caution about performative enthusiasm; his praise of firm-as-rock discernment (line 2) becomes a practice of pausing before gratification hardens into habit. The minister-ruler dynamic in lines 4 and 5 is not a model to imitate but a pattern to contextualize: anyone in a position of informal influence or formal authority can recognize the danger of dependence, the need for sincere consultation, and the cost of lost initiative. Change remains possible even after benightedness.
confucian.advice: Notice where ease is earned and where it becomes noise. Cultivate a firm inner standard before riding collective excitement. When responsibility falls to you, act with transparent sincerity and invite others to gather; when power seems withheld, protect your center without mistaking survival for passivity. If enthusiasm has already hardened into habit, use the earliest sign of discomfort as a door for change.
confucian.shadow: Ease can curdle into self-display, smugness, or dependence. The urge to keep harmony may silence needed correction; the comfort of being carried can hollow out authority and delay change until one merely endures.
confucian.reflection_question: Where has my current ease become a substitute for disciplined alignment?
confucian.evidence_zh: 豫者安和恱樂之義

lines.interpretation: When ease announces itself too loudly, it is often compensation for inner emptiness. This line points to the person who, favored or excited, cannot contain joy and turns it into display. The commentary reads it as shallow and arrogant. In modern terms, notice performative enthusiasm—praise that demands applause, confidence that drowns out uncertainty. Such noise tends to isolate rather than connect. The reflection here is not to suppress joy but to ask whether it rests on solid ground.
lines.reflection: What am I performing when I amplify my ease?
lines.evidence_zh: 是不中正之小人處豫而為上所寵其志意滿極不勝其豫至發於聲音輕淺如是必至於凶也

lines.interpretation: The second line shows a different relation to ease: firmness that can leave pleasure before it becomes compulsion. Cheng Yi praises the one who, though in a time of joy, guards centrality and correctness, acting on subtle signs before patterns harden. Today this suggests discernment in a culture of constant stimulation—knowing when to step away, how to keep boundaries without self-righteousness, and how to trust early unease. It is not rejection of joy but refusal to be owned by it.
lines.reflection: What early sign am I noticing but not acting on?
lines.evidence_zh: 當豫之時獨能以中正自守可謂特立之操是其節介如石之堅也

lines.interpretation: Vacillation in a time of ease creates its own regret. This line looks upward for approval, delays movement, and thereby remains misaligned. Cheng Yi treats it as a problem of position and self-correction: when inner placement is not correct, both advance and retreat produce shame. Contemporary experience may recognize the person who hangs back waiting to be invited, or who reshapes themselves to please those above. The path is not to force a choice but to correct one's relation to value and act from that.
lines.reflection: Where am I waiting for permission instead of ordering my own stance?
lines.evidence_zh: 以不中正而處豫動皆有悔盱上視也上瞻望於四則以不中正不為四所取故有悔也

lines.interpretation: This is the pivot of the hexagram: the one through whom joy can become shared achievement. Cheng Yi reads the fourth as a minister entrusted with great responsibility under a weak ruler, in a position of suspicion and danger. The instruction is perfect sincerity and no doubt, so that companions gather. In modern collaborative life, this suggests the person who holds a group's momentum together—not by dominance but by transparent care and reliable initiative. The danger is isolation and self-reliance hardening into mistrust. Sincere invitation can gather the help that already waits.
lines.reflection: What might become possible if I stopped doubting the support I need?
lines.evidence_zh: 四大臣之位六五之君順從之以陽剛而任上之事豫之所由也故云由豫大有得言得大行其志以致天下之豫也

lines.interpretation: The fifth line describes a ruler whose ease has become illness: authority is ceded to a stronger figure, yet the position survives. Cheng Yi compares this to the late Han and Wei rulers, clearly naming historical decline, not fate. For present readers, this may be a leader, parent, or partner who has let comfort and dependency hollow out their own capacity. The line does not guarantee ruin; it asks whether one is merely holding a role while power has moved elsewhere, and whether that can be faced without false optimism.
lines.reflection: Where am I retaining a title while surrendering my initiative?
lines.evidence_zh: 乃柔弱不能自立之君受制於専權之臣也

lines.interpretation: Darkened ease is not the end if change is possible. The top line suggests a state of indulgence so complete that one no longer sees it; Cheng Yi warns that even the noble person would need caution at this extreme, and the weak yin is lost in it. Yet the entire emphasis falls on transformation. Modernly, this speaks to habits, institutions, or relationships that have become numbed by comfort. The moment one recognizes the benightedness, a door opens. Blame is not the point; change is.
lines.reflection: What pattern of ease have I stopped seeing clearly?
lines.evidence_zh: 乃躭肆於豫昏迷不知反者也在豫之終故為昏㝠已成也若能有渝變則可以无咎矣

original_chinese.title: 伊川易傳 (四庫全書本)/卷2

further_reading.title: The Yi River Commentary on the Book of Changes

hexagrams.essence: Joy is not indulgence but the fruit of timely movement: lower earth receives upper thunder, inner compliance allows true yang to rise. When fire times are exact and the heart rules the body, whole-hearted action becomes effortless.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: The archetype is the heart as a lord or general: one yang among yin, not overpowered, but transforming confusion into gathered order. Joy appears when desire no longer performs; authentic nature moves and ordinary patience follows. The image is thunder breaking from earth—music honoring virtue, inner vitality breaking through stagnation. Yet this is not passive waiting; it requires establishing disciplined inward rule and moving only when the moment is ripe.
hexagrams.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 16 as inner-alchemy instruction. He defines Yu as joy (樂) and identifies its virtue as 'upper Zhen movement, lower Kun compliance.' Following Dayou, he frames this as using yin to attract yang: the heart is master of the body 'like the lord, like the general.' Joy depends on moving in accord with fire times—'haste and slowness have their method, advancing and withdrawing accord with their joints.' The six lines then diagnose false joys: display, envy, stubborn emptiness, darkened indulgence—while the second and fourth lines show true constancy and unifying strength. His final image is thunder emerging beyond earth, yang qi rising, and the world blooming.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: In present-day practice, Ease can be misread as relaxation or emotional comfort. Liu's reading points elsewhere: joy is the signal that one's inward timing is correct. It asks for self-inquiry rather than mood management. The heart-as-lord is not a literal ruler but a metaphor for a centered, ethical core that can coordinate impulses, desires, and relationships. Moving in accord with the time may mean declining an opportunity that flatters desire but violates the moment; it may mean acting firmly when gentleness would only postpone. The discipline is not harshness but precision—recognizing when effort is needed and when effort interferes. Building inner order, as one builds trust in any community, allows joy to arrive without chasing it. Today, joy need not be loud or performative; it can be the quiet steadiness of a rock, the gathered force of scattered attention, the willingness to change a completed pattern. This is practiced only by attending to one's actual nature and timing, not by passive waiting.
hexagrams.advice: Do not advertise an unfelt joy or borrow someone else's. Practice becoming firm as rock toward inner truth: examine what is yours to do now, and what is merely restless desire. When the moment is ripe, move decisively; otherwise, wait without hollow stillness. Gather scattered attention around a single clear intention. Let joy be a sign of right timing, not a goal forced by display or avoidance.
hexagrams.shadow: Ease curdles into performance, envy, and stubborn emptiness. The heart chases borrowed joy or locks itself away, mistaking numbness for peace. Dark indulgence completes then collapses into sorrow; no outer blame absolves the inner flight from timing.
hexagrams.reflection_question: Where am I forcing or displaying joy instead of allowing disciplined inner movement to reveal the season?
hexagrams.editorial_status: integration-candidate — AI-assisted; final human review pending

classical.name: Following
classical.judgment_zh: 元亨。利貞。无咎
classical.judgment_en: Supreme success; beneficial to be firm and correct; no fault.
classical.image_zh: 澤中有雷，隨；君子以嚮晦入宴息
classical.image_en: Within the lake there is thunder: Following. The noble person, as dusk approaches, enters restful repose.
classical.historical_note:
Hexagram 17, Sui (Following), lower trigram Zhen (Thunder), upper trigram Dui (Lake). Translation is limited to the base hexagram judgment, the Great Image, and the six line texts; Tuan commentary and Small Image line comments in the source are omitted. No use-nine or use-six text applies to this hexagram. Note: the classical line 3 text in this base edition punctuates as 隨，有求得利，居貞, while the supplied Taoist commentary quotation punctuates it as 隨有求得，利居貞; the translation follows the standard/commentary segmentation.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.text_zh: 官有渝，貞吉。出門交有功
lines.translation_en: The office changes; perseverance brings good fortune. Going out the gate to interact brings merit.
Bound to the small child, one loses the grown man.

lines.text_zh: 係丈夫，失小子。隨，有求得利，居貞
lines.translation_en: Bound to the grown man, one loses the small child. Following: there is seeking and obtaining; beneficial to abide in firm correctness.

lines.text_zh: 隨有獲，貞凶。有孚在道，以明，何咎
lines.translation_en: Following obtains gain; perseverance brings misfortune. With sincerity on the way, and thereby clarity, what fault is there?
Sincerity toward what is excellent: good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 拘係之，乃從維之。王用亨于西山
lines.translation_en: Seize and bind it; then follow and tether it. The king performs an offering on the Western Mountain.

hexagrams.title: Following
hexagrams.name: Following

taoist.title: Following as Reciprocal Cultivation
taoist.essence: Liu Yiming reads Following as the inner-alchemical art of using nature to seek emotion: by following with disciplined correctness, true yang returns to its origin and the elixir can form. Timing and reciprocal trust matter.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: For Liu Yiming, Following is not drift or compliance but the primal pattern of movement within joy. In the original state nature and emotion were one; after birth, true yang strayed to the 'other family.' Following means first accommodating the other's desire to win trust, then guiding the other back. It is the reciprocal way of using nature to seek emotion and emotion to return to nature, through which lost original yang is restored.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming views Hexagram 17, upper Dui (joy/lake) and lower Zhen (movement/thunder), as the continuation after yang has returned. He describes Following as the method of summoning true yang: Zhen is the Eastern House, nature, self; Dui is the Western House, emotion, other. Because post-cosmic life has lost true yang to the other family, the practitioner must 'go along with its desires and gradually guide it,' then use correctness to transform false emotion and nature into true. The medicinal ingredients may be false, and fire-times, movement and stillness have strict sequence; a hair's-breadth error causes great loss. Each line illustrates a different mode of following.
taoist.modern_meaning: Read as a present-day contemplative practice, Following invites a careful relationship with desire, timing, and attraction. Liu Yiming's language of 'stealing back' true yang may sound manipulative if taken literally; historically it belongs to a hierarchical inner-alchemical cosmology in which emotion is subordinate to nature and the other is a recipient of guided influence. Applied today, we can set aside that framework and receive a more reflective insight: change often begins not by forcing another or oneself to comply, but by first listening to what is actually desired, earning trust, and then gradually redirecting attention toward what is genuine. This is not passive acceptance; it requires clear discernment of true and false impulses, patient timing, and a willingness to give before receiving. For example, in a strained relationship or a stalled creative practice, one might stop preaching at the resistant part and first follow its small willingness, then guide it gently toward integration. No result is guaranteed, but the discipline of correctness prevents the process from becoming manipulation or self-abandonment.
taoist.advice: Before trying to bring anything back—focus, affection, creative energy—first discern whether your following is true or false. Follow with correctness, not with anxious clutching. Give a small honest response to what is genuinely present in the other or in yourself; let trust accumulate. Keep the timing gentle and clear, and stop if attachment replaces sincerity.
taoist.shadow: The shadow of this hexagram is deluded grasping—trying to force another or an inner state to follow you without first following it, producing empty fantasy and strain.
taoist.reflection_question: Where am I trying to force a return instead of first following what is actually present with sincere attention?
taoist.evidence_zh: 以性求情，以情歸性

lines.interpretation: At the very start of following, you are standing at a threshold where direction is not yet fixed. Liu Yiming treats this as the moment to distinguish acceptable from harmful influences and choose correctness before any commitment. Once that is clear, movement outward is not danger but opportunity: engaging with the world can become a method of cultivation rather than distraction. The line invites you to be cautious about what you first say yes to, then to step out and learn through real interaction.
lines.reflection: What initial choice of direction needs clearer discernment before I commit?
lines.evidence_zh: 須當辨別可否，以正而隨，方能得吉。既知其正，於是出門交物，借世法而修道法

lines.interpretation: In this line Liu Yiming sees the danger of a soft, unknowing following that attaches to whatever arises later, losing touch with the original inner strength. The 'little child' names what is small, familiar, and emotionally immediate; the 'husband' names the mature true yang that has been forgotten. When we follow every passing reaction or subordinate desire, we may trade durable growth for momentary comfort. This asks whether your current attachment is nourishing your deeper integrity or only keeping you occupied.
lines.reflection: What passing desire or small attachment is currently crowding out my deeper truth?
lines.evidence_zh: 柔而無知，隨其後起之陰，失其元初之陽

lines.interpretation: Here the yielding disposition is paired with firm intention. Liu Yiming describes the ability to follow what is genuinely valuable in the other—or in a neglected part of oneself—rather than remaining loyal to a lesser internal pattern. Yet this is not an easy victory; those who are naturally yielding often know the way but lack steadiness. Therefore the instruction is to dwell in correctness without shifting, to persist with increasing sincerity over time until what was lost is truly returned. Following here means patient attraction, not quick capture.
lines.reflection: What genuine good am I being asked to follow with patient firmness rather than letting slip?
lines.evidence_zh: 性柔志剛，能隨他家之陽，不隨我家之陰

lines.interpretation: Line Four holds strength to follow, yet Liu Yiming warns that strength turned toward more strength becomes rigidity. Capability can become grasping; even a correct cause turns inauspicious if pursued with too much force. The turn is to use firmness through yielding: stay sincere on the way, see clearly what is true and false, and know when to advance or retreat. This is not weakness but mature use of power. The line invites an honest look at where determination may have become stubbornness, and where a gentler hand might bring more gain.
lines.reflection: Where is my firmness currently excessive, and what would it mean to use it more yielding?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛以柔用，有孚在道，明於是非邪正，知進知退

lines.interpretation: This is the centered, joyful line. Liu Yiming sees it as the fruit of discipline: joy arises not from chasing pleasure but from resting in sincerity toward what is excellent. Here the practitioner can follow both firm and yielding, hiding faults while promoting good, holding the middle so no step is forced. 'Following the heart's desires without overstepping' is not indulgence but an achieved harmony in which spontaneous movement is already aligned with rightness. The line asks what it would feel like to act from that settled inner joy.
lines.reflection: What would be possible if I trusted and practiced sincere appreciation of what is truly good?
lines.evidence_zh: 樂在其中，隱惡揚善，隨剛隨柔，執兩用中

lines.interpretation: The top line shows the failure that comes from trying to possess without first following. Liu Yiming calls it deluded grasping: the mind calculates, tries to bind the other, and demands that the other come to it, yet nothing returns. Imagery of the king sacrificing on West Mountain suggests even noble effort fails if the direction is wrong—the treasure remains outside because one never went out to meet it. This is a caution against forcing emotional, creative, or spiritual union through control. Following cannot begin with capture; it must begin with giving. Where we clutch, we lose.
lines.reflection: Where am I trying to bind or force a connection that first requires me to go out and follow?
lines.evidence_zh: 縱天寶在望，終在西而不歸東，究是落空事業

confucian.title: Following with Principled Timing
confucian.essence: Following is not passive drift; it is deliberate alignment of movement with joy, choosing whom and what to follow through correctness and timeliness, so that influence becomes mutual, accountable, and fitting rather than coercive.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: Thunder inside the lake: movement below stirs joy above, and the lake answers. Cheng Yi sees this as the pattern of all following—leader and follower, caller and responder, person and principle. Following succeeds when the firm willingly yields to the yielding, when what is higher serves what is lower, and when action answers the moment. It is not conformity but correct responsiveness; joy arises because the movement fits the time and the relationship.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi's commentary reflects a hierarchical world of rulers, ministers, wives, and elders. His examples—such as King Tai's people following him to Mount Qi—are historical accounts of their time, not templates for modern authority. What remains transferable is his ethical core: following must be correct and timely; private affection, flattery, and a minister's accumulation of personal loyalty all corrupt right relationship. He urges single-minded attachment to the good, discerning between the near and the truly worthy, and keeping sincerity and clarity in any bond.
confucian.modern_meaning: Today, following speaks to how we choose influences, leaders, traditions, and inner callings. We are always following something—algorithms, relationships, ambition, fear—often without noticing. This hexagram asks that we make that choice conscious. Cheng Yi warns against clinging to what is merely near or familiar: the small child at hand over the grown person of mature principle. It also warns those who gain followers: if you collect loyalty for yourself rather than serving the shared good, suspicion and distortion follow. The remedy is sincerity in the Way and clarity about motives. At its best, following becomes a mutual bond freely renewed, not coercion. The image of dusk rest teaches the wisdom of limits: even commitment needs rhythm and timely withdrawal.
confucian.advice: Name what you are following and whether it draws you toward correctness or merely toward the near and familiar. Release private attachments that block a more mature bond. If others follow you, examine whose purpose your influence serves. Let sincerity guide your choices, and rest at the day's close instead of pushing endlessly.
confucian.shadow: The shadow is clinging to the near and familiar, seeking favor by flattering the powerful, or accumulating followers for one's own sake. What feels like loyalty may be private affection; what looks like closeness may be the loss of a truer bond.
confucian.reflection_question: Whom or what am I following, and does that following make me more correct, clear, and free?
confucian.evidence_zh: 隨之道可以致大亨也君子之道為衆所隨與己随於人及臨事擇所隨皆隨也随得其道則可以致大亨也

lines.interpretation: A change in office or role can be beneficial, but only if it is grounded in correctness rather than restlessness or private preference. When you step beyond familiar circles and engage with people and perspectives you have not privately favored, your following becomes principled and productive. Do not let the affection of family or friends define what is right; public-spirited interaction opens a wider field and brings merit.
lines.reflection: What change am I considering, and is it motivated by principle or by private attachment?
lines.evidence_zh: 故出門而交則有功也出門謂非私暱交不以私故其隨當而有功

lines.interpretation: The near and familiar can dominate simply by being near. Cheng Yi warns that clinging to a small, immediate bond may cost a more significant relationship or mature commitment. Single-mindedness is not stubbornness; it means choosing the correct correspondence and not trying to hold both. In times of following, ask whether your loyalty is going to what is truly due, or to what is easiest to grasp.
lines.reflection: Where am I trading a significant commitment for a nearby distraction?
lines.evidence_zh: 二若志係於初則失九五之正應是失丈夫也

lines.interpretation: Sometimes it is right to leave a lesser attachment and follow what is more mature, more excellent, or higher in principle. The third line does this, but its gain is conditional: seeking must not become flattery or self-advancement. When you seek from a place of inner correctness, your following yields real benefit; when you bend the way to please the powerful, even success becomes petty and corrupt.
lines.reflection: Is my ambition aligned with genuine goodness, or am I currying favor?
lines.evidence_zh: 雖然固不可非理枉道以隨於上苟取愛以遂所求如此乃小人邪謟趨利之為也

lines.interpretation: The danger of gaining followers is that loyalty may attach to you rather than to the shared good. Cheng Yi reads this line as a warning for ministers and, by extension, for anyone with influence. Even correct-looking success becomes misfortune if it provokes rivalry or suspicion. The remedy is not withdrawal but sincerity in the Way and clear communication, so that your actions visibly serve the whole and not yourself.
lines.reflection: Why do people follow me, and whose purpose does that serve?
lines.evidence_zh: 有獲謂得天下之心隨於己為臣之道當使恩威一出於上衆心皆隨於君若人心從己危疑之道也

lines.interpretation: Good fortune here is not luck; it is the fruit of sincere devotion to what is good. Cheng Yi says the way of following has its blessing only in following the good, from ruler to ordinary person. When centrality and correctness meet, leadership and followership become transparent and trustworthy. This line invites you to anchor choices in a love of excellence rather than in preference, convenience, or image.
lines.reflection: What is the good I actually trust with my choices?
lines.evidence_zh: 自人君至於庻人隨道之吉唯在隨善而已下應二之正中為随善之義

lines.interpretation: The extreme of following can look like binding, but the image is of hearts so firmly joined that people follow freely, as King Tai's people followed him to Mount Qi. This is not coercion; it is a union of trust and shared destiny. Yet such intensity is appropriate only toward a genuinely good end. Applied elsewhere, it becomes possessiveness or enforced loyalty.
lines.reflection: What bonds in my life are freely renewed, and where have I mistaken control for loyalty?
lines.evidence_zh: 太王避狄之難去豳來岐豳人老稚扶攜以隨之如歸市盖其人心之隨固結如此

hexagrams.essence: Liu Yiming reads Following as the inner-alchemical art of using nature to seek emotion: by following with disciplined correctness, true yang returns to its origin and the elixir can form. Timing and reciprocal trust matter.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: For Liu Yiming, Following is not drift or compliance but the primal pattern of movement within joy. In the original state nature and emotion were one; after birth, true yang strayed to the 'other family.' Following means first accommodating the other's desire to win trust, then guiding the other back. It is the reciprocal way of using nature to seek emotion and emotion to return to nature, through which lost original yang is restored.
hexagrams.historical_core: Liu Yiming views Hexagram 17, upper Dui (joy/lake) and lower Zhen (movement/thunder), as the continuation after yang has returned. He describes Following as the method of summoning true yang: Zhen is the Eastern House, nature, self; Dui is the Western House, emotion, other. Because post-cosmic life has lost true yang to the other family, the practitioner must 'go along with its desires and gradually guide it,' then use correctness to transform false emotion and nature into true. The medicinal ingredients may be false, and fire-times, movement and stillness have strict sequence; a hair's-breadth error causes great loss. Each line illustrates a different mode of following.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: Read as a present-day contemplative practice, Following invites a careful relationship with desire, timing, and attraction. Liu Yiming's language of 'stealing back' true yang may sound manipulative if taken literally; historically it belongs to a hierarchical inner-alchemical cosmology in which emotion is subordinate to nature and the other is a recipient of guided influence. Applied today, we can set aside that framework and receive a more reflective insight: change often begins not by forcing another or oneself to comply, but by first listening to what is actually desired, earning trust, and then gradually redirecting attention toward what is genuine. This is not passive acceptance; it requires clear discernment of true and false impulses, patient timing, and a willingness to give before receiving. For example, in a strained relationship or a stalled creative practice, one might stop preaching at the resistant part and first follow its small willingness, then guide it gently toward integration. No result is guaranteed, but the discipline of correctness prevents the process from becoming manipulation or self-abandonment.
hexagrams.advice: Before trying to bring anything back—focus, affection, creative energy—first discern whether your following is true or false. Follow with correctness, not with anxious clutching. Give a small honest response to what is genuinely present in the other or in yourself; let trust accumulate. Keep the timing gentle and clear, and stop if attachment replaces sincerity.
hexagrams.shadow: The shadow of this hexagram is deluded grasping—trying to force another or an inner state to follow you without first following it, producing empty fantasy and strain.
hexagrams.reflection_question: Where am I trying to force a return instead of first following what is actually present with sincere attention?

classical.name: Decay
classical.judgment_zh: 蠱：元亨。利涉大川。先甲三日，後甲三日。
classical.judgment_en: Decay: Supreme success. It is favorable to cross great rivers. Three days before the jia day, three days after the jia day.
classical.image_zh: 山下有風，蠱；君子以振民育德。
classical.image_en: Below the mountain is wind: Decay. The noble person thereby stirs up the people and nurtures virtue.
classical.historical_note:

lines.text_zh: 幹父之蠱，有子考，无咎，厲終吉。
lines.translation_en: Setting right the father's decay, there is a son; the deceased father is without blame; danger, in the end good fortune.
Setting right the mother's decay: do not be inflexible.

lines.text_zh: 幹父之蠱，小有悔，无大咎。
lines.translation_en: Setting right the father's decay: there is small regret; no great blame.
Being indulgent toward the father's decay: going will bring humiliation.
Setting right the father's decay: use praise.
Does not serve kings or lords; exalts his own affairs.

taoist.title: Repairing the Inherited
taoist.essence: Hexagram 18, Gu, reads corruption as both arising after original wholeness and as remediable through vigilant, well-timed inner practice. Liu Yiming frames this as abandoning the false and returning to the true, never as passive quietism.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Gu is the archetype of what has gone bad through neglect, inheritance, or accumulated yin, and of the demanding work of mending it. In Liu Yiming's reading, the mountain over wind shows a stopping of encroaching yin and a return to root. The archetype is not merely social reform but the inner restoration of original nature through disciplined, well-timed effort.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming interprets Hexagram 18 within Quanzhen inner alchemy. For him, Gu means corruption; human nature is originally whole but yin arises at maturity, obscuring the original face. Repairing corruption requires active practice amid danger, symbolized by crossing the great river, and precise timing, symbolized by three days before and after jia, understood through lunar phases. The six lines chart excessive firmness, excessive yielding, and balanced repair, ending in the sage who no longer needs repair. This is a historical, androcentric lineage text; its references to father, mother, king, and lord reflect its time.
taoist.modern_meaning: Today, Gu can name the accumulated dysfunction we inherit: family habits, organizational drift, cultural narratives, or inner patterns formed long ago. The commentary suggests that repair begins with honest recognition and is sustained by disciplined attention, not forced control or passive acceptance. It invites a practice of discerning when to act firmly, when to yield, when to praise, and when to step back from roles that compromise integrity. The 'father's' and 'mother's' language can be read as inherited structures rather than fixed gender roles; modern readers may reframe these as early conditioning. The work is not about predicting outcomes but about returning to what is genuine: attending to root causes, choosing timing carefully, and allowing authentic repair to unfold without resentment or self-blame.
taoist.advice: When you notice something decaying—inside or around you—begin by naming it honestly. Do not rush to fix; first strengthen your inner root through steady, small practices. Then act with a blend of firmness and flexibility, paying attention to timing. If a role or relationship asks you to betray your values, consider stepping back. Repair what is yours to repair; release what is not.
taoist.shadow: In repair, we may become harsh and self-righteous, or lapse into indulgence and avoidance, allowing decay to spread. Another shadow is rescuing others' corruption at the cost of one's own root, or mistaking control for restoration.
taoist.reflection_question: What inherited or accumulated pattern in my life is asking, not for blame, but for honest repair?
taoist.evidence_zh: 蠱者，敗壞之義。卦德上艮止、下巽入，有一陰入而陽止之象，故曰蠱。又巽在止中，止其陰而不上進，兼有飭蠱之義。此棄假歸真之卦

lines.interpretation: Line 1 (First Six) describes the moment before visible corruption, when the root is still whole. Liu Yiming reads 'setting right the father's corruption' as preventing yin from entering. A successor who continues the parent's unfinished work can turn inherited blame into freedom from blame. The line warns against empty stillness: one must remain alert and cautious, guarding the root from subtle 'guest qi.' If the beginning is careful, the ending can be stable. This is preventative repair, active before symptoms fully manifest.
lines.reflection: What early, subtle sign of decay am I noticing before it becomes obvious?
lines.evidence_zh: 但飭蠱之道，非是空空無為，必須危厲戒懼，庶乎客氣不生，根本不傷，能謹於始，自吉於終。

lines.interpretation: Line 2 (Nine in the Second) teaches firmness tempered by receptivity. Liu Yiming says yielding is the root and firmness the stem: one should not be so rigid that the softer root is injured. 'Setting right the mother's corruption' calls for flexible persistence rather than inflexible insistence. The line does not mean passivity; it means adapting method to relationship and circumstance. Firmness and yielding become one, allowing truthful action without domination. Repair here is negotiated, not imposed.
lines.reflection: Where am I being too rigid in trying to help someone change?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛以柔用，柔為本而剛為幹，不過於剛，不傷其柔，剛柔如一，通權達變，如幹母之蠱不可貞。

lines.interpretation: Line 3 (Nine in the Third) shows repair through excessive force. When the one repairing is as unbending as the inherited pattern itself, there is friction and small regret. Liu Yiming calls it 'father firm, son firm.' Yet because the intent is to set things right and the direction is correct, no great blame follows. The line suggests that overcorrection is sometimes part of repair, but its heat should be acknowledged and refined. Regret can teach without condemning.
lines.reflection: What recent overcorrection showed me where my firmness became too sharp?
lines.evidence_zh: 以剛幹剛，剛之太過，如父剛子剛。幹父之蠱，未免小有所悔。然在飭蠱得正，雖有小悔，可無大咎耳。

lines.interpretation: Line 4 (Six in the Fourth) warns against yielding without firmness. When decay is present but one postpones repair and tolerates harm, the situation worsens. Liu Yiming calls this 'indulging the father's corruption'; a child who merely accommodates a parent's dysfunction brings humiliation. The line does not advocate harshness, but shows that leniency without boundaries can become complicity. Timely, honest intervention matters; delay and appeasement only deepen the damage and erode self-respect.
lines.reflection: Is there a place where my tolerance has turned into avoidance?
lines.evidence_zh: 獨柔無剛，有蠱而不即飭，姑息養奸，如父有蠱而子裕之，以是往而修道，邊以自取羞吝耳。

lines.interpretation: Line 5 (Six in the Fifth) models skillful use of yielding. One remains open and humble, recognizing one's own blind spots while naming and appreciating the clarity in others. Liu Yiming reads 'using praise' as borrowing the firm brightness of another house to dispel one's own darkness. This is not flattery but strategic receptivity: allowing another's strength to illuminate and support repair. Through such cooperation, corruption can return to wholeness without domination or control.
lines.reflection: Whose honest clarity can I invite into my repair work without losing my own center?
lines.evidence_zh: 柔順虛心，示己之無，稱人之有，如幹父蠱而用譽也。以譽而用，借他家之剛明，以破我家之昏暗，有蠱即可歸於無蠱。

lines.interpretation: Line 6 (Top Nine) points beyond the repair cycle. Firmness rests in yielding; there is no grasping for fame or profit. The person does not serve kings or lords, but exalts the affairs of Dao and virtue. Having returned to the root, no corruption remains and no special mending is needed. This is not self-isolation or worldly contempt, but a mature freedom from roles that compromise integrity. The line invites a life centered in principle, not in external validation.
lines.reflection: What would it look like to make my own life's work 'lofty' in the sense of rooted in integrity, not status?
lines.evidence_zh: 無貪無求，根本不傷，無蠱而亦不飭，是以不事王侯，高尚其事也。不事王侯者，不圖名利之事也。高尚其事者，尚其道德之事也。

confucian.title: The Work of Repair
confucian.essence: Decay names both what has spoiled and the active work of restoring order. Mountain stillness above wind’s gentle penetration models disciplined care: trace causes, prepare consequences, and carry inherited obligations with renewed integrity.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: Beneath a still mountain, wind turns back on itself, stirring disorder from within. The image points to stagnation caused by neglect, entangled affection, or inherited failure. Yet ruin also opens the way to renewal. The archetype asks for a repairer: someone who can face what has spoiled, set right a parent’s or predecessor’s unfinished affairs, and re-establish patterns that can endure.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads the hexagram through filial and ministerial duty. The lower wind is Xun, gentle penetration; the upper mountain is Gen, stillness. The son and minister roles are developed in the individual line commentaries rather than identified with the lower trigram as such. He treats decay as both natural and moral: 'Once there is decay, there is the principle of returning to order.' The classical framing assumes hierarchical relations—father and son, mother and child, ruler and minister—and asks each party to act according to role. Those roles are historical; the underlying principle of responsible repair remains relevant when translated into present-day accountability.
confucian.modern_meaning: In a contemporary context, Decay invites you to notice where inherited systems—families, workplaces, communities, even inner habits—have accumulated dysfunction. It is not an omen of inevitable collapse. It is a call to become a repairer of what has been handed down. You may be the one who can gently but firmly address what others have avoided. This requires both courage and restraint: investigate why patterns developed before changing them, and plan for consequences after you act. If the situation is delicate, do not force a rigid correction; if it has been neglected, do not remain indulgent. Cheng Yi’s emphasis on timeliness means no single rule fits every repair. The task is to discern what the moment requires and to act with sincere accountability, not perfectionism. The image of stirring the people and nourishing virtue suggests that repair includes education, moral development, and restoring trust.
confucian.advice: Approach inherited difficulty as a careful restorer, not a harsh critic. First investigate causes; then prepare for side effects. When relationships call for gentleness, yield without abandoning principle. When firmness is needed, act decisively but with respect. If the situation is beyond your capacity, consider delegating or stepping back with integrity.
confucian.shadow: You may become rigid and moralistic, or too lenient and avoidant. Excessive force breeds regret; excessive indulgence invites shame. A detached refusal to engage can become self-righteous withdrawal.
confucian.reflection_question: What inherited pattern or obligation is asking me to be a responsible repairer rather than a passive heir or harsh critic?
confucian.evidence_zh: 既蠱則有復治之理自古治必因亂亂則開治理自然也

lines.interpretation: The first line stands at the lowest position yet carries the initial responsibility for repair. When you inherit an unfinished task or a damaged legacy, the source of value is not your rank but your willingness to undertake it. If you can bear the difficulty, you relieve those who came before from blame; if you shrink, you add to the burden. Caution and alertness are essential because you occupy a humble place while handling something weighty. This is not about proving yourself heroic; it is about reverent, sustained effort that may eventually restore trust and secure good outcomes.
lines.reflection: What unfinished burden have I inherited, and how can I carry it without either resenting or collapsing under it?
lines.evidence_zh: 子幹父蠱之道能堪其事則為有子而其考得无咎不然則為父之累故必惕厲則得終吉也

lines.interpretation: Here firmness meets a softness that must be honored. The image of remedying a mother’s decay, or any relationship where direct authority would harm trust, calls for gentle persuasion rather than rigid enforcement. You may see exactly what is wrong, but if you push too hard too soon, you damage the bond and lose influence. The middle way is not to abandon principle but to lower your manner, listen, and guide with patience. This line reminds you that effectiveness depends on entering the other’s frame of reference. Strength that cannot bend cannot heal.
lines.reflection: Where am I being too inflexible with someone whose trust requires gentleness rather than proof of correctness?
lines.evidence_zh: 故曰不可貞謂不可貞固盡其剛直之道如是乃中道也

lines.interpretation: This line describes decisive, perhaps excessive, action in repairing a legacy. You may go too far, express too much heat, or correct too forcefully. Small regrets arise, but because your fundamental intention is to honor and restore, the damage is not fatal. Cheng Yi notes that compliance is the root of serving one’s parents; even when you are firm, if you remain rooted in respect, the repair can hold. The invitation is to act with courage while checking your excesses before they harden into lasting harm.
lines.reflection: Where can I act decisively without letting my firmness become harshness or self-righteousness?
lines.evidence_zh: 以剛陽之才克幹其事雖以剛過而有小小之悔終无大過咎也

lines.interpretation: This position warns against treating decay with mere tolerance. If you are too gentle, too attached to comfort, or too willing to preserve appearances, you may keep an ordinary routine but fail when real repair is needed. Cheng Yi says such a capacity can only follow the usual and preserve itself; if it tries to handle extraordinary matters, it may be inadequate and encounter shame. The line invites honest self-assessment: not every problem can be managed by waiting; some require stretching beyond present limits.
lines.reflection: Where am I mistaking indulgence or avoidance for patience and thereby failing to repair what needs attention?
lines.evidence_zh: 柔順之才而處正僅能循常自守而已若徃幹過常之事則不勝而見吝也

lines.interpretation: The fifth line occupies a position of leadership yet may lack the forceful talent to undertake major reform alone. Its strength lies in recognizing and entrusting capable people. You may not be the originator of a new system, but you can become a wise steward who continues what is good and gains a fine reputation through humility and good delegation. Cheng Yi cites Tai Jia and King Cheng as rulers who relied on worthy ministers. The task is not to make yourself the hero but to enable others’ competence while maintaining responsibility.
lines.reflection: Whose capable help can I trust and invite without abdicating my own responsibility?
lines.evidence_zh: 苟能任剛賢則可以為善繼而成令譽也

lines.interpretation: The top line stands outside the machinery of service. When times are corrupt or no role fits, preserving integrity may mean refusing to serve unworthy powers and exalting one’s own principled work. This is not ordinary indifference but a deliberate withdrawal that follows the Way in advancing and retreating. Cheng Yi admires those who do not bend the Way to follow the age. Yet this is not an escape for every moment; it is an option for those whose continued involvement would compromise principle. Such a life can itself become a standard.
lines.reflection: When is my non-participation an act of integrity, and when is it merely avoidance of my share of repair?
lines.evidence_zh: 賢人君子不偶於時而高潔自守不累於世務者也

classical.name: Approach
classical.judgment_zh: 臨：元亨。利貞。至于八月有凶
classical.judgment_en: Supreme success; favorable to persevere. By the eighth month there will be misfortune.
classical.image_zh: 澤上有地，臨；君子以教思无窮，容保民无疆
classical.image_en: Above the lake is earth: Approach. The noble person, by teaching and reflection, is inexhaustible; by embracing and protecting the people, is without limit.
classical.historical_note:
The hexagram name 臨 (Lín) means 'approach' or 'overseeing.' The warning about the eighth month reflects the cyclical waxing and waning of yin and yang in early Chinese calendrical thought.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Approaching together; perseverance is good fortune.
Approaching together; good fortune, nothing unfavorable.

lines.text_zh: 甘臨，无攸利。既憂之，无咎
lines.translation_en: Sweet approach; nothing is favorable. If one grieves over it, no blame.
Utmost approach; no blame.
Approaching with knowledge; what is appropriate for a great ruler; good fortune.
Sincere approach; good fortune, no blame.

hexagrams.title: Approach
hexagrams.name: Approach

taoist.title: Tending the Nascent Yang
taoist.essence: Approach the inner threshold with disciplined timing: nascent yang is strengthening yet yin remains strong. Guard the process with harmony and correctness, neither forcing nor missing the moment, so true inner warmth can mature.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: The archetype is the overseer of the alchemical furnace: a moment when the first returns of vitality become visible and require careful tending. It evokes a responsible, alert caretaker watching the subtle rise of light within body and mind—not grasping, but refining. This is not an external authority; it is the noble person teaching and protecting without limit, embodying a wise, watchful approach to what is just emerging.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 19 not as political approach but as overseeing the furnace to gather medicine. He identifies yuan with the first yang and heng with the second yang: by the time one begins work at the furnace, two yang lines have returned, but yin is still strong. One must guard against danger and risk, use harmony as substance and compliance as function, and act only when the time is right. Rushing causes the growing yang to decline and Approach to turn into Contemplation, the warning of 'the eighth month.' The line commentaries follow the alchemical fire-times from cautious beginning through gathering the medicine to final simplicity.
taoist.modern_meaning: In present-day terms, this hexagram describes the early phase of any meaningful change or recovery: new energy has appeared, but old habits and uncertainties still dominate. Liu's alchemical language—furnace, medicine, fire-times—can be read as a disciplined way of noticing and nurturing what is just beginning. The warning against sweet talk and hurried results remains timely: when we perform rather than practice, quick enthusiasm collapses. Instead, the text points to patient self-refinement, honest timing, and a clear inner observer. This is not passive waiting; it is active, accurate attention that knows when to act and when to restrain. It invites us to become the overseer of our own process, protecting our growing clarity while learning from setbacks without either self-rejection or forced positivity.
taoist.advice: Resist the impulse to force quick results. Establish a regular inner practice that observes your emerging energy without feeding it with harshness or flattery. When the moment is ripe, act simply and directly; when it is not, consolidate and wait. Let sincerity, not sweetness, guide your words and commitments. Tend the small yang like a careful guardian.
taoist.shadow: The sweet approach: a smiling, people-pleasing performance that talks about growth while avoiding real inner work. It produces fake positivity, bypasses timing, and collapses into bitterness when results fail or old patterns return.
taoist.reflection_question: Where am I pretending to approach my own growth while actually avoiding the slow, sincere work of timing and self-honesty?
taoist.evidence_zh: 臨者，監察也。卦德上坤順、下兌悅，悅而順理，順行其悅，故謂臨。此臨爐采藥之卦

lines.interpretation: This line marks the beginning of the practice. Yang energy has just been born, small and easily disturbed. The counsel is to meet it with firm, simple integrity: a single pure thought, influenced only by what is correct. There is no need to amplify or display it. Instead, one guards the first stirring with quiet precision, avoiding false starts. The line's goodness arises from this initial caution. Reflect on how you begin: do you protect your new resolve or dissipate it through scattered enthusiasm?
lines.reflection: What does a single pure thought look like for you right now, and what would it refuse to be influenced by?
lines.evidence_zh: 一念純真，有感即臨，以正而感，不正不感，正而未有不吉者

lines.interpretation: At the second line, the emerging yang has gained enough stability to blend firmness and yielding. The practitioner's stillness is not inert; it can respond accurately when touched. There is a mutual attraction between the new life and the old receptivity, so neither is harmed. The instruction is to let this organic bond happen without interference. Consistent, unhurried practice allows the subtle to become obvious and eventually whole. Ask where you can allow firm resolve and gentleness to move as one, without making the process into a fight.
lines.reflection: Where is my stillness able to respond, rather than merely withdraw?
lines.evidence_zh: 寂然不動，感而遂通，陽戀陰而陰戀陽，大小無傷，生機不息

lines.interpretation: This line warns against the polished, ingratiating approach: saying the right things while inwardly disconnected, performing practice for approval or quick sensations. It is empty and yields nothing lasting. The saving turn is honest grief over this falseness—a lowering of pride and a willingness to learn. Such grief is not self-punishment; it is the beginning of authenticity. Without that, sweetness turns bitter. Consider whether your current efforts have any trace of showmanship that covers an inner split.
lines.reflection: What part of my practice or self-presentation is sweet on the outside but empty within?
lines.evidence_zh: 口是心非，務外失內，是謂甘臨。臨至於甘，能言不能行，一無所利可知

lines.interpretation: The fourth line emphasizes preparation rather than seizure. One refines the self, holds the heart-mind steady, and waits for the precise moment when nascent yang appears. This is not idle waiting but the highest kind of readiness: a clear vessel, a calm will, and no distraction. When the moment arrives, the medicine—the inner resource—is recognized immediately and not missed. It teaches that timing is not luck but the fruit of self-discipline. Where do you need to prepare more deeply so you can recognize an opportunity when it comes?
lines.reflection: How can I prepare now so that when the inner moment ripens, I will not let it pass?
lines.evidence_zh: 柔而守正，煉己持心，以待初生之陽，是為至要之臨。臨於至要，大藥發現，自無當面錯過之咎

lines.interpretation: At the fifth line, the work becomes knowing and centered. It uses emptiness not as blankness but as a receptive clarity that can meet what arrives. The inner observer is calm and luminous; when the arising energy comes, the receptive side receives it without grasping. Urgent or slow, stopping or sufficient—everything fits the moment. The fruit is described as pre-cosmic qi coalescing within open stillness. This is the blending of yin and yang through accurate attention. Ask how your own inner receptivity can be both empty and knowing.
lines.reflection: Can I be empty enough to receive what is arising, and clear enough to meet it with accurate timing?
lines.evidence_zh: 以無求有，以虛求實，是謂能知其臨。能知其臨，則心君清泰，神明內照

lines.interpretation: The final line describes the ripening of the entire process: deliberate effort gives way to effortless stability, and the practitioner returns to simple, original authenticity. It is not ignorance but a direct, uncontrived accordance with deeper order. The text calls this sincere approach—suchness, stable, beyond subject and object. The original face appears when nothing is forced. In practical terms, this is the fruit of long discipline: a kindness and clarity that no longer need to prove themselves. How would it feel to trust the simplicity that remains after the work is done?
lines.reflection: What would it mean to let deliberate effort ripen into simple, uncontrived presence?
lines.evidence_zh: 自有為而入無為，返樸歸醇，至善無惡，不識不知，順帝之則，是謂敦臨

confucian.title: Approach at the Shore
confucian.essence: Yang's quiet growth below meets earth's receptivity above, forming the bank where water nears land. Overseeing requires sincere presence, teaching without end, and protection without limit—while remembering that every fullness begins to turn.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: The lake gathers beneath the earth, and the earth forms its shore: a relation of nearness and containment. Cheng Yi sees this as overseeing the people and affairs, not as distant command. Teaching and reflection should be inexhaustible; embracing and protecting should have no boundary. Yet because two yang lines are just growing, the sage warns against taking growth for permanence—fullness contains the seed of its own decline. The image invites responsible nearness, patient nurture, and early caution at the moment of rising strength.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi, following the Sequence of Hexagrams, reads Lin as what comes after Gu: once affairs are set right, greatness can emerge. He treats the lake below and earth above as a bank bordering water—among things, none approach as closely as earth and water. For him this becomes a model of higher overseeing lower, ruler overseeing people. His commentary reflects Song-dynasty Neo-Confucian confidence in teaching, moral authority, and hierarchical responsibility. The eighth-month warning is his ethical application of the waxing and waning of yin and yang: the noble person should prepare at fullness rather than wait for decline. This historical framing should be understood as a product of its time. Modern evaluation: it is not an endorsement of authoritarian hierarchy.
confucian.modern_meaning: Approach at the shore speaks to moments when we are close to others, to new work, or to growing influence. It asks for a presence that teaches not through control but through steady example and open listening. Cheng Yi's image of inexhaustible teaching and boundless protection suggests that care is not a finite resource; it enlarges when shared. His eighth-month caution reminds us not to mistake a rising phase for a guarantee. The task is to enjoy and use strength while preparing for the turn, without becoming anxious or controlling. In contemporary life this may mean checking whether we are using power to include or to dominate, whether our words are sincere or merely soothing. It also means trusting the knowledge of others rather than believing one person must have every answer. Approach, then, is not passive waiting; it is active, responsible drawing near—with respect for timing, relationship, and the limits of any one standpoint. By doing so, we may foster settings where people can approach us without fear, and where learning is mutual.
confucian.advice: Notice what is coming close. Offer guidance without demanding obedience, and reassure without flattery. When your influence grows, pause to ask what might be fading even as you succeed. Build forms of care that can outlast your own efforts. If you sense you are performing sweetness to avoid conflict, turn back to honest, steady speech. Choose to trust competent others rather than carrying every decision alone.
confucian.shadow: The shadow is sweet-talking authority: performing warmth to win compliance while avoiding difficult truths. At the peak of influence, we may mistake temporary growth for permanence, become complacent in our own knowledge, or use closeness to overwhelm rather than to empower.
confucian.reflection_question: What is approaching that asks for your honest presence rather than your control?
confucian.evidence_zh: 君子以教思无窮容保民无疆

lines.interpretation: At the first step, approach is felt through genuine stirring, not calculated performance. Cheng Yi says the initial yang line occupies a correct position and responds to the fourth, so its purpose is right. This suggests that in new undertakings, integrity matters more than visible results. When you draw near from an upright place, those above and alongside can sense it. The line does not promise effortless success; it points to persevering in what is correct. Let your intention be aligned with what you truly value, and allow trust to grow through steadiness.
lines.reflection: Is your current approach aligned with your core intention, or shaped by hope for approval?
lines.evidence_zh: 以九居陽又應四之正其志正也

lines.interpretation: This line deepens approach through sincere mutual response. Cheng Yi emphasizes that the second yang and the fifth yin respond in feeling; their good result comes from utmost sincerity, not from simply obeying orders. Here authority is shared, not imposed. When we bring growing strength and central balance to a relationship, we need not wait for permission to do good. Yet the line is not about rebellion; it is about acting from inner alignment while remaining in honest connection. A favorable outcome arises because the interaction is real, not because it is compliant. Trust becomes possible where both sides are moved by what is true rather than by rank.
lines.reflection: Where are you tempted to obey outwardly while withholding your true response?
lines.evidence_zh: 至誠相感非由順上之命也

lines.interpretation: At this place, approach may become sweetened performance—saying what soothes while avoiding the harder truth. Cheng Yi calls this a serious loss of virtue and says it brings no benefit. The line is not a final condemnation; it opens a door. If we recognize danger and feel genuine unease, we can return to humility, uprightness, and sincerity, and the fault need not last. This reading asks us to examine where our warmth is placating rather than caring. The way out is not harshness, but a more honest climate in which we can name what is difficult without losing compassion. Change is possible when the unease becomes conscious.
lines.reflection: Is there a place where your kindness is softening truth into flattery?
lines.evidence_zh: 若能持謙守正至誠以自處則无咎也

lines.interpretation: Here approach reaches its full closeness without overreaching. Cheng Yi notes the fourth line dwells near the ruler's position and responds to the capable yang below; it guards correctness, assigns tasks to worthy people, and personally draws near to those below, hence no blame. This is accountable leadership that remains close enough to understand actual conditions. It does not demand that one know everything; instead it values right placement and the courage to delegate to those with genuine ability. Presence matters: overseeing from too far breeds abstraction, but responsible nearness makes mistakes reparable. Proximity combined with humility becomes strength.
lines.reflection: How can you stay close enough to the work to understand it, while trusting others to carry their part?
lines.evidence_zh: 守正而任賢以親臨於下是以无咎

lines.interpretation: The fifth line shows wisdom in leadership: soft and central, it responds to the firm and central below, trusting capable others without abandoning its own discernment. Cheng Yi warns that a single person cannot handle the breadth of the world by relying narrowly on private judgment. To gather the excellence of others and employ their intelligence is to enlarge one's knowledge, not diminish it. This is not mere delegation; it is a willingness to know through relationship. The wise overseer need not be the smartest voice in the room, but must know how to hold the whole together.
lines.reflection: Whose wisdom are you currently leaving outside the room?
lines.evidence_zh: 不自任其知則其知大矣

lines.interpretation: At the close, approach becomes generous rather than controlling. Cheng Yi says the top yin is the utmost of compliance; though not formally paired with the lower yang, it seeks them and honors the worthy with sincere generosity. The position might seem to invite blame because it is soft and at the edge, but its sincere turning toward stronger, better-placed lines keeps the ending free of blame. There is no strain to force further growth. Later periods of involvement can be gracious; we may learn from those we once led and let the work continue through others.
lines.reflection: What might a generous ending ask of you now?
lines.evidence_zh: 以其敦厚於順剛是以吉而无咎

further_reading.title: The Yi River Commentary on the Book of Changes

hexagrams.essence: Approach the inner threshold with disciplined timing: nascent yang is strengthening yet yin remains strong. Guard the process with harmony and correctness, neither forcing nor missing the moment, so true inner warmth can mature.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: The archetype is the overseer of the alchemical furnace: a moment when the first returns of vitality become visible and require careful tending. It evokes a responsible, alert caretaker watching the subtle rise of light within body and mind—not grasping, but refining. This is not an external authority; it is the noble person teaching and protecting without limit, embodying a wise, watchful approach to what is just emerging.
hexagrams.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 19 not as political approach but as overseeing the furnace to gather medicine. He identifies yuan with the first yang and heng with the second yang: by the time one begins work at the furnace, two yang lines have returned, but yin is still strong. One must guard against danger and risk, use harmony as substance and compliance as function, and act only when the time is right. Rushing causes the growing yang to decline and Approach to turn into Contemplation, the warning of 'the eighth month.' The line commentaries follow the alchemical fire-times from cautious beginning through gathering the medicine to final simplicity.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: In present-day terms, this hexagram describes the early phase of any meaningful change or recovery: new energy has appeared, but old habits and uncertainties still dominate. Liu's alchemical language—furnace, medicine, fire-times—can be read as a disciplined way of noticing and nurturing what is just beginning. The warning against sweet talk and hurried results remains timely: when we perform rather than practice, quick enthusiasm collapses. Instead, the text points to patient self-refinement, honest timing, and a clear inner observer. This is not passive waiting; it is active, accurate attention that knows when to act and when to restrain. It invites us to become the overseer of our own process, protecting our growing clarity while learning from setbacks without either self-rejection or forced positivity.
hexagrams.advice: Resist the impulse to force quick results. Establish a regular inner practice that observes your emerging energy without feeding it with harshness or flattery. When the moment is ripe, act simply and directly; when it is not, consolidate and wait. Let sincerity, not sweetness, guide your words and commitments. Tend the small yang like a careful guardian.
hexagrams.shadow: The sweet approach: a smiling, people-pleasing performance that talks about growth while avoiding real inner work. It produces fake positivity, bypasses timing, and collapses into bitterness when results fail or old patterns return.
hexagrams.reflection_question: Where am I pretending to approach my own growth while actually avoiding the slow, sincere work of timing and self-honesty?
