classical.name: Nourishment
classical.judgment_zh: 頤：貞吉。觀頤，自求口實。
classical.judgment_en: Nourishment: Perseverance is auspicious. Observe nourishment; seek food for yourself.
classical.image_zh: 山下有雷，頤；君子以慎言語，節飲食。
classical.image_en: Below the mountain is thunder: Nourishment. The noble person uses this to be cautious in speech and moderate in eating and drinking.
classical.historical_note:
Hexagram 27 (Yí), Thunder below Mountain; base text and Great Image only.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Discard your numinous tortoise and watch my chewing jaws: misfortune.
Nourishment is overturned, going against the constant rule; seeking nourishment from a hill, to march on brings misfortune.

lines.text_zh: 拂頤，貞凶，十年勿用，无攸利。
lines.translation_en: Going against nourishment; perseverance brings misfortune: for ten years do not act; nothing is favorable.

lines.text_zh: 顛頤吉，虎視眈眈，其欲逐逐，无咎。
lines.translation_en: Nourishment overturned is good fortune; the tiger stares intently; its desires continue without cease; no blame.

lines.text_zh: 拂經，居貞吉，不可涉大川。
lines.translation_en: Going against the constant rule; dwelling in perseverance is good fortune; one cannot cross the great river.
Nourishment through it; danger leads to good fortune; it is advantageous to cross the great river.

hexagrams.title: Nourishment
hexagrams.name: Nourishment

taoist.title: Nourishing the True Self
taoist.essence: True nourishment is not filling the mouth but emptying the heart and filling the belly, harmonizing movement and stillness, and seeking correct inner sustenance in due season.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Yi images the cheeks and jaws: stillness above, movement below. When the mouth receives food, it moves; that movement is nourishing only when it remains rooted in stillness. Liu Yiming reads this as choosing the good and holding firmly, seeking the real through emptiness. The archetype asks what we take in—speech, food, impressions—and whether it feeds the true self or merely agitates appetite. Nourishment becomes alchemy when emptiness opens a place for the real.
taoist.historical_core: Hexagram 27, Yi, appears in the received Zhouyi as Nourishment, with the Great Image of thunder below mountain and the caution to be careful in speech and moderate in eating. Liu Yiming, a late imperial Daoist inner alchemist, treats the hexagram as a map of internal cultivation: the mouth is the gate through which either real sustenance or mere food enters. He states that nourishment 'follows from Wuwang,' though in the standard sequence Yi follows Da Chu; this reflects his doctrinal ordering. He distinguishes 'mouth-food' from 'real sustenance,' reads the six lines as six styles of nourishment, and sees only the top line as completing both inner and outer, beginning and end.
taoist.modern_meaning: Today nourishment feels like consumption: information, images, food, relationships. Liu Yiming invites a different inquiry: not 'What am I taking in?' but 'Does it become real in me?' The lower lines describe recognizable patterns—restlessness that reaches for external stimulation, pretense of fullness, obsession with bodily comfort, solitary stillness that avoids action. The top line does not reject the world; it crosses the great river and meets adversity as nourishment. In present terms, this is a practice of inner gathering: notice when hunger is actually for recognition, when movement has no center, or when quiet becomes withdrawal. Then return to the empty center, let the true impulse move at the right time, and rest when rest is due. It is not about dieting the body or the mind, but about what ripens into character, relationships, and quiet usefulness.
taoist.advice: Before feeding any appetite, pause and ask what part of you is hungry. Let stillness gather beneath movement. Speak and consume with economy. When you notice pretending or grasping, return to emptiness without shame. When outer action is needed, do not stay in stillness; when stillness is needed, do not force action. Cultivate the small daily gesture of choosing what is real.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is false nourishment: mistaking attention, food, or information for substance; abandoning inner knowing for jaw-like craving; mistaking solitary withdrawal for completion; or pretending fullness while empty.
taoist.reflection_question: What am I really hungry for, and how would I know if it is being nourished?
taoist.evidence_zh: 虛其心，實其腹，虛實相應

lines.interpretation: The first line is firm and liable to rush outward. Liu Yiming names the mistake plainly: abandoning the numinous tortoise within and watching another's chewing jaw. The tortoise is the quiet, self-contained knowing that needs no external display. When that is set aside, movement becomes restless and false nourishment begins. The line is a caution about beginnings: before any new habit, speech, or appetite forms, check whether the impulse arises from inner fullness or from comparison and craving. Starting in hunger of the wrong kind makes misfortune likely, not as punishment but as consequence.
lines.reflection: What inner resource am I abandoning when I compare my hunger to someone else's display?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛而妄動，不養於內，求養於外，棄真認假

lines.interpretation: The second line sits in weakness but longs to appear substantial. Liu Yiming describes one who lacks virtue yet wishes to nourish virtue, treating emptiness as fullness and seeking nourishment from the hill—a place of imagined height. This is overturned nourishment: it violates the regular way of borrowing firmness to nourish yielding. In present practice, this appears as grandiosity, claiming insights one has not digested, or refusing to ask for help. Real learning requires admitting emptiness first. The hill is not a source; only the low plain of honest practice can feed the work.
lines.reflection: Where am I pretending fullness, and what might honest emptiness allow me to receive?
lines.evidence_zh: 以無德而欲養有德，自高自大，無而為有，虛而為盈

lines.interpretation: The third line moves with appetite and follows desire. Liu Yiming says it busies itself only with clothing and food, not with innate nature and life-destiny; it nourishes the small body and becomes a small person. Even if food is obtained correctly, the path is still misfortune. The 'ten years' marks a wasted season of mistaken priorities. In present life, comfort and consumption can occupy decades while the inner person starves. The antidote is not asceticism but redirecting attention from comfort to character, from acquiring to becoming.
lines.reflection: What comfort am I feeding while my deeper nature is left unattended?
lines.evidence_zh: 只在衣食上打點，不在性命上留心

lines.interpretation: The fourth line shows the honored humbling itself below, not ashamed to ask of those beneath. Liu Yiming reads this as borrowing another's firm brightness to dissolve one's own yielding darkness. But the key is sincerity: the eyes concentrated, the heart true, without strain, first seeking from oneself before taking from others. This is an inversion that leads to good fortune because it reverses pride. In present practice, it looks like seeking guidance or correction from someone we might overlook, while keeping our own intention honest. The tiger's fixed stare is not aggression but single-minded desire for what is real.
lines.reflection: From whom or what am I willing to learn, even if it humbles me?
lines.evidence_zh: 目專一而心真切，出於自然，絕無勉強，未取於人，先求其己

lines.interpretation: The fifth line dwells in emptiness and knows only how to nourish within; it does not nourish outer movement. Liu Yiming honors its ability to dwell in correctness, but names the limit: it cannot cross the great river, cannot accomplish the intentional work of the golden elixir. This is solitary quietism mistaken for completion. Stillness is a stage, not a destination. In present terms, this line warns against a meditation or self-care that becomes withdrawal from relationships and responsibilities. Inner peace that cannot meet the world is incomplete. Let stillness gather strength, then cross at the right time.
lines.reflection: Where has my stillness become a way of avoiding the river I am called to cross?
lines.evidence_zh: 只知養內，不知養外

lines.interpretation: The top line completes the hexagram: it abides in yielding, stops in its place, and movement and stillness become one. It nourishes both inner and outer, self and others. Liu Yiming insists this completion must be accomplished in a place of danger and peril—the great river. If one can nourish in adversity, then one can nourish in prosperity. The image is not of a finished sage untouched by difficulty, but of someone for whom danger has become food. Here the false split between contemplation and action, inner and outer, breaks down, and the great Dao is completed.
lines.reflection: What adversity am I being invited to feed on rather than flee?
lines.evidence_zh: 須要在危厲之處做出，方能得吉

confucian.title: The Mouth's Discipline
confucian.essence: Nourishment asks what truly sustains us. Correctness in feeding body, speech, virtue, and relationships turns hunger into disciplined care; mountain stillness over thunder counsels restrained speech and measured intake.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: The hexagram is a mouth: two firm outer lines hold four open inner lines, with movement below and stillness above. It points to every kind of nourishment—physical, verbal, moral, social. To be fed well is not merely to consume; it is to align intake, expression, and dependence with what is suitable. The noble person watches the mouth because through its two acts, speech and eating, inner character and outward order are either sustained or damaged.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Nourishment as the hexagram of the human jaw: upper Gen halts, lower Zhen moves, outer lines are solid, the interior is empty. In his Confucian cosmos, heaven and earth nourish all beings; the sage nourishes worthy persons and through them the common people. He extends the mouth's discipline to speech and food, then to commands and resources. Some line readings rely on historical roles—ruler, minister, worthy, commoner—and on gendered yin-yang metaphors. These belong to his time; they can be re-read today as relationships of responsibility, dependency, and fitness rather than fixed status.
confucian.modern_meaning: Nourishment speaks to ordinary modern life as a question of sustainability and attention. We are fed by food, media, work, relationships, and self-talk; not all of it nourishes. The hexagram invites a pause at the mouth—what we take in and what we release through words. It asks us to distinguish genuine self-sustenance from craving approval or stimulation, and to see our dependencies clearly. In teams and families, those who hold responsibility for others can still receive support without losing dignity; those who rely on others can do so with integrity by choosing appropriate sources and honoring mutual obligation. The warning lines remind us that hunger, when unexamined, leads to grasping at what cannot truly feed us. The top line's vigilance suggests that carrying influence requires humility, steady effort, and awareness of risk—not domination. Cultivation here is active: regulate speech, moderate consumption, choose worthy nourishment, and accept that timing changes what is fitting.
confucian.advice: Consider pausing before consuming—food, information, or attention—and asking what it will nourish. Notice when words are reaching for approval, and see whether silence or a more measured phrase better serves the moment. If you depend on another, choose a source aligned with your values and honor that relationship. If others depend on you, accept support while staying steady, and hold influence with vigilance rather than pride.
confucian.shadow: Unchecked hunger becomes craving: envy of others' satisfaction, dependence on unsuitable sources, or speech that consumes attention. In such states the mouth is active but the self is diminished, and dignity is traded away.
confucian.reflection_question: What are you currently feeding—by your attention, your words, and your daily choices—and does it truly nourish the life you intend?
confucian.evidence_zh: 頥之道以正則吉也人之養身養徳養人養於人皆以正道則吉也

lines.interpretation: Cheng Yi reads this as squandering innate clarity for external craving. The 'numinous tortoise' names an inner resource that can be self-sustaining; the dangling jaws show hunger aroused by another's supposed plenty. The image is not only about food but about attention and desire. When a person abandons quiet sufficiency to watch what others seem to have, the mind moves before the body, and dignity slips. The present invitation is to notice where envy or comparison makes you drool after something that cannot truly feed you, and ask what native strength is being set aside.
lines.reflection: What inner sufficiency have I been neglecting while watching someone else's plate?
lines.evidence_zh: 心既動則其自失必矣迷欲而失已以陽而從隂則何所不至

lines.interpretation: Here a person cannot yet sustain themselves and must seek nurturing from others. The error is not dependence itself but turning to the wrong source: looking downward to an unsuitable match or reaching upward to a distant patron outside one's circle. Cheng Yi links this to 'kind'—those with whom one has response and fit. Today it asks us to accept legitimate interdependence without grasping for support from relationships that cannot honor who we are. When need is real, seek help from those whose values and position create fitting connection; do not force an alliance that betrays your context.
lines.reflection: Whose support am I seeking, and is it truly fitting for the person I am becoming?
lines.evidence_zh: 隂柔既不足以自養初上二爻皆非其與故往求則悖理而得凶也

lines.interpretation: This line pictures a person whose hunger is coupled with restlessness and self-assertion. The movement is not disciplined but impulsive; the search for nourishment breaks the proper pattern. Cheng Yi says even persistence in such a path is harmful—not because effort is wrong, but because the whole direction is opposed to principle. Modern readers might recognize moments of forcing a plan, habit, or relationship that feeds only anxiety. The 'ten years' is not a literal sentence but a call to stop acting until the underlying orientation changes. No amount of striving along a mistaken path will make it nourishing.
lines.reflection: Where am I persisting in a course whose very direction starves what I most need?
lines.evidence_zh: 三以隂柔之質而處不中正又在動之極是柔邪不正而動者也

lines.interpretation: Cheng Yi presents a leader who lacks full competence and therefore turns to capable people below—an inversion of hierarchy that can be fruitful when done from sincere need and respect. The tiger's glare is not aggression but a consciously cultivated dignity that prevents others from taking the position lightly; ceaseless needs point to dependable follow-through. The modern reading is not about rank but about interdependence: those in responsibility can accept support without pretending self-sufficiency, while still showing steadiness and reliable commitment. Seeking help from the right hands and sustaining that relationship with consistency turns apparent reversal into shared effectiveness.
lines.reflection: What support do I need to accept, and what steadiness do I need to bring in return?
lines.evidence_zh: 必養其威嚴耽耽然如虎視則能重其體貌下不敢易

lines.interpretation: Cheng Yi describes a ruler whose personal capacity falls short, and who therefore must lean on a worthy minister. This is not passive dependence; it requires active constancy: dwelling in correctness, giving steady trust, and avoiding grand ventures until foundations are firm. The historical example of King Cheng and the Duke of Zhou belongs to a monarchic setting, but the principle translates: when we recognize our limits in positions of care, wisdom lies in finding trustworthy partners, honoring their counsel, and not overreaching during fragile seasons. Authority is not weakened by appropriate reliance; it is strengthened by disciplined humility.
lines.reflection: In what area of responsibility do I need to rely on another, and am I giving that reliance steady, respectful commitment?
lines.evidence_zh: 必居守貞固篤於委信則能輔翼其身澤及天下故吉也

lines.interpretation: Cheng Yi casts the top line as the worthy minister who carries the nourishment of the whole. The auspiciousness is not comfort but danger turned to good fortune—won by constant vigilance, honest effort, and awareness of weight. His examples are Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou, who did not settle into entitlement but worked with alert humility. For modern readers this suggests that being a reliable source for others is a heavy trust: remain attentive, sustain effort through uncertainty, and refuse complacency, while still daring to act when the moment demands crossing.
lines.reflection: What responsibility am I carrying for others, and how do I remain vigilant without becoming rigid or self-important?
lines.evidence_zh: 以人臣而當是任必常懐危厲則吉也

original_chinese.title: 伊川易傳 (四庫全書本)/卷2

further_reading.title: The Yi River Commentary on the Book of Changes

hexagrams.essence: True nourishment is not filling the mouth but emptying the heart and filling the belly, harmonizing movement and stillness, and seeking correct inner sustenance in due season.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: Yi images the cheeks and jaws: stillness above, movement below. When the mouth receives food, it moves; that movement is nourishing only when it remains rooted in stillness. Liu Yiming reads this as choosing the good and holding firmly, seeking the real through emptiness. The archetype asks what we take in—speech, food, impressions—and whether it feeds the true self or merely agitates appetite. Nourishment becomes alchemy when emptiness opens a place for the real.
hexagrams.historical_core: Hexagram 27, Yi, appears in the received Zhouyi as Nourishment, with the Great Image of thunder below mountain and the caution to be careful in speech and moderate in eating. Liu Yiming, a late imperial Daoist inner alchemist, treats the hexagram as a map of internal cultivation: the mouth is the gate through which either real sustenance or mere food enters. He states that nourishment 'follows from Wuwang,' though in the standard sequence Yi follows Da Chu; this reflects his doctrinal ordering. He distinguishes 'mouth-food' from 'real sustenance,' reads the six lines as six styles of nourishment, and sees only the top line as completing both inner and outer, beginning and end.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: Today nourishment feels like consumption: information, images, food, relationships. Liu Yiming invites a different inquiry: not 'What am I taking in?' but 'Does it become real in me?' The lower lines describe recognizable patterns—restlessness that reaches for external stimulation, pretense of fullness, obsession with bodily comfort, solitary stillness that avoids action. The top line does not reject the world; it crosses the great river and meets adversity as nourishment. In present terms, this is a practice of inner gathering: notice when hunger is actually for recognition, when movement has no center, or when quiet becomes withdrawal. Then return to the empty center, let the true impulse move at the right time, and rest when rest is due. It is not about dieting the body or the mind, but about what ripens into character, relationships, and quiet usefulness.
hexagrams.advice: Before feeding any appetite, pause and ask what part of you is hungry. Let stillness gather beneath movement. Speak and consume with economy. When you notice pretending or grasping, return to emptiness without shame. When outer action is needed, do not stay in stillness; when stillness is needed, do not force action. Cultivate the small daily gesture of choosing what is real.
hexagrams.shadow: The shadow is false nourishment: mistaking attention, food, or information for substance; abandoning inner knowing for jaw-like craving; mistaking solitary withdrawal for completion; or pretending fullness while empty.
hexagrams.reflection_question: What am I really hungry for, and how would I know if it is being nourished?
hexagrams.editorial_status: integration-candidate — AI-assisted; final human review pending

classical.name: Great Exceeding
classical.judgment_zh: 大過：棟橈，利有攸往，亨
classical.judgment_en: Great Exceeding: The ridgepole bends; it is favorable to have somewhere to go; there is success.
classical.image_zh: 澤滅木，大過。君子以獨立不懼，遯世无悶
classical.image_en: The lake submerges the trees: Great Exceeding. The noble one stands alone without fear and withdraws from the world without distress.
classical.historical_note:
Received Zhouyi text; the Great Image is from the Ten Wings. The Tuan commentary and the individual line images are outside the classical translation scope and are omitted from the translated line objects. No use-nine/use-six text applies because this hexagram is not Qian or Kun.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Use white cogongrass as a mat; no blame.

lines.text_zh: 枯楊生稊，老夫得其女妻，无不利
lines.translation_en: The withered poplar produces shoots; an old man gets a young wife; nothing is unfavorable.
The ridgepole bends; misfortune.
The ridgepole arches upward; good fortune. If there is something else, there is distress.

lines.text_zh: 枯楊生華，老婦得其士夫，无咎无譽
lines.translation_en: The withered poplar puts forth blossoms; an old woman gets a husband; no blame and no praise.
Crossing too far, the water submerges the top of the head; misfortune, but no blame.

hexagrams.title: Great Exceeding
hexagrams.name: Great Exceeding

taoist.title: Excess and the Empty Center
taoist.essence: Excess is not defeated by suppression but by a precise return: honor the small, pair firm with yielding, and restore the empty center before the ridgepole bends.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Great Exceeding pictures four yang lines crowded between two outer yin lines—inner pressure too great for its container. In Liu Yiming’s inner-alchemy reading, this is the moment when advancing yang qi outruns yin, threatening the spirit chamber. The image is not a command to withdraw from all action; it is a signal to rebalance timing and degree, to let emptiness hold fullness, and to use the small, gentle entry of wind beneath the lake’s joy without collapse.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming treats Great Exceeding as a warning anchored in the trigrams and line positions: Dui above is joy, Xun below is entering, four yang within and two yin without show yang surpassing yin. Following Da Chu, which restrains strength, this hexagram addresses the danger of excessive advancing yang in forming the Golden Elixir. If yang is too exuberant and yin too weak, the generative way is lost; the ridgepole bends and the mansion topples. The remedy is not mere quietism but active harmonization—advance with Xun’s gentleness, avoid fierceness and obstinacy, adapt through changes, guard peril—so firm and yielding correspond and nature and destiny may be fulfilled.
taoist.modern_meaning: In present-day terms, this hexagram may describe a season of overreach, intense effort, or one-sided self-discipline that has begun to bend the supporting structure. It does not say to stop caring or to become passive; it points to the neglected yin capacities—receptivity, pause, attention to small details—that allow strong intention to become sustainable. A person may be working honestly yet missing the signals of fatigue, relationship strain, or the inner life asking for space. The medicine is not less commitment but a different distribution of firmness and yielding. Ask what has been overfilled and what has been left empty. Then act: adjust the pace, restore a modest practice, repair a connection, return to the body’s timing. Great effort can succeed when it no longer insists on being great.
taoist.advice: Instead of pushing harder, look for the small, quiet adjustments that let the center hold. Match each forward step with a moment of receptive check. Choose one excessive pattern—overwork, over-control, or over-indulgence—and bring it back into proportion through a concrete, time-bound change.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is the collapse hidden in overextension: rigidity posing as discipline, indulgence posing as joy, self-will mistaking intensity for spiritual progress, until the structure breaks and the person blames circumstance rather than imbalance.
taoist.reflection_question: Where have I confused excess with strength, and what small, genuine yielding would let my life’s ridgepole no longer bend?
taoist.evidence_zh: 大過者，陽氣有過也。卦德上兌悅、下巽入；巽于內而悅於外，順其所欲，樂極生悲，卦體內四陽而外二陰，陽過於陰，陰不及陽，故謂大過。

lines.interpretation: The first line sits at the base, yielding and lowly. Liu Yiming sees an almost excessive caution—like placing white couch grass before acting—that transforms arrogance before it grows. This is not passivity; it is the active discipline of smallness. When you are entering a charged situation, begin by preparing the ground rather than announcing your strength. Genuine humility here protects you from the larger fault. Ask what small ritual of preparation—done without self-importance—would steady the next step.
lines.reflection: What small act of preparation or humility could transform my current momentum before it becomes excessive?
lines.evidence_zh: 如借用自茅，而不敢先人，傲氣悉化，自無過大之時。

lines.interpretation: The second position is firm but reaches for yin’s support. The withered poplar does not revive by doubling its hardness; it receives new shoots through a complementary bond. In human terms, strength becomes generative when it partners with receptivity. This is not a promise of perpetual youth but an image of balance: an established, strong element renews itself by honoring the tender and undone. Where might a seasoned part of you learn from the unformed? Use yielding not as weakness but as the precise aid that keeps firmness from breaking.
lines.reflection: What strong part of my life is asking to be paired with something young, soft, or unformed so it can renew rather than break?
lines.evidence_zh: 過而不過，如枯楊生稊，老夫得其女妻，陰陽相當，生機常存，剛而不傷，自無不利。

lines.interpretation: Third line is the classic excess of firmness: forward only, no retreat. Liu Yiming warns that the elixir gained can be lost again—progress undone by the very force that produced it. This is the moment when discipline becomes stubbornness, when intensity refuses feedback. The ridgepole bends because it carries one-sided pressure. If you find yourself unable to stop or reconsider, you may be in this territory. Real strength includes the capacity to pause without shame. The question is not whether to advance but whether your advance has become a flight from correction.
lines.reflection: Where am I treating retreat as failure, and what would it take to let feedback bend me before something breaks?
lines.evidence_zh: 以剛用剛，只知前進，不知後退，金丹得而復失，棟橈之凶，所不能免

lines.interpretation: The fourth line shows the ridgepole rising rather than bending: greatness learns to be small, the mind settles, and the qi evens out. This is not a final resting place. Liu Yiming adds a caution: after yin and yang have begun to unite, do not now overcorrect into too much yielding, or firmness is harmed and the way becomes blocked. The middle path is dynamic—neither rigid nor limp. If you have recently made space after a period of overeffort, hold that balance consciously rather than swinging into passivity. Continue to act from a calm center.
lines.reflection: After finding balance, how can I avoid the subtle excess of too much accommodation or softness while keeping firmness alive?
lines.evidence_zh: 大而能小，心平氣和，如棟隆不敗，動與吉會矣。

lines.interpretation: Fifth position is firm and centered, but its joy has become self-enclosed. The withered poplar puts out showy blossoms but cannot renew; the older wife who takes a young husband may gain vitality yet also invite overindulgence. Liu Yiming says the center provides an inner ruler, so there is no blame, yet there is also no praise because fullness has not emptied the mind. This is the subtle excess of satisfaction—spiritual or material. When you feel justified and full, ask whether your contentment is producing new life or merely decoration. True-centeredness remains open to correction.
lines.reflection: Where is my sense of centeredness quietly becoming self-satisfaction, and what would it mean to empty the mind just enough to remain teachable?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛於悅而不能柔以悅，如枯楊生華，老婦得其士夫，過於淫奢，自滿自足，陽極生陰，真為假傷

lines.interpretation: The top line reaches the end of excess. Liu Yiming describes a yielding nature turned to deluded fantasy: it will not study the medicine or the degree of the fire, lets the mind run arbitrarily, climbs too high, and is submerged. The misfortune is self-invited, yet no blame attaches to others. Here the fault is not aggressive hardness but undisciplined softness—dreamy, willful exploration without method or timing. Deep inner work cannot be improvised from imagination alone. If you recognize this pattern, the way is not to shame yourself but to return to patient, grounded practice.
lines.reflection: Where has my searching become ungrounded fantasy, and what disciplined small step would return me to right timing?
lines.evidence_zh: 愚而自用，不知藥物火候，任心造作，迷而不返，升之高，傷之甚，過涉滅頂，自招其凶，與人無咎

confucian.title: Great Exceeding
confucian.essence: Greatness beyond the ordinary arises when strong capacities gather centrally, yet weak roots and tips ask whether the structure can bear its load; centrality, gentle movement, and joy make success possible without violating principle.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: This hexagram pictures a marsh above wind and wood—moistening gone too far, water submerging trees. It names the moment when one's powers exceed familiar norms and ordinary structures bend. Cheng Yi does not present this as moral fault; he points to great affairs—abdications, founding acts, deeds that surpass common measure—where the Dao remains constant. The noble person stands alone without fear and withdraws without distress, not from pride but from clarity that great responsibility requires integrity beyond approval.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Hexagram 28 as following Yi because nourishment enables movement, and movement can produce excess. He defines 'great excess' not as violating principle but as the surplus of yang in the four central lines, which leaves the upper and lower yin lines weak; hence the ridgepole bends. Yet the judgment remains favorable: yin weak and yang strong means the noble person flourishes and the petty person declines, so 'it is fitting to have a place to go and there is success.' He insists that the sage does not exceed principle; great acts such as abdications or founding wars follow the Dao, which is never without centrality or constancy.
confucian.modern_meaning: In present terms, this hexagram speaks to seasons when your competence or responsibility has outgrown the supports around you. You may possess real strength—skill, expertise, moral seriousness—but the situation can still bend because the outer conditions are thin: institutional backing is fragile, or personal support is not yet ready. The image does not command withdrawal from the world, nor does it promise success. It invites an honest audit: are you carrying a central load with only weak roots and tips? If so, move forward only by finding a place to go that lets you act with centrality, gentle persuasion, and shared joy rather than force. Standing alone without fear does not mean isolation; it means refusing to let public disapproval distort your ethical center. Withdrawing without distress means you are not dependent on recognition. In modern relationships, work, or community leadership, the question is whether your strong center is connected to humility, consultation, and timing, because a ridgepole that bends may still be true if its weight is balanced.
confucian.advice: Examine the supports around a weight you are carrying. Strengthen the weak ends through quiet, careful groundwork before adding more load. Act through gentle persistence and cooperation rather than solitary force. If you must stand alone, do so without resentment, and withdraw from recognition without bitterness. Keep your own central measure, and let others' responses inform timing without taking away your balance.
confucian.shadow: The shadow is rigidity dressed as greatness—insisting on a heavy central role while ignoring weak supports, or turning principled isolation into resentment. Another form is producing showy flowers without roots: activity that looks impressive but cannot renew itself.
confucian.reflection_question: Where am I bearing a central load on weak supports, and what quiet strengthening does that situation actually need?
confucian.evidence_zh: 大過者陽過也故為大者過過之大與大事過也

lines.interpretation: At the beginning, the soft line dwells below in a position of fearfulness. It mats the ground with white cogongrass rather than placing anything directly on the earth. Cheng Yi sees this as excessive caution, but a caution that completes the way of reverence. The seeming smallness of the reed is not the point; its careful use gives weight to what is slight. In a situation of great excess, beginning with protected, deliberate placement avoids fault. This is not timidity for its own sake; it is the foundation of safety when larger burdens may later descend.
lines.reflection: What small act of careful preparation might protect a much larger undertaking from unnecessary fault?
lines.evidence_zh: 以柔在下用茅藉物之象不錯諸地而藉以茅過於慎也是以无咎

lines.interpretation: The second line shows strength that has not reached its extreme: a withered willow puts out shoots, an image of renewal through relationship. Cheng Yi explains that this yang line attains the center, resides in a soft position, and joins closely with the yin line below. Cheng Yi reads the old man/young wife image as a traditional metaphor for harmonizing firmness and softness, not as a modern social prescription. What proves favorable is that excessive strength learns to use gentleness as a partner, so life can grow again from apparent exhaustion. Without this yielding, strength alone would be too brittle.
lines.reflection: Where might a complementary softness renew what has become withered in me?
lines.evidence_zh: 是剛過之人而能以中自處用柔相濟者也

lines.interpretation: The third line is a warning. Firmness becomes excessive, so it cannot share the burden with others or accept their support. Cheng Yi says even ordinary tasks require help; how much more great undertakings. The image of the bending ridgepole here points to isolation dressed as strength. The line dwells in firmness at the height of a solid core, yet without softness or consultation it endangers the whole structure. This is not a prediction of doom but a diagnosis: when force becomes self-enclosed, it forfeits the alliances that could hold it.
lines.reflection: In what way has my determination stopped seeking the assistance it actually needs?
lines.evidence_zh: 既過於剛強則不能與人同常常之功尚不能獨立况大過之事乎

lines.interpretation: The fourth line offers a better kind of strength. It dwells in a soft position and can use gentleness to assist, so the ridgepole arches upward rather than bending. Cheng Yi calls this bearing great responsibility without rigidity. However, he warns of 'something else': even after balancing firmness and softness, the line risks being pulled back toward the yin at the beginning, entangling its will. The lesson is not to avoid relationships, but to avoid a divided heart once one has chosen the weight one carries. Confidence remains useful only when it stays free of anxious attachments.
lines.reflection: What attachment might quietly draw my center away from the task I have accepted?
lines.evidence_zh: 居柔為能用柔相濟既不過剛則能勝其任如棟之隆起是以吉也

lines.interpretation: The fifth line sits in the center and honored position, yet it lacks responsive help from below and leans toward the exhausted top line. Cheng Yi likens this to a withered willow that produces flowers but no roots: there is display but no renewing depth. The traditional image of an old woman with a husband is a figure for imbalance; Cheng Yi explicitly calls it shameful and unbeautiful, not a social endorsement. Here the result is neither fault nor praise—nothing takes root, nothing is celebrated. The lesson concerns misplaced reliance: even central integrity cannot accomplish great work if it attaches itself to what is already spent.
lines.reflection: Where am I looking for vitality in a relationship or situation that cannot actually renew me?
lines.evidence_zh: 枯楊下生根稊則能復生如大過之陽興成事功也上生華秀雖有所發无益於枯也

lines.interpretation: The top line reaches the extreme of excess. Cheng Yi describes not a noble greatness but a petty overstepping: disregarding danger, treading into peril, wading until the head is submerged. The misfortune is real, yet 'no blame' appears because no one else can be faulted for a choice made in reckless agitation. This is the hardest line: it does not promise rescue, but it does refuse to shift responsibility. It invites honest awareness that some losses follow from overreaching beyond lawful limits, not from external enemies.
lines.reflection: Which of my current risks is self-chosen rather than truly necessary?
lines.evidence_zh: 小人狂躁以自禍盖其宜也復將何尤故曰无咎言自為之无所怨咎也

hexagrams.essence: Excess is not defeated by suppression but by a precise return: honor the small, pair firm with yielding, and restore the empty center before the ridgepole bends.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: Great Exceeding pictures four yang lines crowded between two outer yin lines—inner pressure too great for its container. In Liu Yiming’s inner-alchemy reading, this is the moment when advancing yang qi outruns yin, threatening the spirit chamber. The image is not a command to withdraw from all action; it is a signal to rebalance timing and degree, to let emptiness hold fullness, and to use the small, gentle entry of wind beneath the lake’s joy without collapse.
hexagrams.historical_core: Liu Yiming treats Great Exceeding as a warning anchored in the trigrams and line positions: Dui above is joy, Xun below is entering, four yang within and two yin without show yang surpassing yin. Following Da Chu, which restrains strength, this hexagram addresses the danger of excessive advancing yang in forming the Golden Elixir. If yang is too exuberant and yin too weak, the generative way is lost; the ridgepole bends and the mansion topples. The remedy is not mere quietism but active harmonization—advance with Xun’s gentleness, avoid fierceness and obstinacy, adapt through changes, guard peril—so firm and yielding correspond and nature and destiny may be fulfilled.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: In present-day terms, this hexagram may describe a season of overreach, intense effort, or one-sided self-discipline that has begun to bend the supporting structure. It does not say to stop caring or to become passive; it points to the neglected yin capacities—receptivity, pause, attention to small details—that allow strong intention to become sustainable. A person may be working honestly yet missing the signals of fatigue, relationship strain, or the inner life asking for space. The medicine is not less commitment but a different distribution of firmness and yielding. Ask what has been overfilled and what has been left empty. Then act: adjust the pace, restore a modest practice, repair a connection, return to the body’s timing. Great effort can succeed when it no longer insists on being great.
hexagrams.advice: Instead of pushing harder, look for the small, quiet adjustments that let the center hold. Match each forward step with a moment of receptive check. Choose one excessive pattern—overwork, over-control, or over-indulgence—and bring it back into proportion through a concrete, time-bound change.
hexagrams.shadow: The shadow is the collapse hidden in overextension: rigidity posing as discipline, indulgence posing as joy, self-will mistaking intensity for spiritual progress, until the structure breaks and the person blames circumstance rather than imbalance.
hexagrams.reflection_question: Where have I confused excess with strength, and what small, genuine yielding would let my life’s ridgepole no longer bend?

classical.name: The Abysmal (Water)
classical.judgment_zh: 習坎：有孚，維心亨。行有尚
classical.judgment_en: Repeated Abyss: with sincerity, the heart penetrates; action has merit.
classical.image_zh: 水洊至，習坎；君子以常德行，習教事
classical.image_en: Water flows on and on: the abyss repeated. The noble one thereby keeps constant in virtuous conduct and rehearses the tasks of teaching.
classical.historical_note:
Hexagram 29, the doubled trigram 坎 (Water/Abyss). The source text for 六四 and 九五 includes editorial variants: 六四 一作「樽酒簋貳，用缶，納約自牖」; 九五 禔 一作「祗」. No use-nine/use-six applies to this hexagram.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Repeated abyss: entering into the pit's hollow; misfortune.
The abyss has danger; seeking yields small gain.

lines.text_zh: 來之坎坎，險且枕，入于坎窞，勿用
lines.translation_en: Coming and going: pit upon pit; danger and also a pillow/rest (or deep); entering the pit's hollow—do not act.

lines.text_zh: 尊酒簋，貳用缶。内約自牖一作「樽酒簋貳，用缶，納約自牖」，終无咎
lines.translation_en: A flask of wine and a bowl; a second [vessel] of earthenware; an inner bond (内, not 納) through a window—variant: 'A bottle of wine and two bowls; use an earthenware vessel; receive the bond through a window'—in the end no blame.

lines.text_zh: 坎不盈，禔一作「祗」既平，无咎
lines.translation_en: The abyss is not overflowing; already level (variant 祗 for 禔; commentary reads 祗 as 柢/抵 'reach'), no blame.

lines.text_zh: 係用徽纆，寘于叢棘，三歲不得，凶
lines.translation_en: Bound with cords and ropes, placed among thorny thickets; for three years no release; misfortune.

taoist.title: Trust in the Depths
taoist.essence: The abyss repeated is not fate; it is a field of practice. Sincerity in the heart-mind opens a path through danger, while unexamined habit deepens the pit.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Repeated water is danger within danger, but also the image of continuous flow that can be channeled. As an archetype, it is the soul's descent into depth where the original light is hidden—a place of testing that requires sincerity, practiced trust, and disciplined return. The abyss is not merely external; it forms wherever repeated habits carve a channel. Yet the same repetition can become training: a heart-mind that stays sincere may pass through and act with upward progress.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads this doubled Kan hexagram as an inner-alchemy teaching about returning to true yang from within yin. The 'repeated' character is for him both repeated practice and habituation: practicing evil is the way into danger; practicing good is the way out. Sincerity must be present in the heart-mind, otherwise practice is hollow. His line commentary classifies people by whether they combine sincerity with practice—foolish or wise, firm or yielding—and ends by urging the seeker to find a true teacher and complete the work of nature and life-destiny. He treats the trigram water as the place where the primordial yang has sunk, and 'white within black' as the hidden possibility of recovery.
taoist.modern_meaning: When difficulty repeats, it often exposes the habits we bring to difficulty. The hexagram does not promise that sincerity removes the abyss, but that sincerity changes what the abyss does to the heart-mind. Repeated practice—what Liu calls 習—can deepen the pit or build a path through it. In ordinary life this may show up as recurring conflict, addictive patterns, chronic uncertainty, or inherited wounds. The invitation is not to deny danger or to passively wait, but to practice small, honest acts that restore trust in one's own center. Seeking wise counsel, simplifying one's offerings, and keeping the inner vessel level are all forms of disciplined cultivation. The goal is not to eliminate risk but to learn to move through it without being defined by it. Present-day readers might ask what they are practicing daily, and whether that practice is leading toward openness or further entrapment. No outcome is guaranteed, yet the text suggests that practice, not circumstance, decides whether the abyss becomes a grave or a birthplace.
taoist.advice: Consider what you are rehearsing in your current difficulty. Bring sincere attention to the heart-mind, simplify what you offer, and seek a trustworthy guide if the way is dark. Practice small exits rather than waiting for a dramatic rescue. Hold your inner water level: not overflowing, not stagnant. Let action arise from that centered sincerity.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is habituated despair: meeting danger with danger, boring deeper into the pit, and mistaking cynicism for realism. It may appear as self-abandonment, resignation to bad company, or a secret belief that no practice can help.
taoist.reflection_question: What am I repeatedly practicing in the face of this difficulty?
taoist.evidence_zh: 習惡者，入險之道；習善者，出險之道，出險須要能信其險。

lines.interpretation: This line shows the earliest moment of difficulty, where one's existing disposition meets the abyss. Liu describes a nature already foolish that 'practices foolishness' and sinks day by day. The pit is deepened not only by external danger but by the direction of repeated action. It is a warning against meeting a first stumble with resignation or familiar avoidance. There is no fixed identity here; the pattern is still forming. The line asks whether the first response to danger will be one that bores deeper or one that pauses and looks for another way.
lines.reflection: What habitual first response might be deepening the pit?
lines.evidence_zh: 性質本愚，又習於愚，日習日下，是謂習坎

lines.interpretation: Here one is surrounded by unhelpful influences, yet an inner firmness remains. Liu says this line 'obtains the center' and is not deeply sunk; it has a master within and is not deluded by lower currents. However, it trusts that there is danger without practicing the way out, so its gain is small. It is the condition of one who knows better but does not yet act differently. The line invites movement from awareness to disciplined practice: the center is a resource, not a destination.
lines.reflection: Where am I aware of danger but not practicing a way out?
lines.evidence_zh: 幸其剛而得中，陷之不深，雖不能出險，內有主宰，亦不為下流所惑

lines.interpretation: This line depicts frantic movement in a double pit: forward or backward both contain danger, and the pillow image suggests finding no rest even in what should support. Liu calls it a nature already dangerous that also 'walks danger' through self-reliance. Without trusting that danger exists, further practice only makes the trap deeper. It is the state of restless agitation that mistakes movement for progress. The line counsels stopping the cycle rather than pushing through, because here action itself is the problem.
lines.reflection: Where might my restless motion be digging deeper instead of finding ground?
lines.evidence_zh: 性質本險，又愚而自用以行險，險而又險，是來之坎坎矣

lines.interpretation: This is a turning point: an average nature, capable of either good or evil, shown by the simple image of one cup of wine and two vessels. Liu says that by trusting in good and humbling oneself before wisdom, one can borrow another's light through a narrow window. The offering is modest, not grand. The line suggests that in the middle of the abyss, a small sincere gesture—a shared meal, a transparent encounter—can prevent blame. It is not about escaping alone but about receiving light through an opening.
lines.reflection: What modest offering or honest exchange might open a window now?
lines.evidence_zh: 信於善而虛心下賢，借他人之明智，以破己之昏暗，如用缶納約，自牖以通其明

lines.interpretation: Here the danger is held at levelness. Liu portrays one who is centered and correct, with the handle in hand: neither full nor overflowing, neither shifting nor drifting. The water is not overflowing but just level. Full in the belly yet empty in the heart, this condition comes from the completion of nature. It is the highest wisdom that does not need to practice good because it embodies good spontaneously. The line points to an inner equilibrium that neither suppresses danger nor is swept away by it.
lines.reflection: How can I hold my inner water level: neither overflowing nor stagnant?
lines.evidence_zh: 既能不滿不盈，不見惡於小人，又能不遷不流，大有異於小人，如坎水不盈，只既平

lines.interpretation: This line warns of self-binding. Liu insists even this figure's original nature has never failed to be good, but because it does not know how to practice good, it ties itself up and falls into brambles. It is not merely three years of suffering; it is a final abandonment of one's own nature. The cords are not only external; they are made of repeated refusal to cultivate. The line is severe, yet its root is hopeful: the good nature is still there, only hidden by self-abandonment.
lines.reflection: Where might I be tying myself with cords of self-abandonment?
lines.evidence_zh: 雖系小人，本性未嘗不善，但性善而不知習善，自縛自束

confucian.title: The Abyss Repeated
confucian.essence: Repeated danger holds a solid center: sincerity in the heart is what penetrates. Through steady repetition—of virtue, teaching, and faithful action—one can move within peril without losing trust or purpose.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: Water arrives again and again, deepening rather than overflowing. In the doubled abyss, a single yang line rests between two yin: solid trust enclosed by darkness. The image is not merely danger but practice—repetition that makes constancy. Like water following terrain and wearing channels over time, the heart learns to move through difficulty by returning to its sincere center and by rehearsing the tasks that build reliable character.
confucian.historical_core: In Cheng Yi’s commentary, Kan is repeated danger: one yang trapped between two yin, above and below, with no support. The solid center is sincerity; because the heart is sincere and unified, it can penetrate even danger. Water flows and does not fill; acting with this faithfulness brings merit. The noble person sees water’s repeated arrival and keeps virtue constant while rehearsing teaching. Ministers reach rulers through plain trust and by appealing to the ruler’s bright points; no one, not even a strong ruler, can cross collective peril alone. The line readings distinguish weak sinking, firm self-preservation, and the final imprisonment of yin at the extreme.
confucian.modern_meaning: Modern readers need not adopt the ruler-minister hierarchy Cheng Yi assumes. The structure still speaks: in recurring hard stretches—repeated setbacks, deep uncertainty, environments that feel like pits—the task is not to ignore danger or to expect immediate rescue. It is to locate the inner solid point: a commitment, a standard, a relationship that can be trusted. Repetition itself is not the enemy; it is how water carves a path. Practicing small, honest actions under pressure strengthens that center. Where an older context looked to court protocol, a contemporary context might look to workplace transparency, family trust, or personal integrity. The counsel remains: do not decorate with excessive display; offer what is plain and real. Appeal to what is already bright in another rather than attacking their blindness. And do not assume one strong person can fix a collective problem alone; shared effort and clear communication matter. Danger can become a teacher only when sincerity is repeated, not performed.
confucian.advice: Consider naming the one commitment or relationship you can trust in the current difficulty. Keep returning to it daily, even in small ways. Prefer plain, consistent action over dramatic displays. When you need to influence someone, start from what they already value. If the problem is shared, do not try to solve it alone; invite partnership. Let repetition build depth without becoming stuck.
confucian.shadow: Repetition without sincerity hardens into ritual; the heart can become numb. Peril may seduce one into helplessness or into isolated control. Appealing to others' brightness can become manipulation if it lacks honesty.
confucian.reflection_question: Where is the solid center in my present difficulty, and what small practice can keep it sincere?
confucian.evidence_zh: 陽實在中為中有孚信維心亨維其心誠一故能亨通至誠可以通金石蹈水火何險難之不可亨

lines.interpretation: At the first step, weakness and lack of support make escape unlikely if you react from fear. Cheng Yi reads this line as sinking further into the pit because it has lost the way. In present terms: when a hard situation begins, avoid leaning on imagined rescue or denying the danger. Recognize that the first movement matters. Without a firm center or help, impulsive or passive responses can deepen the trap. The line is not a verdict but a warning about direction.
lines.reflection: What is my first impulse in this difficulty, and does it lead toward a way out or deeper in?
lines.evidence_zh: 初以隂柔居坎險之下柔弱无援而處不得當非能出乎險也唯益䧟於湥險耳

lines.interpretation: Even inside danger, a solid center allows small, real progress. Cheng Yi says the second line is trapped yet, through firmness and balance, can preserve itself and achieve a limited good. This is not escape, but it prevents deeper harm. In practical terms: when surrounded by difficulty, do what is reliably within reach. Protect your core commitments, keep decisions measured, and accept incremental gains. The goal now is not to solve everything but to remain intact and trustworthy.
lines.reflection: What small, solid gain is available now without pretending the larger danger is gone?
lines.evidence_zh: 二當坎險之時陷上下二隂之中乃至險之地是有險也然其剛中之才雖未能出乎險中亦可小自濟不至如初益陷入于湥險是所求小得也

lines.interpretation: Cheng Yi sees this position as neither central nor correct: moving forward or back brings danger, and staying is also unstable. The warning 'do not act' is not about laziness but about refusing futile thrashing. When every visible move leads into another pit, the wise response may be to pause, seek a more solid position, and refuse to act from panic. Action taken merely to relieve anxiety can deepen the trap.
lines.reflection: Am I mistaking motion for progress, and what would happen if I paused to find firmer ground?
lines.evidence_zh: 六三在坎陷之時以隂柔而居不中正其處不善進退與居皆不可者也

lines.interpretation: Cheng Yi reads this line as a minister in danger who wins trust through plain substance rather than elaborate display, and who reaches the ruler by appealing to what is already bright in the ruler's mind. Translated beyond court: in strained relationships, integrity and simplicity build more trust than performance. If you need to influence someone, begin with their existing values and understanding. Offer what is genuine and modest; do not attack their blindness directly. The 'window' is the point of shared light.
lines.reflection: What plain, honest offering could open a window in a relationship that now feels dark?
lines.evidence_zh: 納約謂進結於君之道牖開通之義室之暗也故設牖所以通明自牖言自通明之處以况君心所明處

lines.interpretation: Cheng Yi interprets the fifth line as a ruler with firm central talent, yet unable to fill the abyss because he lacks capable helpers. No single person, however strong, can level systemic danger alone. This is not a failure of personal virtue but a truth about shared crises. Blame arises when a leader assumes solitary control. The path is to build trusted partnerships, recognize interdependence, and aim for gradual leveling rather than dramatic rescue. No blame comes when the danger actually subsides through collective effort.
lines.reflection: Where have I been carrying a collective burden alone, and who might share the work of leveling it?
lines.evidence_zh: 以九五剛中之才居尊位宜可以濟於險然下无助也二陷於險中未能出餘皆隂柔无濟險之才人君雖才安能獨濟天下之險居君位而不能致天下出於險則為有咎必袛既平乃得无咎

lines.interpretation: Cheng Yi reads the top line as yin softness at the extreme of danger, an image of deep imprisonment among thorns. It has lost the way, and the text speaks of three years without release—a vivid picture of prolonged consequence, not a fixed prediction. When difficulty is met with passivity, denial, or accumulated missteps, the trap can feel permanent. Yet the commentary's point is not to accept fate but to recognize how one has contributed to the binding. The first step toward release is honest acknowledgment of the pattern.
lines.reflection: What repeated pattern has bound me, and where might I begin to loosen one cord?
lines.evidence_zh: 上六以隂柔而居險之極其陷之湥者也以其陷之湥取牢獄為喻如繫縛之以徽纆因寘于叢棘之中隂柔而陷之湥其不能出矣

classical.name: Clinging Fire
classical.judgment_zh: 離：利貞。亨。畜牝牛，吉。
classical.judgment_en: Clinging: It is beneficial to be correct. Success. Raising a cow brings good fortune.
classical.image_zh: 明兩作離，大人以繼明照于四方。
classical.image_en: Brightness doubled makes up Clinging; the great person, by continuing brightness, illuminates the four quarters.
classical.historical_note:
For 九三, the supplied text has 差 followed by the editorial note 一作「嗟」; the translation follows the common 嗟 reading. The source text opens with 坎 and includes 咸 around navigation markers ◄ ►; these are adjacent hexagram labels, not the current hexagram identity.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: The tread is confused; if one is reverent, there is no blame.
Yellow radiance: supreme good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 日昃之離，不鼓缶而歌，則大耋之差一作「嗟」，凶。
lines.translation_en: The clinging of the sun at dusk: if one does not beat the earthenware jar and sing, then the lament of the very old—misfortune.

lines.text_zh: 突如其來如，焚如，死如，棄如。
lines.translation_en: It comes suddenly: burning, dying, cast away.
Tears pour down in floods; grief and sighs—good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 王用出征，有嘉折首，獲匪其醜，无咎。
lines.translation_en: The king goes out on a punitive expedition; there is commendation in cutting off the leaders; he does not capture their followers—no blame.

hexagrams.title: Clinging Fire
hexagrams.name: Clinging Fire

taoist.title: Nurture Brightness Within
taoist.essence: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 30 as bright spirit, not raw intellect. True clarity begins by nurturing inner brightness through compliant attention; then outer action illuminates without burnout, and compulsive struggle falls away by root removal, not suppression.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Clinging Fire shows luminosity that depends on what it clings to. As an archetype, it is the mind's ability to illuminate only when its center is empty and receptive. Fire above and below double the call: inner clarity and outer clarity must be one. Without fuel, fire burns out; without humility, brightness becomes glare. The archetype invites a disciplined yin within yang—radiance that serves rather than consumes, and that sees by first being willing to be taught.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming treats Li as the empty-numinous qi of the Li palace, the human spirit and ruler of the mind. Using brightness is outer; nurturing it is inner, and outer must root in inner. The female cow is not mere passivity but utmost compliance that turns light back to shine within. He maps the six lines as stages of interior timing: premature use, humble seeking, rigid excess, sudden false brightness, tearful self-awareness, and kingly clarity that cuts off the chief evil while refusing to forcibly suppress mixed thoughts. The summary formula is knowing the male and guarding the female, firmness containing softness.
taoist.modern_meaning: In modern life Li can describe the relationship between inner clarity and outer presence. Liu Yiming’s warning against using brightness before nurturing it invites a pause before deciding, speaking, or performing. Tend the inner source through honest rest, reflection, and receptive attention. Brightness that leaps ahead becomes burnout; brightness that is nurtured becomes steady illumination. The female cow is not passivity but disciplined compliance—choosing what you feed and letting attention return inward. When confusion signals that you have stepped too soon, learning and careful questioning restore the way. When grief or limitation brings tears, Liu treats that as potentially protective, because it prevents reckless action and keeps you to your present portion. The top line’s king is not external conquest; it is the moment when clarity is so rooted that disturbing impulses lose momentum without being forcibly suppressed. This is not fate; it is practice with timing, knowing when to rest and when to act.
taoist.advice: Consider what you are clinging to for light. Nurture one small inner practice before demanding outer clarity. When confusion arises, slow down, study, ask, reflect. If tears come, let them inform without acting rashly. Let unwanted thoughts fall away by withdrawing their fuel rather than attacking them. Align with authentic nature and timing.
taoist.shadow: Forced brilliance that must perform while inwardly hollow. It rushes in suddenly, burns hot, then dies and is cast away. It clings to past noon, refusing to mourn or sing, and mistakes noise for illumination, attacking followers instead of the root.
taoist.reflection_question: What am I using for light before I have nurtured light within?
taoist.evidence_zh: 夫用明者，外明也。養明者，內明也。外明必本於內明，用明須當先養明，是以又畜牝牛吉也。

lines.interpretation: When fire first rises, eagerness outruns preparation. Liu Yiming says the step becomes confused because one uses brightness without first nurturing it. Caution here is not timidity but the beginning of learning: broad study, careful questioning, prudent reflection, and clear discernment must precede committed action. The line suggests that early missteps are avoidable if you pause long enough to see the path. If you feel tangled, return to inquiry; clarity obtained through patient attention prevents the injury that premature certainty would cause.
lines.reflection: Where am I stepping confusedly and need to seek clarity before acting?
lines.evidence_zh: 惟敬之、博學之、審問之、慎思之、明辯之，自始自終，了然於心，而後篤行之，方無錯然之咎矣。

lines.interpretation: Yellow is the central color, the hue of ripened grain and suspended judgment. Here Liu Yiming does not claim one is already bright; he values the person who knows their own dimness and empties the heart to seek brightness from the worthy. This is not self-erasure but an act of genuine receptivity. By showing one's lack and honoring another's possession, even the dull become bright and the weak become strong. The good fortune lies in trying to learn, not in pretending to know.
lines.reflection: Whose experience or wisdom am I willing to seek out with an open heart?
lines.evidence_zh: 自知不明，而能虛心下賢求人之明，是謂黃離也。黃為中色，明而歸中，示己之無，尊人之有，雖愚必明，雖柔必強，不失其柔順之本質，其吉在於能虛心矣。

lines.interpretation: This line describes brightness past its noon: the sun declining, the pot unstruck, the singer silent. Liu Yiming sees a rigidity that uses brightness without nurturing it, reaching the height only to descend. The old-age lament is not inevitable age but the refusal to honor the turn of the day. Beating the earthenware pot and singing is not forced cheer; it is accepting the season and expressing it. When you cling to a peak, you lose the center and harmony that would let you age with grace.
lines.reflection: What ending am I refusing to mark with grief or song?
lines.evidence_zh: 獨剛不柔，只知用明，不知養明，剛明太過，如日昃過缶之明，高極必下，明極必暗，是不能鼓缶而歌，則有大耋之嗟，不中不和，適以取凶而已。

lines.interpretation: Sudden fire that arrives without an inner hearth burns, dies, and is thrown away. Liu Yiming calls this being firm but not correct, unable to brighten the inner yet rushing to brighten the outer. The brightness that comes suddenly leaps over stages; nature becomes hasty, conduct one-sided. Seeking long life, one harms life. In modern terms, it is the forced breakthrough, the premature announcement, the radical change made from desperation. The line asks you to refuse the shortcut and return to the slow work of preparing the center.
lines.reflection: Where am I forcing an outer change because I have not done the inner preparation?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛而不正，不能明內，即欲明外，是突如其來如也。突來之明，躐等而求，性躁行偏，妄作招凶，焚如、死如、棄如，欲求長生，反而傷命。

lines.interpretation: Tears in floods and sorrowful sighs are here not defeat but a strange protection. Liu Yiming reads this line as dwelling in outer brightness while knowing inward insufficiency; one sees the principle imperfectly or lacks strength. The tears express that honesty. Because the person dares not act recklessly and keeps to their proper portion, the way still leads to good fortune. This is not glorifying despair; it is recognizing that grief can dissolve pretense and hold you back from harmful action until clarity returns.
lines.reflection: What current limitation or grief is quietly protecting me from a rash move?
lines.evidence_zh: 居外明之中，所當明內而又明外者，乃懦弱無能，或見理不真，或力有不及，是以出涕沱若、戚嗟若也。然涕沱戚嗟，不敢妄作妄為，自守本分，亦致吉之道。

lines.interpretation: The top line is not violence but root discernment. Liu Yiming says the true mind is like a king brightening bright virtue; the campaign removes the chief evil—the human mind—but does not seize the lowly followers, meaning it does not forcibly suppress mixed thoughts. When the root is cut, post-cosmic guest qi withdraws and transforms by itself. This is the mature use of brightness: still and unmoved within, responsive and connected without. Instead of fighting every symptom, clear the primary inner pattern, and the scattered struggles lose their charge.
lines.reflection: What root pattern, if honestly removed, would let my scattered struggles fall away?
lines.evidence_zh: 人之真心，如王明明德，如出征，明德而德即明，如有嘉功，除去人心，如折首惡，不強制雜念，如不獲從醜，用明而至折首之明，則後天一切客氣，不退而自化，寂然不動，感而遂通，內外光明，而無一毫根塵之咎矣。

confucian.title: Clinging Fire, Nurturing Compliance
confucian.essence: Every being must cling to something. Correctness in attachment yields penetration; cultivate compliance as one rears a cow. Doubled fire is continuing brightness, not mere repetition; clarity must be handed on through careful, reverent succession.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: The double fire of Li enacts the insight that clarity depends on adherence. Just as fire clings to fuel and the sun and moon cling to heaven, human understanding clings to chosen relationships, paths, and purposes. When attachment rests on central correctness and is cushioned by cultivated compliance, brightness can transform a wider field. But when attachment becomes anxious, forced, or possessive, clarity collapses into flame, grief, or exile.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Hexagram 30 as the necessary sequel to Kan: what is trapped must find something to cling to. He treats Li both as attachment and as empty-centered brightness. For him, every form and person cleaves to something; human flourishing comes only when that clinging is upright. The judgment's cow points to the utmost compliance, developed through practice. Doubled fire means brightness continuing from one bearer to another: ruler and minister, generation to generation. Line by line, he warns against impulsive movement, praises centered yellow beauty, accepts decline as constant principle, rejects violent succession, honors anxious reverence in a vulnerable ruler, and restricts punitive force to ringleaders.
confucian.modern_meaning: Read as mirror rather than prediction, this hexagram asks what you are clinging to—relationship, belief, role, desire—and whether that attachment is life-giving enough to be sustained. Clinging is not failure; fire cannot burn without fuel, and understanding cannot endure without commitments. Yet some attachments burn only themselves. Cheng Yi's emphasis on correctness invites reflection on the ethical quality of our dependencies, not merely their intensity. His cow image suggests that compliance is trained, not assumed: repeated small choices form a disposition. The doubled fire reminds us that clarity must be passed on, developed in succession, and made available to others, not hoarded as private insight. When endings arrive, the sage's way is not denial but honest acceptance of the shared pattern of waxing and waning. Grief may become wise when it opens into reverence rather than terror. And the top line's harsh justice is tempered: hold power accountable to what is central, and do not let necessary firmness slide into cruelty.
confucian.advice: Cultivate one attachment you can honestly affirm as upright, and practice its small disciplines daily. When a phase declines, name the loss without catastrophizing. If you hold influence, let successors see how brightness is maintained; do not force your way, and when you must act firmly, aim at the source of harm, not all who are entangled.
confucian.shadow: The shadow appears when clinging turns possessive, clarity becomes invasive certainty, or needed grief congeals into endless dread. Force that should protect becomes destructive flame, and discernment hardens into cruelty toward those merely entangled.
confucian.reflection_question: What are you clinging to, and is that attachment making you clearer or merely more consumed?
confucian.evidence_zh: 離麗也萬物莫不皆有所麗有形則有麗矣

lines.interpretation: Initial yang is drawn upward by fire's nature, yet still belongs below. Cheng Yi sees the crossed footsteps as impulse before position: movement has already begun inwardly. Reverent caution is not timidity but clarity about one's place; it prevents the blame of reckless advance. In modern terms, when a new project or desire sparks movement, pause to notice what you are moving toward before taking visible steps. What feels urgent may only be impulse.
lines.reflection: Where is your first impulse already carrying you before you have consciously chosen to move?
lines.evidence_zh: 陽固好動又居下而離體陽居下則欲進離性炎上志在上麗幾於躁動其履錯然謂交錯也雖未進而跡已動矣

lines.interpretation: Yellow Li, supreme good fortune. The second line occupies the center and is correct; yellow is the color of the middle, the beauty of patterned clarity. Cheng Yi does not praise brilliance that dazzles, but centeredness that forms beauty through balance. This line asks whether one's clarity is rooted in an ethical center or merely in cleverness. Present-day application: cultivate the quiet confidence that comes from aligning insight with fairness, not from standing out.
lines.reflection: What would it look like for your clarity to be centered rather than conspicuous?
lines.evidence_zh: 黄中之色文之羙也文明中正羙之盛也

lines.interpretation: The sun sinking in the west: when decline comes, the one who understands principle accepts it as constant, even joyful in what remains ordinary. The one who does not understand clings to fear and sighs. Cheng Yi treats this as the way of living toward death and change, not as a prediction of doom. Modern readers might hear an invitation to let phases end without desperate protest, and to find rhythm in the daily jar—the small repeated practices that carry life—rather than needing the sun to stay at noon.
lines.reflection: What phase in your life is ending, and can you meet it with ordinary joy rather than dread?
lines.evidence_zh: 以理言之盛必有衰始必有終常道也達者順理為樂缶常用之器也鼓缶而歌樂其常也

lines.interpretation: Nine in the fourth rushes upward, burning, dying, cast away. Cheng Yi calls this a failure of succession: one who would continue brightness must have yielding sincerity and compliant receptivity, like Shun and Qi. Instead, force arrives suddenly, scorching those above and destroying itself. In contemporary terms, this is the hot takeover, the impatient leap that ignores legitimate process, the ambition that burns its own support. The line does not promise doom; it shows the natural consequence of refusing the slow, humble work of inheriting well.
lines.reflection: Where are you tempted to force your way into a role rather than receive it with humility?
lines.evidence_zh: 以陽居離體而處四剛躁而不中正且重剛以不正而剛盛之勢突如而来非善繼者也

lines.interpretation: A ruler with bright virtue yet in a vulnerable position weeps and sighs, and this is auspicious. Cheng Yi explains: because the ruler is clear, the ruler can fear deeply; because the ruler fears, the ruler can preserve what matters. The tears are not weakness but sober awareness of danger. In present life, when responsibility feels exposed and uncertain, it is not failure to feel the weight. Naming the grief can steady the hands. The line does not promise rescue; it shows that honest dread, checked by reverence for one's office, can itself be protective.
lines.reflection: What vulnerability are you avoiding because you equate tears with defeat?
lines.evidence_zh: 唯其明也故能畏懼之湥至於出涕憂慮之湥至于戚嗟所以能保其吉也

lines.interpretation: The top yang is the extreme of firm brightness: able to illuminate evil and capable of cutting off. Cheng Yi warns that such clarity and decisiveness must be restrained by the center. Punitive action should strike only the main instigators; those dragged along or entangled should not be destroyed. Modern parallel: when using power of office, analysis, or public judgment, aim at the source of harm, not every person swept up. Firmness without proportion becomes cruelty. The praise goes to careful, targeted action, not vengeance.
lines.reflection: When you must act firmly, do you have the discipline to strike only the cause and spare the entangled?
lines.evidence_zh: 故但當折取其魁首所執獲者非其醜類則无殘暴之咎也

hexagrams.essence: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 30 as bright spirit, not raw intellect. True clarity begins by nurturing inner brightness through compliant attention; then outer action illuminates without burnout, and compulsive struggle falls away by root removal, not suppression.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: Clinging Fire shows luminosity that depends on what it clings to. As an archetype, it is the mind's ability to illuminate only when its center is empty and receptive. Fire above and below double the call: inner clarity and outer clarity must be one. Without fuel, fire burns out; without humility, brightness becomes glare. The archetype invites a disciplined yin within yang—radiance that serves rather than consumes, and that sees by first being willing to be taught.
hexagrams.historical_core: Liu Yiming treats Li as the empty-numinous qi of the Li palace, the human spirit and ruler of the mind. Using brightness is outer; nurturing it is inner, and outer must root in inner. The female cow is not mere passivity but utmost compliance that turns light back to shine within. He maps the six lines as stages of interior timing: premature use, humble seeking, rigid excess, sudden false brightness, tearful self-awareness, and kingly clarity that cuts off the chief evil while refusing to forcibly suppress mixed thoughts. The summary formula is knowing the male and guarding the female, firmness containing softness.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: In modern life Li can describe the relationship between inner clarity and outer presence. Liu Yiming’s warning against using brightness before nurturing it invites a pause before deciding, speaking, or performing. Tend the inner source through honest rest, reflection, and receptive attention. Brightness that leaps ahead becomes burnout; brightness that is nurtured becomes steady illumination. The female cow is not passivity but disciplined compliance—choosing what you feed and letting attention return inward. When confusion signals that you have stepped too soon, learning and careful questioning restore the way. When grief or limitation brings tears, Liu treats that as potentially protective, because it prevents reckless action and keeps you to your present portion. The top line’s king is not external conquest; it is the moment when clarity is so rooted that disturbing impulses lose momentum without being forcibly suppressed. This is not fate; it is practice with timing, knowing when to rest and when to act.
hexagrams.advice: Consider what you are clinging to for light. Nurture one small inner practice before demanding outer clarity. When confusion arises, slow down, study, ask, reflect. If tears come, let them inform without acting rashly. Let unwanted thoughts fall away by withdrawing their fuel rather than attacking them. Align with authentic nature and timing.
hexagrams.shadow: Forced brilliance that must perform while inwardly hollow. It rushes in suddenly, burns hot, then dies and is cast away. It clings to past noon, refusing to mourn or sing, and mistakes noise for illumination, attacking followers instead of the root.
hexagrams.reflection_question: What am I using for light before I have nurtured light within?

classical.name: Influence
classical.judgment_zh: 咸：亨。利貞。取女吉
classical.judgment_en: Influence: success. It is favorable to persevere. Taking a wife is auspicious.
classical.image_zh: 山上有澤，咸；君子以虛受人
classical.image_en: On the mountain there is a lake: Influence. The noble person receives others with emptiness.
classical.historical_note:
Zhouyi hexagram 31. The supplied source includes a variant note '一作「母」' for line 1's 拇, omitted from the translated line text; only the Great Image paragraph of the 象曰 is used for image_zh/image_en.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Influence on the big toe.
Influence on the calf. Misfortune. Abiding brings good fortune.
Influence on the thigh. Holding to what follows. Going brings regret.

lines.text_zh: 貞吉悔亡，憧憧往來，朋從爾思
lines.translation_en: Perseverance brings good fortune; remorse disappears. Restless going and coming, friends follow your thoughts.
Influence on the back. No remorse.
Influence on the jaw, cheeks, and tongue.
