lines.text_zh: 晉如，摧如，貞吉。罔孚，裕无咎。
lines.translation_en: Advancing but then thwarted; perseverance is auspicious. If not trusted, be at ease; no fault.

lines.text_zh: 晉如，愁如，貞吉。受茲介福，于其王母。
lines.translation_en: Advancing with sorrow; perseverance is auspicious. One receives this great blessing from one's royal grandmother.
The multitude approves; remorse disappears.
Advancing like a marmot; perseverance is perilous.

lines.text_zh: 悔亡，矢一作「失」得勿恤，往吉无不利。
lines.translation_en: Remorse disappears; whether losing or gaining (reading 矢 as 失), do not be anxious. Going forward is auspicious; nothing is unfavorable.

lines.text_zh: 晉其角，維用伐邑，厲吉无咎，貞吝。
lines.translation_en: Advancing by its horns; only useful for attacking a city. Danger, then good fortune and no blame; perseverance brings humiliation.

hexagrams.title: Progress
hexagrams.name: Progress

taoist.title: Advancing Fire, Growing Clarity
taoist.essence: Progress is not outward promotion but the disciplined inner advance from sincerity to clarity. By emptying the acquired human mind and preserving the Dao-mind, brightness grows naturally through obedient timing—not passive waiting, but active refinement of perception and motive.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Fire over earth images the sun rising above the receptive plain: clarity emerging from humble stillness. In Liu Yiming's alchemy, this is the 'advancing fire' phase—sincerity wells up as a hidden white within black, and the heart, emptied of acquired desire, becomes a clear mirror. Progress is measured not by outer rank but by the daily growth of authentic perception, a light that no external condition can injure.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Jin as an alchemical diagram rather than a social ladder. The lower earth trigram is the receptive, obedient path; the upper fire trigram is bright awareness. Obedience gives birth to brightness, and brightness is exercised through obedience—'from sincerity to clarity, advancing fire' (自誠而明，進火). The image of Marquis Kang receiving horses and three audiences is allegorical: the peaceful lord is the true heart, the horses are clarity, and the three audiences are repeated obedience that keeps out depravity and preserves sincerity. In its historical context, this used imperial and alchemical symbolism; the feudal hierarchy is context, not a present model.
taoist.modern_meaning: Today Jin invites a disciplined inner advance: first become still enough to see clearly, then let that clarity move through ordinary actions. It is not the passive 'go with the flow' of popular wu wei; Liu requires active effort—emptying the heart, distinguishing the acquired mind from the Dao-mind, and obeying the right moment. You may feel thwarted or sorrowful at first; these are signs that internal fuel is being refined, not that you are failing. Progress may come through borrowing another person's clarity, through group assent, or through quiet self-examination. The goal is not guaranteed success but a gradual increase of authentic perception: the sun rising over your inner earth. When clarity is rooted in sincerity, it becomes inexhaustible; no external condition can injure it. This is especially relevant when the impulse is to force visibility; Liu suggests waiting until the heart is empty enough to reflect what is true, then acting decisively.
taoist.advice: Consider pausing to identify what is truly sincere in you before seeking recognition. Cultivate trust by being at ease when unnoticed, as at line one. If sorrow arises, let it deepen stillness rather than provoke escape. Borrow clarity from trusted companions when your own is dim. Do not force brightness; empty the heart and allow the inner fire to advance at its own season.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is the 'shí-mouse' brightness of line four: a light that is real but narrow, mixed with self-interest, and prone to moral blindness. It can become overbearing or forcibly self-righteous, mistaking intensity for insight and alienating others through needless correction.
taoist.reflection_question: What would emptiness reveal about the part of your brightness that is still mixed with self-interest?
taoist.evidence_zh: 晉者，進也。卦德上離明、下坤順，由順而生明，用明而行順，順時順理，其明日增，故謂晉。

lines.interpretation: When first seeking clarity, do not force progress. Being pushed back or mistrusted is not failure; it is an opportunity to deepen understanding and build internal substance. Perseverance in quiet study or self-cultivation prevents errors because it lets principle be exhausted and the inner vessel be filled. Waiting at ease when unrecognized is the required discipline for later genuine advance; outward frustration is refining the fire.
lines.reflection: What inner work am I tempted to skip in my hurry to appear accomplished?
lines.evidence_zh: 初六，在明之初，大理未明，宜靜不宜動，是以晉如摧如，守貞而吉也。夫守貞而吉者，以其未能至信，先須窮理，充裕於內，運火自無差錯之咎矣。此未進明，先求其明也。

lines.interpretation: Sorrow appears when the environment is dark or others misunderstand. Do not rush to dispel it or force progress. By staying centered and refraining from external assertion, one allows inner emptiness and stillness to reveal what is genuine. The 'royal grandmother' symbolizes a deep inherited wisdom that emerges when you stop fighting the gloom. This line is about patience in obscurity and the strange blessing that ripens there.
lines.reflection: What hidden blessing might be ripening in my current sadness or lack of recognition?
lines.evidence_zh: 六二，處於三陰昏暗之中，不但不能增明，而且有以蔽明，是以晉如愁如也。然柔而守正，不為假陰所惑，不進而亦不愁，是以貞而得吉。蓋能貞則致虛守靜，真陰現象，假陰自化，如受茲介福于其王母矣。此處不明，不遽進明也。

lines.interpretation: Here progress comes through receptivity to others. You may not yet have your own clear light; by sincerely following someone or something with genuine clarity, a mutual alignment develops. Group trust and approval emerge not from conformity but from the sincerity of borrowing light. Regret dissolves when you set aside pride and allow wiser guidance to illuminate your path, while your yielding will remains firm in the right direction.
lines.reflection: Whose clarity am I resisting that could help me advance without losing my own center?
lines.evidence_zh: 六三，不能自下而順，乃自上而順，似乎不正而致悔。然性柔志剛，不順陰而順陽，借他家之明，以濟我家之暗，我順他而他即順我，是以眾允其進，有悔可亡。此己不明，順人之明也。

lines.interpretation: Having some clarity can be dangerous if it is mixed with self-interest. Like a nocturnal animal with small vision, one may see enough to act but not enough to avoid error. The peril lies in assuming one's own light is pure when it is still influenced by hidden bias or desire. This line warns against making decisions or asserting truth while in this narrow brightness; pause and purify motive before advancing.
lines.reflection: Where is my current insight still shaped by what I want to see rather than what is true?
lines.evidence_zh: 九四，居於明體，已進於明矣。但在二陰之內。明藏暗中，又應初陰，明而有私，邪正不分，是非相雜，以是進明如鼫鼠夜行，所見不大，其行不遠。雖用明得正，終有危厲。此剛而有私之明也。

lines.interpretation: This is the turning point: recognize both your own obscurity and the availability of real help. By emptying the heart of pride, you can receive substantial insight from another or from deeper practice. Once that inner fullness arrives, you no longer worry about gain or loss; good and ill fortune become transparent, and action can be direct and confident. Progress here is not acquiring more, but emptying to receive.
lines.reflection: What am I still holding onto that prevents me from receiving the fullness this moment offers?
lines.evidence_zh: 六五，居於二陽之內，既明其我家不明，又明其他家有明，借剛濟柔，本有悔者而悔可亡。悔由於心之不虛，若知虛心，則以己求人，即能實腹，既實其腹，則吉凶止足，如在掌上，可以失得勿恤，直行無疑，往而進火下功。吉無不利者。此虛以招實之明也。

lines.interpretation: At the peak, there is a temptation to use brightness as a weapon—against one's own inner demons or against others. The work of self-conquest is valid, but if done through willpower alone, it becomes forced and may lead to a narrow, rigid purity. True advancement of brightness requires not only conquering the self but emptying the heart so the process is natural. Beware of becoming a crusader whose light is sharp but brittle.
lines.reflection: Where am I forcing my own growth through harshness instead of allowing it through emptying?
lines.evidence_zh: 上九，剛強自勝，只知進明，不知虛明，是以維用伐邑也。邑為私邑，伐邑即克己之功。克己之功，虛人心也。若不虛心，獨恃其剛，強制強伏，必危厲而後得吉，得無咎，以是用明，雖克己得正，亦屬勉強，不由自然，未免取吝於大方。此剛而高亢之明也。

confucian.title: Sunrise over Earth
confucian.essence: Jin is the image of light rising above the earth: advance through bright virtue, not forced ambition. Steadiness, timing, and trust—both in oneself and in relationships—allow clarity to grow and be seen.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: The hexagram pictures fire above earth, the sun ascending. It suggests a moment when inner clarity and outer compliance meet: advance becomes possible through alignment with principle rather than personal force. Brightness is not hidden but made visible through steady self-cultivation. Yet each line warns against haste, greed, distrust, or over-scrutiny. The archetype is of faithful, luminous emergence that benefits others and honors the time.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Jin as the time of bright abundance. Li above Kun is the sun rising from the earth. In his social-political interpretation, an enlightened ruler above and compliant ministers below create the image of Lord Kang receiving horses and repeated audiences. The noble person therefore 'makes his own bright virtue shine' by removing concealment and extending knowledge. Cheng emphasizes that this is not outer display but inner luminosity reaching full expression. The feudal language is historical; it describes a hierarchical court order rather than a timeless political prescription.
confucian.modern_meaning: In present-day application, Jin speaks to times when one's abilities, values, or contributions can become visible. The sun does not push its way upward; it rises by nature, gradually and dependably. Likewise, influence grows when inner clarity is cultivated and aligned with trustworthy action rather than self-promotion. The image invites us to remove internal blind spots, develop real capacity, and let recognition follow appropriate timing. It also cautions against performing for approval, clinging to status, or micromanaging outcomes. Where the old commentary reflects a ruler-minister hierarchy, contemporary readers may translate that into transparent leadership, mutual accountability, and respectful relationships. The background of Cheng Yi is Confucian: self-cultivation in community, obligations shaped by role, and progress that must remain principled.
confucian.advice: Let clarity arise from steady practice, not urgency. If trust is slow to come, remain open and composed. Invest in genuine competence, listen to those around you, and delegate rather than control what escapes you. When influence grows, use it to brighten the shared space, not merely to secure your position.
confucian.shadow: Ambition that grasps at prominence becomes the fearful shi-rat; too much brightness turns into invasive scrutiny. Excessive hardness may achieve a narrow goal but loses the mean, leaving progress bright outside yet hollow within.
confucian.reflection_question: Where am I tempted to force visibility instead of letting clarity ripen?
confucian.evidence_zh: 君子觀明出地上而益明盛之象而以自昭其明德去蔽致知昭明徳於己也

lines.interpretation: Initial Six stands at the first movement of advance. Cheng Yi reads 'advancing as if, retreating as if' as the uncertain beginning: one may rise or be held back, and only correctness brings good fortune. Because trust from above cannot be forced, the line counsels composed generosity. Rather than anxiously campaigning for recognition, rest in inner poise and let trust form in its own season. This is not passivity but the discipline of not outrunning one's position.
lines.reflection: What would it look like to remain at ease while waiting for trust?
lines.evidence_zh: 苟上未見信則當安中自守雍容寛裕无急於求上之信也

lines.interpretation: Six Two advances with sorrow because it has no above support and does not force its way. Its strength is central correctness and gentle firmness. Cheng Yi says such virtue will eventually become visible; the 'royal mother' points to Six Five, the great brightness above, which will seek out worthy allies. The line suggests that grief over slow advancement can coexist with faithful self-cultivation. Blessing arrives through the magnetism of integrity, not through loud self-assertion.
lines.reflection: What sorrow may I be carrying that is not a sign to abandon the path?
lines.evidence_zh: 二以中正之道自守雖上无應援不能自進然其中正之德久而必彰上之人自當求之

lines.interpretation: Six Three occupies a compliant position at the top of the lower trigram. It has no central correctness of its own, but its advance is shared with others. The multitude approves, and regret dissolves. Cheng Yi observes that when plans follow the multitude and face the great brightness, they match Heaven's mind. This is collective consent, not peer pressure. The line celebrates advance through shared purpose, where one's private misalignment is corrected by a common movement toward what is right.
lines.reflection: Whose shared purpose is strengthening my sense of right direction?
lines.evidence_zh: 有順上向明之志而衆允從之何所不利

lines.interpretation: Nine Four is a warning. It occupies a high place not its own, greedily clinging to position while fearing the rise of those below. Cheng Yi likens it to a shi-rat: greedy, defensive, and never truly at ease. The danger is not in being watchful but in persisting in an unrightful stance. The line invites self-examination: if advancement feels like guarding a contested perch, the trouble is not other people's ambition but one's own insecure grasp. Reform remains possible.
lines.reflection: Where am I holding a position that makes me fear others' growth?
lines.evidence_zh: 貪而畏人者鼫䑕也

lines.interpretation: Six Five is the soft ruler whose brightness is matched by the compliance of all below. Regret disappears when the leader stops micro-managing and extends sincere trust. Cheng Yi warns against overusing one's own clarity to inspect every gain and loss; the way is to penetrate the aims of others and give responsibility room. This line speaks to wise leadership: the more luminous one is, the less one needs to prove it by controlling outcomes.
lines.reflection: What outcome am I over-inspecting that wants more trust?
lines.evidence_zh: 下既同德順附當推誠委任盡衆人之才通天下之志勿復自任其明恤其失得

lines.interpretation: Top Nine is hard at the extreme of advance, like horns that lead with force. Cheng Yi says such excessive firmness is unfit for general affairs; its only possible use is internal self-governance, where severity may cut away faults. Even then, because it lacks the mean, it remains shameful. The line distinguishes self-correction from public aggressiveness. A sharp edge can prune one's own defects, but it is a narrow instrument, not a way to illuminate others.
lines.reflection: Where has my toughness become useful only for self-correction, and not for shared flourishing?
lines.evidence_zh: 人之自治剛極則守道愈固進極則遷善愈速如上九者以之自治則雖傷於厲而吉且无咎也

classical.name: Brightness Wounded
classical.judgment_zh: 明夷：利艱貞
classical.judgment_en: Mingyi: It is beneficial to be steadfast in hardship.
classical.image_zh: 明入地中，明夷；君子以蒞眾，用晦而明
classical.image_en: Brightness enters into the earth: Mingyi. Thus the noble person, in governing the people, uses concealment and is yet bright.
classical.historical_note:
The received Zhouyi text for hexagram 36 (明夷, Mingyi) has lower Li (fire/clarity) and upper Kun (earth/receptivity). The judgment and line statements are from the base text. The Great Image is from the Xiang commentary; the other Tuan and small-image passages in the supplied source are not translated here. In the appended commentary, King Wen and Jizi are mentioned as exemplars of hidden brightness in hardship.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.text_zh: 明夷于飛，垂其翼。君子于行，三日不食，有攸往，主人有言
lines.translation_en: Mingyi in flight: trailing its wings. The noble person journeys; for three days he does not eat. Though he has somewhere to go, the host has words.

lines.text_zh: 明夷，夷于左股，用拯馬壯，吉
lines.translation_en: Mingyi: wounded in the left thigh. Use a strong horse for rescue; good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 明夷于南狩，得其大首，不可疾貞
lines.translation_en: Mingyi in the southern hunt: he captures the great leader. Do not be hasty in perseverance.

lines.text_zh: 入于左腹，獲明夷之心，于出門庭
lines.translation_en: He enters the left belly and grasps the heart of Mingyi, then leaves through the gate and courtyard.
Jizi’s Mingyi: beneficial to be steadfast.

lines.text_zh: 不明晦，初登于天，後入于地
lines.translation_en: Not bright but dark: first ascending to heaven, afterward entering the earth.

taoist.title: Withdrawing Fire, Hiding Brightness
taoist.essence: Mingyi teaches withdrawal of the alchemical fire: hide achieved clarity in dark receptivity, return fire to its root, and guard the elixir through hardship and correct timing.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Brightness enters the earth: the flame of realized insight is not displayed but stored. Liu Yiming calls this 'withdrawing fire' after the strong movement of Da Zhuang—turning the light inward so that it nourishes rather than burns. The archetype is hidden brilliance: a luminous presence that works from within darkness, remains unhurt by exposure, and returns to its source without trace.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 36 within inner alchemy. He distinguishes yi as both 'hiding' and 'injury,' and sees Kun above Li below as brightness within yielding. After advancing fire to attain clarity, one must withdraw it to a secret place; brightness must not be used lightly. Fire-times are decisive: too little fire cannot form the elixir, too much injures it. Once the elixir forms, one stops the fire, bathes and warms it, and hides brightness in soundlessness. The line texts become stages of withdrawing before injury, rescuing after injury, operating true fire, entering no-mind, and guarding true fire.
taoist.modern_meaning: Modern application reframes the alchemical instruction as a question of rhythm after intensity. When a person has worked hard, gained insight, or become visible, Mingyi suggests storing some of that light rather than letting it burn publicly. This is not passive non-action; Liu explicitly says having brightness and not using it is not empty non-doing. It requires guarding against danger and gathering inward at difficult places. In contemporary life this might mean protecting a creative project from premature critique, softening self-promotion, or leaving space for recovery without abandoning discipline. The ancient fire is a metaphor for inner heat, focus, or passion; too little cannot mature the work, too much damages it. The line readings become stages: early withdrawal, rescue after injury, patient transformation, hidden nourishment, steady center, and the risk of refusing to stop. All are invitations to notice timing, not predictions of outcome.
taoist.advice: Notice where brightness is being spent too openly. Consider withdrawing attention from display and placing it in a protected inner space. Let the work mature before speaking. When criticism comes, register it as surface injury while preserving the inner flame. Do not force; but stay steadily disciplined.
taoist.shadow: If brightness is withdrawn only out of fear or laziness, it can curdle into obscurity—not hidden light but lost light. Overwithdrawal may become evasion, and excessive fire may injure the very clarity one meant to keep.
taoist.reflection_question: Where might your brightest impulse need a season of hidden warmth rather than public exposure?
taoist.evidence_zh: 退火者，藏明於至幽至密之處，而不輕自用也。

lines.interpretation: At the first sign of danger, before visible harm, the bright one lowers its wings. Liu sees this as withdrawing fire before injury. The noble person journeys without eating, aware that withdrawing after the sacred embryo has formed invites misunderstanding and slander. The surface may be criticized, but the inner core remains whole. This is not passive hiding; it is quick, deliberate retreat from premature exposure.
lines.reflection: What early signal is asking you to lower your wings before harm appears?
lines.evidence_zh: 垂翼之飛，不食而往，明於退而急退者。

lines.interpretation: The wound has appeared—brightness is hurt in the left thigh, a sign of limping progress. Liu says yielding emptiness allows immediate recognition and urgent rescue with a strong horse. The error was delay in withdrawing; remedial action can still prevent greater injury. Good fortune belongs to quick, humble correction, not to denying the wound. Withdrawing at the moment of injury requires both soft awareness and strong assistance.
lines.reflection: Where have you delayed a needed withdrawal, and what strong support could still help?
lines.evidence_zh: 用壯馬急拯其不能早退之失，可不至於大傷其明，亦致吉之道。

lines.interpretation: Firmness and clarity combine here. Liu says natural true fire forges away the chief evil of the human mind—the conscious spirit that keeps rebirth alive. This is not a quick purge; trying to remove it too fiercely stirs false fire and harms the true person. The southern hunt captures the great chief, but one must not be hasty. Gradual transformation, not violence, protects brightness while the root pattern is dissolved.
lines.reflection: What ingrained pattern can be dissolved only by steady heat, not by sudden force?
lines.evidence_zh: 惟不可疾貞，漸次化之，人心終有消滅之時。此運真火而明不傷也。

lines.interpretation: Brightness is nourished in the most secret inward place, like entering the left belly where nothing is seen or known. Liu calls this withdrawing false fire: one moves from having mind to no-mind, and false fire has no place to arise. Leaving the gate and courtyard means exiting the domain of visible effort. The heart of Mingyi is found not by seeking more light, but by entering the hidden chamber and letting ordinary cognition rest.
lines.reflection: Can you enter your own hidden chamber without needing to know what will happen there?
lines.evidence_zh: 出有心而入無心，一切邪火，焉得而發之。此退假火而明不傷也。

lines.interpretation: The fifth line is Jizi's Mingyi: guarding the center and embracing unity, not using brightness at all, yet brightness remains. Liu says within there is natural true fire, the furnace blazes ever red. Outwardly insufficient, inwardly abundant. This is not weakness but the culmination of nourishing true fire—steadfastness that keeps the inner light constant while the outer person may appear diminished. It benefits from firm perseverance.
lines.reflection: What could it look like to be outwardly unremarkable while keeping an inner furnace steady?
lines.evidence_zh: 守中抱一，絕不用明，而明常存，所謂內有天然真火，爐中赫赫長紅，如箕子之明夷，利在於貞也。

lines.interpretation: The top line warns against ignoring the fire-times. Knowing only how to push brightness forward and not how to reverse and store it, one becomes not bright but dark. First ascending to heaven, then falling into earth: the elixir is obtained and lost. Liu calls this the ruin of previous work. Overreaching clarity without the discipline of withdrawal ends in injury. Brightness must know its own evening.
lines.reflection: Where might continued pushing turn previous gains into loss?
lines.evidence_zh: 如初登於天而進明，後入於地而傷明，金丹得而復失，前功俱廢矣。

confucian.title: Brightness Hidden in Earth
confucian.essence: When clarity meets a hostile environment, outer concealment may guard inner light; hardship becomes discipline for preserving what is right without pretending the wound is absent.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: The archetype is the clear-sighted person moving through a damaged or darkened order. Brightness is not extinguished but goes underground: outer compliance protects inner principle, and timely restraint prevents useless harm. King Wen and Jizi model two shapes of this—serving without losing inner light, or hiding brilliance to remain upright. It is not passive withdrawal but a discipline of staying whole under pressure.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads the hexagram as brightness entering the earth: Li beneath Kun, the sun wounded into obscurity. He interprets King Wen as one whose inner civilized virtue remained intact while he outwardly complied with a benighted ruler, and Jizi as one who feigned madness to guard his correctness. The commentary warns rulers against excessive scrutiny and ministers against devious influence. Its examples reflect a hierarchical, dynasty-centered world; the enduring principle is ethical self-protection and timing rather than blind loyalty or open defiance.
confucian.modern_meaning: In contemporary life, Mingyi can name a season when speaking openly is punished: a toxic workplace, a polarized community, a family system that cannot tolerate truth. The text does not promise rescue, though the final line depicts a fall into darkness for those who lose the Way. It invites you to practice intelligent concealment—not lying, but not exposing your deepest commitments where they may only be used against you. Inner clarity can remain while outer visibility recedes. You might buy time, preserve relationships needed for later action, or choose indirect influence. The hexagram advises against forced moral correction; entrenched habits rarely change through sudden confrontation. Instead, keep your own standards firm, choose your moments, and avoid becoming the darkness you resist. This is not passivity but a disciplined holding of light in a season that cannot yet bear it.
confucian.advice: Notice early signals before harm becomes obvious. When openness only wounds, lower the flame but keep the wick lit. Use available supports to move if needed. If you stay close to a harmful center, hold inner correctness while softening outward brilliance. Reform gradually, not by coercion.
confucian.shadow: Concealment may slide into self-erasure, cynicism, or complicity. Hidden brightness can become lost brightness if outward dimming is not matched by inner constancy over time.
confucian.reflection_question: Where am I using visible light in ways that wound rather than protect what I most need to honor?
confucian.evidence_zh: 君子當明夷之時利在知艱難而不失其貞正也

lines.interpretation: At the first sign of injury, before the trouble is obvious, the wise response is to leave early. Others may think you are overreacting or disloyal, because they cannot see what you see. This is not fear; it is discernment of incipient harm. You may need to step back from a role, project, or relationship while there is still room to move. Not eating for three days images the cost, but that cost is better than being trapped. Trust your reading of the small signals, even when the group doubts you.
lines.reflection: What early warning have I noticed but let others talk me out of taking seriously?
lines.evidence_zh: 君子見幾故亟去之

lines.interpretation: An injury has occurred, but it is not yet disabling—the left thigh is hurt, not the center of movement. Cheng Yi sees this as the good fortune of a person who manages themselves well enough to limit the damage. The strong horse is a swift means of rescue: a resource, ally, or practice that carries you away before deeper harm. This line does not promise accomplishment in the dark time, only escape from worse injury. Act quickly, use what is available, and do not linger trying to fix the system from a weakened position.
lines.reflection: What strong horse—a trusted ally, a practical exit, a daily practice—can carry me away from this situation while I still have strength?
lines.evidence_zh: 君子為隂闇所傷其自處有道故其傷不甚自拯有道故獲免之疾

lines.interpretation: Here brightness confronts the source of darkness directly. Cheng Yi likens it to a justified hunt that captures the chief offender—an image of overthrowing a tyrant or removing a destructive leader. But the line warns against rushing the moral cleanup. Old corrupt ways have soaked into people and institutions; sudden reform creates only panic and resistance. Even when you are right, proceed gradually. The victory is not in destroying the person but in removing the harm while leaving room for others to change.
lines.reflection: Where am I tempted to force a long-overdue correction too quickly, risking a backlash that would undo the very change I seek?
lines.evidence_zh: 誅其元惡舊染汚俗未能遽革必有其漸

lines.interpretation: This line describes a different kind of injury: not open attack but infiltration. A devious person enters through private, hidden channels—the left belly—and captures the heart of the ruler before acting outwardly. Cheng Yi warns that such influence is never built through open principle but through flattery and secret access. For you, this may be a signal to examine where power is being manipulated behind closed doors, or to check your own motives when you are tempted to win someone over by appealing to their unexamined desires.
lines.reflection: Where is private influence shaping a decision or relationship, and is that influence serving integrity or only serving control?
lines.evidence_zh: 四由隱僻之道深入其君故云入于左腹

lines.interpretation: Jizi feigned madness and became a slave to survive the tyrant Zhou, but inwardly he never abandoned his correct intention. This is the line of those who cannot leave and cannot safely show their full light. Cheng Yi calls it not cowardice but fidelity under extreme constraint. The outward role is diminished; the inner commitment remains unbroken. If you find yourself close to a wounding center, you may need to hide your capabilities not to avoid responsibility but to keep them intact for a future that can receive them.
lines.reflection: What outward role or brilliance am I being asked to soften, and what inner commitment must remain unbroken while I wait?
lines.evidence_zh: 箕子能藏晦其明而自守其正志

lines.interpretation: The final line depicts the fall of the one who should have illuminated but instead wounded others. Brightness that once ascended to heaven now enters the earth—not as a hidden light but as darkness, because it lost its proper way. Cheng Yi sees this as the consequence of abusing clarity and power: the ruler or institution that refuses to illumine becomes blind. For you, this may be a caution about your own authority: when visibility becomes domination, it eventually destroys the capacity to see.
lines.reflection: Where has my own power or visibility begun to darken into control rather than illumination, and what would return me to genuine clarity?
lines.evidence_zh: 明既夷傷故不明而反昏晦也

hexagrams.essence: Mingyi teaches withdrawal of the alchemical fire: hide achieved clarity in dark receptivity, return fire to its root, and guard the elixir through hardship and correct timing.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: Brightness enters the earth: the flame of realized insight is not displayed but stored. Liu Yiming calls this 'withdrawing fire' after the strong movement of Da Zhuang—turning the light inward so that it nourishes rather than burns. The archetype is hidden brilliance: a luminous presence that works from within darkness, remains unhurt by exposure, and returns to its source without trace.
hexagrams.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 36 within inner alchemy. He distinguishes yi as both 'hiding' and 'injury,' and sees Kun above Li below as brightness within yielding. After advancing fire to attain clarity, one must withdraw it to a secret place; brightness must not be used lightly. Fire-times are decisive: too little fire cannot form the elixir, too much injures it. Once the elixir forms, one stops the fire, bathes and warms it, and hides brightness in soundlessness. The line texts become stages of withdrawing before injury, rescuing after injury, operating true fire, entering no-mind, and guarding true fire.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: Modern application reframes the alchemical instruction as a question of rhythm after intensity. When a person has worked hard, gained insight, or become visible, Mingyi suggests storing some of that light rather than letting it burn publicly. This is not passive non-action; Liu explicitly says having brightness and not using it is not empty non-doing. It requires guarding against danger and gathering inward at difficult places. In contemporary life this might mean protecting a creative project from premature critique, softening self-promotion, or leaving space for recovery without abandoning discipline. The ancient fire is a metaphor for inner heat, focus, or passion; too little cannot mature the work, too much damages it. The line readings become stages: early withdrawal, rescue after injury, patient transformation, hidden nourishment, steady center, and the risk of refusing to stop. All are invitations to notice timing, not predictions of outcome.
hexagrams.advice: Notice where brightness is being spent too openly. Consider withdrawing attention from display and placing it in a protected inner space. Let the work mature before speaking. When criticism comes, register it as surface injury while preserving the inner flame. Do not force; but stay steadily disciplined.
hexagrams.shadow: If brightness is withdrawn only out of fear or laziness, it can curdle into obscurity—not hidden light but lost light. Overwithdrawal may become evasion, and excessive fire may injure the very clarity one meant to keep.
hexagrams.reflection_question: Where might your brightest impulse need a season of hidden warmth rather than public exposure?

classical.name: The Family
classical.judgment_zh: 家人：利女貞
classical.judgment_en: Beneficial for a woman to be steadfast.
classical.image_zh: 風自火出，家人；君子以言有物，而行有恆
classical.image_en: Wind emerges from fire: this is the Family. The exemplary person's words have substance and his actions have constancy.
classical.historical_note:
Hexagram 37 in the received Zhouyi; only the base text and Great Image are translated, excluding the appended Ten Wings commentaries (彖曰 and line-specific 象曰).

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Guard the household; regret disappears.
She has nothing to accomplish; she manages the cooking in the household; steadfastness brings good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 家人嗃嗃，悔厲吉；婦子嘻嘻，終吝
lines.translation_en: The household is stern and severe; regret and danger, yet good fortune. Wife and children giggling and playing; in the end there is shame.
Enrich the household; great good fortune.
The king reaches his household; do not worry. Auspicious.
With sincerity and dignity, in the end there is good fortune.

taoist.title: Refining the Inner Household
taoist.essence: The body-mind is a household where essence, spirit, hun, po, and intention must settle into ordered roles. Refining the human mind allows the Dao-mind to appear, so disciplined inner attention becomes the root of authentic presence.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: This hexagram presents the primal scene of internal governance: fire below gives clarity, wind above gives gradual penetration. Like wind coaxing fire, clear awareness and patient practice must work together. The family is not merely kinship but the inner community of psycho-physical forces. Ordering that community—bringing scattered impulses into alignment with a central, quiet authority—is the foundation for any outward vitality, intimacy, or creative work. True steadfastness is not rigid control but the receptive discipline that allows genuine warmth to emerge.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 37 through Neidan (inner alchemy). The received Zhouyi says 'beneficial for a woman to be steadfast'; for Liu this is not primarily about literal domestic roles but about refining the self: the 'woman' is true yin, the household the human body-mind. Essence, spirit, hun, po, and intention are family members ruled by the human mind; refining the human mind lets the Dao-mind appear. Each line stages a phase: initial guarding, yielding inward care, firm severity, yielding-with-firmness, unified harmony, and dignified completion. Historically, this language draws on gendered and hierarchical imagery; those should not be endorsed as social norms, but understood as maps for inner transformation.
taoist.modern_meaning: In contemporary terms, this is a map for recognizing that you are not a single voice but a household of impulses, memories, and intentions. The clarity of fire and the gentleness of wind suggest that inner change requires both honest seeing and patient, repeated practice. Rather than suppressing the 'human mind' with guilt, Liu Yiming asks for gradual refinement: name what distracts you, set a threshold, return to the center. When the inner household is ordered, emotions can move without taking over; relationships become less reactive because the one relating is less internally fragmented. This is not passive quietism but active cultivation of attention, timing, and self-boundary. It invites you to treat daily life—work, conflict, care—as the household where the Dao-mind learns to preside. No outcome is guaranteed; the work is the practice of becoming a more integrated presence.
taoist.advice: Choose one inner pattern—a recurring fear, desire, or story—and give it a named place in your inner household. Meet it with early, calm boundary rather than harshness or indulgence. Pause before speaking or acting from that place; let clarity precede reaction. Let discipline be steady as wind feeding fire, not a crackdown. Gradually, the space that opens is where authentic choice lives.
taoist.shadow: When inner order hardens into severity, the household becomes brittle; the giggling, unruly parts are exiled rather than integrated. True refinement then turns into self-rejection, and hidden impulses await a chance to break through.
taoist.reflection_question: What inner voice is currently running the household, and what would it mean to let a quieter authority preside?
taoist.evidence_zh: 人之身，如家也。人之精、神、魂、魄、意，如一家之人也。

lines.interpretation: At the start of inner work, the self is still present, so the task is preventive: guard the threshold. Liu Yiming says that with a self one can restrain and control; the square inch becomes empty and open, thoughts do not arise, external things do not enter. Applied today, this means creating a small ritual of returning—maybe a breath, a pause, a walk—before the first reactive impulse gathers momentum. Regret is not erased by force but by early, quiet boundary. This is the discipline of beginning.
lines.reflection: What threshold practice would you most benefit from keeping?
lines.evidence_zh: 初九，在家人之初，剛於煉己，如閑有家也。有己即能防閑克制，方寸之中，空空洞洞，內念不生，外物不入，本有悔而悔可亡。此煉已於有己之初者也。

lines.interpretation: This line shows yielding inward care rather than outward striving. The text 'no external pursuits; manages the cooking in the household' becomes, for Liu Yiming, returning the gaze within: heart clear, intention still, not chasing outward goals. By stillness controlling movement, by oneness managing confusion, external things cannot enter. In modern life this is not withdrawal from responsibility but a reordering of attention—tend the inner nourishment first, then act. The quiet center prepares better responses than busy distraction.
lines.reflection: What would it look like to manage your inner 'kitchen' before seeking external results?
lines.evidence_zh: 六二，柔而中正，返觀內照，心清意靜，不專遂於外，而謹慎於內，以靜制動，以一禦紛，外物不納，客氣難入，如婦人在中饋而居貞，未有不得吉者。此煉己而用柔道者也。

lines.interpretation: Here the work requires firmness. Liu Yiming distinguishes two possibilities: if refining is diligent and scattered thoughts do not arise, there is a sternness like a serious household—regret, danger, and fear keep one from doing harm, leading to good. If instead thoughts are indulged, like wife and children giggling without household law, the path ends in shame. This is not about harsh self-punishment but about taking inner tendencies seriously enough not to feed them. The 'firm way' protects the tender work begun earlier.
lines.reflection: What thought-pattern needs firmer, non-negotiable limits right now?
lines.evidence_zh: 九三，煉己功勤，雜念不生，如家人嗃嗃，悔厲驚懼，不敢為惡，自然得吉。否則有念不去，姑息養奸，恣情縱欲，如婦子嘻嘻，略無家法，焉能到得無己之時？如此修道，終不成道，取吝而已。此煉己當用剛道者也。

lines.interpretation: This stage tempers firmness with yielding. Liu Yiming describes using the yielding to seek the firm, borrowing firmness to aid the yielding, neither clinging nor separated, gradually guiding. The result is enrichment—not merely material wealth but accumulating dharma-wealth and heavenly treasures; the empty heart enables a full belly. In practical terms, after establishing discipline, you can relax into a more integrated rhythm: boundaries become less brittle, and practice bears fruit in daily abundance.
lines.reflection: Where might firm structure now need a gentler, more gradual approach?
lines.evidence_zh: 六四，以柔求剛，借剛濟柔，不即不離，漸次導引。虛心即能實腹，富有日新，方且積法財、聚天寶，其吉之大，不僅無己而已。此煉己柔而用剛者也。

lines.interpretation: The fifth line represents centered authority: yang firm and obtaining centrality, the heart correct and the body cultivated. Liu Yiming compares this to a king who extends order from his household, and the world is naturally at peace; good fortune arises from naturalness, not forcing. This is not passive quietism but the mature stage where inner governance flows outward without strain. When the center is clear, actions align without constant effort. In relationships, this shows up as calm, non-anxious presence.
lines.reflection: Where in your life is inner order already allowing spontaneous, unforced effectiveness?
lines.evidence_zh: 九五，陽剛得中，心正而身修，如王者假家施治，而天下自平，其吉出於自然，非有勉強，何憂恤之有？此煉己而剛柔如一者也。

lines.interpretation: The final line seals the work with sincerity and dignity. Liu Yiming says one can trust that refining the self has dignity; being strict at the beginning naturally produces good at the end. This is completion with both beginning and end. In modern terms, this is the earned gravitas of a person who has done the daily inner work—not performance, but a quiet authority that others recognize. It is not about perfection but about consistency over time.
lines.reflection: What ending would you like to be able to look back on as sincere and dignified?
lines.evidence_zh: 上九，剛而居於巽體之上，可信其煉己有威如矣。煉己威如，嚴之于初，自能吉之於終，此煉己而有始有終者也。

confucian.title: Wind from Fire Within
confucian.essence: An inner hearth of clarity and gentle wind: the household is where self-cultivation first takes form. Ordered words, steady deeds, and respectful relations extend from intimate life into the wider world.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: Family is the archetypal threshold where private feeling meets right relationship. The lower trigram fire gives inner clarity; the upper wind gives outward, gentle influence. This image suggests an ethical warmth that does not consume but gradually transforms: love takes shape through roles, limits, and steady care, so that the home becomes a model from which broader order can grow.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Hexagram 37 through the hierarchical family of his time. He places the wife in the inner sphere, centered on the kitchen, and the husband in the outer sphere, with parents as the household’s awe-inspiring rulers. Correct roles, preventive regulation, and strictness over laxity are his central themes. He sees self-cultivation as beginning in speech and conduct, then extending from the household to the state and all under Heaven. This vision assumes a patriarchal order; its ethical weight lies in the demand that power be matched by self-rectification, sincerity, and mutual love, not in the social form itself.
confucian.modern_meaning: Today the oracle invites us to see intimate bonds as a practice ground for truthful speech and dependable action. In shared life, early agreements and clear boundaries often prevent slow erosion of respect. Daily acts of care—cooking, listening, budgeting time, keeping agreements—can carry as much weight as grand gestures. Firmness need not become harshness; the commentary suggests that a respectful structure can preserve affection better than endless permissiveness. Resources can stabilize a household when they are stewarded with transparency and shared purpose. Leadership within a home is less about control than about modeling the order one hopes to see: returning to one’s own words and conduct before demanding change from others. The ancient hierarchy is not a map for today; its live discipline is reciprocal responsibility, plain constancy, and the courage to address what is ordinarily left unspoken.
confucian.advice: Begin with the small domestic things: a clear agreement, a consistent ritual, a repair of a broken promise. Speak with substance rather than performance, and return to your own conduct before asking others to change. Let firmness carry warmth, and let warmth carry limits. If a pattern feels stuck, examine the boundaries and resources you have quietly neglected.
confucian.shadow: The shadow appears as rigid rule-keeping that mistakes control for love, or as indulgent warmth that avoids boundaries. It turns family into a stage for proving virtue rather than a shared practice of honest return.
confucian.reflection_question: What small, faithful act of home would I begin if I stopped waiting for the other person to change first?
confucian.evidence_zh: 正家之本在正其身正身之道一言一動不可易也

lines.interpretation: At the very beginning of a shared life, clarity about limits and roles is not coldness but protection. Cheng Yi calls for preventive order before habits harden. The task is not to control every detail, but to establish fair structures that keep affection from drifting into chaos. Early agreements about time, money, privacy, or the division of labor help prevent resentment. Because intentions have not yet scattered, a few explicit boundaries can save much later regret. This is a moment for simple, honest groundwork rather than grand declarations.
lines.reflection: What clear agreement or boundary would I want to establish before a small friction becomes a fixed pattern?
lines.evidence_zh: 閑之於始家人志意未變動之前也

lines.interpretation: This line honors the quiet center: someone who nourishes the household through reliable, repetitive care. Cheng Yi does not present this as weakness, but as a kind of softness that remains correct and central. Not every contribution is public; cooking, tending, listening, and keeping the daily rhythm can hold a family together. The challenge is not to disappear into service, but to recognize that such care is meaningful work. When it is offered freely from the center, it becomes a stabilizing power rather than an invisible sacrifice.
lines.reflection: Which daily nourishing task have I treated as mere background, and what would change if I did it with full attention?
lines.evidence_zh: 以柔順處中正婦人之道也

lines.interpretation: Here the commentary weighs two dangers: harsh rigidity and loose indulgence. A household ruled by severity may wound affection, yet Cheng Yi still prefers it to a home where no limits hold. The point is not to endorse cruelty, but to recognize that without respectful firmness, patterns of self-indulgence gradually dissolve trust. The line asks us to find a middle way that is neither punitive nor permissive—one where boundaries carry care, and laughter does not become avoidance. Discipline works when it preserves relationship, not when it crushes it.
lines.reflection: Where have I avoided a difficult boundary to keep the peace, and what has that avoidance cost?
lines.evidence_zh: 與其失於放肆寧過於嚴也

lines.interpretation: This line turns to material resources and shared prosperity. Cheng Yi connects wealth with the ability to preserve a household, but the foundation is compliance with right position—stewardship in alignment with shared purpose. Money and assets are not private trophies; they are relational tools that can create security or inequality. The oracle invites an honest look at how resources flow, who decides, and whether use of wealth strengthens or weakens trust. True enrichment includes non-material abundance: time, attention, skill, and fairness.
lines.reflection: How might my use of money, time, or space either stabilize or undermine the relationships I say I value?
lines.evidence_zh: 能保有其富則爲大吉也

lines.interpretation: This line describes a leader whose inner order creates outer confidence. Cheng Yi interprets the king’s arrival not as display, but as perfected presence: the fifth line is reverent outside while the second line keeps the inner home correct. The result is mutual love and freedom from anxious control. For modern readers, this suggests that influence in close relationships grows from self-consistency and genuine reciprocity. When both inner and outer life share the same values, there is less need to force outcomes; trust can be allowed to emerge.
lines.reflection: What would it look like for me to bring my public and private selves into one consistent practice?
lines.evidence_zh: 夫愛其内助婦愛其刑家交相愛也

lines.interpretation: The closing line returns to the root: sincerity and self-rectification. Cheng Yi warns that family life is full of emotional currents, where excessive affection erases awe and kindness can obscure rightness. Lasting order therefore depends on turning back to one’s own conduct. Dignity that is not first practiced in oneself provokes resentment; dignity that arises from self-examination invites respect. This is not a demand for cold authority, but for the quiet authority of a person whose words and deeds have become trustworthy over time.
lines.reflection: Before asking my household or close circle to change, what would I need to turn back and examine in myself?
lines.evidence_zh: 威如之吉反身之謂也

hexagrams.essence: The body-mind is a household where essence, spirit, hun, po, and intention must settle into ordered roles. Refining the human mind allows the Dao-mind to appear, so disciplined inner attention becomes the root of authentic presence.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: This hexagram presents the primal scene of internal governance: fire below gives clarity, wind above gives gradual penetration. Like wind coaxing fire, clear awareness and patient practice must work together. The family is not merely kinship but the inner community of psycho-physical forces. Ordering that community—bringing scattered impulses into alignment with a central, quiet authority—is the foundation for any outward vitality, intimacy, or creative work. True steadfastness is not rigid control but the receptive discipline that allows genuine warmth to emerge.
hexagrams.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 37 through Neidan (inner alchemy). The received Zhouyi says 'beneficial for a woman to be steadfast'; for Liu this is not primarily about literal domestic roles but about refining the self: the 'woman' is true yin, the household the human body-mind. Essence, spirit, hun, po, and intention are family members ruled by the human mind; refining the human mind lets the Dao-mind appear. Each line stages a phase: initial guarding, yielding inward care, firm severity, yielding-with-firmness, unified harmony, and dignified completion. Historically, this language draws on gendered and hierarchical imagery; those should not be endorsed as social norms, but understood as maps for inner transformation.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: In contemporary terms, this is a map for recognizing that you are not a single voice but a household of impulses, memories, and intentions. The clarity of fire and the gentleness of wind suggest that inner change requires both honest seeing and patient, repeated practice. Rather than suppressing the 'human mind' with guilt, Liu Yiming asks for gradual refinement: name what distracts you, set a threshold, return to the center. When the inner household is ordered, emotions can move without taking over; relationships become less reactive because the one relating is less internally fragmented. This is not passive quietism but active cultivation of attention, timing, and self-boundary. It invites you to treat daily life—work, conflict, care—as the household where the Dao-mind learns to preside. No outcome is guaranteed; the work is the practice of becoming a more integrated presence.
hexagrams.advice: Choose one inner pattern—a recurring fear, desire, or story—and give it a named place in your inner household. Meet it with early, calm boundary rather than harshness or indulgence. Pause before speaking or acting from that place; let clarity precede reaction. Let discipline be steady as wind feeding fire, not a crackdown. Gradually, the space that opens is where authentic choice lives.
hexagrams.shadow: When inner order hardens into severity, the household becomes brittle; the giggling, unruly parts are exiled rather than integrated. True refinement then turns into self-rejection, and hidden impulses await a chance to break through.
hexagrams.reflection_question: What inner voice is currently running the household, and what would it mean to let a quieter authority preside?

classical.name: Opposition
classical.judgment_zh: 睽：小事吉。
classical.judgment_en: Opposition: Small matters are auspicious.
classical.image_zh: 上火下澤，睽；君子以同而異。
classical.image_en: Fire above, lake below: Opposition. Thus the noble person is of like mind yet distinct.
classical.historical_note:
Source text from Zhouyi hexagram 38, 睽 (Kuí), lower Dui ☱ (Lake) and upper Li ☲ (Fire). The judgment and line statements are base Zhouyi text; the Great Image is from the Wings. In line 3, the character 𧤊 is accompanied by an editorial variant note giving 掣. In line 6, 說 is read as 脱 (to loosen).

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.text_zh: 悔亡，喪馬勿逐，自復；見惡人无咎。
lines.translation_en: Regret vanishes. Do not pursue the lost horse; it will return on its own. Seeing a bad person: no blame.
Meeting the lord in the lane: no blame.

lines.text_zh: 見輿曳，其牛𧤊一作「掣」，其人天且劓，无初有終。
lines.translation_en: Seeing a cart dragged, its ox pulled back; the man has his forehead branded and his nose cut off. No beginning, yet an end.

lines.text_zh: 睽孤，遇元夫，交孚，厲无咎。
lines.translation_en: Opposition and isolation: meeting a good man, mutual trust; danger, no blame.
Regret vanishes. His kinsman bites through the skin; going forward, what blame?

lines.text_zh: 睽孤，見豕負涂，載鬼一車，先張之弧，後說之弧，匪寇婚媾，往遇雨則吉。
lines.translation_en: Opposition and isolation: seeing a pig covered with mud, a cart loaded with ghosts. First he draws the bow, later he loosens the bow; [they are] not robbers but marriage partners. Going forward, meeting rain brings good fortune.

taoist.title: Rescuing Opposition
taoist.essence: When fire above and lake below pull apart, inner clarity and outer joy are misplaced. Small disciplined work with the human mind—not passive waiting—allows the buried Dao-mind to return and turns opposition into a secret bridge.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Kui is the archetype of mutual opposition: fire above, lake below, each moving away from the other. It names the state where joy is inward but not rightly expressed, and brightness is outward but not rooted within. The work is not to force union but to return clarity to its origin and sweep desire from the belly. In that disciplined reversal, separated yin and yang can communicate secretly; estrangement becomes a threshold to a truer meeting.
taoist.historical_core: In Liu Yiming's alchemical account, Kui follows Mingyi after true clarity has been obscured and the acquired human mind takes charge. The hexagram shows yin and yang separated, yet Liu holds that union is possible: 'if one can empty the mind, one can return brightness to within; if one can fill the belly, one can sweep desire outside.' Because the human mind is both the source of error and the occasion for recovery, 'small matters are auspicious' means first bringing the human mind into order. If this small yin work succeeds, the great matter of full union and completion can follow. Each line offers a specific strategy for rescuing opposition at a different moment.
taoist.modern_meaning: In present-day reflective use, Kui does not predict opposition; it describes a felt condition when inner clarity and vitality seem split apart—bright outwardly but unrooted, or pursuing alien desires while the heart grows dull. The images of a muddy pig, a cartload of ghosts, a lost horse, and a lane meeting can be read as ordinary moments of misunderstanding, suspicion, or self-betrayal. The work is not suppression or passive waiting; it is small, disciplined acts of recognition. See the 'bad person' or 'ghost' as one's own projected habit; restore clarity to its inner source; choose a modest road of repair. This creates conditions for reconciliation without guaranteeing it. In that sense, attending to small daily dishonesties and unexamined reactions is the auspicious 'small matter' that may open a larger union.
taoist.advice: Begin with the small, unglamorous inner task: notice the human mind's desires without feeding them. When suspicion or blame appears, ask what projected image is carrying your own unexamined habit. Take a modest lane of repair rather than forcing a grand confrontation. Let the lost horse return through restored inner correctness; the rain of clear seeing may then wash away what felt like a cartload of ghosts.
taoist.shadow: When the human mind's projections are mistaken for actual enemies, suspicion becomes a cartload of ghosts; the desire to fix others can become a hidden righteousness. In isolation, one may self-brand or cut off the very part needed for reunion.
taoist.reflection_question: What am I projecting onto the 'bad person' or 'ghost' that actually belongs to my own unexamined human mind?
taoist.evidence_zh: 睽者，彼此相違之義。卦德上離明、下兌悅，悅生於內，明用於外，悅非所悅，明非所明，悅明不當，故謂睽。此陰陽相隔，和緩調理之卦，承上明夷而來。明夷者，真明有昧之義。真明有昧，假明即出，識神用事，順其所欲，明於外而不明於內，性亂命搖，與道相隔，此睽之所由來也。

lines.interpretation: At the first moment of estrangement, the Dao-mind is just departing and the human mind is just arriving. Liu Yiming counsels firm self-restraint rather than chasing what has been lost: the horse returns by itself when inner correctness is restored. Seeing the 'bad person' is not about external enemies but about recognizing the five thieves in one's own human mind. Notice them without feeding them, and regret dissolves while opposition is still small.
lines.reflection: What lost part of myself am I pursuing externally instead of allowing it to return through inner correctness?
lines.evidence_zh: 初九，在睽之初，道心方去，人心方來，若能剛而守正，不為人心所惑，道心自復，有悔者可以悔亡，如喪馬勿逐自復也。

lines.interpretation: When yin and yang are in full opposition, harmful qi is strong and correct qi is weak; the Dao-mind is not easily met. Liu Yiming advises using firmness in a yielding manner, advancing along a small path and using the human mind to generate the Dao-mind. Meeting the lord in a lane means accepting an unglamorous, indirect opportunity for connection. What originally carried fault becomes faultless through humble, patient approach rather than forcing a grand encounter.
lines.reflection: Where is an unglamorous 'lane' being offered for a meeting I have been too proud or rigid to enter?
lines.evidence_zh: 當陰陽正睽之時，邪氣盛而正氣弱，道心未易相遇。然剛以柔用，從小道中進步，借人心生道心，如遇主於巷，本有咎者，即能無咎。此濟睽于正盛之時也。

lines.interpretation: Foolish self-will follows its desires like a cart dragged and an ox held back. Joy is sought outside rather than within, and one loses oneself before gaining anything else—like a branded forehead and cut-off nose. Liu Yiming calls this injuring the inner by serving externals, mistaking the false for the true. Though there may be an end in regret, that late regret is less useful than early honesty. The line warns against self-betrayal through external grasping.
lines.reflection: In my pursuit of outside approval or gain, how have I branded or cut off my own deeper nature?
lines.evidence_zh: 愚而自用，順其所欲，如輿曳而牛掣也。不悅于內而悅於外，未得於彼，早失於己，如天頭而劓鼻也。如此之人，務外傷內，認假失真，到頭一著，窮無所歸，始悔自錯，故無初有終也。

lines.interpretation: Yang is trapped within yin: the Dao-mind is buried by the human mind, the solitary yang has no support. Yet Liu Yiming says the subtle Dao-mind can grow if one is quick to learn, unashamed to ask those below, and mutually sincere with a Dao-holding friend. Through such exchange, the human mind daily recedes and the Dao-mind daily increases. Isolation can end through humble association; what had fault becomes without fault.
lines.reflection: Whose company or teaching, if I approached with humility, could help the Dao-mind grow while my human mind loses its grip?
lines.evidence_zh: 陽在陰中，道心為人心所陷，人心惟危，道心惟微，孤陽無依，是睽孤也。然道心雖微，若能敏而好學，不恥下問，交孚抱道之君子，彼此資益，人心日去，道心日增，久之人心化，道心存。

lines.interpretation: Yielding and empty-hearted, one stands between two yang lines: aware that one's own house is pure yin and that the other house has yang. Here one empties the human mind and seeks the Dao-mind; regret dissolves. Liu Yiming calls the Dao-mind the ancestor of the human mind. To take that root and transform the false is as easy as biting through skin. When the root is touched, going forward carries no fault; small sincere work releases large stuckness.
lines.reflection: What 'skin' of false identity can I let be bitten through to reach the root of kinship with my own deeper nature?
lines.evidence_zh: 柔順虛心，居二陽之中。既明其我家純陰，又明其他家有陽，虛人心而求道心，本有悔者，而悔可以亡矣。夫道心者，人心之宗，厥取道心之宗，點化人心之假，如噬膚之易，以是往而行道，有何睽之咎乎？

lines.interpretation: At the extreme, the Dao-mind has been buried so long that habits and suspicious projections arise like a pig in mud and a cartload of ghosts. The work is not to deny these images but to see them clearly as the harm of the human mind. First one draws the bow; then, recognizing the projection, one loosens it. The feared robber is actually a marriage partner—the human mind, seen honestly, can restore the Dao-mind. Meeting rain washes away old contamination and brings union.
lines.reflection: What 'ghosts' am I seeing in others that are actually my own unexamined habits, and how might relaxing the bow lead to meeting rain?
lines.evidence_zh: 處睽之極，道心埋沒已久，人不反顧，是睽孤也。道心埋沒，人心用事，習染成性，疑慮百出，如豕負塗，載鬼一車矣。

confucian.title: Estrangement's Small, Deep Work
confucian.essence: In opposition, fire and lake move apart; shared principle remains. Cheng Yi reads small success not as weak passivity but as disciplined, timely union through difference, indirect meeting, mutual trust, and the reversal of suspicion.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: Fire above and lake below move in contrary directions; two daughters dwelling together hold different intentions—estrangement assumes an original unity. The noble person 'shares with the common while preserving difference,' not sameness for its own sake. Heaven and earth, man and woman, and the myriad things are separated yet their work, longing, and kind correspond. Opposition is therefore not absolute rupture; it is a field in which principled differentiation can be held within a deeper commonality and eventually reunite.
confucian.historical_core: In a Song-dynasty Confucian reading, Cheng Yi interprets Zhouyi 38 as the principle of estrangement emerging after the exhaustion of family order. He grounds this in hexagram structure: fire tends upward, lake downward; the two younger daughters will marry into different households. His commentary assumes a hierarchical ruler–minister and male–female order, which we can treat as the language of his time rather than a present norm. What remains ethically live is his claim that division occurs within an original unity and that a junzi unites with common humanity while maintaining principled difference. He insists on active cultivation: indirect approaches, sincere alliances, and reversal of extreme suspicion, not passivity.
confucian.modern_meaning: Today, estrangement appears in families, workplaces, online conflict, and political fragmentation. Cheng Yi's lens suggests that opposition is not proof of hopeless difference; it may presuppose forgotten shared ground. The work begins with small matters that can actually be repaired—a conversation, a boundary, a shared task—rather than demanding total reconciliation. 'Meeting the lord in the lane' means indirect, respectful approaches that preserve integrity rather than flattery or coercion. Mutual trust between people of good will can carry intention even in danger. At the extreme, suspicion manufactures enemies and ghosts; the advice is not to ignore harm, but to question the stories we project onto others. When suspicion dissolves, relationship may be restored—not guaranteed, but made possible through honest, principled effort.
confucian.advice: Stay close to what is small and repairable. Do not chase what has temporarily withdrawn; create conditions for its return. Move toward others through honorable, indirect paths rather than forcing a confrontation. Trust must be earned and mutual, especially with allies of good character. When suspicion becomes extreme, pause and ask whether you are seeing mud and ghosts where there may instead be a potential partner.
confucian.shadow: The shadow is proud isolation: rejecting everyone who seems 'bad,' fabricating enemies from suspicion, drawing the bow too quickly, or using hierarchy to force compliance. Extreme clarity becomes paranoid overreading; estrangement then becomes self-imposed loneliness disguised as principled separation.
confucian.reflection_question: Where am I mistaking my own projection for another person's reality?
confucian.evidence_zh: 暌者暌乖離散之時非吉道也以卦才之善雖處暌時而小事吉也

lines.interpretation: At the first move of estrangement, regret fades because the firm line below meets the fourth, a fellow yang of the same virtue, though the two are not formal correspondents. The lost horse returns without pursuit: do not anxiously force recovery. 'Seeing the bad person' means remaining connected even to those who differ, not out of naivety but to avoid making the whole world an enemy. The ancient sage-kings transformed enemies into subjects by not cutting them off. This is active inclusion, not passivity.
lines.reflection: Whom have I avoided that I might need to see without endorsing their harm?
lines.evidence_zh: 古之聖王所以能化姦凶為善良革仇敵為臣民者由弗絶也

lines.interpretation: The second and fifth are proper correspondents—minister and ruler—but in estrangement their tie is weakened and must be rebuilt indirectly. The lane is a winding path, not corruption; it is the practice of flexible, honorable seeking. One clarifies rightness, removes obstruction, and uses sincerity to elicit trust. The goal is meeting in order to carry out shared work, not flattering or bending the Way. Integrity matters more than directness.
lines.reflection: What indirect, honorable path might open a blocked relationship without compromising my principles?
lines.evidence_zh: 所謂委曲者以善道宛轉將就使合而已非枉已屈道也

lines.interpretation: The third line is caught between two strong forces; its cart is dragged from behind and its ox held back from the front. It suffers injury—head shaved and nose cut—a vivid figure of being blocked and marked by conflict. Yet it holds to its proper correspondent above, and despite the bad beginning, union comes at the end. The commentary says one who joins through the correct Way has no ground for permanent estrangement; the worthy follows principle calmly, the wise perceive the incipient and hold fast.
lines.reflection: What wounds am I carrying from being caught in the middle, and what ending do I still intend?
lines.evidence_zh: 合以正道自无終暌之理故賢者順理而安行智者知幾而固守

lines.interpretation: The fourth is isolated, without a correct response, and surrounded by yin. But in this lonely position it meets a 'good man'—the first line, also yang, a companion of like virtue. Their bond is not formal but substantial: mutual trust born of shared character. With utmost sincerity joining above and below, no danger cannot be crossed. The worth of this meeting is that intention is carried out, not merely blame avoided; companions of good will can rescue the time.
lines.reflection: Is there a companion of good will whose trust I have not yet fully accepted or reciprocated?
lines.evidence_zh: 同德相遇必須至誠相與交孚各有孚誠也上下二陽以至誠相合則何時之不能行何危之不能濟

lines.interpretation: The fifth is a yielding ruler in the honored place, regretful because estrangement requires more than position. Its proper response is the firm and central second, called 'his kinsman,' who assists by 'biting through skin'—entering deeply into the sovereign's own person, not merely advising from outside. In a time of estrangement, unless one enters deeply, how can union occur? The commentary cites the Duke of Zhou and Zhuge Liang as examples of wise ministers whose deep influence enabled a young or weak ruler to act.
lines.reflection: Where am I being asked to let trusted counsel enter beneath the surface rather than remaining politely outside?
lines.evidence_zh: 當暌之時非入之者深豈能合也

lines.interpretation: At the extreme of estrangement, suspicion sees a pig covered in mud and a cartload of ghosts; what has no form is imagined to exist. The top line draws its bow against its proper partner, then loosens it when it realizes the other is not a robber but a marriage counterpart. Cheng Yi reads this as the principle that extremes reverse; suspicion, being delusion, cannot last. Rain is the harmony of yin and yang after the crowd of doubts dissolves. The good ending is not forced but becomes possible when projections are relinquished.
lines.reflection: Which ghost am I ready to unload from the cart so that a real meeting can occur?
lines.evidence_zh: 雨者隂陽和也始暌而能終和故吉也所以能和者以羣疑盡亡也

classical.name: Obstruction
classical.judgment_zh: 利西南，不利東北；利見大人，貞吉
classical.judgment_en: It is beneficial to go to the southwest; it is not beneficial to go to the northeast. It is beneficial to see the great person. Perseverance brings good fortune.
classical.image_zh: 山上有水，蹇；君子以反身修德
classical.image_en: Water on the mountain: Obstruction. Thus the noble person turns back to himself and cultivates virtue.
classical.historical_note:
Received Zhouyi hexagram 39: lower Mountain, upper Water. Traditional title: Jian/Obstruction. The source block also includes the Tuan and Xiang commentaries; only the Great Image from the Xiang is translated here.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Going: obstruction; coming: praise.
The king's servant is obstructed again and again; it is not for his own sake.
Going: obstruction; coming: return.
Going: obstruction; coming: connection.
Great obstruction; friends come.
Going: obstruction; coming: greatness; good fortune. It is beneficial to see the great person.
