hexagrams.essence: Increase ripens by adding the genuine and subtracting the false. Move with disciplined calm, increase the Dao mind and correct qi, diminish the human mind and acquired qi, and advance gradually until no fault remains.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: Wind above thunder images movement joined to gentle entrance. Increase is not piling up achievements; it is the patient, phased work of adding what is genuine while removing what is false. The aim is not endless growth but the point where there is nothing left to add or remove—a return to original wholeness through rightly timed effort.
hexagrams.historical_core: In Liu Yiming’s commentary, hexagram 42 is a manual of inner alchemical refinement. He holds that from beginningless kalpas, accumulated samsaric seeds make authentic cultivation necessary; it cannot be empty speculation. The work has fire-phases and stages. One must increase the Dao mind and correct qi while decreasing the human mind and heterodox qi, advancing gradually without haste or slack. Line two describes the union of yin and yang as a hibernating tortoise storing spirit; line six warns against trying to benefit others before self-correction. His ruling principle is increase by way of diminution, never passive quietism.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: Today this hexagram can be read as an invitation to slow, honest self-shaping. Increase is not necessarily more productivity, more influence, or more advice given to others. It may mean identifying what in your attention, speech, and habits is genuine and what is acquired noise, then feeding the first while gently withdrawing from the second. Wind over thunder suggests that real change needs both movement and gentle penetration—neither abrupt force without sensitivity nor endless reflection without action. There may be a season for correcting your own faults before you can be truly useful to others. Difficulty need not be merely endured; approached with sincerity and careful conduct, it may become a refining stone. The promise is not a guaranteed outcome but a path in which inner alignment and outer expression gradually come to support each other.
hexagrams.advice: Give your increase a foundation. First correct your own inner fault, then offer benefit. Let the work be gradual—neither hurried nor slack. When difficulty comes, use it to refine sincerity and careful conduct. If the urge to improve everyone before tending yourself arises, pause and return to the first task.
hexagrams.shadow: When resolve to benefit others outruns self-correction, the gesture turns hollow. A forced increase may attract criticism, and an unsteady heart loses the constancy that makes benefit real. Arrogance can disguise itself as service.
hexagrams.reflection_question: Where am I trying to increase outward effectiveness while neglecting a fault that only I can diminish?
hexagrams.editorial_status: integration-candidate — AI-assisted; final human review pending

classical.name: Decisive Breakthrough
classical.judgment_zh: 夬：揚于王庭，孚號，有厲，告自邑，不利即戎，利有攸往
classical.judgment_en: Breakthrough: Proclaim it in the king's court; with sincere call, there is danger. Announce from your own city: it is not favorable to take up arms; it is favorable to have somewhere to go.
classical.image_zh: 澤上于天，夬；君子以施祿及下，居德則忌
classical.image_en: The lake has risen above heaven: Breakthrough. The noble person bestows emoluments and reaches down to those below; dwelling in virtue is taboo.
classical.historical_note:
The base text of Hexagram 43 (夬, guài) is translated from the received Zhouyi. The Great Image is from the Ten Wings and is rendered separately from the judgment and line statements; the small-line images are omitted.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Strong in the front toes; going without prevailing is blame.
Cry out in alarm; at night there are soldiers; do not worry.

lines.text_zh: 壯于頄，有凶。君子夬夬，獨行遇雨，若濡有慍，无咎
lines.translation_en: Strength in the cheekbones; there is misfortune. The noble one is thoroughly resolute; walking alone, he encounters rain; if he is soaked, there is indignation, but no blame.

lines.text_zh: 臀无膚，其行次且。牽羊悔亡，聞言不信
lines.translation_en: The buttocks have no skin; his gait is halting. Leading the sheep, remorse disappears; hearing words, he does not believe.
The amaranth is resolute; walking in the middle is without blame.
No cry; in the end there is misfortune.

hexagrams.title: Decisive Breakthrough
hexagrams.name: Decisive Breakthrough

taoist.title: Resolute Cutting of Acquired Yin
taoist.essence: Hexagram 43 teaches gradual, discerning removal of acquired mental habit—the discriminating spirit—by gathering correct qi, refining the self, and waiting for the right moment; hardness must be tempered by softness.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: The image of five yang lines pressing upward against one remaining yin expresses the moment when clarity is almost fully restored. This is not violent expulsion but disciplined, timed resolution: proclaim at the inner court of the heart, announce from your own city, refuse armed haste. Breakthrough succeeds through sincere watchfulness and balanced strength.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming of the Longmen tradition reads Guai not as political declaration but as inner alchemy: 'the hexagram virtue is strong and harmonious: harmony carries out strength, strong but not violent.' The one yin above five yang is the discriminating spirit (識神) that must be cut off. Because this acquired spirit has deep roots, one cannot 'cut it off abruptly'; one must refine the self (告自邑) and wait for the proper moment (不利即戎). The process advances yang and retreats yin gradually, with both urgency and slowness, so original spirit returns and the Dao-mind is complete.
taoist.modern_meaning: This hexagram can be read as a map for working with entrenched mental-emotional habits. In present-day terms, the 'one yin above five yang' symbolises a lingering pattern—compulsive reactivity, self-criticism, addiction to certainty—that remains even after much personal growth. The text does not promise instant transformation. It advises first to bring the issue into the clear light of awareness ('proclaim at the king's court'), then gather honest intention ('sincere call'), acknowledge realistic risk, and work from one's own base ('announce from your own city') rather than seeking external battle ('not favorable to resort to arms'). Timing matters: some patterns soften only when the moment is ripe, and forcing them may feed what one opposes. The practice is disciplined, not passive; it asks for patient self-refinement, consistent attention, and the discernment to make small decisive cuts when opportunity appears. Each line probes a different stance—rash force, alert patience, impatience, self-doubt, divided will, and final release—so that one can locate one's own edge and choose a balanced path.
taoist.advice: Resist the urge to attack the habit in one heroic blow. Instead, clarify your values, tighten your daily routines, and watch for the small opening when the pattern shows itself. Act then with both firmness and gentleness. Do not over-water the seed of self-blame; simply remove what clouds the true heart.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is a compulsive inner critic that dramatises breakthrough but remains entangled with desire—excessive force, anxious vigilance, or paralysis before the final remaining flaw. It may mistake self-punishment for discipline.
taoist.reflection_question: What single acquired habit or inner argument is ripe for a small, decisive act of cutting away this week?
taoist.evidence_zh: 夬者，決也。卦體一陰居於五陽之上，陽將純而陰將盡，卦德健而和，和以行健，健而不猛，均有以陽去陰之義，故謂夬。

lines.interpretation: At the first movement toward inner change, the ordinary tendency is to charge ahead with pure willpower. Liu Yiming warns that such 'strength in the front toes' is one-sided; it not only fails to remove the acquired pattern but may feed it. This line is not a call to abandon effort, but to recognize that decisive cutting requires preparation, humility, and an honest assessment of one's position. Without that, apparent boldness becomes self-created blame. Begin by studying the habit rather than attacking it.
lines.reflection: Where am I rushing to fix something before I have understood its roots?
lines.evidence_zh: 初九，在決陰之初，獨剛不柔，冒然前進，是壯於前趾矣。前趾之壯，不但不能決陰，而反有以助陰，陽不勝陰，無咎而自致咎。此剛而不謹于決陰者也。

lines.interpretation: Here firm intent learns to be flexible. The line's alert call and night-time readiness describe a state of prepared watchfulness, not anxiety. When the internal opponent is still hidden, one keeps guard: regular practice, clear boundaries, and self-observation. This allows the discriminating pattern to be noticed before it erupts. Liu Yiming calls it 'hard yet able to be slow.' Do not rush, but do not sleep; maintain the inner watch and the timing will not be forced.
lines.reflection: What daily guard could I keep so that an old reaction loses its power to surprise me?
lines.evidence_zh: 九二，剛而能柔，儆惕自號，戒備嚴密，雖莫夜有戎，已伺於未發之先矣。何憂恤之有？此剛而能緩于決陰者也。

lines.interpretation: This line portrays a person whose resolve is visible in the face—too much heat, too much urgency. The path toward a clean cut is blocked by the very intensity; 'walking alone, meeting rain' means that harshness gets soaked and slowed by circumstances. Yet the commentary sees a saving feature: if the underlying intention is upright, the encounter with discomfort can cool the excess and lead to a harmonised resolution. The task is to convert impatient force into mature discernment.
lines.reflection: What in me is trying so hard that it creates the very obstacle it fears?
lines.evidence_zh: 九三，剛躁太過，急欲成功，壯氣現之於頄，宜有凶道，幸其以正去邪，為君子夬夬之決，但嫌其獨剛不柔，其行遇雨，若濡不能遽遂其志而有慍。然行既遇濡，始雖不能剛決，終必和決之，亦可無壯頄之咎矣。此剛而速于決陰者也。

lines.interpretation: Here the will to cut away is present but the foundation is uncomfortable: 'buttocks without skin' makes every step hesitant. The Dao-mind is burdened by ordinary human concerns, so decisions are postponed. The line does not condemn; it notes that if the true heart has not been extinguished, it can still draw on and strengthen positive influences. The danger is failing to trust the very guidance one has received. Change requires accepting support and acting despite awkwardness.
lines.reflection: What piece of honest guidance am I hearing but not yet believing?
lines.evidence_zh: 九四，剛居不正，道心為人心所累，如臀無膚，其行次且而決陰不果。幸其道心未抿，能以牽引陽氣而增長，本有悔而悔可亡。但嫌其不信決陰之言，道心中猶雜人心耳。此剛為柔傷，不知決陰者也。

lines.interpretation: This line sits directly below the final yin, the stubborn remnant of acquired habit. The mind is 'sometimes cutting, sometimes not,' pulled back by hidden attachment to the very pattern it wants to remove. Liu Yiming sees the contest as a hair's breadth: this side Dao-mind, that side human mind. Because yang is almost pure, principle can eventually prevail, but only by a sustained, determined choice made in the center. No dramatic victory; only repeated, conscious return to the true direction.
lines.reflection: In which small moment today did I almost choose differently and then slip back?
lines.evidence_zh: 九五，切近上陰，陰尊陽卑，道心為人心所瞞，貪戀識神，或決或不決，如莧陸夬夬。一時不能決斷其根然。

lines.interpretation: The final yin no longer calls out; its time is exhausted. In Liu Yiming's reading, this is not a disaster for the sage but the natural dissolution of the acquired discriminating spirit when the true yang advances. The line can unsettle if taken literally as a personal loss, but within this practice it marks completion: the old narrative has no voice, and without that voice it ends. Let the old pattern fall silent rather than dramatising its last protests.
lines.reflection: What would it look like to let an exhausted inner narrative end without giving it one more microphone?
lines.evidence_zh: 上六，在決之終，群陰退盡，只有識神一陰未消，其時當決，其勢必滅，陽氣一進，陰氣即化，是以無號終有凶。陰氣之無號，即陽氣之孚號，陰氣之終凶，即陽氣之終吉。此陽氣純全，陰氣悉化之決者也。

confucian.title: Resolute Cutting of the Last Remnant
confucian.essence: Five firm lines rise against one lingering yielding line. This oracle calls for public clarity, prior self-correction, restrained force, and persistent advance; even in strength, danger remains and requires vigilant warning.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: The lake has risen above heaven—pressure at the point of overflowing. Five strong elements move to expose and remove one final weak remnant. The image is not violence but a disciplined breakthrough: accumulated integrity must now become open, warned, self-governed action. Because the remnant still rides above the strong, the decisive cut must combine courage with restraint, never relying on force alone.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads the moment as noble ways increasing while petty influence fades. He says one should act openly in the public court so good and evil are clear, yet still warn the multitude of danger. First set one’s own domain in order; do not esteem aggressive military force; continue advancing. The Great Image teaches distributing benefits downward and not dwelling on one’s virtue. Line comments warn against rash forward movement, forgetful ease, private sympathy with the remnant, hesitant softness, inner attachment at the center, and the exhausted end of a harmful way.
confucian.modern_meaning: Historically, this text speaks within a ranked court society of rulers, ministers, and petty persons, and its language should not be read as endorsing that hierarchy. For present-day practice, it names a threshold in a relationship, institution, team, or inner habit where a lingering dysfunction has become exposed. The counsel is to make the issue visible in the appropriate shared space, but only after first correcting one’s own side. Warn those affected honestly rather than threatening; danger remains. Avoid militarized responses—literal aggression, brittle ultimatums, or performative toughness. Keep moving, but do not assume the last remnant is harmless. The lake above heaven suggests pressure that cannot be contained by denial; it is best released through clarity, preparation, and steady ethical advance rather than force.
confucian.advice: Place your own house in order before naming the fault elsewhere. Bring the matter into the open with measured warning, not threat. Avoid rashness and self-righteous force. If private attachment remains, sever it visibly. Advance steadily, and let the final pattern end through reform, not humiliation.
confucian.shadow: Urgency masquerading as courage; brittle self-righteousness; secret sympathy with the very thing one condemns; hesitation that chafes without moving; or an attachment to power that makes one’s center dull.
confucian.reflection_question: Where am I still bound to a pattern I claim to be removing?
confucian.evidence_zh: 告自邑先自治也

lines.interpretation: At the first moment, strength sits in the lower position and is tempted to lunge forward. Cheng Yi warns that this is restless movement, not principled decision. If one goes before measuring whether the matter can be accomplished, the resulting inability to prevail is self-created blame. The yin remnant may be weak, but one’s own impatience produces the failure. In practice this asks you to distinguish urgency from readiness: decide only after measuring the actual conditions, and do not let eagerness become a fault.
lines.reflection: Am I acting from disciplined readiness or from impulsive agitation?
lines.evidence_zh: 九居初而壯於進躁於動者也故有不勝之戒隂雖將盡而已之躁動自宜有不勝之咎不計彼也

lines.interpretation: The second line holds the center and is not excessively firm. It models alertness that is not the same as anxiety. Inwardly it harbors caution; outwardly it issues clear warning. Because this inner and outer preparation is already in place, an unexpected armed threat at night can be faced without worry. The point is not that threats are unreal, but that genuine readiness removes the need for panic. For modern life, this is the difference between cultivating disciplined awareness and rehearsing catastrophe. When preparation is real, worry can be set down.
lines.reflection: What readiness, if truly completed, would allow me to release persistent worry?
lines.evidence_zh: 内懐兢惕而外嚴誡號雖莫夜有兵亦可勿恤矣

lines.interpretation: The third line is strong but has a private correspondence with the very yin line being removed. Cheng Yi reads this as walking alone and meeting rain—an illicit harmony with the remnant. The noble person must be decisively decisive, cutting that private tie even at the cost of appearing soaked and indignant. The teaching is not self-punishment but clarity: you cannot claim to oppose a harmful pattern while secretly depending on it. If you emerge stained by contact, let that stain be visible and let your displeasure with it mark the separation.
lines.reflection: What private alliance am I still protecting while publicly standing against it?
lines.evidence_zh: 唯君子處斯時則能夬夬謂夬其夬果决其斷也雖其私與當遠絶之若見濡汚有愠惡之色如此則无過咎也

lines.interpretation: The fourth line is a yang line in a soft place, lacking firm decision. It cannot rest because others below are advancing, yet cannot move because it has lost its strength. The result is painful chafing and halted steps. Cheng Yi adds that even when told to pull itself along with the flock, this position cannot trust the counsel. The image of pulling the sheep shows the cure: join a larger, shared movement rather than standing alone. But that requires enough inner firmness to hear and accept help.
lines.reflection: What movement or support am I refusing to join, even though it could release my stagnation?
lines.evidence_zh: 臀无膚居不安也行次且進不前也次且進難之狀

lines.interpretation: The fifth line occupies the central place of authority but is dangerously close to the last yin. It should be the chief agent of decisive removal, yet instead it is attached. Cheng Yi says it must be decisively decisive, like purslane that is easily broken. Outwardly it can walk the middle and avoid blame, but the center is not yet bright; inner desire still dims its radiance. The task here is not only right action but the purification of motive, so that proximity and privilege do not erode judgment.
lines.reflection: What inner attachment is keeping my otherwise correct action from becoming fully clear?
lines.evidence_zh: 五為决隂之主而反比之其咎大矣故必决其决如莧陸然則於其中行之徳為无咎也

lines.interpretation: The last yin is at its exhausted end. Cheng Yi says no amount of wailing or fear can preserve what is already depleted. Yet he also refuses to read this as a call to harm persons. The way of the petty person must die, but that can occur through reform and transformation rather than annihilation. When a pattern has lost its sustaining principle, grief alone cannot extend it. The present task is to allow an outdated way to end without turning the moment into cruelty or triumphalism.
lines.reflection: What am I prolonging that has already lost its principle and needs to be released?
lines.evidence_zh: 夬者小人之道消亡之時也决去小人之道豈必盡誅之乎使之變革乃小人之道亡也道亡乃其凶也

hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: The image of five yang lines pressing upward against one remaining yin expresses the moment when clarity is almost fully restored. This is not violent expulsion but disciplined, timed resolution: proclaim at the inner court of the heart, announce from your own city, refuse armed haste. Breakthrough succeeds through sincere watchfulness and balanced strength.
hexagrams.historical_core: Liu Yiming of the Longmen tradition reads Guai not as political declaration but as inner alchemy: 'the hexagram virtue is strong and harmonious: harmony carries out strength, strong but not violent.' The one yin above five yang is the discriminating spirit (識神) that must be cut off. Because this acquired spirit has deep roots, one cannot 'cut it off abruptly'; one must refine the self (告自邑) and wait for the proper moment (不利即戎). The process advances yang and retreats yin gradually, with both urgency and slowness, so original spirit returns and the Dao-mind is complete.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: This hexagram can be read as a map for working with entrenched mental-emotional habits. In present-day terms, the 'one yin above five yang' symbolises a lingering pattern—compulsive reactivity, self-criticism, addiction to certainty—that remains even after much personal growth. The text does not promise instant transformation. It advises first to bring the issue into the clear light of awareness ('proclaim at the king's court'), then gather honest intention ('sincere call'), acknowledge realistic risk, and work from one's own base ('announce from your own city') rather than seeking external battle ('not favorable to resort to arms'). Timing matters: some patterns soften only when the moment is ripe, and forcing them may feed what one opposes. The practice is disciplined, not passive; it asks for patient self-refinement, consistent attention, and the discernment to make small decisive cuts when opportunity appears. Each line probes a different stance—rash force, alert patience, impatience, self-doubt, divided will, and final release—so that one can locate one's own edge and choose a balanced path.
hexagrams.advice: Resist the urge to attack the habit in one heroic blow. Instead, clarify your values, tighten your daily routines, and watch for the small opening when the pattern shows itself. Act then with both firmness and gentleness. Do not over-water the seed of self-blame; simply remove what clouds the true heart.
hexagrams.shadow: The shadow is a compulsive inner critic that dramatises breakthrough but remains entangled with desire—excessive force, anxious vigilance, or paralysis before the final remaining flaw. It may mistake self-punishment for discipline.
hexagrams.reflection_question: What single acquired habit or inner argument is ripe for a small, decisive act of cutting away this week?

lines.text_zh: 系于金柅，貞吉，有攸往，見凶，羸豕，孚，蹢躅一作「𨅙𨄃」。

The buttocks have no skin; one walks with difficulty. Danger, but no great blame.
lines.text_zh: 臀无膚，其行次且，厲，无大咎。

Wrapping melons with qi tree; harboring hidden excellence; something falls from heaven.

taoist.title: Guarding the First Stirring
taoist.essence: At the peak of clear yang, one small yin arises without announcement. Gou teaches early, disciplined containment—not suppression, not indulgence—so the subtle stirring can be met and transformed before it scatters the whole.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Gou is the encounter that happens without appointment: one yin arises beneath five yang just as strength reaches its full expression. The archetype warns that peak clarity contains the seed of its own turning; the task is to meet that seed with early, clear-eyed restraint, neither fearing it nor feeding it, so the strong can remain whole.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 44 as a warning within inner alchemy: after yang has been increased to fullness, one yin secretly arises beneath the five yang lines. He calls it a hexagram of guarding yin and protecting yang, continuing from Increase (42). The ideal is not to destroy yin but to borrow yin to preserve yang, reversing the post-heaven course. The lines are graded by whether and when one guards against yin: early prevention (line 2) and centered correct transformation that uses yin without being used by yin (line 5) are praised; self-reliance, negligence, indulgence, or overbearing rigidity lead to injury or loss of the golden elixir.
taoist.modern_meaning: In present-day practice, Gou names not a literal woman but any fresh yin tendency that appears quietly after a peak of clarity or success: a small excuse, an unexamined resentment, a mental drift that feels too slight to matter. The historical text speaks of guarding yang; today that can mean protecting the clear, warm, committed intention from being quietly colonized by the first flicker of avoidance or appetite. Liu Yiming's counsel is not to become paranoid or to repress the yin. Early noticing, like binding a cart to a brake, prevents a tiny restlessness from becoming a herd. In moments of strength, it is tempting to ignore the first descent; the practice is to remain sober and gentle, not to wait until the fish has left the wrapper. This is active inner cultivation: discern the barely visible, contain it without cruelty, and let centered presence transform it.
taoist.advice: Notice the first small turning away from clarity. Treat it as a signal for early, gentle restraint rather than as an enemy to suppress. If a restlessness is already stirring, do not dramatize it; return to a simple, steady practice, giving it no further food. In moments of strength, be especially watchful: peaks are where the quiet descent begins.
taoist.shadow: Spiritual pride that enjoys being above weakness, or fear that turns every small inner movement into a threat. The hidden danger is not the yin itself but the neglect or rigidity that lets a tiny stirring become a wandering compulsion.
taoist.reflection_question: What is the barely visible yin I am tempted to call too small to attend to just now?
taoist.evidence_zh: 此防陰保陽之卦，承上益卦而來。

lines.interpretation: At the first moment, a single yin line stirs beneath five strong yang. The commentary reads this not as a threat to be crushed but as a cue for early restraint: the metal brake is an inner discipline that stops the cart before movement scatters the yang. The danger lies in underestimating the subtle impulse; like a lean sow, a small restlessness can stir companions. Preservation lies in steady integrity, not in dramatic intervention.
lines.reflection: What first small restlessness am I tempted to dismiss as too slight to matter?
lines.evidence_zh: 初六，一陰潛生，其力足以敵五陽，如金柅能以止車於不行。

lines.interpretation: The second line shows firmness expressing itself through gentleness. It does not attack yin or pretend it is absent; it notices the fish while it is still contained. Vigilance here is quiet and exact, not anxious; because the host sees it early, the fish cannot do harm. The advantage is with the host, not the guest.
lines.reflection: Where can firmness in me learn to act through gentleness instead of force?
lines.evidence_zh: 九二，剛以柔用，戒慎恐懼，能防始生之陰，如魚在包中不能為害，其利在主不在賓，蓋已伺之於早矣。

lines.interpretation: By the third line, the moment for easy prevention has passed. The sense of self has relied too much on its own firmness, so the arising yin has already mixed with awareness; walking is halting because the inner ruler is no longer stable. Yet the line does not fall into blame if it accepts the labor of daily vigilance and honest fear. What cannot be removed quickly can still be contained through renewed discipline.
lines.reflection: What has already arisen that I have been relying on my own strength to handle alone?
lines.evidence_zh: 九三，剛而自恃，不能防閑于早，陰氣已發，制伏甚難，道心中人心相雜，如臀無膚，其行次且，主宰不定矣。

lines.interpretation: The fourth line describes a collapse of attention. The fish has escaped the bundle, and the commentary names the fault as failure to guard, not the power of yin. The real trouble arises from within: when the Dao-mind dims, scattered human impulses seem to come from every direction. This is not fate but an inner neglect that turns a contained stirring into wandering.
lines.reflection: Where have I stopped watching and allowed a contained impulse to wander?
lines.evidence_zh: 九四，剛而失守，不能防陰而縱陰，坐觀成敗，道心有昧，人心亂生，禍起蕭牆，如魚出包中，無所不至矣。

lines.interpretation: Line five is the image of completed inner order: the strong clear awareness does not fight the yin but wraps it, like willow covering the melon, while containing its own light. The commentary says clear hearing and clever discernment are deliberately set aside, not because awareness weakens, but because quiet radiance makes yin unable to approach. This is disciplined transformation rather than suppression: yin changes by being held within centered presence.
lines.reflection: What would it look like to hold a difficulty in quiet radiance rather than fight it?
lines.evidence_zh: 九五，剛健中正，天人混合，以道心而制人心，如以杞之陽，包瓜之明，黜聰毀智，光華內含，陰氣不得而近之，以是處姤，人力可以回天，陽氣不傷，陰氣自化矣。

lines.interpretation: At the top, too much yang has become rigidity. The commentary says the golden elixir is gained and then lost again, not because yin is evil, but because high, overbearing firmness missed the early turning point. This is a caution about spiritual pride: after strong attainment, the very sense of being above weakness opens the door. No external enemy is blamed; the loss is owned.
lines.reflection: Where has attainment begun to harden into pride or distance from my own weakness?
lines.evidence_zh: 上九，剛而高亢，不能防陰於早，陽極必陰，剛極必敗，金丹得而復失，自取其咎，與陰無咎。

confucian.title: The First Yin Stirring
confucian.essence: Cheng Yi reads Gou as encounter after separation: one yin begins below, small but capable of growth. Timely restraint, undivided sincerity, humble seeking, and central correctness shape genuine meeting; unchecked incipience or haughty distance brings harm.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: The hexagram pictures wind beneath heaven, touching everything, and one yin line below meeting five yang lines above. It represents the moment of first encounter—of a person, influence, opportunity, or pattern. Cheng Yi sees the fragile yet growing yin as something to watch carefully: what begins subtly can strengthen. The archetype calls for honoring the timing of meetings, guarding against premature or possessive attachment, and cultivating enough inner balance to meet others without losing one's center.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi comments within a cosmology of yin and yang: after decisive separation there must be encounter. He interprets the one yin at the base as a woman growing strong, warning against marrying her, and extends this to petty persons and barbarians whose power gradually rises. His line readings emphasize controlling yin while subtle, exclusive encounter, avoiding improper attraction, losing the people through lack of centrality and correctness, humbling oneself to seek worthies, and isolation through topmost arrogance. The Image teaches the sovereign to issue commands everywhere. The historical frame includes ruler-minister and husband-wife hierarchies, which should be contextualized rather than approved.
confucian.modern_meaning: Present-day readers can set aside the historical gender and political hierarchies while retaining the core insight: small beginnings shape later events. A restless impulse, an unexamined bias, a promising connection, or a leadership opportunity all begin as faint first stirrings. Cheng Yi encourages noticing incipience and acting while patterns are still pliable—not through anxious control, but through clear boundaries, faithful attention, and honest self-correction. Genuine encounter requires undivided presence; scattering to too many outside claims undermines trust. Where we hold influence, losing connection with those we serve often reflects our own lack of fairness or humility. The image of wind under heaven suggests that a meeting is not just private but can become a public blessing when commands and care reach all quarters. This is not passive waiting: it is disciplined readiness, inner sincerity, and the courage to lower oneself toward what one hopes to meet.
confucian.advice: When a new influence or pattern first appears, name it clearly and set a firm boundary if it leans toward harm. Give genuine relationships your undivided loyalty without shutting out all others from principle. If you feel uneasy in an attachment, withdraw and correct course early. Lead with humility and central fairness, not by demanding recognition. Sincere seeking prepares the way for worthy encounter.
confucian.shadow: Unchecked small influences grow into dominant patterns; possessiveness masquerades as loyalty; uneasy attachments linger through indecision; leaders blame others for their own loss; pride isolates, and the resulting shame is one's own doing.
confucian.reflection_question: What faint first stirring am I tempted to overlook, and what would faithful attention ask of me before it strengthens?
confucian.evidence_zh: 一隂始生自是而長漸以盛大

lines.interpretation: The first line is the single yin just born. Cheng Yi urges restraint while it is still subtle, before it grows strong. The metal brake stops the carriage before movement gains momentum. If allowed to advance, a small imbalance will gradually harm what is upright. The weak pig is not yet fierce, but its heart is already restless and leaping. In modern application, notice the first flicker of a harmful habit or unexamined impulse. Early, clear boundaries are not rigidity; they protect what is still formable. Timely attention at the threshold prevents a later, harder struggle.
lines.reflection: Which small restlessness in me is asking to be named and gently restrained before it gains momentum?
lines.evidence_zh: 制之當於其微而未盛之時

lines.interpretation: The second line holds the first close, like a fish wrapped in a bundle. Cheng Yi says the way of encounter is to be exclusive and sincere; the fish should not reach outside guests. This is not possessiveness but undivided loyalty. A genuine meeting, resource, or commitment loses its integrity when scattered among too many claims. He also cautions that yielding influences may not remain firm, so trust must be cultivated, not assumed. In modern application, give chosen connections full attention, protect what is entrusted to you, and resist diluting them by serving every outside demand.
lines.reflection: What relationship or work am I scattering by admitting too many outside 'guests,' and where is undivided attention needed?
lines.evidence_zh: 相遇之道主於專一

lines.interpretation: The third line is caught between the second, which has already met the first, and its own attraction to that same first line. Cheng Yi describes the discomfort as buttocks without skin: one cannot sit still, yet walking halts and hesitates. It should leave but cannot quickly abandon the desired object. Because the third is firm and correct, it can avoid great blame if it recognizes the impropriety, feels caution, and stops reckless movement. In modern terms, unease in a competing or inappropriate attachment is information. Hesitation prolongs risk; clear-sighted withdrawal is not weakness but correction.
lines.reflection: Where am I hesitating in a relationship or situation that I already know is not right, and what would a clean step back look like?
lines.evidence_zh: 若知其不正而懐危懼不敢妄動則可以无大咎也

lines.interpretation: The fourth line should correspond with the first, but the first has already met the second. Cheng Yi reads this as a wrapping with no fish: a holder of high position loses those below. The cause is not bad luck but the fourth's lack of centrality and correctness. When one is not fair and balanced, people depart; disaster arises from that rupture. The superior has caused the separation. In modern terms, when trust dissolves in a team, family, or institution, examine your own integrity before blaming others' disloyalty. Repair begins with self-correction and renewed responsibility toward those you serve.
lines.reflection: When those around me withdraw, what might my own lack of fairness or attention have contributed, and what can I repair now?
lines.evidence_zh: 四之失者不中正也以不中正而失其民所以凶也

lines.interpretation: The fifth line occupies the ruler's place but lacks a corresponding helper below. Cheng Yi says it obtains the way of encounter by humbling itself to seek worthies. The image is a tall qi tree wrapping a melon lying beneath: greatness stoops to serve what is lowly. This humility must be paired with hidden inner splendor—centrality, correctness, and utmost sincerity. Only then does the meeting arrive as if from heaven. This is not passive waiting but disciplined self-lowering that makes genuine encounter possible. Modern leadership finds talent in overlooked places through sincere invitation and inner integrity.
lines.reflection: Whom or what have I overlooked because it seemed beneath my attention, and how might sincere humility prepare a genuine meeting?
lines.evidence_zh: 以至髙而求至下猶以杞葉而包瓜

lines.interpretation: The topmost line is firm and high, like a horn. Cheng Yi says encounter comes from lowering oneself and receiving the other with harmony, but this line is haughty and rigid to the extreme. No one wants to meet it; its isolation is shameful, yet no blame attaches to others because the line itself caused the distance. In modern terms, when we find ourselves repeatedly alone or unapproachable, ask what in my stance keeps others away. The remedy is not self-abasement but willingness to soften, listen, and meet others partway without sacrificing principle.
lines.reflection: In what situation has my own rigidity or pride made me unapproachable, and what would softening look like without losing integrity?
lines.evidence_zh: 上九髙亢而剛極人誰與之以此求遇固可吝也

classical.name: Gathering
classical.judgment_zh: 萃：王假有廟，利見大人，亨。利貞。用大牲吉，利有攸往。
classical.judgment_en: Cui: The king approaches his ancestral temple. It is beneficial to see the great person. Success. It is beneficial to be steadfast. Using a great sacrifice is auspicious. It is beneficial to have somewhere to go.
classical.image_zh: 象曰：澤上于地，萃；君子以除戎器，戒不虞。
classical.image_en: The lake rises above the earth: the image of Gathering. Thus the noble person puts his weapons in good order and guards against the unexpected.
classical.historical_note:
Hexagram 45 in the King Wen sequence, 萃 (Cuì), lower trigram Kun (Earth) and upper Dui (Lake). The judgment and line texts are the received Zhouyi base text; the Great Image is from the Ten Wings '象曰' (Xiang) commentary. No separate Use Nine or Use Six text applies. Line 6 contains a source variant note: after 齎 the source gives 資, with '一作「咨」'; the translation follows the standard reading 齎咨涕洟, no blame.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.text_zh: 有孚不終，乃亂乃萃，若號一握為笑，勿恤，往无咎。
lines.translation_en: Sincerity does not last to the end; now confusion, now gathering. If one cries out, one clasp of hands brings laughter. Do not worry; going brings no blame.
Drawing is auspicious; no blame. With sincerity it is beneficial to present a meager sacrifice.

lines.text_zh: 萃如，嗟如，无攸利，往无咎，小吝。
lines.translation_en: Gathering and sighing; nothing is favorable. Going brings no blame, but there is slight regret.
Great good fortune; no blame.

lines.text_zh: 萃有位，无咎。匪孚，元永貞，悔亡。
lines.translation_en: Gathering has its place; no blame. If not trusted, be supremely and enduringly steadfast; regret disappears.

lines.text_zh:
齎
資
一作「咨」
涕洟，无咎。
lines.translation_en: Sighing and lamenting, tears and snivel; no blame.

taoist.title: Gathering the Scattered Essence
taoist.essence: Gathering is the disciplined work of calling back dissipated spirit and qi, restoring the original root through compliance, sincerity, and step-by-step cultivation—not a sudden stroke.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Gathering arises when joy above and receptivity below allow scattered forces to be assembled. It images a king entering a temple to honor ancestors, at once a return to source and a harmonizing of community. The inner equivalent is collecting body-mind’s dispersed energies around a true center.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Cui as the hexagram of ‘gathering the medicinal ingredients’ following Guai. He equates the king’s approach to the ancestral temple with remembering the root of one’s original heavenly innocence, and he links each line to different qualities of gathering: initial confusion, yielding sincerity, borrowing firmness, forming the elixir, warming the sacred embryo, and entering side doors. For him, true gathering is not an empty thought but a gradual practice of repaying the root; knowing must be followed by walking.
taoist.modern_meaning: This hexagram speaks to any period in which life feels scattered—attention fragmented, energy leaking, purpose unclear. The alchemical language is not about external laboratory alchemy but about an internal energetic discipline that gathers essence, qi, and spirit; in modern terms, this can also be understood as gathering the forces of attention, desire, and intention back to a felt center. Historically, Liu Yiming framed this as a return to the ancestral root; today that root may be one’s deepest values, a spiritual practice, a creative discipline, or a community of mutual fidelity. The text does not promise that one dramatic act will fix the scatter. Instead it describes a sequence: admit the confusion, make a small sincere offering, stop clinging to private ideas, allow firmness and softness to work together, and then protect what has gathered without meddling. This is not passive waiting; it is disciplined cultivation in which timing and right relationship matter more than force. It also asks us to notice why we gather—not to accumulate, but to restore authentic nature.
taoist.advice: When life scatters, pause and choose one trustworthy center. Return not by heroic effort alone but by steady, sincere habits. Ask what has been neglected, and bring attention back gradually. Let honest grief or confusion become a doorway, then move toward what you know is true.
taoist.shadow: Filling time with fragments, chasing many teachings without commitment, or mistaking false comfort for real gathering. The shadow is honoring roots only in words while avoiding daily cultivation.
taoist.reflection_question: What inner root am I currently neglecting, and what one step would return me to it?
taoist.evidence_zh: 萃者，聚也。卦德上兌悅、下坤順，我順人而人即悅，故謂萃。此攢簇藥物之卦，承上夬卦而來。

lines.interpretation: At the beginning, trust is unstable and attention jumps from one object to another, so what gathers is confusion rather than true order. Liu Yiming calls this the gathering of ‘turning from evil and returning to correctness’: honest distress may first express as weeping before it becomes the quiet laughter of recognition. The line does not promise an easy start, but shows that sincere regret and a willingness to be guided are enough to change direction. Present-day attention scattered by competing claims can be gathered only after admitting the scatter.
lines.reflection: Where has my sincerity not lasted, and what would it mean to let that be seen rather than hidden?
lines.evidence_zh: 初六，陰柔無斷，不辨是非，或信此，或信彼，乃亂乃萃，信非所當信，聚非所當聚矣。

lines.interpretation: When the situation is dark and resources are few, Liu Yiming highlights a different kind of gathering: not through force but through obeying one’s genuine inclination and gradually transforming acquired temperament. The image of the yue sacrifice suggests that sincerity, not lavish display, is what establishes connection. This line warns against despising small beginnings; steady faithful yielding can slowly gather true-suchness. Present-day practice often looks unremarkable—showing up, listening, small honest offerings to one’s deeper nature—but it creates the condition for transformation while preserving one’s integrity.
lines.reflection: What small sincere offering have I been underestimating?
lines.evidence_zh: 一身純陰，而能順其所欲，漸次導引，化其氣質之性，聚其真如之性，其利如用禴祭神，以誠感通。

lines.interpretation: This stage describes gathering that begins from self-enclosure: one holds to a narrow, empty idea of progress and then meets frustration. Liu Yiming is blunt: such self-will ends in sighing. Yet the line also leaves a door open: if a person can move toward a worthy companion or firmer inner principle, softness can borrow strength and avoid deeper harm. The remaining ‘slight regret’ belongs to waiting too long before asking for help. This is a call to recognize that gathering with the right people or principles is not weakness but repair.
lines.reflection: What private stubbornness is currently producing more sighing than growth?
lines.evidence_zh: 愚而自用，執著一己之陰，妄想成道，空而不實，是萃如必終嗟如，其無所利可知。

lines.interpretation: Here firmness and yielding are no longer split but balanced, so the scattered ingredients come together as a whole. Liu Yiming reads this as the condensing of the returning elixir, a state in which inner forces support rather than fight each other. Neither rigid control nor passive drifting, this line points to a gatheredness that feels steady and alive. It is not a final reward to be grasped, but a quality of integration that can be recognized and protected. In present terms, it is the moment when disparate parts of a life begin to cooperate.
lines.reflection: Where in my life are firmness and receptivity already forming a working alliance?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛而能柔，陰陽相當，還丹凝結，大丹有望，不但聚之如意而大吉，必將聚於一無所咎之地矣。

lines.interpretation: Line five describes a mature gathering: centered, correct, not relying on outer proof. Liu Yiming cautions that joy can turn into self-satisfaction; the work then is to ‘fill the belly and empty the heart’—preserve inner substance while releasing pride—and to warm the sacred embryo without meddling. This is not passive quietism but a precise, patient nurture after the main gathering has occurred. It reminds that later stages ask for less visible effort and more faithful timing, so that hidden residues are refined rather than repressed.
lines.reflection: What inner residue am I tempted to force away instead of patiently refining?
lines.evidence_zh: 若知實腹而又虛心，行無為之事，溫養聖胎，永於貞一，用天然真火，鍛盡後天余陰，號曰無漏真人，何悔之不亡乎？

lines.interpretation: The final line is a warning, not a prediction. Liu Yiming calls it the outcome of carelessness at the beginning: pursuing false substitutes until, at the end, only sorrow remains. Yet the phrase ‘no blame’ suggests that even this mourning carries no external guilt; the harm is self-inflicted and the lesson arrives late but honestly. It is a sober reflection on how a whole life can scatter itself in side paths. The image invites recognition of one’s own false refuges before they calcify, and it restores agency: no one else is responsible for the choice to turn.
lines.reflection: Which false refuge am I still defending as if it were the real path?
lines.evidence_zh: 愚而無知，誤入旁門，以假為真，雖天寶在望，未許我聚，空空一世，臨死方悔，齎咨涕洟，自致其傷，與人無咎。

confucian.title: Gathering by Sincerity and Rightness
confucian.essence: Gathering is not mere assembly; it becomes stable through trust, shared principle, and reverent order. Cheng Yi sees the lake above the earth as the moment when hearts converge and need a great person's governance.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: The lake rising above the earth is water gathering in a basin, an image of convergence. In the ancient setting, the king approaches the ancestral temple, the highest focal point for loyal hearts; sacrifice expresses abundance fitting the time, while weapons must be readied against the unexpected. The hexagram suggests that true gathering is not automatic. It requires a great person to order it, rightness to prevent careless union, and sincerity to bind diverse wills. Without these, gathering becomes contention and disorder.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi explains Cui as 'gathering': things meet, then form groups. The judgment's king entering the temple marks the utmost way to gather hearts; ritual sacrifice returns people to reverence. He treats the 亨 after 萃 as an interpolation. Gathering must be governed by a great person; otherwise people, goods, and affairs fall into strife. Abundance calls for generous offering, matching Heaven's decree. The Great Image calls the noble person to put weapons in order against unforeseen conflict. Each line traces the moral dynamics: lasting trust, mutual drawing through central correctness, the shame of last-resort belonging, the insufficiency of mere position, and the isolation of the self-seeking.
confucian.modern_meaning: In present-day life, Gathering names those moments when people, resources, or attention converge—an organizing effort, a family reconciliation, a social movement, a team under pressure. Cheng Yi does not promise that convergence will naturally succeed. He asks what principle is gathering it. A group that assembles only through convenience, shared grievance, or a charismatic figure may look unified but is already tending toward confusion and contention. His answer is multi-layered: trust must be sincere and lasting, leadership must be more than position, and shared practices must be simple enough to express genuine care rather than display. At the same time, he warns that all gatherings have unforeseen edges, so we need sober preparation—clear agreements, accountability, conflict readiness—not just shared enthusiasm. Historically, the commentary assumes a ruler and minister; today, those roles can be translated into any accountable leadership in communities, workplaces, or partnerships. The goal is not to dominate or predict outcomes, but to ask whether the form of gathering matches its inner principle. When it does, even a small sincere offering may hold people together; when it does not, abundance becomes noise.
confucian.advice: When you notice people or resources gathering around you, pause and ask what holds them together. Prefer sincere simplicity over impressive display. Check whether those with influence are using it rightly or merely occupying a convenient spot. Prepare for the unexpected without becoming suspicious. If trust is missing, turn inward and cultivate steady, principled conduct before demanding loyalty.
confucian.shadow: Gathering can become crowd-thinking, careless union, or manipulation. A person may collect followers while remaining inwardly crooked; another may chase belonging so desperately that they settle for shameful company or end isolated and weeping.
confucian.reflection_question: What is gathering in my life right now, and is its center sincere enough to hold without coercion?
confucian.evidence_zh: 王者萃聚天下之道至於有廟極也

lines.interpretation: Cheng Yi sees First Six as originally bound to its correct partner, Fourth Yang, but tempted by nearby yin company. Its trust does not last: one moment confused, the next clustering with sameness. If it holds firm and moves toward the correct connection despite the group's laughter, blame is avoided. In modern terms, early in a gathering we may face pressure to conform. Enduring sincerity can mean leaving comfortable resemblance to seek a more demanding, trustworthy relationship. The call and clasped hands point to a brief opening in which mockery can become shared laughter.
lines.reflection: Where am I tempted to trade a trustworthy commitment for the comfort of the crowd?
lines.evidence_zh: 若能勿恤而往從剛陽之正應則无過咎不然則入小人之羣矣

lines.interpretation: Cheng Yi contrasts Six Two with First Six. Although yin and soft, it is central and correct; it still needs to be drawn by its partner, Nine Five. The phrase 'being led is auspicious' means mutual seeking, not passive waiting. Their gathering is ruler and minister in harmony, but Cheng Yi grounds it in sincerity. The thin yue sacrifice shows that a simple, honest offering outweighs display. In modern terms, trustworthy belonging grows through mutual invitation and simplicity. When groups prize ornament over truth, they are not yet gathered. Even modest, consistent gestures—a clear word, a shared task—may hold people more firmly than grand performances.
lines.reflection: What would change if I approached a current gathering with quiet sincerity rather than impressive display?
lines.evidence_zh: 孚信者萃之本也不獨君臣之聚凡天下之聚在誠而已

lines.interpretation: Six Three is neither central nor correct. It seeks to gather with others but is rejected by Four, its non-partner, and by Two, rightly bound to Five. Cheng Yi says it sighs because it grasps at companions who cannot receive it. Turning to Top Six, another soft line with no partner, gives a place, but the text calls this small shame. Modern readers may recognize the pattern: after repeated rejection, we settle for mere similarity or convenience. Belonging gained only as a last resort still leaves a sting. The lesson is to notice when we trade integrity for relief.
lines.reflection: What rejected pursuit might be leading me to settle for a less fitting form of belonging?
lines.evidence_zh: 惟往而從上六則得其萃為无咎也

lines.interpretation: Nine Four sits close to the ruler above and gathers the people below. Cheng Yi warns that this broad gathering is not enough. Because the line is yang in a yin place, its position is not correct; it must achieve great, all-pervasive rightness before blame is removed. He cites Chen Heng of Qi and the Ji clan of Lu as gaining ruler and people by crooked paths—impressive gathering, but not great auspiciousness. Today, popularity or institutional power may attract many without moral legitimacy. The question is whether gathering is held by rightness or by convenience.
lines.reflection: When I hold influence over others, is my position earned by rightness or only by convenience?
lines.evidence_zh: 四以陽居隂非正也雖得上下之聚必得大吉然後為无咎也

lines.interpretation: Nine Five has the honored place and central correctness. Cheng Yi says that even a legitimate ruler may face those who do not yet trust or submit. The response is not coercion but self-reflection: cultivate the primal, perpetual, and correct virtue—lasting, principled leadership—until regret dissolves. He cites Shun and the Miao people, where virtue, not force, drew the distant. For modern readers, authority that rests only on position is fragile. Trust grows when leaders consistently embody principle over time. The line distinguishes rightful place from realized trust; the former is given by role, the latter earned by character.
lines.reflection: What untrusting person or group is inviting me to deepen my own integrity rather than demand their assent?
lines.evidence_zh: 如是而有不信而未歸者則當自反以修其元永貞之徳則无思不服而悔亡矣

lines.interpretation: Top Six is a yin-soft line at the top of joy, delighting in a high place but gathered by no one. Cheng Yi calls it the petty person who craves belonging, is cut off, and ends in sighing and tears. The situation is self-inflicted, so no external blame is assigned; yet the tears show inner shame. In modern terms, isolation at the end of a gathering often comes from seeking status without right relationship. Absence of blame does not mean peace. A more mature response is to choose one's place with care and remain calm in hardship.
lines.reflection: Is there a place I cling to because it flatters me, even though it leaves me uneasy and alone?
lines.evidence_zh: 人之絶之由己自取又將誰咎

hexagrams.essence: Gathering is the disciplined work of calling back dissipated spirit and qi, restoring the original root through compliance, sincerity, and step-by-step cultivation—not a sudden stroke.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: Gathering arises when joy above and receptivity below allow scattered forces to be assembled. It images a king entering a temple to honor ancestors, at once a return to source and a harmonizing of community. The inner equivalent is collecting body-mind’s dispersed energies around a true center.
hexagrams.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Cui as the hexagram of ‘gathering the medicinal ingredients’ following Guai. He equates the king’s approach to the ancestral temple with remembering the root of one’s original heavenly innocence, and he links each line to different qualities of gathering: initial confusion, yielding sincerity, borrowing firmness, forming the elixir, warming the sacred embryo, and entering side doors. For him, true gathering is not an empty thought but a gradual practice of repaying the root; knowing must be followed by walking.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: This hexagram speaks to any period in which life feels scattered—attention fragmented, energy leaking, purpose unclear. The alchemical language is not about external laboratory alchemy but about an internal energetic discipline that gathers essence, qi, and spirit; in modern terms, this can also be understood as gathering the forces of attention, desire, and intention back to a felt center. Historically, Liu Yiming framed this as a return to the ancestral root; today that root may be one’s deepest values, a spiritual practice, a creative discipline, or a community of mutual fidelity. The text does not promise that one dramatic act will fix the scatter. Instead it describes a sequence: admit the confusion, make a small sincere offering, stop clinging to private ideas, allow firmness and softness to work together, and then protect what has gathered without meddling. This is not passive waiting; it is disciplined cultivation in which timing and right relationship matter more than force. It also asks us to notice why we gather—not to accumulate, but to restore authentic nature.
hexagrams.advice: When life scatters, pause and choose one trustworthy center. Return not by heroic effort alone but by steady, sincere habits. Ask what has been neglected, and bring attention back gradually. Let honest grief or confusion become a doorway, then move toward what you know is true.
hexagrams.shadow: Filling time with fragments, chasing many teachings without commitment, or mistaking false comfort for real gathering. The shadow is honoring roots only in words while avoiding daily cultivation.
hexagrams.reflection_question: What inner root am I currently neglecting, and what one step would return me to it?
hexagrams.editorial_status: integration-candidate — AI-assisted; final human review pending

classical.name: Ascending
classical.judgment_zh: 元亨，用見大人，勿恤，南征吉
classical.judgment_en: Supreme success. For seeing the great person, do not worry. Going south is auspicious.
classical.image_zh: 地中生木，升；君子以順德，積小以高大
classical.image_en: A tree grows from within the earth: Ascending. Thus the noble person, in accordance with virtue, accumulates the small to become high and great.
classical.historical_note:
This is Zhouyi hexagram 46, Sheng, with lower Xun and upper Kun. The supplied line 4 text includes the variant note 一作「亨」; the translation renders the base sense of the king offering at Mount Qi. The Great Image is kept separate from the line translations; the small line images are not included.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Trustworthy ascent; great good fortune.
Sincere confidence, then it is favorable to use the yue sacrifice; no error.
Ascending into an empty town.

lines.text_zh: 王用享一作「亨」于岐山，吉无咎
lines.translation_en: The king performs the offering at Mount Qi; good fortune, no error.
Perseverance brings good fortune; ascending the steps.
Darkened ascent; it is favorable to be unceasingly persevering.

hexagrams.title: Ascending
hexagrams.name: Ascending

taoist.title: Cautious Ascent in Fire-Phases
taoist.essence: Liu Yiming reads Ascending as cautious inner-alchemical progress: first make yin compliant, then climb gradually from lowliness to sagehood. Accurate fire-phases, humility, and a true teacher are indispensable; without them, ascent becomes empty or darkened.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: The image is a tree growing from earth: lower Xun's gentle penetration meets upper Kun's receptivity. Ascent is organic, not forced. The noble person in accordance with virtue accumulates the small to become high and great. Progress arises through patient nurturing, correct timing, and inner sincerity rather than willful leaps.
taoist.historical_core: In Liu Yiming's commentary, this hexagram follows Gou and marks the stage after yang has reached its extreme and yin is born. The Golden Elixir path requires first making yin compliant so human desires do not arise, then advancing step by step. This ascent is not for guesswork or blind cultivation; it demands oral transmission from a true teacher and precise fire-phases. Each line shows a mode of ascent or failure: trust, sincerity, self-conceit, correct sacrifice, empty heart, and dark self-will.
taoist.modern_meaning: Today this hexagram speaks to any long-term growth—spiritual, ethical, professional—that cannot be rushed. It cautions against self-directed striving that mistakes activity for progress. A trustworthy mentor, honest feedback, and disciplined practice provide the fire-phases. Sincerity matters more than grand gestures: a simple offering given wholeheartedly outweighs elaborate display. Humility opens the way; arrogance leads into an empty city where nothing real is gained. When growth feels dark or compulsive, the counsel is not to push harder but to curb anger and desire, guard against evasion, preserve sincerity, and return to basics. The ascent is not a guarantee but an orientation: small consistent steps, aligned with authentic nature and right timing, may gradually accumulate into genuine high standing. This is the slow work of character, not a shortcut.
taoist.advice: Refrain from solitary self-certainty. Seek out those whose insight is tested and who correct without flattery. Practice small sincere actions repeatedly rather than dramatic leaps. When progress feels empty or dark, pause and ask whether pride has replaced receptivity. Curb anger, restrain desire, and protect sincerity as the foundation for any real ascent.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is stubborn self-will dressed as advancement: refusing teachers, clinging to one's own limited yin, and ascending more and more into darkness. One mistakes empty confidence for high standing and may defend arrogance while believing one is growing.
taoist.reflection_question: Where am I mistaking self-will for genuine ascent, and what trustworthy guidance am I avoiding?
taoist.evidence_zh: 升者，自卑登高之義。卦德上坤順、下巽入，徐緩進步，順時而行，不即不離，漸入真常，故謂升。

lines.interpretation: The first line shows a gentle nature with firm intent. One approaches accomplished mentors with an empty and receptive heart, not pretending to know. Because the seeker is sincere in humility, the wise do not withhold genuine teaching. This is ascent through yielding to firm guidance. Applied today, it suggests that the earliest stage of growth is not about accumulating information but about becoming a trustworthy student: listening, asking, and allowing oneself to be corrected. Trustworthy ascent begins with recognizing someone worth following.
lines.reflection: Who do I trust enough to learn from, and am I actually listening or merely performing humility?
lines.evidence_zh: 性柔志剛，虛心自下，親近有道之士，而高明者，未有不允其升，不授其真者。此柔而順剛之升也。

lines.interpretation: Here inner firmness is balanced by gentleness. The practitioner understands the subtle ingredients and timing of practice, entering with sincerity and applying with softness. Progress is gradual, like making a simple yue sacrifice: wholehearted sincerity, not elaborate display, moves the process forward. This line commends a disciplined but non-coercive approach. In modern terms, consistent honest effort—showing up fully for ordinary tasks—carries more transformative power than sporadic heroic gestures. When sincerity is present, even modest actions become a path without blame.
lines.reflection: Is my effort sincere but gentle, or am I forcing outcomes that need gradual cultivation?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛而有得於中，深明藥物火候，以誠而入，以柔而用，漸次下功，如以禴祭神，用誠感通，必升於一無所咎之地矣。此剛而用柔之升也。

lines.interpretation: This line warns against self-appointed sages. One who considers oneself already enlightened, avoids teachers and peers, guesses privately, and rushes ahead actually falls behind. Ascending into an empty city means entering a place with no substance, no real attainment, only a hollow sense of progress. The counsel is to check pride and seek genuine dialogue. Without external correction, inner certainty can become a closed loop. Growth requires relinquishing the fantasy that one already knows.
lines.reflection: What private beliefs have I protected from examination, and whom am I avoiding because they might challenge me?
lines.evidence_zh: 予聖自雄，不知尋師訪友，妄猜私議，冒然前進，欲向其前，反落於後，如升於虛邑，何能進于高明之地？此不知求師之升也。

lines.interpretation: Here gentleness is paired with rectitude. The practitioner refines the self and holds the mind steady, advancing in accord with the time, moving from lowliness toward height without haste. The image of the king offering at Mount Qi suggests that even one in authority bows in reverence to something greater. This is a model of disciplined humility: doing the inner work, honoring what transcends the ego, and letting progress unfold. Applied today, it points to steady practice and respectful acknowledgment of sources, mentors, and traditions.
lines.reflection: What regular practice or offering of reverence keeps my ascent grounded rather than ego-driven?
lines.evidence_zh: 柔而守正，順時進步，煉己持心，自卑登高，漸入佳境，如王用亨於岐山，未有不升於上者。此吉而無咎之升也。

lines.interpretation: This line describes emptying the acquired human mind to seek the Dao mind. When the heart is empty, inner fullness can settle; a single turning of awareness returns one to what was originally present. Moral and spiritual growth becomes as straightforward as climbing steps—not because effort is absent, but because resistance is removed. The key is prioritizing inner simplicity over mental clutter. In modern language, quieting the chattering mind and returning to core values allows clear, incremental progress, rather than wresting enlightenment through will.
lines.reflection: What mental clutter am I holding onto that makes genuine growth feel heavy or complicated?
lines.evidence_zh: 虛人心而求道心，虛心即能實腹，所謂一念回機，如同本得，其增益道德，如升階之易，此柔而虛心之升也。

lines.interpretation: This top line depicts darkened ascent: stubborn self-will clings to its own yin and imagines it is progressing in virtue and destiny. The more it climbs, the darker it becomes. To emerge from gloom one must seek a teacher's oral formula, curb anger and desire, guard against evil, and preserve sincerity. This is not passive surrender but active correction—returning from error to rectitude. The line warns against compulsive self-improvement that bypasses real feedback and humility. Persistence alone is not enough; persistence aligned with truthful guidance can still restore the light.
lines.reflection: Where has my determination become a dark compulsion, and what correction am I resisting?
lines.evidence_zh: 愚而自用，執著一己之陰，妄想增升道德，了命了性，升之不息，冥之不息，愈升愈冥，焉能出晦暗而進于高明？

confucian.title: Timely Rising through Accumulation
confucian.essence: Rising succeeds by gentle compliance, timeliness, and gradual accumulation. Trust the worthy, act with sincere simplicity, and restrain blind ambition so that small virtues become lasting greatness.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: The hexagram shows wood beneath earth, a tree growing upward from within. It images how a person of principle accumulates small acts of virtue according to the time, rising through faithful relationships and orderly support. The movement is not forced expansion but responsive growth—honoring what is above, nurturing what is below, and staying within one's place.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Sheng as Xun below and Kun above: wood under earth, a tree rising. For him, the hexagram's 'great success' comes from its gentle compliance and firm center; one uses this way to meet the great person and advance without anxiety. The Commentary highlights 'the yielding rises according to the time.' Lines describe stages: trusting a worthy, sincere unadorned service, unimpeded ascent, King Wen's compliant restraint at Mount Qi, a ruler's reliance on worthy steps, and dark endless striving. This hierarchical imagery—ministers serving rulers, King Wen under the Son of Heaven—reflects his historical ethical framework, not a modern endorsement.
confucian.modern_meaning: In present terms, this hexagram speaks to growth that is not ego-driven but rooted in the soil of relationships and self-cultivation. Rising begins by trusting those who embody integrity, offering sincere effort without ornamental self-promotion, and knowing when to climb through empty openings. The fourth line's King Wen image becomes a reflective model: one may advance others and serve larger purposes while remaining within one's role, not inflating oneself. The fifth line suggests that firm correctness and reliance on capable collaborators make advancement orderly, like steps. The top line warns against blind striving: the momentum of desire can become a discipline if redirected to ceaseless moral improvement. Each stage is conditional, inviting examination rather than predicting outcomes. As a modern ethical reframing, authority and rank can be read as contextual roles, not as inherent superiority, though Cheng Yi's own framework accepts hierarchical position as normatively significant; the ethical content remains trustworthy support, restraint, and timely service.
confucian.advice: Cultivate what is small and genuine. Trust trustworthy models, speak and act with simplicity, and let advancement follow from service rather than self-assertion. When close to responsibility, resist the urge to rise further; instead support the growth of others. Channel restless ambition into steady ethical practice. Attend to timing: move when structure and relationships align.
confucian.shadow: Blind upward drive that knows advance but not rest; forced ambition entering empty spaces; serving without sincerity; overstepping one's position; restless craving mistaken for progress. These exhaust rather than enrich.
confucian.reflection_question: Where am I striving to rise, and is my effort rooted in sincere service and timely accumulation rather than restless self-advancement?
confucian.evidence_zh: 君子觀升之象以順修其徳積累微小以至髙大也

lines.interpretation: The first line is yielding at the beginning of Xun, with no strong support of its own. Cheng Yi reads it as trusting and following the firm, central second line. Rather than seeking isolated self-advancement, it joins its will to a worthy person and rises together. Great good fortune here is not solitary success but shared purpose shaped by trust in genuine character. The line values receptive trust as a form of active alignment with what is dependable.
lines.reflection: Whose integrity do I trust enough to follow, and does that trust lead to shared growth rather than dependency?
lines.evidence_zh: 初之柔㢲唯信從於二信二而從之同升乃大吉也

lines.interpretation: A firm person serves a more yielding superior—a situation that can tempt flattery or ornament. Cheng Yi says the second line should keep utmost sincerity within and not borrow outward decoration. The yue sacrifice is simple and plain: once trust is real, no elaborate display is needed. In this way a strong minister can serve without blame and even bring benefit beyond the immediate relationship. Sincerity becomes the channel that makes hierarchical service ethically possible.
lines.reflection: When I relate to people in authority, is there any gap between my inner intent and my outward expression?
lines.evidence_zh: 當内存至誠不假文飾於外誠積於中則自不事外飾故曰利用禴謂尚誠敬也

lines.interpretation: The third line has strong yang capacity, correctness, and gentleness; above, all are compliant; it also has support and response. Cheng Yi compares rising here to entering an uninhabited city—no one blocks it. The image points to moments when circumstances open easily. Yet the ease itself calls for discernment: an empty city can mean fruitful advance or the shallowness of no resistance. The line asks whether one is rising through real merit or merely through an unresisting environment.
lines.reflection: When progress feels easy, do I examine whether the path is truly aligned with principle, or only convenient?
lines.evidence_zh: 如入无人之邑孰禦哉

lines.interpretation: The fourth line is yielding and correct, close to the ruler but not seeking further ascent. Cheng Yi uses King Wen at Mount Qi as the model: above, compliant to the Son of Heaven; below, supportive of worthies; for oneself, humble and within one's position. Its good fortune lies in compliant undertaking. As a modern reflection, this is not passive subordination but active ethical restraint: one may raise the way of those above and nurture those below without inflating one's own rank. Restraint here is a form of service.
lines.reflection: In a position of influence, do I use it to lift others while remaining appropriately humble about my own advancement?
lines.evidence_zh: 上順天子而欲致之有道下順天下之賢而使之升進已則柔順謙恭不出其位

lines.interpretation: The fifth line, though yielding, has a firm central response below. Cheng Yi says it must hold to correctness and constancy, otherwise trust in worthies is shallow and employment of them not lasting. Steps are the means by which one rises: relying on a worthy of firm centrality is like ascending by steps. The line teaches that genuine advancement depends on sustained reliability and on using capable helpers rather than forcing oneself upward. It also dignifies the role of support as essential to leadership.
lines.reflection: Do I remain constant in my reliance on trustworthy people, or do I abandon them when growth becomes difficult?
lines.evidence_zh: 任剛中之賢輔之而升猶登進自階言有由而易也

lines.interpretation: The top line is yin at the extreme of rising: darkened, knowing to advance but not to halt. Cheng Yi warns that such blind upward drive leads only to diminishment. Yet he redirects the unceasing urge—if the mind that seeks endlessly is applied to correct and constant moral strengthening, it becomes fitting. The line does not condemn effort itself, only its direction. What looks like restless ambition can be converted into disciplined self-cultivation.
lines.reflection: When I feel driven to rise without stopping, can I turn that same energy toward inner improvement rather than external gain?
lines.evidence_zh: 昏冥於升知進而不知止者也

The ascent is not a guarantee but an orientation: small consistent steps, aligned with authentic nature and right timing, may gradually accumulate into genuine high standing. This is the slow work of character, not a shortcut.
hexagrams.advice: Refrain from solitary self-certainty. Seek out those whose insight is tested and who correct without flattery. Practice small sincere actions repeatedly rather than dramatic leaps. When progress feels empty or dark, pause and ask whether pride has replaced receptivity. Curb anger, restrain desire, and protect sincerity as the foundation for any real ascent.
hexagrams.shadow: The shadow is stubborn self-will dressed as advancement: refusing teachers, clinging to one's own limited yin, and ascending more and more into darkness. One mistakes empty confidence for high standing and may defend arrogance while believing one is growing.
hexagrams.reflection_question: Where am I mistaking self-will for genuine ascent, and what trustworthy guidance am I avoiding?
