classical.name: Oppression
classical.judgment_zh: 困：亨，貞大人吉，无咎，有言不信。
classical.judgment_en: Oppression: Success. Perseverance of the great person brings good fortune; no blame. When one has words, they are not believed.
classical.image_zh: 澤无水，困；君子以致命遂志。
classical.image_en: The lake has no water: Oppression. Thus the noble person stakes his life on fulfilling his will.
classical.historical_note:
The Zhouyi base text (judgment, Great Image, and six line statements) is quoted from the supplied source; the Great Image belongs to the Ten Wings but is included as requested. Lines 3 and 4 in the source include minor textual variants (e.g., 蒺蔾/藜; 荼荼/徐徐, 轝/車); those variants are embedded in the quoted Chinese, while the English renderings follow the main reading.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.text_zh: 臀困于株木，入于幽谷，三歲不覿。
lines.translation_en: The buttocks are trapped by a tree stump; one enters a dark valley; for three years one does not see anyone.

lines.text_zh: 困于酒食，朱紱方來，利用亨祀，征凶，无咎。
lines.translation_en: Oppressed by wine and food, the vermilion knee-covers are just arriving. It is favorable to perform sacrifice; going forward brings misfortune; no blame.

lines.text_zh: 困于石，據于蒺蔾一作「藜」，入于其宮，不見其妻，凶。
lines.translation_en: Oppressed by a stone, leaning on thorns, he enters his house and does not see his wife: misfortune.

lines.text_zh: 來荼荼一作「徐徐」，困于金轝一作「車」，吝，有終。
lines.translation_en: Coming slowly, trapped by a metal chariot: distress, but there is an end.

lines.text_zh: 劓刖，困于赤紱，乃徐有說，利用祭祀。
lines.translation_en: Nose cut off, foot cut off; oppressed by the scarlet knee-covers. Then gradually there is joy; it is favorable to make sacrifice.

lines.text_zh: 困于葛藟，于臲卼，曰動悔。有悔，征吉。
lines.translation_en: Entangled by creeping weeds, in a rocky and precarious place, he says, 'If I move, regret.' There is regret; going forward brings good fortune.

hexagrams.title: Oppression
hexagrams.name: Oppression

taoist.title: Integrity in Exhaustion
taoist.essence: Oppression tests whether outer exhaustion can become inner tempering: the noble person stays centered, trusts the process, and lets joy emerge from danger instead of forcing escape.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: This archetype names the condition where vital movement is obstructed and speech is not believed. Lower water is one yang held inside two yin; upper lake is one yin above two yang, so yang qi cannot flow. Yet the lake's joy is not lost; it must be rediscovered from within danger. The noble person stakes life on fulfilling will, not to guarantee rescue but because integrity inside exhaustion is itself a hidden path. This is a furnace for tempering body and mind.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Oppression as exhaustion and difficulty: lower Kan is one yang sunk between two yin, upper Dui is one yin above two yang; yin soaks yang and yang qi cannot flow. He frames this as the hexagram of tempering body and mind, following Gathering. The proper response is centered correctness: the great person meets hardship with correctness and moves with the times, while the petty person complains, takes risks, and adds blame. Across the six lines he traces self-inflicted hardship, endurance through want, arrogant inner emptiness, gradual rescue, untimely capacity, and repentance that turns to the Way.
taoist.modern_meaning: In a modern life, oppression may look like chronic constraint, unrecognized work, or moments when honest words are dismissed. The text does not ask for passive endurance or reckless flight. It invites disciplined inner cultivation while external conditions remain unfree. Practically, this could mean maintaining a simple routine of reflection, refusing to perform competence for approval, and choosing trustworthy companions who can reflect truth. Timing matters: some efforts cannot move quickly, and forcing them brings only regret. Joy here is not denial; it is clarity and steadiness that can grow inside difficulty. The six lines chart common traps: small self-neglect becoming isolation, scarcity producing panic, arrogance covering ignorance, impatience damaging a gradual rescue, untimely capacity breeding bitterness, and delusion hardening into crisis. Working with them means distinguishing what can be changed from what must ripen, using restraint not as passivity but as precise timing, and turning regret into honest learning. It is the difference between being crushed by a season and being shaped within it.
taoist.advice: Treat this season as a tempering, not a verdict. Keep your inner practice regular even when results are invisible. Refuse self-contempt and self-dramatization. Say less, listen more, and let your actions carry what words cannot. If you feel forced, slow down before acting; if regret arises, turn it into a course correction toward honest learning.
taoist.shadow: Bitter resentment disguised as resilience, self-isolation mistaken for depth, spiritual arrogance covering inner emptiness, rash risk-taking under pressure, and a refusal to repent or seek guidance until the entanglement tightens further.
taoist.reflection_question: Where in this difficult season am I trying to force an exit before my inner alignment is ready?
taoist.evidence_zh: 以正處困，以正而亨，困而與時偕行也。

lines.interpretation: At the first stage, hardship is still small and support may be near, but the line is soft and lacks inner firmness. Instead of using available help, it sinks into self-abandonment, like sitting on a stump and entering a dark valley. The commentary warns that a small difficulty can become self-inflicted long isolation. The work here is to recognize early neglect before it hardens, not to wait three years in the dark.
lines.reflection: What small neglect am I allowing to become a long isolation?
lines.evidence_zh: 初六，在困之初，其困不大，又近二陽，不宜受困，乃柔弱無剛，自暴自棄，甘居人下，如臀困於株、木入于幽谷矣。

lines.interpretation: This line is yang hidden in yin, a time of scarce resources and bodily pressure. Yet firmness and centrality remain: the body may be oppressed, but the mind is not. One who can forget the body for the Way endures want without losing purpose. The commentary pictures first bitterness, then sweetness—heaven's clothing and emolument arriving. The practice is patient sincerity like sacrifice, not anxious flight. Trying to escape the hardship prematurely invites misfortune.
lines.reflection: Where am I being asked to endure scarcity without abandoning my inner firmness?
lines.evidence_zh: 幸其剛而得中，為道忘軀，身困而心不困

lines.interpretation: This line describes self-willed arrogance that refuses teachers and friends. The person is disliked by upright people and enters hardship on their own, like leaning on thorns. Having no real learning, they claim to possess the Way, pursue externals, and lose the inner. The image of entering one's palace and not seeing one's wife points to a hollow, ruined inner life. This is not oppression imposed from outside; it is self-created ruin through certainty without substance.
lines.reflection: Where has my own certainty closed me off from correction and genuine relationship?
lines.evidence_zh: 本無實學，自負有道，務外失內

lines.interpretation: The line has left the lower danger and enters the joyful upper trigram, so rescue is timely. But firmness dwelling in yielding cannot rush; movement is slow, as if caught by a metal carriage. There is distress, yet an end will come—not by force but by gradual progress. The teaching is to allow the long hardship to loosen in its own sequence, staying present without forcing speed.
lines.reflection: What can I allow to move slowly now rather than forcing abrupt escape?
lines.evidence_zh: 乃剛居於柔，不能速濟

lines.interpretation: Here yang is centered and correct, yet the time is not right. There is capacity for great work but no outward arena. The image of mutilation by red knee-covers suggests a bearer of value confined by roles and honors. Liu calls this the great hardship of one who cherishes the Way. The response is hidden cultivation: wear coarse cloth while holding jade inside, accept bitterness and self-effort, and let sincerity accumulate until gradual joy arises.
lines.reflection: What seed of authentic work am I carrying that cannot yet be shown outwardly?
lines.evidence_zh: 有大作之道，而無大作之時

lines.interpretation: The top line is stuck in entangled weeds and precarious ground, tangled by its own cleverness and private judgments. It distorts the Way and claims truth, then cannot move forward or back. The commentary says movement brings regret; better to turn early, seek teachers and friends, and become clear before acting. Through sincere repentance, even a side-path crisis can open into hearing the great Way. This is regret as a gate.
lines.reflection: What arrogance or distortion in me is ready to become sincere repentance?
lines.evidence_zh: 不若及早自悔，尋師訪友，明而後行

confucian.title: The Lake Without Water
confucian.essence: Adversity arises when what is solid is covered by what is soft. The great person remains centered, sincere, and constant, refusing to force outcomes or plead for belief, until like-minded allies arrive.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: The hexagram shows a lake emptied of its water: the source has sunk beneath the vessel, leaving dryness where there was abundance. Yang firmness is covered by yin softness, and the noble person is hemmed in by small-minded constraints. Yet the image is not only loss; it is a call to know the difference between what can be changed and what must be accepted, and to commit entirely to one's deepest purpose.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Kun as the time when firm yang is covered by soft yin, so the noble person is obstructed by the petty person. He anchors the reading in the Sequence: rising without stopping must end in oppression. For him, success in oppression belongs to the great person who keeps firm centrality and constancy, rests in Heaven's decree, and uses utmost sincerity rather than clever speech. The lower danger and upper joy show how one may dwell in danger with joy. Each line tests this discipline: some trap themselves through rashness or misplaced reliance, while the central lines and the top line open paths through sincerity, patience, or timely change.
confucian.modern_meaning: In contemporary life, this hexagram names the familiar experience of being stuck in a situation where effort seems fruitless and one's words carry little weight. It may appear in a constrained workplace, a strained relationship, or a long season of caregiving or unemployment. The older language of rulers and ministers can be read today as a reminder that authority and support are not automatic; one must build trust through steady conduct rather than demand belief. The text does not promise a dramatic rescue. It invites a quieter discipline: name what is truly within your power, refuse to add self-harm to external pressure, and keep faith with your own standards. When possible, seek companions whose values match yours, but do not chase recognition or force a resolution. The line between patient endurance and harmful passivity requires ongoing discernment. Ask what loyalty, honesty, and responsibility require now, and let those commitments shape your choices.
confucian.advice: Withdraw from the urge to explain yourself to those who cannot hear. Tend the inner spring: rest, restore, and return to your core commitments. Discern which constraints are alterable and which must be accepted for now. Move only when movement can be truthful. When an opening appears through trustworthy people, receive it with sincerity, not desperation.
confucian.shadow: Oppression can curdle into bitterness, self-dramatizing endurance, or reckless attempts to prove oneself. The shadow confuses being stuck with being worthless, and may either collapse into silent despair or batter against immovable obstacles.
confucian.reflection_question: Where am I being invited to keep my integrity while no longer needing to be believed?
confucian.evidence_zh: 君子為小人所揜蔽窮困之時也

lines.interpretation: This line shows a person without support, perched on a dead stump, sinking into a dark valley. When no external aid is available, the danger is not simply hardship but the inner slide into confusion and self-pity. The three years symbolize a long obscurity. Cheng Yi warns that a yielding nature, if it cannot rest in its circumstances, becomes increasingly deluded and reckless. The wise response is to stop adding motion to despair, refuse to mistake one's own darkness for the whole landscape, and seek whatever small clarity remains.
lines.reflection: When I cannot find outside help, how do I avoid turning a difficult season into a dark identity?
lines.evidence_zh: 幽不明也謂益入昏暗自䧟於深困也

lines.interpretation: Here a person of real ability is blocked, not by poverty or enemies, but by abundance that cannot yet be shared. The wine and food represent generous intentions with no outlet. Cheng Yi reads this as a time to remain sincere and self-possessed rather than to chase recognition. The vermilion knee-covers point toward like-minded help forming, but it cannot be forced. Sacrifice suggests that inner truthfulness, not urgent action, creates the connection. Going forward aggressively would bring misfortune; waiting in integrity does not.
lines.reflection: Where am I tempted to push for recognition instead of letting sincerity do its quiet work?
lines.evidence_zh: 雖困于所欲未能施惠於人然守其剛中之徳必能致亨而有福慶也

lines.interpretation: This line warns against fighting to advance when the way is blocked by something hard, while resting on a foundation of thorns. The more one struggles, the more entangled one becomes; the home one hoped to protect may slip away. Cheng Yi says the problem is not the outside obstacles alone, but a wrong use of force from a non-central, soft position. To act with danger against unyielding realities is to bring disaster on oneself. The line asks for humility, retreat, and a refusal to turn difficulty into aggression.
lines.reflection: Where am I treating aggression as strength, when the situation calls for honest withdrawal?
lines.evidence_zh: 據于蒺藜謂乗九二之剛不安猶藉刺也

lines.interpretation: This line describes a hesitant approach. The person wishes to move toward a proper connection, but an obstacle—here called a metal carriage—makes progress slow and awkward. There is shame in the hesitation, as if one is not enough. Yet Cheng Yi insists the correct relationship can eventually hold. The lesson is not to abandon an upright bond for a more powerful-looking option just because the path is obstructed. Slow, uncertain movement can still be faithful movement; the end is not lost.
lines.reflection: What am I hesitating to pursue, and is the hesitation caution or fear of not being enough?
lines.evidence_zh: 四欲從初而阻於二故其來遲疑而徐徐是困于金車也

lines.interpretation: This line speaks to those in authority or responsibility who feel cut off from both higher and lower support. The injuries of nose and feet suggest public shame and inability to act. Yet the ruler here has firm centrality and a like-minded helper below. The remedy is not command but sincere invitation, symbolized by sacrifice. Only by extending genuine reverence and seeking worthy allies can the oppression be relieved. The release is gradual, not immediate; it appears after integrity has made space for it.
lines.reflection: When I hold responsibility but feel unsupported, how can I invite rather than demand?
lines.evidence_zh: 人君在困時宜念天下之困求天下之賢若祭祀然致其誠敬則能致天下之賢濟天下之困矣

lines.interpretation: At the extreme of entanglement, every movement seems to bring regret. The creepers bind and the ground is unsteady. Cheng Yi says this is the point where oppression turns, provided one recognizes the pattern and lets regret become a turning point. The line does not counsel frozen stillness; it counsels changed movement. If you see that repeating the same responses only tightens the knot, then the very regret can lead you out. Going forward, after honest correction, may open a way.
lines.reflection: What old movement am I repeating, and what would a true change of direction require?
lines.evidence_zh: 困極而征則出於困矣故吉

classical.name: The Well
classical.judgment_zh: 改邑不改井，无喪无得，往來井井。汔至亦未繘井。羸其瓶，凶。
classical.judgment_en: The settlement may be changed, but the well is not changed. No loss, no gain. Coming and going, they draw from the well. Almost reaching [the water], yet the well rope is not yet lowered; the pitcher is broken, there is misfortune.
classical.image_zh: 木上有水，井；君子以勞民勸相。
classical.image_en: Water above wood: The Well. Thus the noble person comforts the people and urges them to assist one another.
classical.historical_note:
Hexagram 48, Jing (The Well), lower Xun (Wind) above upper Kan (Water). The judgment and six line statements belong to the base Zhouyi text; the Great Image is from the Ten Wings and is translated separately. Quotations preserve the source characters, including 无 for 無.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: The well is muddy; no one drinks from it. An old well has no birds.
In the well valley, one shoots small fish; the jar is broken and leaks.

lines.text_zh: 井渫不食，為我心惻，可用汲，王明，並受其福。
lines.translation_en: The well is dredged, but no one drinks from it. This makes my heart sad. It may be drawn from; if the king is wise, all together receive its blessing.
The well is lined; no blame.
The well is clear; its cold spring water is drunk.
The well is drawn from; do not cover it. With sincerity, there is great good fortune.

hexagrams.title: The Well
hexagrams.name: The Well

taoist.title: The Unchanged Well
taoist.essence: A well with a source nourishes without loss. Cultivate your own depth first; only when the Dao is complete can you offer others what will truly sustain them. Timing and sincere preparation prevent a broken vessel.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: The Well is the archetype of sustainable nourishment drawn from a hidden source. It cannot be moved or exhausted; it neither gains nor loses as people come and go. Its water must be kept clear, its walls lined, its rope intact, and its mouth opened only at the right time. The image says: cultivate the inner source, then share from fullness without depleting yourself.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 48 as 'accumulating merit and cultivating virtue.' The lower Xun is gradual penetration; the upper Kan is danger that can be passed through, like wood entering below water to draw it out. For him the well is 'water that has a source,' and every line is graded by self-nourishment: from the muddy first line to the clear fifth and open sixth. The central claim is that nourishing others must be rooted in nourishing oneself; before the Dao is completed, one has no root and trying to guide others brings the broken-pitcher misfortune. This belongs to his inner alchemy commentary on the Zhouyi.
taoist.modern_meaning: In contemporary life, the Well may ask where one draws from. Offering guidance, creativity, or care from an unreplenished place is like lowering a broken pitcher into a muddy well: the gesture looks right, but little of value reaches anyone. This is not a call to withdraw into passive waiting. Liu Yiming's reading is disciplined: the lower trigram is gradual penetration, the upper is danger passed through by cultivation. One might learn to recognize the difference between readiness and compulsion—between a season for lining the well and a season for opening it to others. The image of no loss and no gain suggests that true nourishment is not about heroic depletion or accumulation. A person may give without losing their center when the giving flows from a completed inner source. Timing matters: premature helping, teaching for validation, or caretaking out of unresolved need may reproduce emptiness rather than meet it. The well remains well when the source is tended first, and only then shared.
taoist.advice: Consider noticing what is not yet clear within you before offering it outward. Let discipline, not urgency, set the pace. In quiet confusion, repair the vessel; in clarity, let the water be drawn. It may help to ask whether a current impulse to serve is rooted in fullness or in a need to be needed.
taoist.shadow: The muddy well of unexamined inner life; premature teaching that leaks through a broken vessel; helping from emptiness; accumulating without use; hiding a clear spring out of distrust or control.
taoist.reflection_question: What am I attempting to offer from a source I have not yet cleared or lined?
taoist.evidence_zh: 養人必本於自養，養己如是，養人如是，如井無喪無得也。

lines.interpretation: At the first step, there is a risk of pretending to be a source before any clarity has been gathered. The image is of a muddy abandoned well: even birds shun it. The shadow here is not laziness but a kind of premature imitation—offering from emptiness while lacking the honest work of self-cultivation. One may feel an eagerness to guide, but this line suggests first admitting the mud. Without that admission, the attempt to help becomes polluted from the start.
lines.reflection: Where might I be imitating clarity instead of doing the slower work of clearing myself?
lines.evidence_zh: 如舊井有泥無水，積汙百端，禽亦不顧，焉能養人乎？此絕不知自養者也。

lines.interpretation: Here the self-cultivation is underway but incomplete. There is a real impulse to give, yet the vessel leaks and the water only reaches the small and nearby. The line warns against comparing one's inner stirring to readiness. Service attempted from a half-filled container may wet a few things but loses more than it gives. It may be a moment to stop outward movement and tend the leaks—attending to consistency, inner honesty, and the integrity of the container itself before deciding that one has something to offer.
lines.reflection: Which leak in my own vessel am I ignoring while trying to water others?
lines.evidence_zh: 自養未足，即欲養人，無益於彼，先傷於我，如井穀外射，僅能養鮒，甕敝水漏，浸潤有限

lines.interpretation: The water is clear now, but no one drinks. This is not failure; it is a timing gap between readiness and recognition. The line describes a person whose inner work has reached a point where others could benefit, yet no fitting relationship or audience has arrived. The heart grieves, but the text also trusts that clear water has a silent influence: it may be noticed and eventually used. This stage may ask one to let clarity remain available without forcing it upon the unready, and to keep the vessel liftable.
lines.reflection: Can I wait without bitterness when my clarity is not yet received?
lines.evidence_zh: 養己已到可以養人之時，但近於險，未遇知音，限於不得養，如井水渫泛而無人食之也。

lines.interpretation: This is a quieter position: not yet ready to nourish others, but able to repair and fortify oneself. Lining the well is unglamorous work—no one drinks, no one is impressed—yet it prevents collapse and protects the source. The line suggests that a period of consolidation is not avoidance. When inner resources feel thin or one is surrounded by unstable circumstances, strengthening boundaries and steadying one's own structure may be the most responsible offering one can make, because it ensures no one falls into the pit.
lines.reflection: What protective repair is being asked of me before I can safely serve?
lines.evidence_zh: 居於險體，雖無養人之德，幸其柔而守正，能知自養，如井之甃以防險，內不傷而外不損，可無陷人之咎矣。

lines.interpretation: The well is now clear, cold, and drinkable. Liu Yiming treats this as the completed inner work: yang residing within yin, emptiness and fullness unified, firmness and yielding mixed. The source is deep and abundant; drawing does not exhaust it. This is not a final moral achievement but an alchemical state of balanced presence. From here, offering to others can be natural, because the water comes from a depth that is not diminished by use. In ordinary life, this might look like a person whose help strengthens rather than drains them.
lines.reflection: What would it feel like to give from a source that is not depleted by giving?
lines.evidence_zh: 陽居陰內，外虛內實，虛實如一，剛柔混合，大道完成，是謂有本之水，如井冽寒泉，所養深厚，取之不盡，用之不竭。

lines.interpretation: The final line opens the well. The discipline of self-nourishment has become a finished work, so the cover may be removed; guidance can flow according to another's capacity without harm to the source. The line's trust is that the good fortune was already present at the start of inner cultivation, not manufactured at the moment of giving. It may point to a stage where one's lived practice itself becomes an open resource, and sharing is simply not obstructing the spring. The well remains a well when the source is shared, not hoarded.
lines.reflection: What cover am I still holding over a spring that is ready to be shared?
lines.evidence_zh: 養己已到，如井功已收，可以勿幕井口，因人開導，自能有益於人，無傷於我。特以其吉已在於養己之初矣。

confucian.title: The Constant Nourishing Well
confucian.essence: A well stays put while settlements change; drawn without being depleted, filled without overflowing. Its virtue is constancy; its use is thorough mutuality. Only when water rises and is shared does the well fulfill its work.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: The Well images an inexhaustible common source—a point of stable nourishment that outlasts changing structures. Cheng Yi reads the image of wood entering beneath water and raising it upward as the drawing of well water: usefulness depends on drawing what is below into open circulation. The archetype points to constancy of character, the discipline of remaining serviceable, and the patient work of making one’s inner resources available to others. Without that upward movement and sharing, even abundant endowment remains ineffective.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi treats the Well as a figure for constancy and nourishing usefulness after oppression forces a turn downward. For him Kan above and Xun below show a wooden vessel entering beneath water and raising it, the image of drawing water. He stresses the hexagram statement’s 'no loss, no gain' as constancy of virtue and 'coming and going, welling' as thorough, all-reaching use. The noble person imitates this by comforting the people and urging mutual aid. Each line is measured by whether water rises and benefits others; mud, leakage, or unaccessed clarity marks unused or misdirected capacity. Only the top completes the well’s work through broad, constant giving.
confucian.modern_meaning: As a present-day reflection, the Well can represent the institutions, skills, relationships, and inner practices that remain dependable amid changing circumstances. Cheng Yi’s historical framework assumes a ruler and ranked roles, but the underlying discipline can be translated into modern terms: maintain the shared sources you draw on, keep them clean and accessible, and do not hoard what is meant to circulate. The image asks not merely for inner depth, but for the consistent effort of raising that depth into usable contribution. When a person feels undervalued, the third line’s waiting for a 'wise king' may be re-read as seeking the right opening and the right community rather than waiting for a superior. The fourth line’s repair work suggests that even modest maintenance is meaningful. Mature character, in this reading, is not a private reservoir; it becomes real only through steady, transparent sharing and the relationships that make sharing possible. The Well cautions against confusing constancy with stagnation, or depth with withdrawal.
confucian.advice: Consider the shared sources you rely on and tend them without needing visible reward. If your capacities feel muddied, misdirected, or unaccessed, notice what is blocking upward movement—lack of support, broken containers, or timing—and repair what is repairable. Let clear, consistent contribution be more important than recognition. In relationships, offer steady, transparent support; do not cover or privatize what can nourish others.
confucian.shadow: The shadow is becoming an abandoned well: talent or tradition left muddy, unused, or leaking away; resentment at not being recognized; waiting for permission instead of repairing and offering; constancy hardening into stagnant self-enclosure.
confucian.reflection_question: What is one steady resource I can keep clean and available, and where am I letting it sink or go unused?
confucian.evidence_zh: 井之為物常而不可改也邑可改而之他井不可遷也故曰改邑不改井汲之而不竭存之而不盈无䘮无得也至者皆得其用往來井井也无䘮无得其徳也常往來井井其用也周常也周也井之道也

lines.interpretation: At the bottom, the well is muddy and no one drinks; even birds stay away. Cheng Yi sees this as unused capacity: yin softness below, without response or support above, cannot raise water to benefit others. The mud is not simply lack of talent but accumulated neglect, and the absence of birds shows that what is not renewed stops attracting even small life. This line warns against letting a useful source become stale through isolation, self-doubt, or lack of care, and asks what has been left untended too long.
lines.reflection: What part of my life has become like an old, muddy well that no one visits—and why do I leave it untended?
lines.evidence_zh: 井本濟人之物六以隂居下无上水之象故為不食井之不食以泥也猶人當濟物之時而才弱无援不能及物為時所舍也

lines.interpretation: The second line has firm substance but, situated below with no response above, it turns downward and sideways like valley water rather than rising. Cheng Yi compares this to shooting at minnows in the mud and to a broken earthenware jar: the water that ought to be contained and drawn upward leaks away. The issue is not lack of talent but misdirection and lack of support. Good intention, without an upper connection or a sound vessel, cannot become public benefit. The line asks where energy leaks into small, muddy aims.
lines.reflection: Where is my energy leaking into low, narrow outlets because I lack a sound container or supportive connection?
lines.evidence_zh: 二雖剛陽之才而居下上无應而比於初不上而下之象也井之道上行者也澗谷之水則旁出而就下二居井而就下失井之道乃井而如谷也

lines.interpretation: The third line is clean and ready—a dredged well—but no one drinks from it, and the heart grieves. Cheng Yi describes a capable person anxious to act, not yet in a position where water reaches others. The line does not say the person is wrong to sorrow; it says the situation needs an enlightened opening above. If an able person is recognized and used, ruler and people together receive the blessing. This is not a call to force oneself upward, but to watch for the right alignment between readiness and a receptive context, and to grieve honestly without becoming bitter.
lines.reflection: What am I ready to offer, and what would a truly receptive opening look like for that gift?
lines.evidence_zh: 三以陽剛居得其正是有濟用之才者也在井下之上水之清潔可食者也井以上為用居下未得其用也

lines.interpretation: The fourth line is neither brilliant nor abundant, but it is well placed and able to maintain the well. Cheng Yi says that although this position cannot broadly bestow benefits, it can still repair and guard the well, and this earns no blame. Repair here is not glamorous; it is bricking, cleaning, preventing waste. The teaching is that modest maintenance of a shared source is a real moral task. Quiet repair keeps the structures sound so others can draw from them.
lines.reflection: What small repair or maintenance task, if left undone, would quietly undermine a larger shared work?
lines.evidence_zh: 四雖隂柔而處正上承九五之君才不足以廣施利物亦可自守者也故能修治則得无咎

lines.interpretation: The fifth line is the clear, cold spring: central, correct, and utterly drinkable. Cheng Yi calls its endowment and virtue wholly good, yet he notes the text does not fully say 'auspicious' because the water is still below the opening that completes the well’s work. There is a subtle tension: excellence is present, but fulfilment waits on delivery. This is a moment of mature quality that must still become available beyond its own place. The line asks us not to confuse purity with completion.
lines.reflection: Where am I mistaking inner clarity or correctness for actually reaching others with what I have?
lines.evidence_zh: 五以陽剛中正居尊位其才其徳盡善盡美井洌寒泉食也洌謂甘潔也井泉以寒為美甘潔之寒泉可為人食也於井道為至善也

lines.interpretation: The top line completes the well: water is drawn and the cover is not replaced. Cheng Yi reads 'no covering' as the refusal to privatize or hoard the source, making giving broad and inexhaustible. 'Trust' here is constancy—not a one-time act but a steady way of being that does not change. Broad giving with constancy is, for him, the mark of a great person. This is the culmination of the whole hexagram: a self that has become a reliable public resource, not an isolated reservoir.
lines.reflection: After I draw what I need, do I leave the well uncovered and available, or do I close it from fear of scarcity?
lines.evidence_zh: 井以上出為用居井之上井道之成也收汲取也幕蔽覆也取而不蔽其利无窮井之施廣矣大矣有孚有常而不變也博施而有常大善之吉也

hexagrams.essence: A well with a source nourishes without loss. Cultivate your own depth first; only when the Dao is complete can you offer others what will truly sustain them. Timing and sincere preparation prevent a broken vessel.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: The Well is the archetype of sustainable nourishment drawn from a hidden source. It cannot be moved or exhausted; it neither gains nor loses as people come and go. Its water must be kept clear, its walls lined, its rope intact, and its mouth opened only at the right time. The image says: cultivate the inner source, then share from fullness without depleting yourself.
hexagrams.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 48 as 'accumulating merit and cultivating virtue.' The lower Xun is gradual penetration; the upper Kan is danger that can be passed through, like wood entering below water to draw it out. For him the well is 'water that has a source,' and every line is graded by self-nourishment: from the muddy first line to the clear fifth and open sixth. The central claim is that nourishing others must be rooted in nourishing oneself; before the Dao is completed, one has no root and trying to guide others brings the broken-pitcher misfortune. This belongs to his inner alchemy commentary on the Zhouyi.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: In contemporary life, the Well may ask where one draws from. Offering guidance, creativity, or care from an unreplenished place is like lowering a broken pitcher into a muddy well: the gesture looks right, but little of value reaches anyone. This is not a call to withdraw into passive waiting. Liu Yiming's reading is disciplined: the lower trigram is gradual penetration, the upper is danger passed through by cultivation. One might learn to recognize the difference between readiness and compulsion—between a season for lining the well and a season for opening it to others. The image of no loss and no gain suggests that true nourishment is not about heroic depletion or accumulation. A person may give without losing their center when the giving flows from a completed inner source. Timing matters: premature helping, teaching for validation, or caretaking out of unresolved need may reproduce emptiness rather than meet it. The well remains well when the source is tended first, and only then shared.
hexagrams.advice: Consider noticing what is not yet clear within you before offering it outward. Let discipline, not urgency, set the pace. In quiet confusion, repair the vessel; in clarity, let the water be drawn. It may help to ask whether a current impulse to serve is rooted in fullness or in a need to be needed.
hexagrams.shadow: The muddy well of unexamined inner life; premature teaching that leaks through a broken vessel; helping from emptiness; accumulating without use; hiding a clear spring out of distrust or control.
hexagrams.reflection_question: What am I attempting to offer from a source I have not yet cleared or lined?
hexagrams.editorial_status: integration-candidate — AI-assisted; final human review pending

classical.name: Radical Change
classical.judgment_zh: 革：已日乃孚，元亨。利貞。悔亡
classical.judgment_en: Ge: On the day of the change, there is trust. Supreme success. It is favorable to be steadfast. Regret vanishes.
classical.image_zh: 澤中有火，革；君子以治歷明時
classical.image_en: Fire is in the lake: Ge. Thus the junzi regulates the calendar and clarifies the seasons.
classical.historical_note:
Translated from the received Zhouyi base text (hexagram judgment, line statements, and Great Image), with the Great Image kept distinct from the base text; Tuan and small line images are omitted. The base-text reading 已日 is ambiguous; the commentary reads it as 'after the day has passed.'

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Bind it with the hide of a yellow ox.
On the day of the change, then change it. To go forward is auspicious. No blame.

lines.text_zh: 征凶，貞厲，革言三就，有孚
lines.translation_en: To go forward is ominous; to persist is perilous. The words on change reach completion three times; there is trust.
Regret vanishes. Having trustworthiness, changing the mandate is auspicious.
The great person changes like a tiger; even without divination there is trust.

lines.text_zh: 君子豹變，小人革面，征凶，居貞吉
lines.translation_en: The junzi changes like a leopard; the small person changes his face. To go forward is ominous; to remain and be steadfast is auspicious.

hexagrams.title: Radical Change
hexagrams.name: Radical Change

taoist.title: Radical Change as Self-Refinement
taoist.essence: Radical Change removes the old by refining selfish desire until no self remains. Clarity governs joy, fire smelts metal, and returning to brightness makes trust possible again.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: No self, no old stain: Liu Yiming reads Ge as the alchemical process of removing what has accumulated. Upper Dui is joy, lower Li is clarity; joy rooted in clarity cannot become reckless, and clarity cannot remain obscured. Fire smelting metal symbolizes refining yin qi, undoing the defilement that arises whenever a fixed 'I' takes charge.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming’s historical commentary presents Ge as 'refining and forging yin qi,' succeeding Kun. He locates the root of defilement in having a self: after the acquired state takes charge, 'a hundred anxieties disturb the heart and ten thousand affairs weary the body.' Change therefore means 'changing the non-brightness of one's self in order to return to brightness.' Only a change done correctly—restraining the self, returning to propriety, removing falseness, preserving sincerity—can reveal the original numinous nature and dissolve regret.
taoist.modern_meaning: Rather than demanding that circumstances, institutions, or other people change, this hexagram asks where an old pattern within oneself still repeats. The alchemical image of fire smelting metal suggests that excessive heat or impatient force is not the point; the work is gradual, and clarity must precede trust. When the heart is empty enough to recognize its own self-interest, change begins without forcing outward events. This may mean noticing where one is bound by the hide of the yellow ox, or whether one is changing only the face while the heart remains unchanged. Historical hierarchy and language of 'great person' and 'petty person' reflect Liu Yiming’s era; today they can be read as degrees of inner sincerity—whether one changes only the outer face or the root. The text offers no guaranteed outcome, only a way of working with timing, self-knowledge, and the removal of accumulated habits.
taoist.advice: Before trying to change others, let clarity return by asking what old self-interest is active. Trust the process enough to soften where you have been rigid. Act from inner center, not from the need to be seen as right. Allow change to become steady and undramatic.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is changing only the surface—binding oneself tighter with duty or appearance while leaving the inner self intact—or trying to reform others from self-importance, so that change words return three times and nothing deep shifts.
taoist.reflection_question: Where am I trying to change the outside while leaving the inner pattern untouched?
taoist.evidence_zh: 革者，去而不用之義，所以去舊也。卦德上兌悅、下離明，悅本於明，以明制悅，悅而不得有妄，明而不得有昧，明中出悅，悅中有明，故謂革。

lines.interpretation: Initial Nine is firm but not bright: it cannot turn inward to change the root, so it binds itself outwardly like ox hide. This is change that abandons the root and pursues the branch. In present terms, tightening one’s duties, appearance, or discipline may create a temporary container while the inner confusion remains untouched. The result is rigidity, not renewal. The first movement of change asks whether one is truly willing to enter the inner heat, or only fortifying the outer shell.
lines.reflection: What outer binding am I using to avoid the inner change?
lines.evidence_zh: 初九，剛而不明，不能逆革其內，乃順革於外，如鞏用黃牛之革，顧外失內，固執不通。此捨本逐末之革也。

lines.interpretation: Six in the second place empties the heart. By first removing selfish desire, there is no fixed self; when there is no fixed self, one can genuinely meet others. Liu calls this 'seeking brightness through an empty heart.' The belly is filled—not with more opinions, but with a substantial inner clarity. Change at this stage is relational and receptive: it begins by clearing space, then moves toward others and into the work. Going forward in this way carries no blame.
lines.reflection: What selfish desire can be set down so that I can meet another without grasping?
lines.evidence_zh: 六二，虛心自處，明於革而先能去其私欲，私欲能去，則無己，無己則有人，有人則以己求人，即能實腹，實腹而己愈明，是以征吉，而且無咎。此虛心求明之革也。

lines.interpretation: Nine in the third place is too firm. It knows how to reform others but not itself. Even if its outward cause is just, there is danger; intended change becomes a mirror in which repeated words come back to reform the one who will not reform. Liu calls this the change of self-importance. The present-day pattern is recognizable: the stronger the urge to fix others, the more likely one is avoiding one’s own knot. The threefold repetition is an invitation to stop and listen.
lines.reflection: What repeated feedback have I heard as a demand that others change, when it may be asking me to change?
lines.evidence_zh: 九三，剛而太過，只知革人，不知革己，雖革事得正，亦有凶屬。蓋以不能革己，即欲革人，不但人不受我革，且將有言來革我，雖欲不自革而不能。是以革言三就也。三就之革，可信其終於不能革己矣。此自大自尊之革也。

lines.interpretation: Nine in the fourth place possesses firmness but does not force it. Regret can vanish when one trusts inner change enough to allow firmness to become yielding. This is not weakness; it is the transformation of disposition, no longer chained to reactive yin–yang cycles. A felt direction may change—Liu speaks of 'changing the mandate'—not by fiat, but by releasing a fixed self-image. The opportunity here is to let a long-held solidity become pliable, so that something genuinely new can take shape.
lines.reflection: Where have I been rigid because I did not yet trust that yielding could change my direction?
lines.evidence_zh: 九四，有剛不用，是以有悔可亡，悔出於不信革己。若信革己，剛即能柔，可以變化氣質，而不為陰陽所拘，豈僅有己之悔可亡，方且有改命之吉。此剛以柔用之革也。

lines.interpretation: Nine in the fifth place is centered, firm, and active. The ruling power is within; it opens the gate of life, closes the door of death, and lets guest qi dissolve on its own. This is not external dominance but deliberate inner sovereignty. A tiger’s presence needs no argument. In modern terms, this stage may appear as a clear, unhurried decision that reorders priorities and lets distractions fall away. Change here is active, yet its strength lies in correction of one’s own center, not in attacking others.
lines.reflection: What clear inner decision, made from center, would allow distracting forces to dissolve without struggle?
lines.evidence_zh: 九五，陽剛中正，主宰在內，扶陽抑陰，開生門、閉死戶，留人道、塞鬼路，一切客氣，自消自化，如虎威常在，不變之變，無容占信其已革矣。此大人用剛有為之革也。

lines.interpretation: Top Six completes the work. Liu describes a leopard’s change without ferocity: sincere within, transformed without, sense-roots and dust cleared. This is the gentleman’s yielding, non-forcing completion. Petty change alters only the face; sincere change remains steadfast and grows more vigorous with time. In present-day practice, this suggests that the deepest changes may be quietly visible, while surface compliance without inner shift eventually fails. Persistence rooted in trust, not drama, is what endures.
lines.reflection: Is my current change reaching the face only, or is it ripening quietly from within?
lines.evidence_zh: 上六，在革之終。柔而得正，煉己功勤，虛極靜篤，如豹不威之變，誠中達外，氣質俱化，根塵全消，淨倮倮、赤灑灑，形神俱妙，與道合真矣。此君子用柔無為之革也。

confucian.title: Change That Earns Trust
confucian.essence: Radical change becomes trustworthy only after preparation, consensus, and shared confidence. Imposed alteration breeds doubt; timely reform aligned with principle dissolves regret and preserves what renewal has won.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: Fire beneath the lake heats and extinguishes; incompatible forces meet, and what was old is transformed. The hexagram names change not as novelty but as renewal after decay—like cleaning a neglected well or regulating the calendar so seasons remain legible. Its core movement is not sudden rupture but earned, well-timed alteration that people can trust and maintain.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Ge through the Neo-Confucian lens of principle, timeliness, and the trust binding ruler and people. He argues that changing what is old meets initial suspicion, so reforms must be announced and repeated until 'after the day has passed' hearts assent. In his hierarchical world, a minister waits for trust, a ruler embodies transforming authority, and Tang and Wu's dynastic change obeys Heaven and responds to people. His distinction between noble and petty persons reflects his historical social order; the ethical argument, however, turns on legitimacy through trust, not on endorsing that order.
confucian.modern_meaning: In present-day organizations, communities, and personal life, this hexagram does not demand perpetual revolution; it describes how a needed change becomes legitimate. Before announcing a change, we can test whether people have had enough time to see the problem and voice their reservations. Repeated, clear explanation—not spin—builds confidence. Where the fourth and fifth lines suggest sincerity and visible alignment, authority flows from coherence rather than coercion. After the change is made, the wise move is often to consolidate, to tolerate outward compliance while inviting deeper consent, and to avoid driving the change until it breaks. This is not passivity but disciplined timing: clarity about what is decaying, patience for public trust, and firmness in preserving the good that has been won. Historical hierarchy can be translated as differentiated responsibility—those with more power still answer to shared principle and must earn trust.
confucian.advice: When you contemplate change, distinguish urgency from readiness. Ask whether the day of shared understanding has truly arrived. Use consultation as a discipline: bring the proposal back repeatedly until it is tempered by public reasoning. If you have authority, let the change show its pattern rather than forcing belief. Once change occurs, guard it with steady correctness; do not push the unwilling deeper than circumstance allows.
confucian.shadow: Impatience disguised as courage, forcing change before trust forms, or endlessly demanding internal transformation from people who can only offer outward compliance. The reformer may become coercive or, after success, overreach and undo the gain.
confucian.reflection_question: Where am I mistaking my own readiness for a shared readiness to change?
confucian.evidence_zh: 革者變其故也變其故則人未能遽信故必已日然後人心信從

lines.interpretation: At the first impulse toward change, the text says to bind with yellow ox hide. Cheng Yi reads this as a start that lacks deliberation, support, and weight. The yellow is centrality, the ox compliance; binding is not fear but securing oneself in focused patience. Rash action invites fault because time, position, and capacity are not yet aligned. Restraint here is disciplined non-action: protect the possibility of change by refusing to spend it prematurely.
lines.reflection: What first move could I bind with patience until it can be made whole?
lines.evidence_zh: 變革事之大也必有其時有其位有其才審慮而慎動而後可以无悔

lines.interpretation: This line holds a favorable position: yielding, central, correct, and capable of clarifying what should change. Yet Cheng Yi warns that a minister should not be first; she must wait for trust between above and below before acting. Readiness without earned credibility is not yet authority. When the day of shared understanding comes, moving becomes auspicious; holding back solely from caution would then be a fault of missed timeliness.
lines.reflection: What readiness am I withholding because trust has not yet caught up with my insight?
lines.evidence_zh: 臣道不當為革之先又必待上下之信故已日乃革之也

lines.interpretation: The third line sits in the lower trigram's top, rash and strongly opinionated. Cheng Yi says moving alone invites harm; persisting rigidly is perilous. The remedy is repeated consultation: let the words of change be examined three times until they agree. That repetition is not weakness but a discipline that turns private urgency into public trust. If the affair truly needs change, refusing out of fear is also harmful. So consult, refine, then act.
lines.reflection: Where could repeated consultation turn my solitary certainty into shared confidence?
lines.evidence_zh: 稽之衆論至於三就事至當也又何之矣

lines.interpretation: At the fourth line, change moves from proposal to mandate. Cheng Yi sees firmness tempered by yielding, nearness to the ruler without brashness, and no private attachment blocking action. When an affair is fitting and ills are real, regret can dissolve if one acts with utmost sincerity. 'Changing the mandate' is not seizing power but aligning conduct with principle so those above trust and those below comply. The gift of this line is the convergence of authority, timing, and truthful purpose.
lines.reflection: Does my authority for this change rest on sincere alignment rather than private will?
lines.evidence_zh: 革之既當唯在處之以至誠故有孚則改命吉

lines.interpretation: The fifth line is the great person changing like a tiger. Cheng Yi describes a centered, correct figure whose transformation blazes visibly, like a tiger's markings, so that trust arises without divination or persuasion. This is not charisma detached from principle; it is authority made legible. When inner alignment with what is fitting is complete, the pattern shows. Others may still need time, but the work of coercion is no longer needed.
lines.reflection: What change in me could become so visibly aligned that persuasion would be unnecessary?
lines.evidence_zh: 以大人中正之道變革之炳然昭著不待占决知其至當而天下必信也

lines.interpretation: At the end of change, Cheng Yi distinguishes deep transformation from surface compliance. The noble person's pattern deepens like a leopard; the petty may only change face. He warns not to march further: pressing outward compliance into inward change is excess. Instead, remain upright and steady, because what has been changed can revert. The wise response to incomplete consensus is consolidation, tolerance, and faithful preservation, not another campaign.
lines.reflection: Where might I overreach by trying to force an inward change that can only be invited over time?
lines.evidence_zh: 天下之事始則患乎難革已革則患乎不能守也故革之終戒以居貞則吉也

hexagrams.advice: Before trying to change others, let clarity return by asking what old self-interest is active. Trust the process enough to soften where you have been rigid. Act from inner center, not from the need to be seen as right. Allow change to become steady and undramatic.
hexagrams.shadow: The shadow is changing only the surface—binding oneself tighter with duty or appearance while leaving the inner self intact—or trying to reform others from self-importance, so that change words return three times and nothing deep shifts.
hexagrams.reflection_question: Where am I trying to change the outside while leaving the inner pattern untouched?

classical.name: The Cauldron
classical.judgment_zh: 鼎：元吉，亨
classical.judgment_en: The Cauldron: supreme good fortune; prosperity.
classical.image_zh: 木上有火，鼎；君子以正位凝命
classical.image_en: Above wood there is fire: the Cauldron. The noble one thereby rectifies his position and consolidates the mandate.
classical.historical_note:

The Great Image and Tuan comments in the source are separate; only the Great Image is included here, not the small line images or Tuan commentary. This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. lines.text_zh: 鼎顛趾，利出否，得妾以其子，无咎
lines.translation_en: The cauldron's feet are overturned; it is beneficial to expel the stale; one obtains a concubine on account of her son; no blame.

lines.text_zh: 鼎有實，我仇有疾，不我能即，吉
lines.translation_en: The cauldron has substance; my enemy has an ailment; he cannot come near me; good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 鼎耳革，其行塞，雉膏不食，方雨虧悔，終吉
lines.translation_en: The cauldron's ears are altered; its movement is blocked; the pheasant fat is not eaten; when rain is about to fall, regrets wane; in the end, good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 鼎折足，覆公餗，其刑一作「形」渥，凶
lines.translation_en: The cauldron's legs break; the duke's stew is overturned; the punishment is heavy; misfortune.
The cauldron has yellow ears and a metal carrying-bar; beneficial to be steadfast.
The cauldron has a jade carrying-bar; great good fortune; nothing is unfavorable.

hexagrams.title: The Cauldron
hexagrams.name: The Cauldron

taoist.title: The Alchemical Cauldron
taoist.essence: Liu Yiming reads Hexagram 50 as the inner vessel where true yang is cooked, yin is dissolved, and old conditioning becomes new clarity through disciplined fire-phases, empty-solid balance, and careful timing.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: The Cauldron is the vessel of transformation: it receives raw ingredients and, through heat and patience, turns them into nourishment. In this inner reading, the lower Xun wind feeds the upper Li fire, producing steady, penetrating clarity. To refine the elixir, one must balance firmness and yielding, empty awareness and solid virtue, and adjust the process according to precise phases. The image is not passive; it is the disciplined cooking of the untamed self into a mature, integrated life.
taoist.historical_core: In Liu Yiming's Qing-era inner alchemy, the Zhouyi Cauldron is a manual for refining the Great Medicine. The commentary follows from the Well hexagram: once true yang emerges from danger, one must apply fire to transform post-cosmic yin. Each line maps a stage—self-refinement, return of true yang, one-sided firmness, loss through the human mind, harmonized fire and medicine, final transcendence. Attention to fire-times, advance and retreat, increase and decrease is paramount. The source block prints Nine Four as 其形渥, while the supplied classical line text has 其刑 with a variant note reading 一作「形」; this textual variation is noted without altering the quoted source.
taoist.modern_meaning: For a contemporary reader, the Cauldron speaks to any long-term work of transformation: a creative project, a health practice, a relationship, or an ethical habit. Liu Yiming's framing cautions against relying only on passive letting-go; renewal requires the steady heat of attention, the right timing, and a willingness to remove what has become stale. The lower wind can be felt as the penetrating questions that enter our fixed identities; the upper fire as the clarity that comes when we sit with what those questions reveal. The middle lines show familiar traps: becoming too rigid after some progress, or allowing old reactive patterns to overturn what we have built. The final lines point toward a state where effort and ease no longer feel opposed because the practice has become natural. This is not a promise of perfection, but an invitation to notice where the ingredients of our lives are being cooked, and to adjust the heat with care.
taoist.advice: Tend your current transformation with both firmness and yielding. Remove what is stale before adding what is new. When progress makes you feel full or certain, deliberately empty the mind and listen again. Watch for moments when the human mind—reactivity, pride, fear—threatens to overturn the work. Let fire and medicine meet in a steady, single-pointed practice, adjusting timing rather than forcing outcomes.
taoist.shadow: Rigid certainty after early gains, or a sudden collapse when reactive desire overturns the vessel; mistaking the container for the elixir, and over-manipulating the process until the original spirit is lost while outward form remains.
taoist.reflection_question: Where are you being asked to empty the mind and adjust the fire, rather than simply wait or push?
taoist.evidence_zh: 鼎者，烹煎鍛煉之器，所以取新也。

lines.interpretation: The first line describes a beginning marked by instability: the cauldron's feet are overturned, but this overturning can serve a purpose. Liu Yiming reads it as the stage of refining the self, when old yin must be poured out before the new can be established. The image of a concubine who gains honor through bearing a son reflects that even a lowly or confused beginning can become worthwhile if it produces something true. The work here is to correct the foundation, stop shifting, and remove what is stale rather than chase what is not yet ripe.
lines.reflection: What stale residue in your foundation needs to be poured out before new life can be welcomed?
lines.evidence_zh: 初六，在鼎之下，為下德之人，性質昏愚，其趾多顛而不正，欲立其鼎，不利於取新，利於去舊

lines.interpretation: When the cauldron has substance, the work has gained real content: true yang has returned and the belly is full. Liu Yiming calls this nourishing the Dao-mind, so that the human mind no longer arises. The adversary's illness and inability to approach are understood inwardly: the reactive, desiring mind loses its foothold when the deeper mind is present. This is not about defeating an external enemy, but about so regularly nourishing the true center that what once disturbed us cannot draw near. The good fortune is quiet and steady, not a dramatic victory.
lines.reflection: What practice or attention is currently keeping your deeper mind steady enough that reactive thoughts cannot come near?
lines.evidence_zh: 九二，剛而得中，真陽返回，已實其腹矣。腹既能實，道心常存，人心不生，如我仇有疾，不我能即矣。此養道心，自無人心也。

lines.interpretation: This line warns against a one-sided firmness that completes the lower work but forgets the empty, receptive side. The cauldron's ears are removed, so the vessel cannot be moved; movement is blocked, and the rich pheasant fat goes uneaten. Liu Yiming describes a person who may have real longevity but remains a foolish man because inner nature is not yet complete. The saving turn comes through regret and the willingness to empty the mind again. Then movement opens, and what began as obstructed can end in good fortune.
lines.reflection: Where has your progress become too rigid, and what would it mean to empty the mind enough to move again?
lines.evidence_zh: 九三，獨剛無柔，實腹之後，不知虛心，是革去鼎耳，雖能了命，未能了性，其行塞窒，不能通前達後，壽同天地一愚夫，如不食雉膏也。

lines.interpretation: At this stage the Golden Elixir has an image, and one should be especially alert to danger. Yet the firm is dragged by the yielding, and the cauldron's legs break. The duke's stew overturns; the treasure of life-destiny is lost. Liu Yiming says the form may remain while the spirit is already lost. This line is a sober warning: after real achievement, a single rising of the human mind—pride, desire, distraction—can overturn the entire work. The misfortune is not external punishment but inner loss.
lines.reflection: What recent rise of reactivity or pride could overturn the good you have already built?
lines.evidence_zh: 乃剛為柔牽，鼎足又折，起人心而傷道心，如公餗覆傾命寶，得而復失，形雖存而神已喪，其凶不可言矣。

lines.interpretation: Here the cauldron has yellow ears and a metal carrying-bar: the central empty ear receives the solid bar, so firm and yielding support each other. Liu Yiming says fire is precisely the medicine, and the medicine is precisely fire. The work no longer needs extra additions or subtractions; it calls for single-pointed steadfastness and watchful care. This is the stage where the human mind is emptied and the Dao-mind is nourished, not by suppressing desire but by aligning inner emptiness and solidity so that they respond to each other.
lines.reflection: Where is your practice asking you to stop adding or subtracting and simply remain single-pointed?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛柔相濟，虛實相應，火即是藥，藥即是火。當此之時，利於貞一不二，防危慮險，不必分外增減矣。

lines.interpretation: The final line describes the end of the cauldron work: the jade carrying-bar. Firm and yielding are no longer two; physical disposition is transformed; body and spirit become subtle. Liu Yiming says being and non-being are both not established, and object and self return to emptiness, yet this emptiness is not passivity—stillness is without contrived action, movement is natural. One has reached utmost sincerity, able to know beforehand, not by prediction but by being aligned with the Dao. This is the great good fortune of complete transformation.
lines.reflection: What would it feel like for your firmness and yielding to become one, so that effort and ease are no longer separate?
lines.evidence_zh: 上九，在鼎之終，鼎新之功已盡，有無俱不立，物我悉歸空，靜則無為，動則自然，剛即是柔，柔即是剛，不用剛而剛全，不用明而明通，已到至誠可以前知地位，如鼎之玉鉉也。

confucian.title: The Cauldron of Timely Transformation
confucian.essence: A vessel that transforms through fire and wood: overturn what is stale, contain substance, and match the moment. Correct your position and make commands weighty; use the right people, guard talent, and temper firmness.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: The cauldron is the vessel that changes raw into cooked and hard into soft. Its form—planted feet, solid belly, upright ears, crossbar—models stability; its wood-fed fire models the use of heat for nourishment. As a norm, it asks for correct positioning, weighty commitment, and the capacity to hold substance until it matures. Transformation, in this image, requires a container strong enough not to break under the work.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Ding as a 'normative image,' not merely a kitchen pot. The hexagram follows Ge because it transforms the raw into the cooked and brings water and fire into cooperative use. Its shape—feet, belly, ears, carrying bar—teaches uprightness and calm weight, while wood under fire teaches disciplined transformation. The noble person corrects his position and consolidates commands, giving commands the weight of a seated vessel. Cheng Yi even treats 'ji' in the judgment as a textual error, saying the vessel supports 'yuan heng' rather than promising effortless good fortune. Within the hierarchical world of early imperial Confucianism, the lines repeatedly speak through ruler, minister, and subordinate roles; those roles are historical and should not be copied as present-day social prescriptions.
confucian.modern_meaning: For a modern reader, the cauldron can stand for any situation where change requires a stable container: a team, a household, a practice, a role. Before adding new substance, it may be necessary to empty what has gone stale; this is not destruction for its own sake but timely clearing. The hexagram also cautions against carrying a load through one person alone. Fit matters more than brilliance: ability blocked by a wrong fit can turn bitter, while a trustworthy helper can make the whole venture lift. Correct your position—where you stand, what you are responsible for—and make your commitments weighty rather than scattered. In relationships built on historical hierarchy, the commentary’s images can be translated into mutual responsibility, honorable dependence, and the duty of those with power to choose helpers wisely rather than demand obedience.
confucian.advice: Consider what needs to be emptied and what substance deserves protection. Choose helpers for actual capacity rather than convenience, and do not accept a load beyond what the vessel can carry. When influence comes, keep the center firm and receive capable support without becoming soft. Let completed work be handled with measured warmth, not brittle self-assertion.
confucian.shadow: The shadow of Ding is rigidity posing as discipline, or warmth without structure. It may tip the vessel unnecessarily, employ the wrong person out of comfort, or break under the weight of authority while shaming the community it promised to nourish.
confucian.reflection_question: What stale contents am I ready to pour out in order to hold what truly nourishes others?
confucian.evidence_zh: 君子觀鼎之象以正位凝命

lines.interpretation: The base line appears as an overturned foot, which Cheng Yi does not read as simply wrong. There are moments when the vessel must tip so stale contents can flow out and clean substance enter. Cheng Yi does regard the line as lacking inherent talent or virtue, but its timely, lowly receiving service can create no blame. The 'concubine' image belongs to the historical household hierarchy and should be read as a relational figure: helpfulness from a modest position, not an endorsement of that social arrangement.
lines.reflection: What stale or spoiled part of my current situation needs to be tipped out before new growth can begin?
lines.evidence_zh: 有當顛之時謂傾出敗惡以致潔取新則可也

lines.interpretation: Firm central substance is the cauldron's real content, and Cheng Yi turns it into a caution about direction. The strong second line must not let an improper neighboring influence draw near, even if that influence seeks closeness. Talent and enterprise need to be aimed toward a fitting relationship rather than given to whatever approaches. Guarding oneself with correctness is not aloofness; it preserves the vessel’s value until the right partner appears. This is good fortune built on restraint and selectivity.
lines.reflection: What solid ability or resource am I risking by allowing the wrong closeness to draw near?
lines.evidence_zh: 鼎之有實乃人之有才業也當慎所趨向

lines.interpretation: The third line is able but not aligned with the ruling line; the vessel’s movement is blocked and its rich nourishment uneaten. Cheng Yi sees this as a temporary lack of fit, not a final verdict. The noble person keeps his virtue; after long time it will show, and the rain of mutual rapport will eventually fall. The line’s initial regret belongs to possessing talent while lacking the right opening. Its auspicious end comes from combined brightness above and compliant strength below.
lines.reflection: How can I keep my capability from turning bitter while I wait for a fitting alignment?
lines.evidence_zh: 君子藴其徳久而必彰守其道其終必亨

lines.interpretation: The fourth line occupies the minister’s place and bears public trust. Cheng Yi warns that no one person can carry the world’s affairs alone; seeking worthy helpers is essential. If the wrong person is employed, the load breaks, the nourishment spills, and the failure is both practical and shameful. In historical terms the blame falls on the high official, not the low helper; the present-day point is to assess capacity honestly before accepting responsibility.
lines.reflection: Where might I be overloading myself or relying on someone unsuited to the weight I am asking them to carry?
lines.evidence_zh: 居大臣之位當天下之任而所用非人至於覆敗乃不勝其任可羞愧之甚也

lines.interpretation: The fifth line is the vessel’s ear, the place where the whole cauldron is lifted. Cheng Yi praises its central virtue and responsiveness to a firm assistant, but also warns against softness that fails to solidify. Yellow ears and a metal bar are only useful if correctness remains firm. Authority, in this reading, becomes sustainable through the center: listening to capable support while holding to uprightness. The historical ruler–minister relation can be translated today as any leadership that must remain principled while receiving help.
lines.reflection: In my position of influence, how can I receive strong help while remaining firmly centered rather than yielding to pressure?
lines.evidence_zh: 五文明得中而應剛二剛中㢲體而上應才无不足也相應至善矣所利在貞固而已

lines.interpretation: The top line completes the vessel’s work. Cheng Yi compares jade to a firmness that has become warm: the line is yang but rests in a yin place, so it does not harden into rigidity. When the task is nearly done, the danger is overreach or self-assertion. The line’s 'great good fortune' is not automatic victory but the result of regulated firmness and softness. Movement and stillness stay within measure; usefulness continues even without official position.
lines.reflection: Am I allowing my recent effectiveness to become overconfidence, or can I temper it with warmth and restraint?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛柔適宜動静不過則為大吉无所不利矣
