classical.name: Thunder
classical.judgment_zh: 震：亨。震來虩虩，笑言啞啞。震驚百里，不喪匕鬯
classical.judgment_en: Thunder: Success. Thunder comes, alarming and fearful; then laughter and talk, at ease. Thunder shocks a hundred li, but one does not lose the ladle and sacrificial wine.
classical.image_zh: 洊雷，震；君子以恐懼修省
classical.image_en: Repeated thunder: Thunder. The noble one, with fear and trembling, examines and corrects himself.
classical.historical_note:
Translations follow the received Zhouyi base text for Hexagram 51. The Great Image is taken from the 象 commentary; the 彖 and line-specific Wing comments are excluded.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.text_zh: 震來虩虩，後笑言啞啞，吉
lines.translation_en: Thunder comes, alarming and fearful; afterwards laughter and talk, at ease. Good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 震來厲，億喪貝，躋于九陵，勿逐，七日得
lines.translation_en: Thunder comes, bringing danger. A great number of cowrie shells are lost [or estimate: cowrie shells are lost]; climb the nine hills; do not pursue; in seven days you will recover them.
Thunder comes, dazed and afraid; moving through the thunder is without calamity.
Thunder sinks into mud.
Thunder comes and goes, bringing danger. There is no great loss [or estimate: no loss], but there are affairs to attend to.

lines.text_zh: 震索索，視矍矍，征凶。震不于其躬，于其鄰，无咎。婚媾有言
lines.translation_en: Thunder comes, causing trembling; one looks with alarm. Going forward is ominous. Thunder does not strike his own body, but his neighbor; no blame. Marriage alliances bring words of reproach.

hexagrams.title: Thunder
hexagrams.name: Thunder

taoist.title: Thunder's Inward Discipline
taoist.essence: Liu Yiming reads Thunder as disciplined movement in inner cultivation: internal fear of one's own stirring thoughts, outward composure amid shock, and active self-examination that fulfills nature and destiny without quietist withdrawal.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: The double thunder is not random noise but the call awake. It shakes what is asleep, splits the shell of habit, and asks whether you will tremble as a victim or examine yourself as a cultivator. In stillness, a single yang stirs beneath two yin, so shock is the beginning of movement, not its end.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming treats Hexagram 51 as the hexagram of 'moving and practicing the Way, of fear and self-examination.' He distinguishes internal movement—the stirring of thoughts—from external movement—the arrival of things. True movement arises when the dao-mind governs and the human mind does not stir; then outer shocks cannot move one within. For Liu, stripping old defilements must happen in movement, not by forgetting objects or deadening the heart. Among the six lines, only the First Nine perfectly embodies inward fear and outward fearlessness, careful at the beginning and complete at the end. The rest show various failures of fear—too high, too weak, too stuck, too speculative—all still pathways of cultivation.
taoist.modern_meaning: When disruption arrives—a sudden loss, an unexpected message, a public crisis—the first tremor is often internal. Liu Yiming invites you to separate the inner stirring from the outer event. Instead of asking only 'What just happened?' ask 'What thought has been awakened in me?' This is not quietism. It is disciplined awareness inside ordinary movement. You do not need to withdraw from activity or silence your mind; you need to observe the stir and let the dao-mind, not the human mind, answer. That might mean pausing before speaking, delaying a hasty decision, or returning to a practice you had neglected. It also means respecting timing: some frights are not losses but calls to self-examination. When you hold your inner center, a public shock can roll through without stealing your offering. The thunder then becomes a teacher, not a threat.
taoist.advice: When the thunder comes, do not first manage the noise outside; first notice the movement within. Guard the unseen and unheard. Do not chase scattered shells or climb lofty fears. Let composure be your sacrificial vessel. In action and stillness, let the dao-mind preside, so that each shock becomes an occasion for self-examination rather than panic.
taoist.shadow: Trembling without practice; speculating without deciding; sinking into muddy entanglements; or faking fearlessness while refusing inner examination. Fear then becomes a habit of paralysis, and shock merely repeats without teaching.
taoist.reflection_question: When thunder comes, do I fear my inner stirring or the outer event?
taoist.evidence_zh: 內無妄動，自有真動，真動之動，終日動未嘗動

lines.interpretation: At the first stir, calm attention is not timidity but timing. Recognize the shock before it becomes noise. When you examine the unseen and unheard, you prepare the ground. Later, ease arises not from avoidance but from having begun in honesty. This is the most auspicious movement: firm, centered, and true to your nature. Invite the beginning carefully, and the ending will carry its own laughter.
lines.reflection: What inner movement is asking for my careful attention right now?
lines.evidence_zh: 初九，在動之初，而能戒慎恐懼，於不睹不聞之中，是以震來虩虩，後笑言啞啞也。

lines.interpretation: When you overreach, the shaking exposes a loss of direction. Do not chase the scattered shells or climb imaginary heights. Stay with what you know is correct, even if it feels insufficient. The life-impulse is already present; no need to seek another. In seven days—within a natural cycle—what was dislodged returns if you do not grasp. The yielding center holds when ambition quiets.
lines.reflection: What am I chasing that would return on its own if I let go?
lines.evidence_zh: 幸其柔而守正，雖億而不敢妄行，即此便是生意，不必再尋生意，而危厲可無，是以勿逐七日得。

lines.interpretation: You may feel shaken because you see both your limits and the difficulty of the task. That double fear can paralyze. Yet when you let go of self-sufficiency and seek wise companionship, firmness borrowed from others steadies your own movement. The shaking then becomes a way through, not a calamity. In trembling, there is also a hidden will that can learn.
lines.reflection: Who or what can offer the steadying firmness I lack right now?
lines.evidence_zh: 然性柔志剛，能親有道之士，借剛濟柔，不能行者亦能行，是以震行而得無眚。

lines.interpretation: Strength without direction or companions of substance sinks into habit. You may have the capacity to practice, yet daily absorption in petty concerns bogs you down. The thunder is not something to ignore; without the will to examine yourself, your movement becomes heavy, obscured, and ineffective. This line calls for waking from the mire of comfortable complicity. Petty alliances cannot carry the practice.
lines.reflection: Where has my capacity for practice become stuck in muddy surroundings?
lines.evidence_zh: 九四，剛居不正，又在二陰之間，日與小人為伍，有行道之力，而無行道之志，是遂泥之動，一步不能前進矣。

lines.interpretation: In the middle of ongoing shock, the danger lies in endless speculation. Going or coming, you calculate without deciding. Yet centered yielding can keep you from reckless action. There are affairs to attend to, not losses to lament. Tend to the inner fear, let outer conduct remain composed, and your basic substance stays intact. Do not confuse caution with indecision.
lines.reflection: What decision am I postponing by repeatedly weighing it?
lines.evidence_zh: 幸其柔而得中，不敢妄為，無喪行於外，有懼事於內，亦不失其柔之本質。

lines.interpretation: At the height of alarm, tremors without practice leave you peering sideways, unable to move far. Yet if shock has struck your neighbor, not your own body, the lesson can be borrowed. Fear that restrains harm, not fear that paralyzes, opens a path for wiser counsel. Even uneasy alliances may speak a needed truth. Let a near-miss school you without claiming your body as its target.
lines.reflection: How can I let a near-miss teach me without becoming consumed by it?
lines.evidence_zh: 無咎者，以其懼人，不敢為惡。則賢人君子，必將導引為善，是以婚媾有言矣。

confucian.title: Repeated Thunder, Awakened Heart
confucian.essence: Sudden awe opens a path to success only through reverent self-examination; fear is not paralysis but preparation, and sincerity held through the shake preserves what matters.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: This hexagram is the eldest son amid the vessel: movement rising from below that startles, not merely motion. It names the moment when life's foundations quake and the unexamined self would drop its ladle. Properly received, the shock becomes a call to cultivate vigilance: look around, correct your conduct, let dread become blessing. The one who can remain sincere and reverent through the hundred-li reach of disturbance demonstrates the way to hold responsibility amid upheaval.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi reads Zhen as one yang arising beneath two yin, the eldest son succeeding Ding as vessel-keeper. He insists success belongs to the hexagram's inherent meaning: fear, self-cultivation, preserving a presiding lord all lead to success. He sets a hierarchy in which centrality outweighs correctness, as seen in lines two and five, and treats the Tuan as having dropped the ladle phrase. For him the noble person fears Heaven's awesomeness, examines and corrects himself; in sacrifice, sincerity and reverence keep one from dropping the ladle even when thunder shakes a hundred li.
confucian.modern_meaning: Today this is not about literal sacrifices or eldest sons; it is about those moments when an internal or external shock breaks ordinary composure. A health scare, a public failure, a sudden loss—these cannot be bypassed by pretending calm. Cheng Yi's model is active: turn around and look, estimate honestly, avoid chasing what is already falling away, climb to higher ground if needed, and hold the center. Reverence here means taking the moment seriously enough to examine ourselves without self-contempt. The aim is not to suppress fear but to let it complete its work, after which speech and laughter return with a rule. Where the classical text speaks of ruler, eldest son, or marriage alliance, contemporary readers can translate these as roles of responsibility, care, and intimate negotiation, not as fixed hierarchies. In a world of sudden shocks—news, relationships, work—this hexagram invites a disciplined alertness that neither panics nor withdraws.
confucian.advice: When the first wave of shock arrives, pause before acting. Let alarm become attentiveness: survey what is actually at risk, preserve your central commitments, and refuse to chase losses merely to undo them. Move toward integrity rather than away from discomfort. If you can hold sincerity through the shaking, your words afterward will be steadier and more gracious.
confucian.shadow: Shock can become overwhelm or collapse. When fear is indulged without discipline, it dissolves presence, mires resolve, or makes one mistake the neighbor's trouble for exemption. Trembling then exhausts the will instead of refining it.
confucian.reflection_question: What am I being asked to examine, not merely endure, in this disturbance?
confucian.evidence_zh: 君子觀洊雷威震之象以恐懼自修飭循省也

lines.interpretation: At the outset you are the one who feels the shock most directly, and also the one who can set the pattern. If you meet it with immediate, attentive fear—looking around, not seeking comfort too soon—the disruption can complete its refining work. The laughter afterward is not forced cheerfulness; it arises because self-examination has produced a rule for moving forward. Good fortune here is the fruit of disciplined alertness, not accidental rescue.
lines.reflection: How can I meet this initial shock without numbing myself or rushing to reassurance?
lines.evidence_zh: 若能以為恐懼而周旋顧慮虩虩然不敢寧止則終必保其安吉

lines.interpretation: You may be well placed in principle, but a forceful upheaval rides against you. Cheng Yi does not urge heroic resistance; he counsels estimating the real loss, moving to higher ground, and guarding your central correctness. Do not chase after what is already gone, because chasing makes you lose your own center. Recovery may come in its own time, after the wave passes, through a return to constancy rather than through anxious recovery efforts.
lines.reflection: What do I need to stop pursuing in order to preserve my inner center?
lines.evidence_zh: 不失其守雖一時不能禦其來然時過事已則復其常

lines.interpretation: Here the shock shows you are not in a sustainable position; ordinary times were already unstable, and now the nerves go slack. The remedy is not to stay frozen in self-loss but to let the shaking move you out of what is incorrect—toward a more truthful stance. Moving through the thunder, rather than merely being dazed by it, puts error behind. The line offers a chance to use fear as direction.
lines.reflection: What in my current position is being revealed as unsustainable, and what step toward integrity does it invite?
lines.evidence_zh: 若因震懼而能行去不正而就正則可以无過眚過也

lines.interpretation: This is a warning about losing the very capacity to be shaken into action. You may be surrounded by heaviness—conflicting demands, low energy, repeated discouragement—and instead of rousing yourself, you sink. Cheng Yi treats it as a loss of firmness and centrality: the will is mired between double yin. Without self-arousal, shock becomes stagnation, not transformation. The task is to recover an active, yang-like resolve instead of waiting for circumstances to lift you.
lines.reflection: Where am I sinking into heaviness, and what one firm move could break the mire?
lines.evidence_zh: 陷溺於重隂之間不能自震奮者也

lines.interpretation: In the middle of ongoing turbulence, neither advancing nor withdrawing feels safe. Cheng Yi says the ruler of this moment should not force a great breakthrough; instead, estimate carefully and hold the central virtue. Being soft in a demanding role can still be effective if you remain centered and avoid losing what matters. The danger is real, but calamity is not fated; it is averted by deliberate self-preservation of principle rather than by dramatic victory.
lines.reflection: Amid the back-and-forth danger, what central commitment must I refuse to lose?
lines.evidence_zh: 苟不失中雖有危不至於凶也

lines.interpretation: At the far edge of shock, exhaustion may have already set in; the text describes looking around with unsteady gaze and notes that pressing forward would be harmful. The saving grace is indirect: seeing trouble approach a neighbor can wake you before it reaches your own body. This is a late but real chance to change—less about heroic action, more about heeding early warnings and adjusting course before the extreme. Intimate relationships may complain, but that is preferable to disaster.
lines.reflection: What warning near me am I ignoring because it has not yet touched me directly?
lines.evidence_zh: 若能見鄰戒而知懼變於未極之前則无咎也

further_reading.title: The Yi River Commentary on the Book of Changes

hexagrams.essence: Liu Yiming reads Thunder as disciplined movement in inner cultivation: internal fear of one's own stirring thoughts, outward composure amid shock, and active self-examination that fulfills nature and destiny without quietist withdrawal.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: The double thunder is not random noise but the call awake. It shakes what is asleep, splits the shell of habit, and asks whether you will tremble as a victim or examine yourself as a cultivator. In stillness, a single yang stirs beneath two yin, so shock is the beginning of movement, not its end.
hexagrams.historical_core: Liu Yiming treats Hexagram 51 as the hexagram of 'moving and practicing the Way, of fear and self-examination.' He distinguishes internal movement—the stirring of thoughts—from external movement—the arrival of things. True movement arises when the dao-mind governs and the human mind does not stir; then outer shocks cannot move one within. For Liu, stripping old defilements must happen in movement, not by forgetting objects or deadening the heart. Among the six lines, only the First Nine perfectly embodies inward fear and outward fearlessness, careful at the beginning and complete at the end. The rest show various failures of fear—too high, too weak, too stuck, too speculative—all still pathways of cultivation.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: When disruption arrives—a sudden loss, an unexpected message, a public crisis—the first tremor is often internal. Liu Yiming invites you to separate the inner stirring from the outer event. Instead of asking only 'What just happened?' ask 'What thought has been awakened in me?' This is not quietism. It is disciplined awareness inside ordinary movement. You do not need to withdraw from activity or silence your mind; you need to observe the stir and let the dao-mind, not the human mind, answer. That might mean pausing before speaking, delaying a hasty decision, or returning to a practice you had neglected. It also means respecting timing: some frights are not losses but calls to self-examination. When you hold your inner center, a public shock can roll through without stealing your offering. The thunder then becomes a teacher, not a threat.
hexagrams.advice: When the thunder comes, do not first manage the noise outside; first notice the movement within. Guard the unseen and unheard. Do not chase scattered shells or climb lofty fears. Let composure be your sacrificial vessel. In action and stillness, let the dao-mind preside, so that each shock becomes an occasion for self-examination rather than panic.
hexagrams.shadow: Trembling without practice; speculating without deciding; sinking into muddy entanglements; or faking fearlessness while refusing inner examination. Fear then becomes a habit of paralysis, and shock merely repeats without teaching.
hexagrams.reflection_question: When thunder comes, do I fear my inner stirring or the outer event?

classical.name: Keeping Still
classical.judgment_zh: 艮其背，不獲其身，行其庭，不見其人，无咎
classical.judgment_en: Keep the back still; he does not perceive his body; walking in his courtyard, he does not see another person; no blame.
classical.image_zh: 兼山，艮；君子以思不出其位
classical.image_en: Paired mountains: Gen. The noble person’s thinking does not go beyond his position.
classical.historical_note:
The source text includes variant annotations: line 3 一作「列」 for 裂, 一作「薰」 for 閽; line 5 一作「序」 for 孚. Translations follow the primary readings except at line 3, where the received/interpreted reading 薰 is adopted; the primary graph 閽 is likely a corruption.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: Keeping the toes still: no blame; beneficial to be ever correct.
Keeping the calves still: he does not rescue what follows; his heart is unhappy.
lines.text_zh: 艮其腓，不拯其隨，其心不快。

lines.translation_en: Keeping the waist still: the spine is torn; danger; the heart is agitated.
lines.text_zh: 艮其限，裂一作「列」其夤，厲閽一作「薰」心。

lines.translation_en: Keeping the body still: no blame.
Keeping the cheeks still: speech has sincerity; regret vanishes.
lines.text_zh: 艮其輔，言有孚一作「序」，悔亡。

lines.translation_en: Solid keeping still: good fortune.

hexagrams.title: Keeping Still
hexagrams.name: Keeping Still

taoist.title: Resting in the Proper Place
taoist.essence: True stillness is not empty quietism; it is disciplined stopping in one's own place. Movement and stillness alike rest on principle, dissolving self and other, so the Dao-mind can refine the inner elixir.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Paired mountains describe an archetype of layered stillness. The image is not frozen isolation but a boundary that holds; one yang above two yin shows inner command joined with outward composure. Stopping here means choosing the good and holding firmly, moving and resting by one principle. It invites a person to return from restless reaching to a stable inner center, not by suppressing life but by letting action arise from that center.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming reads Gen as the hexagram of nourishing qi through stillness and of choosing good and holding firmly, continuing the refining work of Ding (though the received order places Zhen immediately before Gen). He insists that resting in one’s proper place is not bare non-action: movement and stopping are both ways of resting there. By keeping the back still, the distinction between self and other is transformed; the human mind departs, the Dao-mind is born, and one moves and stops by principle alone. He grades the six lines from the toes to the whole body: constant adherence, compelled yielding, compelled firm, self-governance, benefiting others, and complete stillness, culminating in the place of utmost good without evil.
taoist.modern_meaning: In present life, Gen can be read as a call to recover a disciplined center amid pressures to react, perform, and exceed boundaries. It does not mean withdrawal from relationships or obligations; it means pausing long enough to know what is genuinely yours to do. The cultivated pause helps distinguish the acquired human mind—impulsive, anxious, self-referential—from the Dao-mind that can move and stop with principle. When you keep still at the back, you stop grabbing at a fixed self and stop seeing others only through that self’s demands. This empowers clear action: speech becomes ordered, promises are kept, attention stays within your position without abandoning care for others. It is a practice of intentional restraint followed by purposeful movement, not passive quietism. Timing matters; there is a moment to hold the toes and a moment to walk the courtyard. The outcome is not guaranteed, but the practice refreshes inner clarity, repairs relationships, and returns you to your own ground.
taoist.advice: When urgency rises, pause and ask which principle should hold you here. Let your outer movement be tested by inner stillness. Speak only when words are ordered and useful. Take responsibility for your own state before correcting others. Cultivate a daily moment of quiet that is not escape, but preparation for deliberate action.
taoist.shadow: Stillness can harden into cold withdrawal or rigid control. The shadow is either suppression—holding so tightly that life stops—or its opposite, a compulsive push for success that tears the spine. Both lose the middle and mistake stopping for ending.
taoist.reflection_question: Where is your proper place, and what would it mean to move and rest entirely from that place?
taoist.evidence_zh: 止於其所，非空空無為，其道有行有止，行之止之，皆止於其所也。

lines.interpretation: First Six, low and humble, shows stopping at the toes before a step is taken. Liu sees this as not treading where propriety forbids; the first thought is already true. Because yielding positions often lack a steady master, the line adds a caution: beneficial to be perpetually steadfast. The discipline here is not a single pause but an enduring commitment to keep returning to one's ground, so that the beginning and the end remain aligned. It asks for small, consistent acts of self-restraint rather than dramatic gestures.
lines.reflection: What small step can you consistently decline, so that your first impulse stays aligned with your deeper values?
lines.evidence_zh: 止之於趾，非禮不履，初念已真，止而即能無咎。

lines.interpretation: Six in the Second describes yielding without firmness; the stopping is not secure. Liu uses the calf that cannot walk by itself but follows the foot: the person must stop because there is no clear-minded companion to rescue him, and his heart is unhappy. This is not joyful stillness but compelled restraint. It reveals that stopping from weakness feels like deprivation. The line invites honest acknowledgment: if you cannot move freely, can you use the pause to find clarity rather than resent the constraint?
lines.reflection: When you stop only because you cannot go on, how might you transform that unwilling pause into a source of insight?
lines.evidence_zh: 腓不自行，隨足而行，止之於腓，由於無則明者以拯援，是以其心不快，不得不止耳。

lines.interpretation: Nine in the Third is firm without yielding, restless and reckless. Liu compares it to the waist/spine: knowing advance but not retreat, the strong person's force defeats itself. The line speaks of tearing the spine muscles and smoke choking the heart—danger arising from love of victory and hasty desire for success. It is a warning against using stillness as another weapon of ambition. True stopping at the center cannot be forced by willpower; it requires surrendering the need to be right or first.
lines.reflection: What hasty ambition might be choking your heart, and what would it mean to pause without secretly using the pause to win?
lines.evidence_zh: 知進而不知退，必敗其剛，有限而止，如列其夤也。列夤之止，其厲在於熏心好勝，急欲成功耳。

lines.interpretation: Six in the Fourth is yielding and guarding correctness: although it moves, it does not change its direction. Liu calls this keeping the body still. It is self-governance—demanding much of oneself and blaming others lightly, which keeps resentment away. This is stillness applied to one's own conduct, not to controlling the world. The body here is the seat of ordinary behavior; resting there means acting from a centered, accountable place. It yields no blame because the person tends to their own alignment before involving others.
lines.reflection: How might you hold yourself to a higher standard while remaining gentle in your expectations of others?
lines.evidence_zh: 能止於身，躬自厚而薄責於人，則遠怨矣，是以無咎。

lines.interpretation: Six in the Fifth is yielding and attaining the center. Liu takes the image of keeping the jaws still: the mouth does not open recklessly, so words are not spoken recklessly. If words come, they are ordered—perhaps benefiting the world’s way and people’s hearts, or concerning body-mind and nature-destiny. Even if one cannot fully practice what one says, leading others toward good is a form of accumulating merit. Here stillness becomes responsible speech, poised between silence and helpful expression.
lines.reflection: Which words of yours are ordered and useful, and which simply fill the air because stillness felt uncomfortable?
lines.evidence_zh: 口不妄開，必言不妄發。即或有言，是有序之言

lines.interpretation: Top Nine sits at the summit of doubled Gen. Liu calls this 'stout stillness': inner and outer are one stopping. Firm and yielding are wholly transformed; nature is settled and feelings forgotten; one rests in the place of utmost good and does not shift. It is not a fragile quiet but a mountain-like endurance without arising or ceasing. This line completes the work from toe to body to speech, returning stillness to its root—not as suppression but as a return to an unshakable center.
lines.reflection: What would it be like to rest so fully in your own principle that inner and outer no longer argue?
lines.evidence_zh: 止而至敦，剛柔悉化，性定情忘，止於至善之地而不遷，無生無滅，如崇高大山，與天地同長久。

confucian.title: Keeping Still in Place
confucian.essence: Gen is not forced restraint but resting in your assigned place. Turn your back on the pull of external objects; with outer desire quieted and inner craving unawakened, stillness becomes possible.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: Double mountains stand one over another: above stops, below remains still. The one yang has risen to the top and can go no further. This archetype is not arrested motion but the weight of a life that knows its own edge. It turns the back on enticing objects, forgets the self, and meets nothing in the courtyard. Within that non-engagement, desire loses its foothold and stillness becomes perhaps possible.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi opens by placing Gen after Zhen: things cannot end in movement, so stopping follows. He insists Gen is not called simply 'stopping' because the mountain image carries calm weight and solidity beyond the word. Against Xü’s forceful restraint, he defines Gen as resting in one’s proper place. In his hierarchical framework, father, son, ruler, and minister each have a norm in which to rest; to gain it is peace, to lose it is disorder. Timeliness governs all—movement and stillness must not miss their time. The commentary reads the six lines as a body rising from toes to jaws and ending in thick continuance.
confucian.modern_meaning: For present-day readers, this hexagram invites reflection on boundaries, attention, and relational place rather than literal social rank. Cheng Yi’s father-ruler examples belong to his time; today they may be held lightly as a call to discern the limits proper to each relationship or context. The back turned toward obsession is a psychological move: withdraw attention from what feeds desire so the heart can settle. Walking through the courtyard without meeting people suggests not absence of others but non-intrusion—letting things be. Applied to daily life, this might look like pausing before reaction, speaking with order, avoiding the rigidity that severs connection, and sustaining commitments to the end. It is not a promise of success, but an orientation toward integrity within limits.
confucian.advice: Notice what you are turning your back toward, not only what you face. Stillness here is not force but placement: find the boundary that allows desire to quiet and speech to become ordered. Let movement and stopping follow the actual time. If a stance has become rigid or isolated, ask whether it is still your place, or only a wall.
confucian.shadow: Stillness can harden into rigid severing: too fixed to advance or retreat, cut off from others, heart smoked by anxiety. Or it can shrink into private composure that neglects public responsibility. The shadow mistakes isolation for peace and silence for order.
confucian.reflection_question: What place, if honored with stillness rather than forced restraint, is asking for my attention now?
confucian.evidence_zh: 安止之義止其所也

lines.interpretation: Stopping at the toes means pausing at the very start of motion, before an impulse has built momentum. Cheng Yi reads the lowest soft line as the first movement, where stopping is still easy and has not yet led to error. The caution is toward constancy: because yielding energy may not hold, the benefit lies in enduring correctness. Modern readers may recognize this as the early pause before a reactive word, purchase, or commitment—when a small boundary can prevent drift from one’s center.
lines.reflection: What first impulse in me is asking to be paused before it becomes habit?
lines.evidence_zh: 事止於初未至失正故无咎也

lines.interpretation: The second line is centered and correct, but it lacks support above and cannot rescue the rigid third line. Like a calf that follows the thigh’s motion, its movement is not free; it must force itself to follow even though its heart is not in it. Cheng Yi names this constraint without blame, but also without joy. Modern readers may think of times when relational or institutional limits make genuine consent impossible, and the honest response is sadness rather than submission dressed as agreement.
lines.reflection: Where am I following rigidly because rescue is not possible, and what would honesty require?
lines.evidence_zh: 股動則腓隨動止在股而不在腓也

lines.interpretation: Nine in the third place embodies stopping that has become hard and absolute. It severs the waist, dividing upper and lower, and can no longer advance or retreat. Cheng Yi calls this not stillness but stubbornness: too rigid to adapt, it becomes perverse and cut off, the heart smoked by danger. Modern readers might see this as a warning against making boundaries into walls, or mistaking isolation for peace. Strength without flexibility isolates; true stopping remains timely and relational.
lines.reflection: Where has my effort to hold still become a wall that cuts me off from life?
lines.evidence_zh: 艮其限是確乎止而不復能進退者也

lines.interpretation: At the fourth line, the subject stops only its own body. Cheng Yi sees a high minister who, because soft yin lacks a strong ruler’s support, cannot still the world but can still itself. This earns no blame through correctness, yet he is blunt: occupying a high position while only improving oneself is not worthy of the role. Modern readers may ask how personal composure relates to public responsibility—inner stillness may be honest, but it is not yet enough where wider duties call.
lines.reflection: Where am I content with private composure when my position asks for wider responsibility?
lines.evidence_zh: 唯自止其身則可无咎

lines.interpretation: The fifth line turns to speech. At the ruler’s place, the source of words is stilled, so speech does not issue recklessly but has order; regret vanishes. Cheng Yi says the jaws are where words come from, and stopping there means stopping in the center. Modern readers may recognize this as measured communication—not silence for its own sake, but words that fit the moment and respect relationship. When speech is deliberate and ordered, misunderstanding loses much of its power.
lines.reflection: What words in me are currently too quick, and what order would make them true?
lines.evidence_zh: 艮於輔則不妄出而有序也

lines.interpretation: The top line is thick keeping still—generous, solid, not excessive. Cheng Yi says human stopping is hard to maintain to the end: integrity may shift late, guard may fail at the close, affairs may be abandoned after long effort. But this line can be thick at the ending, and therefore is auspicious. Modern readers might see maturity: not intermittent restraint, but steadiness that holds without rigidity. The reward is not reward, but the trust that accrues to consistency.
lines.reflection: What commitment asks me to remain steady at its ending, long after the first effort has passed?
lines.evidence_zh: 難於久終故節或移於晚守或失於終事或廢於久

classical.name: Gradual Advance
classical.judgment_zh: 漸：女歸吉，利貞
classical.judgment_en: Gradual Advance: the marriage of a young woman is auspicious; it is beneficial to be steadfast.
classical.image_zh: 山上有木，漸；君子以居賢德，善俗
classical.image_en: Above the mountain there is wood: Gradual Advance. Thus the noble person abides in worthy virtue and improves the customs.
classical.historical_note:
The judgment and six line statements belong to the Zhouyi base text. The Great Image is from the Ten Wings and is not part of the earliest layer. The source repeats 陸 in both 九三 and 上九; some editions vary.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.text_zh: 鴻漸于干，小子厲，有言，无咎
lines.translation_en: The wild goose gradually advances to the riverbank. The young one is in danger; there are words, but no blame.
The wild goose gradually advances to the boulder. Eating and drinking with joy: good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 鴻漸于陸，夫征不復，婦孕不育，凶；利禦寇
lines.translation_en: The wild goose gradually advances to the dry land. The husband campaigns and does not return; the wife conceives but does not give birth: misfortune. It is beneficial to resist robbers.

lines.text_zh: 鴻漸于木，或得其桷，无咎
lines.translation_en: The wild goose gradually advances to a tree; perhaps it finds a flat branch: no blame.

lines.text_zh: 鴻漸于陵，婦三歲不孕，終莫之勝，吉
lines.translation_en: The wild goose gradually advances to the high mound. The wife for three years does not conceive; in the end nothing can overcome her: good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 鴻漸于陸，其羽可用為儀，吉
lines.translation_en: The wild goose gradually advances to the dry land. Its feathers can be used as ceremonial adornment: good fortune.

hexagrams.title: Gradual Advance
hexagrams.name: Gradual Advance

taoist.title: The Goose Alights Slowly
taoist.essence: Gradual progress is not weakness but ordered return: halt within, allow gentle penetration, and let true yin and true yang meet through unhurried, correct practice until the elixir condenses from emptiness.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: The image of a wild goose moving from shore to boulder, high land, tree, hill, and high land again maps an inner migration. It portrays a journey that cannot be rushed: each foothold is partial, yet each step refines the practitioner. True union, like marriage, requires courtship, matchmaking, and timing; forced speed produces false union, while patient sequence turns effort into naturalness and forms the golden elixir.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming, an 18th–19th-century Daoist, reads Hexagram 53 as the hexagram of cultivating in proper sequence and gradual cultivation. He links its lower Gen (stopping) and upper Xun (entering) to alchemical fire-times and the return from post-celestial to pre-celestial. He explicitly compares gradual practice to a maiden's marriage: the man seeks the woman through a matchmaker, families communicate, and only then does union occur. This reflects his historical context of inner alchemy and Neo-Confucian vocabulary such as exhaust principle, fulfill nature, arrive at destiny. The text values ordered effort, ritual mediation, and correct timing.
taoist.modern_meaning: Today this hexagram speaks to any deep change that requires sequencing: recovery, learning, relationship repair, or creative mastery. It does not promise that waiting alone suffices. Instead it invites you to discern the difference between imposed haste and authentic timing. Where have you been forcing a union—between work and rest, assertiveness and receptivity, ideal and reality—before the necessary preparation has occurred? Gradual progress means honoring small, concrete footholds even when they look unglamorous, like a goose resting on a boulder or a flat branch. The inner alchemy language suggests that real transformation happens when firm intention is held within a yielding, patient container, not through self-punishment or aggressive acceleration. It also warns against false quick fixes that bring temporary excitement but later collapse. The correct question is not simply what should I do, but what is the proper sequence, and what is my next stable step. The outcome is not guaranteed; yet attending to order and timing makes genuine maturation more possible.
taoist.advice: Pause on the current foothold. Name one action you have been rushing and one point of stability you already possess. Allow a small, properly sequenced step to emerge; do not force a big leap. Let your firm intent be carried by gentle, persistent effort. Create a ritual or communication that honors timing before acting.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is disguised impatience: endless gradualness that avoids risk, or rigid sequence used to control outcomes. It also appears as false gradual practice—years of effort without correct direction—ending in emptiness and blame.
taoist.reflection_question: Where am I mistaking forced speed for progress, and where am I mistaking avoidance for patience?
taoist.evidence_zh: 漸者，徐緩不速之義。卦德上巽入、下艮止，止於其所而徐入，故謂漸。此循序漸修之卦

lines.interpretation: At the beginning, the seeker lingers at the water's edge, low and uncertain. This is not the proper sequence of high flight; starting without care invites later failure. The danger is not external blame but self-inflicted frustration—when the work does not ripen, one blames the teaching rather than examining the first step. The line invites honest assessment: have I chosen a foundation too low, too scattered, or too passive? Correcting this does not require dramatic force, only a firmer, clearer beginning aligned with the gradual path.
lines.reflection: Am I blaming conditions or teachings for an unripe result, when my first step was not well chosen?
lines.evidence_zh: 初六，在漸之至下，如鴻漸於幹也。幹為水涯下流之地，漸之於幹，失其高飛之序。始不謹而終必凶，及至年滿月盡，反怨丹經之謬，是小子危厲而有言矣。

lines.interpretation: The second line rests on a boulder: stable but not final. This is the work of refining oneself and waiting for the right time. When the mind is emptied of grasping, the inner belly can be filled; nourishment is received quietly and joyfully. The good fortune here is not a destination but a state of being fed while waiting. It invites trust in the current plateau, not as laziness but as replenishment. There is enough to sustain the next step, and joy itself is a sign of alignment.
lines.reflection: Can I let this stable, temporary ground feed me without demanding that it be the summit?
lines.evidence_zh: 六二，止而得中，如鴻漸於磐矣。磐為平穩之石，磐亦非鴻止之處，漸之於磐，煉己待時，虛心即能實腹，是以飲食衎衎，樂在其中，其吉可知。

lines.interpretation: Here firmness overreaches, climbing to high land before the lower stages are complete. The commentary names a split: the husband campaigns and does not return, the wife conceives but does not give birth—two halves of the self pursuing false alliances. Hurrying to succeed creates inner disharmony and wastes true energy on counterfeit unions. The line does not condemn strength itself but strength used without guarding its proper place. The practitioner is warned to stop self-willed action and instead defend against internal and external bandits that would steal attention from the real work.
lines.reflection: Where am I using strength to bypass an inner split, creating a false union that cannot bear fruit?
lines.evidence_zh: 九三，剛而不中，漸之太高，如鴻漸于陸矣。陸為平頂之大山，漸之于陸，失其自卑登高之序，急欲成功，陰陽不和，涉假傷真，如夫征不復，貪戀外妻，婦孕不育，私通姦夫，適以取凶而已。

lines.interpretation: Finding a flat branch in a tree is not a goose's natural home, yet it offers temporary rest. This line counsels yielding within yielding—a moment of deliberate retreat. When the inner world becomes empty and still enough, the return of yang energy can be noticed rather than missed. The key is not to mistake rest for final arrival, nor to despise needed shelter. It describes a pause that prevents burnout and prepares the next stage, free from blame because it is consciously chosen and correctly timed.
lines.reflection: What temporary support am I refusing to use because it is not where I expected to land?
lines.evidence_zh: 六四，以柔居柔，如鴻漸於木，或得其桷矣。桷為屋角之平，木亦非鴻止之處，漸之於桷，或可暫時休歇，虛極靜篤，以待陽複，自無當面錯過之咎矣。

lines.interpretation: At the high mound, firmness and yielding merge. What was too hard or too soft is transformed at the center; true yin and true yang are no longer blocked by their false counterparts. The image of three years without conception then final victory is not a guaranteed timeline but a symbol of long gestation that cannot be overthrown. This is the stage where nature and emotion, intention and receptivity, become one, and the elixir forms. The line asks for alignment with the central, correct path rather than chasing results.
lines.reflection: Can I allow a long unseen maturation to reach its own term without forcing signs of progress?
lines.evidence_zh: 九五，陽剛中正，如鴻漸於陵矣。陵為山之高而得中者，剛漸於中，燥氣俱化，真陰真陽，性情和合，不復為假陰假陽所隔，如婦三歲不孕，終莫之勝也。

lines.interpretation: The final line does not climb further; it alights on level ground. After the ascent, firm and yielding are fully transformed, and the sacred embryo is complete. Now the task shifts from striving to embodying and offering what has been cultivated. The feathers become ritual ornament—a visible, graceful sign that can guide others. This is not retirement into emptiness but the harvest of practice, where one's lived presence becomes a ceremony. The line invites completion not as personal achievement alone, but as service.
lines.reflection: What in my life, once fully ripened, is now meant to be offered as an example or support for others?
lines.evidence_zh: 上九，在漸之終，剛柔悉化，自卑登高，漸無可漸，聖胎完成，如鴻漸于陸，棲於平穩之處矣。漸於平穩，正當休歇罷功，修德修行，接引方來之時，是以其羽可用為儀吉。

confucian.title: Patient Ascent, Rooted Order
confucian.essence: Gradual Advance teaches that lasting growth rises from sequence and correct timing. Like wood on a mountain, each step builds on solid ground; stillness within and gentle responsiveness without keep movement from exhaustion.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: The wild goose moves by season and flock order, never overstepping. Cheng Yi reads the hexagram as the pattern of all principled advance: a maiden's marriage, a minister's service, a person's growth in virtue. The mountain below gives stillness; wind above gives gentle penetration. True progress is not slow passivity but ordered, timely movement secured by inner stability and outer compliance. The archetype asks: what foundation are you standing on, and what sequence honors it?
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi, in his Yichuan Yizhuan, interprets Hexagram 53 through principle, position, and timeliness. He defines gradual advance as sequence without overstepping, not merely slow pace. Marriage is his central example: a woman's going to her proper home must be correct and ordered, patterned after the interaction of yin and yang central lines. Ministers and people likewise advance by holding right position and awaiting the time. The line texts follow a wild goose from riverbank to high land, with Cheng Yi citing Hu Yuan's reading of the top-line 陸 as 逵 (cloud-road), each stage a moral test. This interpretive frame assumes a gendered hierarchy of husband and wife, superior and inferior, belonging to its historical setting.
confucian.modern_meaning: Today the wild goose's ascent offers a model for patient formation in work, relationships, and self-cultivation. Rather than forcing immediate results, one can ask what ground has been prepared, what sequence is appropriate, and who is truly aligned. The marriage example need not be read as prescribing gender roles; its deeper claim is that trustworthy bonds and institutional commitments grow by ordered steps, mutual correctness, and shared timing. The lower mountain suggests inner stability—knowing one's values before moving; the upper wind suggests gentle influence that does not batter doors down. Obstacles are not always failures; the third and fourth lines warn against impulsive attachments, while the second and fifth show that centered partners can be temporarily blocked yet not ultimately overcome. In periods of transition, small consistent actions build custom and character. One does not simply wait passively; one cultivates the conditions for the next right step.
confucian.advice: When urgency tempts you to leap, return to sequence. Identify the solid ground beneath this stage and the next ordered step. Keep still within, respond gently without, and let timing, not pressure, set the pace. Where bonds matter, cultivate trust through steady presence. Where obstacles appear, guard your integrity rather than forcing a union. Move like the wild goose—never alone, never disorderly.
confucian.shadow: Slowness can harden into avoidance; order can become rigid hierarchy. The shadow of gradual advance is using patience to justify timidity, or invoking sequence to delay necessary change until opportunity is lost.
confucian.reflection_question: What ground am I standing on, and what is the next ordered step that this ground makes possible?
confucian.evidence_zh: 漸者進也止必有進屈伸消息之理也止之所生亦進也所反亦進也漸所以次卦也進以序為漸今人以緩進為漸進以序不越次所以緩也

lines.interpretation: At the water's edge, the first step is close to danger because it is small and unsupported. Cheng Yi says the weak yin at the bottom has no helper above; ordinary people fear and gossip, while a wise person understands that gentleness and lack of premature alliances make gradual progress possible. In modern terms, an early-stage move may look precarious and invite criticism. The task is not to silence all voices but to discern whether they reflect real danger or simply discomfort with a slow beginning. Trust the arrangement; no blame arises from keeping still and not rushing.
lines.reflection: When others call my early step dangerous, can I distinguish genuine risk from their discomfort with unhurried beginnings?
lines.evidence_zh: 用柔所以不躁也无應所以能漸也於義自无咎也

lines.interpretation: The second line rests on a broad rock, eating and drinking with ease—yet this is not idle comfort. Cheng Yi reads it as a centered, correct person in correspondence with a centered, correct ruler. Their advance is peaceful because each has found a true counterpart. In modern relationships or collaborations, deep alignment creates a joy that is not merely private satisfaction; it is the joy of shared purpose about to unfold. The image warns that eating not in vain means this nourishment is for the work ahead, not self-indulgence.
lines.reflection: Does my current contentment feed a shared purpose, or has it become a comfortable pause without forward meaning?
lines.evidence_zh: 二居中得正上應於五進之安裕者也但居漸故進不速磐石之安平者江河之濱所有象進之安自干之磐又漸進也

lines.interpretation: The third line reaches dry high land but finds no proper response. Cheng Yi warns against grasping at an improper nearby union—the fourth yin. To advance, one must guard correctness and wait for the right time; otherwise it is like a husband who leaves and does not return or a wife who conceives yet cannot give birth. The benefit lies in resisting what is contrary to principle. In modern terms, an impatient alliance or forced project at the wrong time can appear to produce results but cannot mature. Boundaried patience is not isolation; it protects what is still forming.
lines.reflection: What tempting nearby alliance or shortcut might make me forget my orderly return path?
lines.evidence_zh: 三在下卦之上進至於陸也陽上進者也居漸之時志將漸進而上无應援當守正以俟時安處平地則得漸之道若或不能自守欲有所牽志有所就則失漸之道

lines.interpretation: The fourth line sits in a precarious place—yin soft above firm yang, like a wild goose on a tree branch it cannot grip. Cheng Yi says the only safety is to find a flat, horizontal branch through compliance and gentleness. This is not passive accommodation but an adaptive search for stable footing. In a modern role where one feels unsupported or out of place, forceful grabbing only worsens the wobble. Instead, look for the level surface—the practice, community, or strategy that allows rest without pretending the tree is the ground.
lines.reflection: Where am I trying to grip a branch that cannot hold me, and what level support is actually available?
lines.evidence_zh: 桷者平安之處求安之道唯順與㢲若其義順正其處卑㢲何處而不安如四之順正而㢲乃得桷也

lines.interpretation: The fifth line is the ruler on the high mound, yet Cheng Yi says the Way is not sudden. The correct bond with the second is blocked by the third and fourth—hence three years without birth. Nonetheless, the central and correct has a principle of certain prevalence; wrong alignments cannot ultimately obstruct it. The line does not promise a quick breakthrough, and it offers no fixed timetable; it affirms that centered alignment remains worthy of trust even when blocked. In modern terms, mature commitments may be delayed by intermediaries, misunderstandings, or structural obstacles. Patience here is active trust, not defeat.
lines.reflection: In a long-blocked relationship or purpose, what central correctness am I called to keep trusting?
lines.evidence_zh: 然中正之道有必亨之理不正豈能隔害之故終莫之能勝但其合有漸耳終得其吉也

lines.interpretation: The top line leaves the high ground and flies into the cloudy sky, seemingly beyond all positions. Cheng Yi cites Hu Yuan reading 'land' as 'cloud-road'—an open passage. In any other time this would be excessive, but in Gradual Advance the utmost of gentle order transforms departure into a model for others. Feathers are the instruments of progress; the path itself becomes ceremonial. In modern terms, those who have completed a long arc of development may step beyond conventional roles, but their example is useful only because it remains ordered, not chaotic.
lines.reflection: When I reach a stage beyond established roles, does my departure still show an order others can learn from?
lines.evidence_zh: 上九在至髙之位又益上進是出乎位之外在他時則為過矣於漸之時居㢲之極必有其序如鴻之離所止而飛于雲空在人則超逸乎常事之外者也進至於是而不失其漸賢達之髙致也故可用為儀法而吉也

classical.name: The Marrying Maiden
classical.judgment_zh: 征凶，无攸利
classical.judgment_en: Going forward: misfortune; nothing is beneficial.
classical.image_zh: 澤上有雷，歸妹；君子以永終知敝
classical.image_en: Above the lake there is thunder: The Marrying Maiden. Thus the noble person, by attending to lasting outcomes, recognizes deterioration.
classical.historical_note:
Line 2 in the supplied source contains an inline editorial variant note: 一作「而」, indicating an alternate reading '眇而視' for '眇能視'. The translation follows the primary reading '眇能視'. No use-nine or use-six special line occurs for this hexagram.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.translation_en: The maiden is married as a secondary wife; the lame can walk; going forward is auspicious.
The one-eyed can see; beneficial is the constancy of the secluded person.
lines.text_zh: 眇能一作「而」視，利幽人之貞。

lines.translation_en: The maiden is married off in a waiting role; she turns back and is married as a secondary wife.
The maiden delays the marriage past the due time; a late marriage will have its own time.
Di Yi gives his daughter in marriage; the sleeves of the principal bride are not as fine as the sleeves of the secondary wife; the moon is almost full; good fortune.
lines.text_zh: 帝乙歸妹，其君之袂，不如其娣之袂良，月幾望，吉。

lines.translation_en: The woman carries a basket with nothing in it; the man slaughters a sheep with no blood; nothing is beneficial.
lines.text_zh: 女承筐无實，士刲羊无血，无攸利。

taoist.title: Improper Union, Sacred Return
taoist.essence: Underneath the image of an imbalanced courtship lies an alchemical map: when dispersed longing seizes inner stillness, true yang is spent. Yet reversal is possible—stillness can reclaim what emotion took, restoring nature and forming the sacred embryo.
taoist.archetypal_meaning: Guimei shows a movement stirred by pleasure rather than principle—yin before yang, emotion displacing nature. In Liu Yiming’s reading, this is the human condition after the primordial unity fractures: the guest (emotion) consumes the host (nature). The archetype is not a prediction of disaster but a mirror of misalignment, and within that mirror the outline of return.
taoist.historical_core: Liu Yiming treats Guimei not as a literal marriage but as ‘improper union’ (交合不正): lower Dui joy rises to seek upper Zhen movement, so feeling moves before clarity. He traces this to the shift from pre-cosmic wholeness to post-cosmic dispersion, where the western house of emotion drains the eastern house of nature. The sage’s reversal means turning this seeking around: Zhen takes back from Dui the true yang that was lost, uniting metal and wood, emotion and nature, to congeal the sacred embryo.
taoist.modern_meaning: Today this hexagram asks where enthusiasm runs ahead of discernment—when the desire for connection, validation, or intensity leads one to give away inner clarity. Liu Yiming’s language of inner alchemy points to a discipline of noticing these movements before acting on them. Rather than suppressing feeling, one may learn to return it to its source, letting the still, host-like awareness receive the guest of emotion without being ruled. The ‘improper union’ becomes a working edge: not every attraction must be acted on, and not every delay is failure. The line images—lame but walking, one-eyed but seeing, the delayed marriage—suggest that incomplete conditions can still hold integrity if one returns to the root. From a modern perspective, the maiden’s subordinate roles reflect patriarchal structures; read inwardly, they speak of willingness to take a quieter position in one’s own psyche so that something truer can grow.
taoist.advice: Before acting on an impulse, pause and ask whether it seeks to fill a lack by grasping outward. Allow a slow, deliberate return: gather attention, let emotion settle into its root, and wait for a moment when movement and stillness align. Small acts of integrity during confusion are often more useful than heroic corrections.
taoist.shadow: The shadow is compulsive reaching: mistaking intensity for truth, selling inner gold for outer glitter, and forcing premature unions. The result is a basket empty of fruit or a sacrifice without blood—activity without substance, and eventual depletion.
taoist.reflection_question: Where is my enthusiasm outrunning my clarity, and what would it mean to let the quiet host within receive that energy without being captured by it?
taoist.evidence_zh: 歸妹者，交合不正之義。卦德上震動、下兌悅，內悅而外動，以動而遂說，順悅之動，如以女求男，陰先陽後，交合不正，故謂歸妹。

lines.interpretation: A firm beginning placed beneath others suggests a time when one’s true position is not recognized, yet integrity can be kept through humility. The image of the lame person able to walk points to moving from a diminished but honest base. One does not need perfect circumstances to take a first step, only the refusal to be defiled by what seeks to stain. Joy, when channeled rightly, becomes a support rather than a snare.
lines.reflection: Where might accepting a lower, less visible role actually preserve my integrity?
lines.evidence_zh: 時不正而德正，非禮不履，又如跛而能履，外物不得點染

lines.interpretation: Here firmness clothes itself in gentleness: outwardly unremarkable, inwardly perceptive. The one-eyed person can still see, meaning that even partial clarity, guarded in seclusion, is enough to stay aligned with what matters. This line does not demand public success; it honors the constancy of the hidden person who takes nature and life as one great matter, finding true joy without depending on external approval.
lines.reflection: What true joy might be available to me if I stop performing my practice for others?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛以柔用，外暗內明，如眇而能視，抱道幽居，守貞不二

lines.interpretation: This line begins with misdirection: softness separated from principle reaches outward and mistakes the false for the true. The image of returning and taking the attendant role suggests that recovery starts with repentance, not perfection. By drawing near to those with clearer insight—symbolized by the attendant’s humbler place—one may not yet enter the great way, but can avoid further harm. The turn itself is the medicine.
lines.reflection: When I notice I have chased outer show, what humble act of turning back is available now?
lines.evidence_zh: 柔而不正，務外失內，認假傷真，自取下賤，如歸妹以須矣。若能反而悔悟，以須歸娣

lines.interpretation: Firmness dwelling in yielding indicates a period of refining the self and waiting. The delayed marriage is not failure but timing: one refrains when the moment is not ripe, removing the human mind’s urgency; one moves when the time arrives, restoring the Dao-mind. This is the discipline of utmost emptiness and deep quietude, observing the return rather than forcing it.
lines.reflection: What in me rushes when stillness is needed, and what might mature if I wait?
lines.evidence_zh: 剛居於柔，煉己待時，如歸妹愆期，遲歸有時也。愆期者，一非時不動，去人心也。遲歸者，動必有時，複道心也。

lines.interpretation: This line shows a sovereign or accomplished person lowering themselves to learn from others. The principal’s sleeves compare less favorably than the attendant’s, yet there is no humiliation: by borrowing another’s strength, even the foolish can become bright and the weak strong. The nearly full moon suggests luminosity that grows through receptive partnership with another’s light. It is a return to proper alignment through relationship.
lines.reflection: Whose insight or capacity am I willing to honor as finer than my own in order to grow?
lines.evidence_zh: 柔順虛心，屈尊下賢，由不正而求其正，如帝乙歸妹，其君之袂，不如其娣之袂良，借人濟己，雖愚必明，雖柔必強

lines.interpretation: The top line warns of a forced, dim-witted grasping: working solely within post-cosmic yin and yang, forcing union, and deludedly hoping for long life while hastening death. The basket without fruit and the sheep without blood are images of activity emptied of substance. When union is secret, forced, or borrowed from the wrong source, both life and nature are harmed. The only remedy is to recognize the mistake and turn back before depletion.
lines.reflection: What forced efforts, if continued, would leave me holding an empty basket?
lines.evidence_zh: 昏愚無知，誤入旁門，在後天陰陽中作活計，強求強合，妄冀長生，反而促死。如女承筐無實，士刲羊無血

confucian.title: The Marrying Maiden's Timing
confucian.essence: Hexagram 54 pictures thunder above lake: movement through pleasure. For Cheng Yi, wrong positions and soft riding firm invite misfortune. The remedy is propriety, centrality, patient waiting, and attending to lasting outcomes—knowing where joy-led action deteriorates.
confucian.archetypal_meaning: This hexagram presents an archetype of eager union where attraction and momentum outrun appropriate placement. Thunder stirs the lake's surface, yet depth remains vulnerable. The pattern is not merely about marriage: any initiative moved primarily by delight may start with brightness but lack firm foundations. It calls for discernment between genuine vitality and impulsive pleasure, and for preserving long-term bonds through restraint, humility, and ritual structure.
confucian.historical_core: Cheng Yi, writing as a Song Confucian commentator, treats Guimei as the auspice of a young woman's marriage. He contrasts its movement-by-joy with Xian's stillness and Heng's constancy, and finds fault in improper line positions and yin riding yang. The commentary repeatedly frames women's virtue through humility, compliance, and ritual office: a secondary bride assists her lord, a wife carries sacrificial baskets, and a delayed marriage waits for a worthy match. These social arrangements belong to his historical gender order and should be understood as his context, not as a present-day directive.
confucian.modern_meaning: Today, Guimei invites reflection on any relationship or venture entered mainly because it feels exciting. Pleasure can launch a beginning, but without alignment between intention, position, and shared responsibility, early delight may curdle. The hexagram asks us not to renounce joy, but to bring it into a larger frame of self-cultivation: Are we acting from genuine integrity or from a desire to please? Do we allow time for the right conditions, or do we force a premature union? The image of knowing deterioration while extending the end suggests that sustainable commitments require honest attention to where they may weaken, not just to their attractive surface. In partnerships, friendship, work, or community, we can honor mutual obligation, ritual care, and patient waiting—without reproducing historical gender roles. The task is to move from eager beginnings toward endings that can be renewed.
confucian.advice: When enthusiasm rises, pause and check the structure underneath. Seek the center rather than the excitement. Let waiting be active: refine your character, clarify obligations, and avoid forcing others into roles. Tend the small rituals that sustain connection over time. If something feels too charming too quickly, ask what will remain when the initial thrill fades. Act only when joy aligns with uprightness.
confucian.shadow: The shadow is refined self-deception: using charm, status, or emotional intensity to bypass proper process. One may play the pleasing secondary role, trade dignity for acceptance, or perform ritual without substance—until the empty basket and bloodless sacrifice reveal hollow union.
confucian.reflection_question: Where is my current joy leading me—toward a durable bond or merely a pleasing disruption?
confucian.evidence_zh: 君子觀男女配合生息相續之象而以永其終知有敝也

lines.interpretation: Line 1: In Cheng Yi's reading, the secondary bride who is lame can walk; though lowly, she makes herself good and assists her lord, so action is auspicious. The line does not promise outward reach but honors faithful work within one's actual sphere. In present terms, when a situation offers no prominent platform, one can still cultivate integrity, support shared purposes, and take the next small step. The outcome is not guaranteed, but such grounded action avoids the hexagram's characteristic excess.
lines.reflection: What small, unglamorous role am I currently filling, and can I act from its own integrity rather than envying a larger stage?
lines.evidence_zh: 如跛之能履言不能及逺也然在其分為善故以是而行則吉也

lines.interpretation: Line 2: Cheng Yi sees a worthy woman matched with an unsuitable partner; like the one-eyed, she sees but not far. Her skill is inner quiet and correctness, not changing the other. Rather than forcing recognition or demanding a better match, she guards her own standards and remains hidden in constancy. The line suggests that when external circumstances limit full expression, the beneficial move is to preserve clarity and not distort oneself to fit a mismatched situation. It is constancy as boundary, not withdrawal out of fear.
lines.reflection: Where have I been trying to make an unsuitable situation work by dimming my own perception?
lines.evidence_zh: 二自守其幽靜貞正乃所利也

lines.interpretation: Line 3: This line describes a woman who seeks marriage through charm and insistence but finds no proper receiver. Cheng Yi reads her as out of position, aspiration without compliance, and therefore waiting in vain. The remedy is to turn back and accept a more modest, fitting role. In modern terms, chasing a position or relationship for which one is not prepared, or using persuasion rather than self-cultivation, often leads nowhere. A humbling reorientation—stepping back, reassessing one's worth, and accepting a smaller but legitimate place—may be the necessary correction.
lines.reflection: Is there a place I keep forcing myself into, and what would it mean to turn back and accept a humbler but more fitting path?
lines.evidence_zh: 柔而尚剛行不順也為說之主以說求歸動非禮也

lines.interpretation: Line 4: Cheng Yi interprets the delayed marriage as a worthy woman who waits for a good match, not because she cannot be married. Her delay is self-chosen, rooted in inner worth and high standards. The line affirms that postponing a commitment can be a form of strength when it is oriented toward right timing and not avoidance. In modern application, it may be right to let a partnership, project, or decision ripen rather than rushing to meet external deadlines. The waiting is fruitful only if it truly refines and prepares, not if it masks fear.
lines.reflection: Which current delay in my life is an expression of wise waiting, and which is an expression of avoidance?
lines.evidence_zh: 待得佳配而後行也

lines.interpretation: Line 5: For Cheng Yi, the royal bride's sleeve is plainer than her attendant's because she honors ritual over display. The moon 'almost full' means she does not let her position swell into arrogance toward her partner. This line points to modesty at the top: true dignity doesn't need outward ornament, and power should not overreach. In contemporary terms, whatever status or advantage one holds, its best use is humble, central, and relationally considerate. Avoid letting success become overfull, and let substance speak more than appearance.
lines.reflection: Where might my success or position be becoming 'too full,' and how can I return to simplicity and restraint?
lines.evidence_zh: 尚禮而不尚飾

lines.interpretation: Line 6: The empty basket and bloodless sacrifice show a union that has lost ritual substance. Cheng Yi says a wife who cannot serve the ancestral rite is not able to carry the marriage to its end; the relationship is hollow. This line does not promise rescue, but names the condition: when form remains without content, nothing beneficial follows. In modern terms, a partnership, institution, or commitment reduced to ritual without sincerity may need honest reckoning—either to restore meaningful practice or to let the empty form go.
lines.reflection: What currently feels empty in my life, and am I filling the basket with genuine care or merely carrying an empty form?
lines.evidence_zh: 筐无實是空筐也空筐可以祭乎言不可以奉祭祀也

hexagrams.essence: Underneath the image of an imbalanced courtship lies an alchemical map: when dispersed longing seizes inner stillness, true yang is spent. Yet reversal is possible—stillness can reclaim what emotion took, restoring nature and forming the sacred embryo.
hexagrams.archetypal_meaning: Guimei shows a movement stirred by pleasure rather than principle—yin before yang, emotion displacing nature. In Liu Yiming’s reading, this is the human condition after the primordial unity fractures: the guest (emotion) consumes the host (nature). The archetype is not a prediction of disaster but a mirror of misalignment, and within that mirror the outline of return.
hexagrams.historical_core: Liu Yiming treats Guimei not as a literal marriage but as ‘improper union’ (交合不正): lower Dui joy rises to seek upper Zhen movement, so feeling moves before clarity. He traces this to the shift from pre-cosmic wholeness to post-cosmic dispersion, where the western house of emotion drains the eastern house of nature. The sage’s reversal means turning this seeking around: Zhen takes back from Dui the true yang that was lost, uniting metal and wood, emotion and nature, to congeal the sacred embryo.
hexagrams.modern_meaning: Today this hexagram asks where enthusiasm runs ahead of discernment—when the desire for connection, validation, or intensity leads one to give away inner clarity. Liu Yiming’s language of inner alchemy points to a discipline of noticing these movements before acting on them. Rather than suppressing feeling, one may learn to return it to its source, letting the still, host-like awareness receive the guest of emotion without being ruled. The ‘improper union’ becomes a working edge: not every attraction must be acted on, and not every delay is failure. The line images—lame but walking, one-eyed but seeing, the delayed marriage—suggest that incomplete conditions can still hold integrity if one returns to the root. From a modern perspective, the maiden’s subordinate roles reflect patriarchal structures; read inwardly, they speak of willingness to take a quieter position in one’s own psyche so that something truer can grow.
hexagrams.advice: Before acting on an impulse, pause and ask whether it seeks to fill a lack by grasping outward. Allow a slow, deliberate return: gather attention, let emotion settle into its root, and wait for a moment when movement and stillness align. Small acts of integrity during confusion are often more useful than heroic corrections.
hexagrams.shadow: The shadow is compulsive reaching: mistaking intensity for truth, selling inner gold for outer glitter, and forcing premature unions. The result is a basket empty of fruit or a sacrifice without blood—activity without substance, and eventual depletion.
hexagrams.reflection_question: Where is my enthusiasm outrunning my clarity, and what would it mean to let the quiet host within receive that energy without being captured by it?
hexagrams.editorial_status: integration-candidate — AI-assisted; final human review pending

classical.name: Abundance
classical.judgment_zh: 豐：亨。王假之，勿憂，宜日中。
classical.judgment_en: Abundance: success. The king attains it. Do not grieve; it is fitting to be like the midday sun.
classical.image_zh: 雷電皆至，豐；君子以折獄致刑。
classical.image_en: Thunder and lightning both arrive: Abundance. The noble person uses this to decide legal cases and administer punishments.
classical.historical_note:
The base text of Zhou Yi hexagram 55 (Feng, lower Li, upper Zhen) is quoted from the received text; the Great Image is from the Xiang commentary. Small line images and Tuan commentary are not translated. The source writes 无 for 無.

This edition translates the received hexagram judgment, the six original line statements, and the special use-nine/use-six passages where applicable, plus the Great Image from the Ten Wings. The Tuan (Commentary on the Judgment), individual line Images, and other Wings passages are outside the shared classical translation scope; they may appear in the separately translated historical commentaries. The shared translation is not a complete translation of the Ten Wings.

lines.text_zh: 遇其配主，雖旬无咎，往有尚。
lines.translation_en: Meeting his matching lord; even for ten days no blame; going forward brings reward.

lines.text_zh: 豐其蔀，日中見斗，往得疑疾，有孚發若，吉。
lines.translation_en: He makes abundant the screen; at midday he sees the Dipper; going brings suspicion and sickness; with sincerity made manifest, good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 豐其沛，日中見沬，折其右肱，无咎。
lines.translation_en: He makes abundant the veil; at midday he sees the dim star; his right upper arm is broken; no blame.

lines.text_zh: 豐其蔀，日中見斗，遇其夷主，吉。
lines.translation_en: He makes abundant the screen; at midday he sees the Dipper; he meets his equal lord; good fortune.
Brightness comes; there is celebration and praise; good fortune.

lines.text_zh: 豐其屋，蔀其家，窺其戶，闃其无人，三歲不觌，凶。
lines.translation_en: He makes abundant his house and screens his household; peering through the gate, it is still and empty of people; for three years he does not see anyone; misfortune.
